en: Preface to *The Morning Bell of the Pure Land* (Jingtu chenzhong):
At the turn of the Wu and Ji years, I compiled various records of the efficacious experiences of upholding the *Vajracchedikā* and the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*.

Furthermore, because among all the teachings of the Buddha, none are more concise, expedient, and universally penetrating than the single gate of the Pure Land, I have selected and annotated writings from both ancient and modern times.
This teacher has gathered the essential points of these teachings and arranged them into this work titled *The Intent of the Morning Bell*.
His desire was to use the morning vigor of worldly people to awaken those in sweet dreams, thereby sounding the bell. In the early winter, the book was completed;
I, without modesty, have humbly borrowed the spirit of the discussions by former worthies to compose this preface. The preface says: [The rest of the text follows.]
The Tathāgata appears in the world for the sake of one great cause and condition. What is this "great matter"? It is precisely birth-and-death.

Out of compassion for sentient beings who are mired in delusion, the Tathāgata points out the path of transcendence and reveals the place of swift return, calling him "Great Compassion" and "Able One.
He is so named because he takes pity upon us, his sentient beings; how truly true this is!
Thus, sentient beings do not practice benevolence toward their own persons; throughout their lives they remain immersed in delusion, acting in defiance of the Tathāgata’s teaching.

Amidst the vast waves of birth and death, the abyss is deep and the sea is wide. They wander throughout China as if passing a bronze statue that sinks while its head and topknot remain long above the water.
Alas! To hear such cries—how truly lamentable! Now, when people rise in the morning, they must necessarily...
It is certain that evening will follow the heat, youth will be followed by maturity, maturity by old age, and old age by death;

from antiquity to the present, it has always been thus. If a person does not plan for the evening while in the morning, nor plan for the cold while in the heat, they will surely be ridiculed by the multitude as a fool.
Yet, from youth through maturity to old age, one approaches death without realizing that one must prepare for it.

Is their strategy not even more foolish than that? Yet, when people do not plan for death, it is either because they are so muddled as to forget it, or because they are so afraid as to avoid speaking of it.

If one forgets it until it finally arrives, or avoids it until it ultimately leaves no room for escape, then even if one wished to forget or avoid it, how could one possibly succeed? Moreover, people’s fear of death is not something they can truly overcome.

Those who fear death must inevitably pass through a sudden birth, a dull growth, and a weary old age until they die—flitting and fluttering, drowning endlessly in the river of love and the sea of desire, and dragged incessantly by the halter and shackles of fame and profit.
In a single instant, the embers grow cold, the fire is passed, and the fuel is replaced; at the final move, who remains?
If a person cannot escape from this point forward the cycle of death and rebirth within the six realms and three miserable paths—revolving like a waterwheel—who then can?

To follow the tracks of one's own actions, daily pursuing the karma of birth and death without seeking the means for liberation, may truly be called "pitying oneself while fearing death not at all. Those who truly fear death will surely seek liberation.
If one seeks liberation from the cycle of birth and death, what path can one follow if one abandons the recitation of the Buddha's name?
To whom can one turn for refuge if one abandons the Pure Land? By reciting the Buddha’s name and being born in the Pure Land, one attains liberation.
Having attained liberation, one transcends birth and death while remaining serenely within them; thus, what need is there to fear death? It is only those who truly fear death who [seek this path].
This person is one who can fear death and contemplate it so as to ultimately attain fearlessness;
this person is one who can comprehend the great matter; this person is one who does not contradict the teachings of Great Compassion and Benevolence.
Now, if worldly people could escape birth and death, that would be one thing; but since worldly people cannot escape birth and death, [they must seek] the Pure Land.
How could one fail to cultivate karma, and how could one fail to read this book? Someone may ask:
"If the Pure Land can be cultivated by everyone, then the method for resolving birth and death seems to be so easy. I reply:

The *Zhongyong* speaks of the "paths that lead everywhere" (*dadao*) and the "virtues that reach everywhere" (*dade*), citing those who possess innate knowledge and act with ease (*shengzhi anxing*), yet it follows this by mentioning those who learn through effort and act with strenuous exertion (*xuekun jiangjian*).
One reason for success is that there is no distinction between the holy and the ordinary; thus, Mencius further said, "The Way is one.
It can be seen that this Dharma is neither difficult nor easy; in reality, it can be practiced by everyone.

This is what the sutras mean when they say that sentient beings are the Pure Land, and that within the afflictions of sentient beings' minds, the virtues and marks of the Tathāgata are fully present. As the Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra says:

"To deliver immeasurable sentient beings, yet in reality there are no sentient beings who attain deliverance"—this is because the act of delivering others is contained within one's own self-deliverance.

For those who cultivate the Dharma-gate of the Pure Land, although they may focus solely on their own deliverance, they cause all others to study this same Dharma-gate so that they too may deliver themselves.
Is this not, therefore, a vast means of delivering others? Thus, let alone those who have not yet attained awakening, even for those who have already awakened:
If one insists on saving others only after having saved oneself, that salvation is small;

if one does not necessarily create a form of "saving others" but instead uses the very means by which one saves oneself to save others, that salvation is great. The principle expressed in the *Prajñāpāramitā* does not go beyond this.
Thus, when those who discuss the Pure Land say, "One must first save oneself before one can save sentient beings," they have only explained it partially.
"Half. Or it is said:
"People nowadays prefer to talk about 'impurity being identical to purity' (jizhu jijing), rather than 'abandoning impurity to take up purity' (shezhu qujing), which has practical benefit.

Is this [Perfect Teaching] not inferior to the Separate Teaching? It is replied: "Within the Gate of Buddha-Recitation, all faculties are fully encompassed and the realization of principle returns to the same source; thus it is capable..."
To abandon turbidity and grasp purity while simultaneously embodying the principle that "turbidity is itself purity" is the most perfect of perfections.
Thus, even the teaching of "turbidity as purity" is but a provisional perfection; this perfection of the Pure Land, however, is the true perfection.
Someone might ask: "Is the teaching of the 'Mind-Only Pure Land' not truly erroneous? I reply: No. Ultimately, it is simply Mind-Only Pure Land.

Among the writings of the T'u [Taoist] school, millions of words are nothing other than a desire for people to take refuge in the Buddha; taking refuge in the Buddha is nothing other than the realization that mind is itself the Buddha.
Master Hui-kuang (Hua-ken) most vehemently refuted the T'u school's doctrine of "mind," yet he stated: "Single-mindedness without distraction is the secret key of the *Amitābha Sūtra*;
'This mind is the Buddha' and 'This mind creates the Buddha' are the secret keys of the *Contemplation Sūtra*. From this, it can be known.
Because the mind and the Buddha are one, one is able to maintain single-mindedness without distraction. This undistracted mind is precisely the mind that becomes a Buddha;
it is the mind of non-abiding equality; it is the mind of the Pure Land of Mind-Only. Thus, the *Vimalakīrti Sūtra* states:
"If you wish to obtain a pure land, simply purify your own mind. These are words of solid iron, allowing no room for contradiction.
Someone asked: "If that is so, then were not the great masters of all ages wrong when they vigorously debated the doctrine of 'mind-only'?

I replied: "No. The error of those who have spoken in the past lies solely in their empty talk regarding this mind. They did not consider that the Pure Land of Mind-Only cannot be described through mere words;
it is not a hollow, headstrong assertion. There must be the actual work of cultivation, such as the practice of *nianfo* (reciting the Buddha's name) to seek rebirth in the Pure Land."
The Land is precisely the place where one cultivates the realization that self-nature is mind-only. When the mindfulness of the Buddha in this land is fresh, the Pure Land flourishes;
when the mindfulness of the Buddha slackens, the Pure Land withers. This flourishing or withering arises from whether or not one is mindful of the Buddha.
Since mindfulness must be exercised through the mind, how can it be said that the doctrine of "mind-only" is erroneous? Therefore, those who cling to [such views]...
To deliberate upon the mind while regarding the land as secondary, or to grasp the land while deliberating upon the mind—their errors are equally great.

Daimai said, "Let them have their 'neither mind nor Buddha'; I simply maintain 'this very mind is Buddha. I also say: "Let them have their 'neither mind nor land'; I simply maintain 'this very mind is the land.
I request that you submit this for evaluation to the venerable masters of Lianchi and Longshu; what do you think?
If one were to say that this, too, is merely "discourse that circles about under people's feet," then it would be appropriate to sweep it all away at once, declaring, "It is not so;

it is not so. Yet, the *Amitābha Sūtra* takes the sixteen contemplations as the primary cause, while also mentioning the three blessings and the three types of mind, and so forth—none of which [are dismissed].
Furthermore, by practicing contemplation through various skillful means, all practices of the six pāramitās and ten thousand deeds can be dedicated toward the Western Land.

Moreover, during the Dharma-ending age, while the *Banzhou sanmei jing* (Pratyutpanna Samādhi Sūtra) has already ceased to circulate, the *Wuliangshou jing* (Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra) remains preserved as a "lotus pond.

This is because reciting the name is easy to learn, whereas visualization and contemplation are difficult to accomplish. The *Banzhou* first contemplates the wheel-mark on the soles of the feet; this is merely a category of sutras for contemplation, similar to the [other] six [practices].
Since even a child of three feet can distinguish a name when it is uttered, the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra* specifically saves those of the final age.
Viewed from this perspective, one cannot say that the Tathāgata’s establishment of the teachings was not broad, nor can one say that the gate of the Pure Land is not expansive;

yet, the single method of invoking the Name alone is simple and essential, capable of universal application. Therefore, the venerable masters of antiquity and today have often [relied] solely upon this.
This is merely an introduction to this gate.

One must know that outside of principle there are no phenomena, and outside of the shallow there is no depth; therefore, it accommodates both those of sharp and dull faculties, being neither difficult nor easy.

If one realizes that phenomena return to principle, then the three types of merit and so forth all enter the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*); this is itself wondrous contemplation and is equivalent to the invocation of the Name.
Contemplation does not belong to two minds; its ultimate destination is one. Furthermore, how could there be a "final dharma" (mofa) within the Dharma?
As for the term "final dharma," it refers to the world of humans reaching its end, and thus the Dharma reaches its end as well.

When it is said that [the teaching] will first perish, etc., this is perhaps a pre-emptive warning intended to serve as a caution. It is not because of this that one should immediately abandon the difficult and rush toward the easy. However—
Students should enter through one gate and practice it with single-minded diligence; thus, their pure karma will naturally be perfected.
One must not, within the same hall, treat others as if they were from Qin or Yue, exalting oneself while disparaging others.
Therefore, that which possesses principle but lacks practice is not the ultimate Dharma; that which is a realm but not the mind is not the ultimate Dharma;

that which may be profound but not shallow, distinct but not universal, provisional but not real, saintly but not ordinary, or self-cultivated but not shared with others—these are not the ultimate Dharma.
To act is equally contrary to the ultimate Dharma; yet, when one studies non-arising, there is no extinction—how can birth and death be two?
When one realizes that delusion is itself reality, how can reality and delusion be two? Though the mountain streams differ, the bright moon is the same—how can Chan and Pure Land be two?
Even across ten million *koṭi* lands, one can be reborn in a mere snap of the fingers—how can far and near be two? With a single toe...
When one presses the earth, it becomes a golden world; are the Sahā and Sukhāvatī worlds two? How could they not both be lands of purity and peace?

After Gautama attained the treasury of the Dharma, were Śākyamuni and Amitābha two? Within the *dharmakāya* of eternal quiescence (*nitya-śānti-prabhā*), the three lands are universally encompassed, and these lands mutually support one another;
are the Land of Common Dwelling (*sahā-loka*) and the Land of Quiescent Light (*śānta-prabhā*) two? Such is the nature of the Dharma.

The ultimate realization is that the sage and the ordinary person are one; things and the self are one; principle and phenomena, mind and environment, are one; depth and shallowness are one; provisional and real are one;
the Separate and the Perfect are one. Extending this, death and life are one; truth and delusion are one; Chan and Pure Land are one;
the distant and the near are one; Śākyamuni and Amitābha are one; the Sahā world and Sukhāvatī are one; and the Shared Residence and the Land of Quiescent Light are one. This is it.
This refers to "single-mindedness without distraction.
If one can truly practice according to this, it begins with gathering the mind to recite the Buddha’s name. When one recites the Buddha’s name, the mind naturally becomes pure;
when the mind is pure, the land follows in becoming pure. As Master Dahui said: "If for even a single day a person's mind does not wander..."
If you seek to be free from deluded thoughts and do not take various objects as conditions, you will immediately accord with all Buddhas of the three periods of time and all great Bodhisattvas.
Thus, this very house on fire—the dust and toil of the world—is itself the place of liberation and the exit from the triple world.

Those who cultivate the Pure Land should likewise rely upon the mind of a single Buddha and practice without interruption. Once this has been maintained for a long time, one may then [regard] the four elements...
The body formed by the union of the four elements is pulverized with a single fist; the world formed by the union of the four elements is overturned with a single kick.

Thereafter, whatever is heard or seen—the chirping of birds, the singing of cicadas, the songs of cowherds, and the chants of woodcutters—is the Dharma-sound of impermanence, suffering, and emptiness, as well as the celestial music of the Western Paradise.
Bamboo fences and thatched roofs are the golden terraces and pavilions of the Western Paradise. To fly...
The sound of springs and waterfalls is the precious pond of the Western Paradise with its waters of virtue;
the fragrance of wild flowers and the beauty of noble trees are the precious nets interlacing there, and the wonderful blossoms are the rain from heaven.

Companions such as enlightened teachers and virtuous friends, and associates such as trees, stones, deer, and pigs, are the various superior and good people of the West. What suffering is there? What joy? What need is there? What opposition? What demons or hindrances?
If the three poisons and other afflictions are entirely absent from before one’s eyes, it can be known that rebirth in the Pure Land in the future is certain.
When the time comes to grow weary of the world, one will be without fear or agitation, neither faltering nor distressed, but will return to one's native land with serene composure and folded hands.
There is no need to inquire whether a Buddha will come to welcome one at that moment, nor whether one can know the exact date in advance. Have you heard this?
Whether it be extraordinary fragrances or marvelous music, these are all places where one has gained strength throughout life;

when arriving here, they will certainly be put to use and there will surely be good news—there is no doubt that one will be reborn in the highest grade of the Pure Land. Nevertheless, such clamor is merely a distraction for those who have not yet seen through things.

Once a person can see through them and maintain steadfastness, then regarding all suffering and joy, purity and impurity— (Note: The provided source text ends abruptly. The translation reflects the available portion.)
As for the various conflicting theories regarding doubt and faith, let them be swept away with a single stroke.
Written on the eleventh month of the Jihai year of the Shunzhi era by the disciple of the Pure Land, Zhou Kefu of Yangxian, who has washed his head and bathed his body in reverence.

An Introduction to Encouraging the Circulation of *The Morning Bell of the Pure Land*:
Since the circulation of the scriptures wherever they may be found constitutes a virtuous condition that yields immeasurable merit and blessings, it is said: "One who is able to [use] the Great..."
Transmitting the Dharma-door of the Vehicle to one person is equivalent to ten good deeds; transmitting it to ten people is equivalent to a hundred good deeds;
transmitting it to those of great nobility, great heroism, and great power is equivalent to a thousand good deeds; and reprinting it for wide distribution is equivalent to ten thousand good deeds.
How much more so for the Pure Land Dharma-door, which transcends the cycle of birth and death, ensuring one never regresses until the attainment of Buddhahood.
To exhort a single person to cultivate the Pure Land is to bring one sentient being to the realization of Buddhahood.
All who attain Buddhahood must necessarily deliver immeasurable sentient beings; those beings whom they deliver all originate with me.
Therefore, the merit and reward of this are truly inexhaustible. For this reason, I desire to exhort all who see or hear of this to broaden their minds toward the Buddha.

If people were to know that their own minds are what drive them, they would all be reborn in the Pure Land. One should therefore believe with earnest conviction the words of Longshu (Lung-shu) as being free from falsehood.
As for the two sutras of the *Lotus* and the *Avataṃsaka*, they are the most supreme among the wondrous teachings spoken by the Buddha.

Regarding the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara’s universal salvation of the world—appearing in every land—and the accounts of how past worthies experienced his spiritual resonance, these matters are recorded throughout history.

It is clear that each has compiled these accounts to encourage the cultivation of practice; this is truly a most convenient gateway for those yet to come, serving as a bell and chime and a bridge across the final path.
In the autumn of the Wuxu year, I compiled the *Records of Experiences in Holding the Vajra*, which has already been circulated with a brief preface.
I now respectfully entreat my fellow practitioners to publish these records of experiences in holding the Pure Land, the Lotus, the Avataṃsaka, and Avalokiteśvara.

I have searched through the archives and collected records, verifying the evidence across ancient and modern times, exhausting the subtle labors of both mind and hand so that my devotion might find its place among the imperishable.
However, as these woodblocks were produced here in this locality, they could not be widely disseminated to other provinces.

Since we all dwell together within the adorned Buddha-land, how could we allow for a deficiency in the excellence of the Dharma’s circulation? I therefore appeal once more to the virtuous and faithful of the present age to [preserve and propagate them].

Having encountered a spiritual friend, I have heard the name of Amitābha Buddha and the merit of his original vows; with single-minded devotion, I invoke his name and pray for rebirth in his land.
May the Buddha, out of compassion, not forsake me but take pity on and accept this disciple, [Name].

Unaware of the Buddha’s physical marks, secondary characteristics, and radiance, I pray that the Buddha will manifest himself so that I may behold him, as well as the Bodhisattvas Avalokiteśvara and Mahāsthāmaprāpta.
I shall clearly perceive the assembly of bodhisattvas in that world, with their pure adornments, radiant light, and wondrous marks;
(entering into contemplation with right mindfulness while sleeping, without allowing for distracting thoughts, but with long-term single-minded devotion, it shall surely be as I wish).
The Morning Bell of the Pure Land, Volume One.
Compiled by the Wayman of Shared Goodness from Jingxi, Zhou Kefu; reviewed by his son, Zhou Shi;
and collated by the Layman Qianque of Wu County, Chen Jisheng.

The primordial Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss is my own hometown; Amitābha is called my compassionate father. Therefore, for those who wish to transcend birth and death, there is nothing like the single gate of the Pure Land.
Worldly people are submerged within the den of the five turbidities, like a young child who has lost his way. Thus he asked.

The ancestral villages, districts, and dwellings of our forebears have become so remote that they can no longer be recalled; though one may wish to travel toward them, by what means could one find the way?

Now, by synthesizing the scriptural canons and tracing their origins and currents, we shall ensure that the history of the Land of Joy appears vividly before our eyes, after which true faith may arise.
This concludes the first section, "Accounting for the Origins."
Regarding the beginning of Amitābha Buddha’s attainment of Buddhahood, the *Drum-Sound King Sūtra* states: "In a past kalpa, there was a land named Abhirati; the king was named Kauśika.
His grandfather was King Viśuddhadeva, his father was the Cakravartin King Candrottarā, and his mother was Viśeṣacārumukhī. At that time, a Buddha appeared in the world."

In the world, he was known as the World-Lord King Kauśika; he resolved his mind upon the Way, renounced his royal throne, and went forth under the Buddha, being named the Bhikṣu Dharmākara (who is Amitābha Buddha). Furthermore, the *Mahā-amitābha-sūtra* states:
"When the Bhikṣu Dharmākara, in the presence of the Buddha Sovereign King (Īśvararāja), resolved upon the unsurpassed mind, none in all the worlds could equal him. At that time, the Buddha..."
He proclaimed that he would attain Buddhahood in two hundred and ten billion Buddha-fields according to his heart’s vows;

he prostrated before the Buddhas and extensively expounded the Dharma-treasury of the forty-eight vows (as fully recorded in the original sutra), vowing that if it were not so, he would never become a Buddha.
At that time, the great earth shook, the heavens rained exquisite flowers, and from the air, voices in unison praised him, saying: "You shall certainly become a Buddha."
Regarding the beginning of Amitābha manifesting the Pure Land and Śākyamuni manifesting the Defiled Land, the *Karunāpuṇḍarīka Sūtra* states:

"In a past kalpa, there was a universal monarch named Araṇemin and a great minister named Ratnasāgara who, with him as a spiritual friend, together with him gave rise to the bodhicitta in the presence of the Buddha Ratnagarbha. Then, Araṇemin made this vow:"

"I vowed that I would practice the Mahāyāna to take hold of a Pure Land, never wishing to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* in a defiled land where the sentient beings of the world were free from all suffering and affliction; until I had attained such a Buddha-field, I would not achieve perfect enlightenment.
Now that my fruition is fulfilled and I am named Amitābha, I therefore manifest this Great Treasure Ocean of the Pure Land."

"I, your servant, vowed to bring sentient beings to maturity in this defiled land; now that this vow has been fulfilled, I am known as Śākyamuni, having attained the Bodhi of Buddhahood within this turbid and evil world.
For the sake of the noble Queen Vaidehī, the Buddha has expounded the primary cause for pure karma."
The *Sūtra on the Visualization of the Buddha of Immeasurable Life* states: At that time, Vaidehī wept and cried out toward the Buddha, saying:

“World-Honored One, I pray that you will extensively expound for me the place free from sorrow and affliction; I shall be reborn there, for I take no pleasure in this turbid and evil world of Jambudvīpa.
Thereupon, the World-Honored One emitted a light from between his eyebrows, which shone everywhere throughout the immeasurable worlds and buddha-lands of the ten directions.
All these lands appeared therein. Having seen them, Vaidehī addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Although these Buddha-lands are all pure and possess radiance, I now wish to be born in the world of Ultimate Bliss where Amitābha Buddha resides.
I only pray that the World-Honored One will teach me how to contemplate and teach me how to enter right concentration. The Buddha told Vaidehī: "Amitābha Buddha is far away..."
This is not far; you should fix your mindfulness and contemplate that land with care.

I shall now explain it to you in detail, so that ordinary people of the future who cultivate pure karma may be born in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss. Those who wish to be born in that land should cultivate the three types of merit:
first, being filial and obedient toward one’s parents, serving one’s teachers and elders, possessing a compassionate heart, refraining from killing, and practicing the ten [wholesome actions].
The second type of wholesome karma consists of: first, upholding the three refuges and fully observing all precepts without violating dignified conduct;
second, generating the bodhicitta, having deep faith in cause and effect, reciting and studying the Mahāyāna, and exhorting practitioners to advance;
third, these three matters are called the primary causes for pure karma. The Buddha said to Ānanda and Vaidehī: “Listen attentively, listen attentively, and reflect upon this well.”

The *Contemplation Sutra on Rebirth in the Nine Grades* states regarding those of the highest grade of the highest birth: "If there are sentient beings who give rise to three kinds of mind, they shall immediately attain rebirth:
first, the mind of utmost sincerity; second, the mind of deep faith; third, the mind of dedication and aspiration. Furthermore, there are three kinds of assemblies."

If one is born [in this world], one shall attain rebirth [in that land] by fulfilling these three conditions: first, possessing a compassionate heart, refraining from killing, and maintaining all precepts;

second, reading and reciting the Mahāyāna Vaipulya sūtras; third, practicing the six mindfulnesses (mindfulness of the Buddha, the Dharma, the Saṅgha, heaven, giving, and the precepts), dedicating these merits and making a vow to be born in that land.
If one possesses these merits for even one day up to seven days, one will immediately attain rebirth. (End of upper section)
Those of the middle grade of birth need not necessarily uphold, read, or recite the Vaipulya sutras;

yet they well understand their meaning and intent, their minds are not shaken regarding the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), they have deep faith in cause and effect, and they do not slander the Mahāyāna.

By dedicating these merits toward seeking rebirth in the Land of Ultimate Bliss, those who practice in this way will immediately attain rebirth. [Regarding] those of the lower grade of the upper class of birth, it is likewise...

Those who believe in cause and effect, do not slander the Mahāyāna, and give rise to the aspiration for the Unsurpassed Way, shall dedicate these merits toward the vow to be born in the Land of Ultimate Bliss;
when such practitioners are on the verge of death, they will immediately attain rebirth there. Regarding those of the Middle Grade, Superior Birth:
if there are sentient beings who uphold the five precepts, observe the eightfold fast, practice various other precepts, and refrain from committing the five [grave offenses]...
Being free from all faults and calamities, they dedicate these roots of goodness with the vow to seek rebirth in the Western World of Ultimate Bliss;
at the moment their lives end, they shall immediately attain rebirth there. Regarding those born in the middle grade of the middle level:
if there are sentient beings who, for one day and one night, observe the eight precepts of the fast, or for one day and one night, observe the śrāmaṇera precepts, or for one...

If one observes the complete precepts for a single night with perfect deportment, and dedicates this merit toward the aspiration to be born in the Land of Ultimate Bliss, such a practitioner—perfumed by the fragrance of the precepts—will attain rebirth there at the very moment their life comes to an end.
As for those of the lower grade of the middle class: if there are good men or good women who filially support their parents and practice benevolence and kindness in the world;

When this person’s life was about to end, they encountered a spiritual friend who extensively explained for them the blissful matters of Amitābha Buddha’s land and also spoke of the forty-eight vows of the Bhikṣu Dharmākara. Having heard these things, they immediately passed away and attained rebirth there.
Regarding those of the highest grade of the lowest class (*adhamāgra-jāti*): there may be sentient beings who have committed grave evil deeds; although they do not...
Those who slander the Vaipulya sutras are such fools who commit many evil dharmas without shame or remorse.
When their lives are about to end, they encounter a virtuous friend who recites for them the titles of the twelve divisions of the Mahāyāna sutras.
Because they have heard the names of these various sutras, they eliminate the most grievous evil karma of a thousand kalpas. The wise person further instructs them to join their palms in reverence.

Joining the palms, one recites "Namo Amitābha Buddha. By reciting the Buddha’s name, the sins of birth and death accumulated over fifty billion kalpas are eliminated, and one immediately attains rebirth [in the Pure Land].
Regarding those of the Middle Grade of the Lower Class: there may be sentient beings who violate the five precepts, the eight precepts, or the full set of monastic precepts.
Such foolish people steal the property of the Saṃgha at large or the property belonging to the resident monks.
They preach the Dharma with impurity and lack shame or remorse, adorning themselves with various evil karmas.
Such sinners, on account of their evil karma, ought to fall into hell; yet when their lives are about to end, the various fires of hell arrive all at once.
If they encounter a virtuous friend who, out of great compassion, immediately praises and explains for them the ten powers and majestic virtues of Amitābha Buddha in detail...
They praise the light and spiritual power of that Buddha, as well as his precepts, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation.

Upon hearing this, such a person eliminates the offenses of birth and death accumulated over eighty billion *kalpas* and immediately attains rebirth there. Regarding those of the lowest grade of the lowest class:
there may be sentient beings who commit unwholesome deeds, including the five heinous crimes and the ten evil acts, being fully possessed of all manner of unwholesomeness—such foolish people...
Due to their evil karma, people ought to fall into the evil realms, where they will experience endless suffering for many kalpas.
At the moment of death, they may encounter a spiritual friend who comforts them in various ways, preaching the sublime Dharma and instructing them to practice mindfulness of the Buddha.

However, being oppressed by suffering, those people have no leisure to practice mindfulness of the Buddha. The virtuous friend then tells them: "If you are unable to mindfully recollect that Buddha, you should instead invoke the name of Amitābha."
If one recites "Namo Amitābha Buddha" with such sincere devotion as to keep the voice uninterrupted for ten full recitations,
by virtue of invoking the Buddha's name, the offenses of eighty billion kalpas of birth and death shall be eliminated in every thought-moment;
at the time of death, one will immediately attain rebirth [in the Pure Land].

In the *Buddhānusmṛti-ratnakoṭi-sūtra*, which the Buddha preached for his father, the King, it is said: The World-Honored One’s father, the King, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, joined his palms with single-minded devotion, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"By what practice may one attain the Way of all Buddhas? The Buddha replied: "All sentient beings are themselves the Buddha."
"Now you should keep in mind Amitābha Buddha of the western world and always apply yourself with diligent effort; you shall surely attain the path of Buddhahood.
The King asked, "How is it that all sentient beings are Buddhas? The Buddha replied, "All dharmas are unarisen and without movement;
they are without grasping or abandoning, without marks, and without self-nature. Within this Buddha-dharma, one should cause the mind to abide securely; do not believe [in other teachings]."

At that time, the father-king and seventy thousand Śākyas, having heard this Dharma being preached, believed, understood, and rejoiced, realizing the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharmakṣānti*).
The Buddha manifested a smile and spoke these verses: "The Śākyas possess decisive wisdom; therefore, they abide with resolute faith in the Buddha-Dharma.
Having ended their lives among humans, they shall be born in the Land of Peace and Bliss (*Sukhāvatī*), where they will personally attend upon Amitābha."
Dharmatrāta attained Bodhi through fearlessness.

In the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, the Bodhisattva Nāgārjuna exhorted mindfulness of the Buddha, stating: "The Buddha is the unsurpassed Dharma King; the great Bodhisattvas are his ministers. These ministers...
That which is most worthy of reverence is none other than the Buddha, the King of Dharma; therefore, a bodhisattva should practice the recollection of the Buddha (*buddhānusmṛti*).

Furthermore, it is said that there were certain bodhisattvas who, having slandered the *Prajñāpāramitā* in the past, fell into the evil realms and remained there for immeasurable eons. Although they practiced other dharmas, they were unable to escape.
Later, encountering a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*), they were taught to practice the *Buddhānusmṛti-samādhi*, whereby they immediately and simultaneously expelled their offenses.

Only when obstacles are removed does one attain liberation. Furthermore, a verse says: "If a person aspires to become a Buddha and brings Amitābha to mind, he will immediately manifest his body before them;
therefore, I take refuge and pay homage. If one wishes to swiftly attain the stage of non-retrogression, one should maintain the name with a heart of reverence.
If a person plants roots of goodness but harbors doubt, the flower will not bloom; it is through the heart of faith that [the fruit] is realized.
Regarding those who are pure, they see the Buddha as soon as the flower blooms.
The *Sūtra on the Ten Kinds of Meritorious Benefits of Mindfulness of the Buddha* states:
"If there are people who receive and uphold the name of even a single Buddha, they shall obtain ten kinds of meritorious benefits in this present life."
First, they shall constantly receive the protection of the great powerful divine generals of the heavens and their retinues, who will remain hidden from view day and night;
second, they shall constantly be followed and protected by the twenty-five great bodhisattvas, such as Avalokiteśvara, and all other bodhisattvas;
third, they shall always be protected and mindful of by all Buddhas day and night, and Amitābha Buddha shall constantly radiate light upon them.
1. This person will be protected such that none of the four types of all malevolent spirits—whether yakṣas or rākṣasas—will be able to harm them;
2. No venomous snakes or poisonous dragons whatsoever will be able to harm them; 3.

All calamities of fire, calamities of water, enemies, bandits, swords, arrows, imprisonment, shackles, and untimely or unjust deaths will not befall them at all; 4. All previously committed sins will be entirely extinguished.
The life-force of the enemy they have slain shall attain liberation; no further enmity or opposition shall arise.

For seven nights, their dreams will be upright and clear, or they may dream of Amitābha Buddha’s most sublime and wondrous physical form. Their hearts will be constantly joyful, their complexion radiant, and their vital energy abundant.
All their undertakings will be auspicious and successful. Ninthly, they will always be honored, supported, and paid homage by all the people of the world.
By prostrating as if revering the Buddha, at the time of death one will be free from fear; with right mindfulness manifest before them,
they shall behold Amitābha Buddha and the assembly of holy bodhisattvas, who will hold a golden platform to welcome and lead them to rebirth in the Western Pure Land,
where they shall enjoy supreme and wondrous bliss until the end of the future.
Regarding the causes for rebirth in the Pure Land, the Tripitaka states that matters concerning the Western Pure Land are addressed in more than ten sutras;

their general purport is that that realm is adorned with the seven treasures and is devoid of hells, hungry ghosts, birds, beasts, and even the smallest crawling and wriggling insects. It is eternally...
Because it is pure, naturally detached, and free from all defilement and impurity, it is called the Pure Land (*śuddhāvāsa*). Its inhabitants are all born and grow within lotus flowers;
they do not age, and their food, clothing, and dwellings are manifested according to their wishes. Its climate is eternally spring-like, with no further alternation of cold or heat.
Because they experience great bliss and are free from all suffering and affliction, it is named the World of Ultimate Bliss (*Sukhāvatī-lokadhātu*). The Buddha there is named A... [Amitābha].

"Amitābha" is a Sanskrit term; in this [language], it means "Immeasurable. Because the light of this Buddha illuminates and perceives the worlds of the ten directions without limit, and because all sentient beings who practice mindfulness of the Buddha know it thus, he is also called the Buddha of Immeasurable Light.
The lifespan of this Buddha, as well as the lifespans of the people within his land, are both immeasurable, even though they are eternal.
Because even kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges never come to an end, he is also named Amitāyus Buddha.
This Buddha possesses great vows to deliver sentient beings, and his majestic spiritual power is inconceivable.

Therefore, those who with a sincere heart place their faith and orientation toward him, and recite his name, will certainly eliminate disasters and calamities in this present life, ward off vengeful spirits, bring peace to body and spirit, and increase their blessings, longevity, and prosperity in the Western [Paradise].
Within the pool of the seven treasures, a single lotus flower shall bloom; one day, by being reborn within it, one will directly escape beyond the cycle of saṃsāra.
Such instances have all been documented in historical accounts and are not empty words.

Among the eighty-four thousand dharma-gates contained within the entirety of the Tripitaka, none is more essential or swift than this; yet people do not know of it, or knowing it, they do not practice it.
It is truly lamentable (from the *Longshu Jingtu Wen*).
Regarding the causes for Amitābha Buddha’s deliverance of sentient beings,
the sutras state that the Bhikṣu Dharmākara made forty-eight great vows before the Buddha Lokeśvararāja, each vow...
Having made this vow for the sake of delivering all sentient beings, one then applies diligent effort to bring an end to birth and death;
subsequently, one enters the stages of a Bodhisattva. To "bring an end to birth and death" means that birth and death become as natural as they are.

To "enter the stages of a Bodhisattva" means to cultivate wisdom internally and cultivate merit externally. Cultivating wisdom causes the nature of wisdom to expand day by day until the time of attaining Buddhahood.
Thus, the nature of wisdom encompasses the void-like world such that there is nothing it does not know and nothing it does not see.
Those who cultivate merit take birth among all sentient beings, assuming their physical forms and mastering their languages in order to establish teachings and transformations;
therefore, from the celestial emperors above down to the most minute insects and ants below, they take birth within them in such infinite ways.

Since the beginning of the kalpas, he has established his teachings to transform sentient beings. Now, in transforming sentient beings, there is nothing that does not result in the acquisition of merit.
Because he acquires merit but does not consume it for himself, his merit accumulates ever more and becomes ever greater; after a long time, it will pervade the worlds of empty space.
When merit is great, majestic spiritual power is likewise great. Furthermore, a sutra states: "Amitābha Buddha practiced the bodhisattva path throughout great asaṃkhyeya kalpas."
Having accomplished the power of patience, they disregard all suffering; they always benefit sentient beings with a serene countenance and loving speech;
they well-guard their verbal karma by not mocking the faults of others; they well-guard their physical karma by not losing their moral discipline (*śīla*);
they well-guard their mental karma so it is pure and undefiled; and from their hands constantly emerge all clothing, food, drink, precious banners, music, and everything else.
By bestowing whatever is most needed as gifts upon sentient beings to bring them joy and thereby carry out their transformation, one causes immeasurable beings to resolve upon unexcelled bodhicitta.
Through such virtuous conduct over countless kalpas, when merit is perfected and majestic power is blazingly intense, one finally accomplishes one's vows and enters the rank of a Buddha. This is...
From the initial generation of the vow until the attainment of Buddhahood, there is nothing that is not for the sake of sentient beings;
therefore, throughout the infinite worlds of the ten directions, from the devas and humans down to the crawling and wriggling insects, there are none who are not saved.
If a person can contemplate their name with a sincere mind and visualize their physical form, they will surely behold the Buddha’s true body in this present life through the Buddha’s majestic power.
The numinous spirit is omnipresent; when the human mind’s contemplation and the Buddha reach a state of pure maturity, they naturally communicate.
If, after death, one passes through births in that land, one will be miraculously born within lotus flowers in the precious ponds.

One’s appearance will be upright and beautiful, beyond comparison with that of devas or humans; one will receive a body of natural purity and emptiness and enjoy infinite longevity throughout that buddha-field.

Within it dwell only the most excellent and virtuous beings; there are no women. They possess the power of clairvoyance and clairaudience, seeing one another from afar and hearing one another’s voices.
Even if ten thousand kalpas have passed, they know exactly where each other has come from.

Furthermore, because their nature of wisdom is all-pervasive and penetrating, they also know all matters of the past, future, and present throughout the worlds of the ten directions. This is due to the power of Amitābha.

The Buddha’s vow states: "Those who have already been born in my land and wish to go to other directions to be born there shall, according to their wishes, never again fall into the three evil realms.
Why is this? Those born in the Pure Land will necessarily realize the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).

The patience of the non-arising of dharmas is the thorough understanding of birth and death. One who thoroughly understands birth and death, even though they enter the realm of birth and death, possesses this single nature."

Since [the mind] is no longer obscured, and its nature is not obscured, by what means could it commit evil? Furthermore, because one relies upon the power of the Buddha, falling into the lower realms is impossible.

Thus, he establishes a transformation for all sentient beings and enters into the realm of birth and death among all sentient beings—whether being born in the heavens, or in the human world, or among those of great wealth and nobility, or in states of purity.
Within this [cycle], one may experience long life without extinction, or die only to be born again, according to one's own desires; such is the nature of birth and death.
This is why the cultivation of the Pure Land is so highly esteemed (from the *Lungshu wen*).
The reason Śākyamuni exhorts people to practice mindfulness of the Buddha is that Amitābha Buddha currently resides in the West, which is the Pure Land.

The land where Śākyamuni was born and our own Middle Kingdom belong to the same realm, both being part of the Sahā world; as such, they are all defiled lands. Beings in defiled lands must necessarily keep [the Buddha] in mind.
When the Buddha contemplated Amitābha with single-minded concentration without distraction, Amitābha came to welcome him and lead him to rebirth in the Western Land.
Yet, who in this world would have known of Amitābha’s sacred name and the matter of rebirth in the Pure Land were it not for Śākyamuni Tathāgata?

Because he preached the various sutras concerning Amitābha, urging people with earnest and compassionate speech to practice mindfulness of the Buddha, these teachings are not false and can be relied upon as certain.
This is the origin of the Buddha-remembrance practice (nien-fo) in China. "A" means non-existence; "Mida" means measure.
Amitābha Buddha is thus the Buddha of Immeasurable Enlightenment. There are two meanings to "immeasurable": it is the essence of immeasurable life and the function of immeasurable light.
These four characters—Immeasurable Light and Life—are precisely the Great Name of the Tathāgata’s myriad virtues; one should focus [upon them].
Why is it that by holding these four characters one is immediately born in the Pure Land? It is because Amitābha Buddha made forty-eight vows to gather in sentient beings, among which it is said:

"If sentient beings wish to be born in my land, they need only sincerely recite my name, and they shall be born in my land, receiving blessings, happiness, and an immeasurable lifespan. Because the Buddha possesses this fundamental vow, sentient beings...
That one attains rebirth through mindfulness of the Buddha is due to relying on the power of the Buddha’s vows, rather than the self-power of sentient beings;
for while self-power is difficult to accomplish, reliance upon the Buddha makes it easily achieved.
This is the teaching of Śākyamuni that opens the way to the causes of the Pure Land.

Tang Yizhi’s *Namo Pian* states: "In the Pure Land scriptures, I have heard that Amitābha Buddha took charge of the Pure Land while Śākyamuni Buddha took charge of the defiled land, with their sovereign and minister-like great vows encompassing sentient beings in both realms; yet I had not understood this in detail.
Furthermore, upon reading the *Karunāpuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, I first learned that when Amitābha Buddha was a Cakravartin King, he made offerings [to the Buddhas]."
The Tathāgata Ratnagarbha had a ground of gold and towers made of the seven precious gems;

he offered his own body as a lamp throughout the entire night, yet even so, he dedicated the merit only for the sake of becoming a Great Brahmā King of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven who rules over the four continents.

At that time, because Śākyamuni Buddha requested a dream from the brahmin Ratnasāgara and presented it to the Wheel-Turning King, the King attained realization and subsequently [sought refuge] in the Jewel...
The Tathāgata of the past took the Western Pure Land before his eyes; thus, while the Western Pure Land was established by Amitābha himself, it was through Śākyamuni that beings were guided.

It was not only so at that time: among the thousand sons of the universal monarch and the eighty-four thousand minor kings, there was not a single one who did not resolve their minds toward enlightenment through the instruction of Ratnasāgara. This crown prince is none other than Avalokiteśvara.
The second prince was Mahāsthāmaprāpta; the third prince was Mañjuśrī; and the eighth prince was Samantabhadra.

It was not only that at that time, among the eighty sons of Ratnasāgara and his three hundred million disciples, there was not a single one who did not follow Ratnasāgara’s instruction and simultaneously resolve their minds for enlightenment;
it extended to all the thousand Buddhas of the Bhadrakalpa and the future Maitreya as well.

The Honored Buddhas are all disciples of Ratnasāgara; it was simply because all those bodhisattvas resolved to take up pure buddha-fields that this Sahā world—its afflictions so dense and heavy—was cast aside by the Buddhas and bodhisattvas.
Thereupon, Ratnasāgara became sorrowful and haggard, and made a vow to remain long within saṃsāra to endure all sufferings without abandoning them, as follows:
These sentient beings vow to enter Avīci Hell; they vow to become animals, to become hungry ghosts, to become impoverished spirits, or to be born as lowly and humble among humans.
They vow to bestow the seven treasures as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, and to sacrifice their own lives as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, in order to deliver all sentient beings.
Now, people morning and evening pay homage to Amitābha, Avalokiteśvara, and Mahāsthāmaprāpta, regarding them as their great refuge. If...

If one does not read this sutra, how could one know that the causes for the three sages’ realization of the fruit were their constant mindfulness of Śākyamuni Tathāgata’s giving of his feet, his head, his hands, his ears, his nose, his tongue, his flesh and blood, and his marrow and brain?
How could we not weep bitterly at the thought of him taming us? Thus, on that day, Śākyamuni first used the Pure Land to guide the three sages, and subsequently spoke [of the Dharma].
Furthermore, the various sutras concerning Amitābha were specifically expounded for the sake of sentient beings in this Sahā world;

thus, that which was revealed to Buddhas and Bodhisattvas is now being revealed to us. When the great power of Amitābha’s welcoming guidance is joined with the compassionate heart of Śākyamuni’s pointing of the way, how could sentient beings possibly辜负 (betray or fail) such profound kindness?
The *Sūtra on the Origin and End of Rebirth in the Four Lands* states:

"One should contemplate that the nature of the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) is entirely created by mind alone. Within the dharma-realm there are ten lands, which are further divided into four types of lands:
first, the Land of Constant Quiescent Light (*nityapraśāntaprakāśa*), which is the Buddha-dharma realm; second, the Land of True Reward and Non-obstruction (*bhūtaniṣyanda-asaṅga*)."
The Bodhisattva Dharma-realm is the land of skillful means with remainder for three days; the two Dharma-realms of Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas are called the Four Noble Realms.

Fourth is the Land of Common Residence for Ordinary Beings and Sages, which refers to the six Dharma-realms of devas, humans, asuras, hell-beings, hungry ghosts, and animals—these being called the Six Ordinary Realms. Thus, these ten realms and four lands reside within the single [mind] of an ordinary person.

Because the mind of mindfulness and consciousness is fully endowed [with all qualities], every single land possesses all four lands; they are distinguished as pure or defiled solely according to the conditions of defilement or purity.
As Vimalakīrti said, "According to the purity of one's own mind, so is the Buddha-land pure"—this is precisely what is meant. Each of the four lands has its own aspects of purity and defilement.

That which is the Land of Eternal Quiescent Light is the dwelling place of all Buddhas and Tathāgatas. "Eternal" refers to the virtue of the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*); "Quiescent" refers to the virtue of wisdom (*prajñā*).

Liberation is the virtue of prajñā (wisdom). True permanence and ultimate consummation constitute the Pure Land; yet there are distinctions between pure and impure within it, because of the differences between ultimate realization and partial realization.

The ultimate realization is that which the Tathāgata has realized, namely the superior grade of *jigō* (the land of tranquil light); what is realized by those of the Perfect Teaching (*enkyō*) is called the middle grade of *jigō*, while according to the Separate Teaching (*bekkyō*), one realizes only the inferior grade of *jigō*.

As for the "Land of Real Reward Without Obstruction," Bodhisattvas dwell therein; because they practice the true Dharma and thereby evoke a supreme reward in which matter and mind do not obstruct one another, it is called "without obstruction. And so forth.

The ten stages (*bhūmi*) are all categorized under the Mahāyāna; their purity or impurity is distinguished by whether one enters them gradually or instantaneously (the gradual entry refers to Bodhisattvas of the Separate Teaching [Bie-jiao], while the instantaneous entry refers to Bodhisattvas of the Perfect Teaching [Yuan-jiao]).

Regarding the "Residual Realm of Expedient Means" (*upāya-avaśeṣa-bhūmi*), it is the dwelling place of the Two Vehicles who have already transcended the Three Realms (it is called "expedient means" because they have cultivated the path of expedients to sever the delusions of the four abodes, and it is called "residual" because ignorance has not yet been exhausted). As for the characteristics of its purity or impurity, they consist in the essence of skillfulness or clumsiness (the essence being the contemplation...).

Regarding the "Pure Land where ordinary beings and sages dwell together," this refers to the Land of Ultimate Bliss (Sukhāvatī). It is a pure land with tranquil ponds of water possessing the eight virtues and rows of trees made of the seven treasures.

It is ranked next to *nirvāṇa* and consists entirely of those in the stage of right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*). Those born in Sukhāvatī have their afflictions subdued and are close to *nirvāṇa*; therefore, it is called the "stage next [to nirvāṇa]. There are three such stages:

in this world, ordinary beings at the level of common ground belong to the stage of wrong determination (*mithyātva-niyāma*); those who have resolved to practice and have not yet fallen back belong to the stage of indeterminate determination (*aniyata-niyāma*); and those who are non-retrogressive are termed those in the stage of right determination.
The defiled land is the Sahā world; its purity or defilement is distinguished by the relative weight of the five turbidities (*pañcakaṣāya*).
Nevertheless, the Buddha-dharma pervades all realms, for the lower three lands are all pervaded by the eternal *dharmakāya* (constant tranquil light).

Thus, when the Tathāgata dwells in the *dharmakāya*, he manifests responsive transformations (*nirmāṇa*) in the lower three lands: Śākyamuni manifests his body to respond to the Sahā world, and Amitābha manifests his body to respond [to the Pure Land].

This is precisely the Land of Ultimate Bliss. Those dwelling in this defiled land who wish to be born in the Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss must do so by means of the samādhi of Buddha-remembrance, or by single-mindedly holding the name of the Buddha without distraction, or by sitting upright facing west and visualizing Amitābha.
Only through these two practices can one lighten the three poisons and clarify the five turbidities; thus, at the moment of death, one will attain right mindfulness and be reborn there.
Regarding rebirth through this samādhi: if one breaks both the delusions of views and thought, one can immediately be reborn in the Land of Expedient Means (*upāya-bhūmi*).
If one further breaks the dust-like afflictions (*rajas-kleśa*) as well as the fundamental ignorance (*mūla-avidyā*), one attains birth in the Land of True Reward (*vipāka-bhūmi*).

Only when ignorance is completely exhausted does one attain birth in the Land of Tranquil Light (*prabhāsvara-bhūmi*). Furthermore, there is a Pure Land that extends horizontally beyond the triple world, while the defiled land extends vertically.
Regarding those who emerge from the three realms vertically, they ascend from the bottom to the top like climbing a nine-tiered platform; their emergence is difficult.

Regarding those who emerge horizontally, they proceed from east to west like walking upon a level path; their emergence is easy. According to the *Amitāyurdhyāna Sūtra*, there are three types of horizontal emergence among the nine grades of rebirth.
As for the highest grade of the highest birth (*śreṣṭha-uttama-upapatti*), at the point of death one boards a diamond throne (*vajra-maṇḍala*) and is reborn in that land, whereupon one beholds...
Having heard the wondrous Dharma, the Buddha immediately realized non-arising; this is to transcend the triple world horizontally and be born in the Land of True Reward and Adornment.

As for those of the highest grade of middle birth, they sit upon a purple-golden platform and are reborn in that land; after one night has passed, the platform opens, and after the lapse of one small kalpa, they attain the patience of the non-arising of dharmas.
This is to transcend the triple world horizontally and be born in the Land of Expedient Means with Remainder. The highest [grade]...
From the "Lower Grades" section below, all [practitioners] emerge horizontally from the three realms to be born in the Pure Land where ordinary beings and sages dwell together.

(Although there are distinctions between devas and humans in the Land of Ultimate Bliss, because there is no sexual desire, there is no birth there belonging to the Desire Realm. Next, since those who attain *nirvāṇa* therein are all of the "rightly settled" category (*samyaktva-niyata-rāśi*), they do not take birth according to the stages of dhyāna;

thus, there is neither the Form Realm nor the Formless Realm, and one can immediately realize and enter the upper three lands while remaining in this same dwelling. There are four types of people who emerge vertically from the three realms—namely, those of the *Zang*, *Tong*, *Bie*, and *Yuan* teachings. Although...
The sudden and gradual approaches differ, each having its own stages; only after passing through them can one emerge from the cycle of birth and death within the triple world.

Since cultivation is difficult while falling back is easy, how would it be better to single-mindedly recite the Buddha’s name and rely on the Buddha’s guidance, thereby transcending all obstacles to be born in that lotus pond, the realm of true recompense, and the realm of serene light, where one constantly perceives the ten stages and may ascend directly? Consider this according to the principles.
The teaching of the ten realms and four lands is frequently omitted and not recorded in many texts on the Pure Lands;

however, since sentient beings aspire to be born in those lands, they must take the attainment of Buddhahood as their goal. Those dwelling in the Land of Common Residence cannot yet be said to have reached the ultimate state if they have not been born into the Land of Peaceful Light.
Therefore, practitioners who cultivate after having attained rebirth must understand this—how much more so regarding the [remaining] four [lands].

"Earth is but earth; it does not emerge apart from that which is created by the mind. This is truly the path upon which ordinary beings and sages alike converge, and the principle in which the sudden and gradual teachings are harmoniously integrated.
It concerns the fundamental and derivative aspects of the cycle of rebirth within the three realms and six paths.

Sentient beings, due to their emotional attachments, give rise to the twelve links of dependent origination, thereby creating the karma for the cycle of rebirth within the three realms and six paths that cannot be severed.
By proceeding to the Western [Pure Land], these emotions are extinguished and the true nature manifests; thus, throughout eternal kalpas, there is no further cyclic existence.
Because the karma of the twelve links of dependent origination creates the retribution of the three realms and six paths, one fails to attain liberation and is born into the Western [Pure Land].
Thus, as karma is severed and retribution becomes empty, one shall never again fall into the abyss for eternal kalpas. The twelve links of dependent origination are:

ignorance (*avidyā*), volitional formations (*saṃskāra*), consciousness (*vijñāna*), name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*), contact (*sparśa*), sensation (*vedanā*), craving (*tṛṣṇā*), grasping (*upādāna*), becoming (*bhava*), birth (*jāti*), and old age and death (*jarāmaraṇa*).
Ignorance refers to the obscuration of true nature; volitional formations refer to mental and physical activity; and consciousness refers to the soul.
"Consciousness" refers to sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness; "form" refers to the physical body; the "six sense bases" refer to the six faculties:

eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind. "Contact" refers to that which contacts the six faculties; because it obscures the true nature, one cannot remain tranquil and unmoving, and thus the soul-consciousness arises.
Because of name-and-form, there are the six sense bases; because of the six sense bases, there is contact. Because of [contact], [feeling arises].
Contact is the cause of feeling; feeling is the cause of craving; craving is the cause of grasping; grasping is the cause of becoming;

and becoming is the cause of birth. Birth is the cause of old age and death; because these conditions are mutually linked and their continuity is never severed, they are called the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination. As for the three realms:
from the Great Avīci Hell up to the Heaven of Controlling Others' Emanations, all are termed the Desire Realm (*kāmadhātu*) because of the presence of sentient beings.
In the realm of desire (*kāmadhātu*), there exists a physical body with form, yet it lacks male or female characteristics.
Above that is the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), where there is likewise no physical body, but only the soul-consciousness (*vijñāna*), much like a ghost or spirit.
These are called the three realms. As for what is meant by "saṃsāra," it refers to: devas, humans, asuras, hungry ghosts (*preta*), animals (*tiryagyoni*), and hell-beings (*naraka*).

They are called the six realms of hungry ghosts (*preta*) and below; they are also termed the three miserable paths (*durgati*). Those who commit acts of anger, killing, and arrogance while possessing slight merit are reborn in the realm of asuras.

Those who are stingy, greedy, and refuse to relinquish their wealth, harming others to benefit themselves, are reborn in the realm of hungry ghosts. Those who are foolish, dull-witted, and ignorant, repaying their karmic debts from past lives, are reborn in the realm of animals.
Those who commit the five heinous crimes (*ānantarya*) and the ten evil deeds (*daśākuśala*), varying in degree of gravity, are reborn in the realm of hell. Fourth.
All paths are suffering. In the heavenly realm, one attains the retribution of joy by practicing the ten wholesome deeds;
yet when that joy is superior, there is no leisure for cultivation, and when merit is exhausted, one falls back down. In the human realm, joy is slight and suffering is abundant;

though one could cultivate with courageous diligence, one lacks the resolve to do so, and when karma is exhausted, one falls further into the three miserable realms. Thus, among the five destinies, the realms of humans and devas are superior to the other four.

Whether it be the inferior seeking to challenge the superior upon repenting their faults, or the superior seeking to challenge the inferior for having committed evil—like a wheel revolving, rising and sinking is not uniform.
As the Sutra says: "The three realms have no peace; they are like a burning house. This is precisely what is meant.
Since the retribution of karma is so terrifying, why do you not turn back with a sudden realization and seek rebirth in the Western Pure Land? (Above from *Kefu Zan*).
The Morning Bell of the Pure Land, Volume One;
The Morning Bell of the Pure Land, Volume Two;
Part Two: Arousing Faith in the Pure Land.
Lianchi held that for those who seek rebirth in the Pure Land, faith, aspiration, and practice constitute the three provisions, none of which may be lacking, yet faith is the most essential.
Without faith, the power of aspiration does not arise and practice lacks its foundation. Zhuan’an said: "There is nothing difficult or easy about the Pure Land;
difficulty and ease depend on the person. For those with doubt, it is ten thousand *li* away though it be but a few paces; for those without doubt, it is close at hand."

For those with faith, ten thousand *li* are but a few inches away; thus, one who realizes the stage of non-retrogression must have a mind of non-retrogression as their precursor—this is precisely what faith is. Faith arises from within oneself and is not produced by others.
Yet, during the long night, one must hold a candle, and in the dark valley, one must await the sunlight. Such is the teaching of the Pure Land, the golden word of the Tathāgata.
That which has been proclaimed by my mouth and discussed by the great masters of antiquity and the present is as clear as the sun or a candle;
yet, the true faith still fails to open in some. These are merely those who strike at a wooden basin or feel their way with a rattle—those who do not truly strike upon the essence.
Now, taking what is recorded in Longshu’s work and supplementing its deficiencies, I compose this second section, "Opening Faith."
The Pure Land is beneficial even before one’s death;

thus, one must not fail to believe in the teaching of the Pure Land. Those who do not understand it merely regard it as a matter for after death, failing to realize that it is of great benefit even during one's lifetime.
Why is this? For that which the Buddha teaches to instruct humanity is nothing other than goodness, which is identical to that of the Confucian teachings.
In what way does this instruction of others differ? It is only that the names are different.

Therefore, if one takes the Pure Land as the core of one's mind, then whatever appears in daily life—whatever the mind intends, whatever the mouth speaks, and whatever the body performs—will invariably be good.
Being good, one becomes a gentleman or a great sage; in this world, people will revere one and the spirits will protect one.
Fortune and rank may increase, and the lifespan may be prolonged. However, next, there are those who are deprived by karmic conditions and thus cannot apply themselves single-mindedly to this;
yet if they possess the will, they may from this point diminish adverse conditions and from this point increase favorable conditions.
If one continues to diminish adverse conditions without ceasing, one will ultimately reach the point where such evil is severed; if one increases favorable conditions without ceasing—
Having reached the end of life, one must surely arrive at a state of pure goodness; who else could this be if not the Great Sage and the Superior Man?

Furthermore, those of the next grade do not know where propriety and ritual reside, nor do they realize that punishments are to be feared; they esteem only physical strength and pursue only power and profit.
However, if they come to take the Pure Land as their heart’s focus, they will surely also come to know how to examine themselves and reproach their own conduct.
Although they may not fully conform to ritual propriety, they will certainly be close to it; although they may not entirely transcend the reach of punishment, they will certainly remain far from it.
Gradually, they can escape the realm of the petty person and ultimately find their way back to that of the superior man.
When an ordinary person possesses even a slight understanding of Buddhist principles, the world will surely regard them as a virtuous person—this is because...
Judging from this, for those who follow the words of the Buddha and take the Pure Land as their core concern, who would say that this is of no benefit to one's life before death?
Someone might ask: "Does not Confucianism also benefit one's life before death? Why must it be the Pure Land? I reply:
This is merely a worldly dharma (*laukika-dharma*), not a supramundane dharma (*lokottara-dharma*). Worldly dharmas do not transcend the cycle of birth and death (*saṃsāra*).
The method for turning toward supramundane dharmas leads directly to liberation beyond saṃsāra;
that the Pure Land benefits both one's present life and future existences is because it encompasses both mundane and supramundane dharmas.
The Pure Land does not obstruct worldly affairs; one must not fail to believe in the doctrine of the Pure Land.
It possesses both principle and evidence. To discuss its principle, it is seen in daily life and never departs from what was stated in the preceding chapter—this is so.
To discuss its evidence, it is discernible even within the brief interval of a single morning cup of tea.
This must refer to the "Dharma Gate of Ten Recitations for the Full Day. For indeed, there are nine grades of Dharma gates for cultivation and practice that all people can undertake;
even those who are sinful, the Buddha does not abandon, for if they turn their hearts toward goodness, they become virtuous.
Thus, this Dharma Gate of Ten Recitations is accessible to everyone, just as a single lamp can illuminate a room long shrouded in darkness.
If one illuminates it, it is clear. Thus, that which is cultivated does not depart from nor obstruct any worldly affairs:

for those in office, it does not obstruct their duties; for scholars, it does not obstruct their studies; for merchants, it does not obstruct their trade; for farmers, it does not obstruct their cultivation;
for those in public service, it does not obstruct serving their superiors; and for monastics, it does not obstruct their Zen practice. In all cases...
Since all activities do not obstruct one another, even the brief interval of a single cup of tea or a single meal does not consume a moment of time;
thus, it can serve as a resource that remains indestructible for ten million kalpas. Why would anyone not cultivate this?
Consider now a merchant who gains two coins of profit from one coin: he surely rejoices, considering it a doubled gain; or if he gains two [coins]...
If one gains a single coin’s worth from a sum of money, one will surely worry about it as a loss of the principal;
this is because one cannot overcome the anxiety or joy over minor gains and losses regarding external things.

Why then, when the light and time of our own lives are limited, do we allow them to be wasted and pass away—this being a loss of great magnitude—without feeling anxiety? Furthermore, the causes and conditions for the Pure Land are difficult to encounter.
To encounter such good fortune and yet recognize it, thereby attaining something of great significance, and not feel joy—how can this be anything but extreme folly?
It is truly lamentable.
One must believe in the Pure Land Buddha, for he does not speak falsely.
When people suddenly hear descriptions of the Pure Land, many do not believe them;
this is because they are constrained by what they currently see, leading them to assume that what they do not presently perceive must likewise be nothing more than that.

One who dwells in a humble alley amidst filth and mire knows not the splendor of a grand mansion, and one whose vessel holds but meager food of wild herbs knows not the abundance of a meal before which such things are set.
How could one know that the mere trifles stored in the humble casket of this abbot can equal the overflowing abundance of a celestial treasury?

How could one believe that while dwelling in this defiled world of Saṃsāra, there exists a pure Buddha-land? Thus, one is born from a womb and remains unaware of the transformation-birth from lotuses;
one’s lifespan does not exceed a hundred years and remains unaware of lifespans as vast as the sands of the Ganges.
One must rely on labor for clothing and food, yet one does not realize that others possess clothing and food provided spontaneously;
one constantly mingles with sorrow and affliction, yet one does not realize that others possess singular, pure happiness.

Thus, that which the Buddha has spoken cannot be disbelieved simply because it is not seen before one's eyes. How much more so when the Buddha strictly admonishes people against false speech—he would certainly not [speak falsely] himself.
False speech is used to deceive people of the world; those who speak falsely do so either to seek profit or to avoid harm.
The Buddha has no desires for the world, so what profit could he seek? The Buddha regards birth and death as a sword cutting through empty space;

what harm could he possibly avoid? Thus, the Buddha has no occasion to employ false speech. Therefore, the ancient sages said: "If one does not believe the words of the Buddha, what else can one believe?"

Regarding the credibility of his words: in the past, there was one who branded loyal ministers as members of a treacherous faction and engraved this upon stone; yet Heaven sent a thunderbolt to strike it down.

Now, using gold, jewels, and colorful pigments to carve and embellish [the scriptures], he has fashioned them into wheel-caskets (cakrakaṣāyas) to store the Buddha’s words, making offerings of incense and flowers and adorning them with divine dragons.
If his words were false, would they not be even more egregious than that inscription on the "treacherous faction" monument?
Is it not because his words were so sincere that celestial thunder did not strike him for a thousand or ten thousand years?

Therefore, there is no longer any room for doubt regarding the teaching of the Pure Land; moreover, from antiquity to the present day, those who have practiced this have experienced numerous spiritual responses, which makes it all the more impossible not to believe.
One must not fail to believe that one will certainly be born in the Pure Land through a single thought-moment.

The *Pure Land Tradition* states: "Amitābha Buddha, together with the two Bodhisattvas Avalokiteśvara and Mahāsthāmaprāpta, boards the great vessel of the Vow and sails upon the sea of birth and death;
from this Sahā world, they call out to and lead sentient beings onto the great vessel of the Vow, escorting them to [the Pure Land]."

In the Western Quarter, those who are willing to go will all attain rebirth. Observing this, one sees that the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, out of compassion for sentient beings submerged in the ocean of suffering with no means of escape, personally employ the power of their vows to beckon and entice those who would be born in the Pure Land;
it is only to be feared that people will lack faith. If one possesses faith and is willing to go, even if they have committed evil deeds, [they shall still be reborn].
There is nothing that cannot be brought forth: for if one lacks compassion, one is unfit to be a Buddha; if one does not deliver sentient beings, one is unfit to be a Buddha;
and if one lacks great majestic power, one is unfit to be a Buddha. Because of his compassion, he beholds sentient beings submerged in the sea of suffering and resolutely desires to deliver them;
because he possesses great majestic power, he is able to fulfill his heart’s resolve to deliver them.
The accomplishment of the merit of salvation is precisely what constitutes a Buddha. As the Sūtra says:
"The Great King of Physicians can cure all illnesses, yet he cannot cure one whose life has reached its end; the Buddha can deliver all sentient beings, yet he cannot deliver those who lack faith.
Faith consists of a single thought-moment (*ekacitta*). If, while a person is still alive, their mind intends to depart from the body, [then...]

If the mind follows its thought of going, the body will follow accordingly; this body always follows the mindfulness. Yet, there may still be cases where the mind desires to go while the body remains bound by attachments.
When the body perishes, there is only a single thought-moment. Since that single thought reaches the destination, there is nowhere it cannot reach.
Therefore, if one single thought is directed toward the Pure Land, one will certainly be born in the Pure Land—how much more so when the Buddha and the Bodhi [are present]?
The Bodhisattva further earnestly exhorts people to be reborn in the Pure Land.
One must take this as a firm foundation and not fail to believe it.
There are those who are exclusively devoted to Zen meditation who claim that "the Pure Land is mind-only" and ask, "How could there be any Pure Land other than one's own self-nature?"
The statement that "Amitābha need not be seen again" appears to be plausible yet erroneous. Why is this? Regarding the Western Pure Land, there is both principle (*li*) and manifestation (*ji*).
If one discusses its principle, because it can purify the mind, all things are pure; thus, it is truly the "Pure Land of Mind-Only.
If one discusses its manifestation, there actually exists the World of Ultimate Bliss (*Sukhāvatī*); the Buddha spoke of this with great earnestness.
Is this not a false claim? That every person can become a Buddha—this so-called "intrinsic nature Amitābha" (svabhāva-amitābha) is certainly not false.
Yet, one cannot suddenly reach this state; it is like fine timber that can be carved into objects of extreme beauty, but which must undergo the labor of carving before it can be realized.
