One cannot point to the fine timber and immediately claim it is the finished masterpiece.

Regarding the splendor of phenomenal forms, some may believe in the existence of the Pure Land yet become mired in the doctrine of "mind-only," claiming that the Western Paradise is not a place where one can be reborn;
others claim that through Zen meditation and the awakening of one's nature, one transcends Buddhas and patriarchs, asserting that Amitābha is not worth beholding.
All such views are erroneous. Why is this? These words are exceedingly lofty, and I fear they are difficult to realize; as for that Western Pure Land, it is truly accessible.
"Without greed, without attachment, without anger, and without delusion—can my mind be free from greed, attachment, anger, and delusion?
That Western Pure Land: when one thinks of clothing, one obtains clothing; when one thinks of food, one obtains food; if one desires stillness, there is stillness; if one desires to go, one may go.
If I think of clothing but have no clothing, I am distressed by the cold; if I think of food but have no food, I am distressed by hunger."
When the mind desires stillness yet cannot attain it, the turmoil of the multitude of phenomena vexes it;
when the mind desires to depart yet cannot do so, the shackles of attachment vex it. This is what is meant by the "Pure Land of Mind-Only," which is truly not easy to reach.
That Amitābha Buddha possesses blessings as vast as mountains and seas, and his power encompasses heaven and earth; he transforms the hells into lotus blossoms with ease.

To perceive the infinite worlds as if they were before one's eyes with the flip of a palm—though my own power of merit cannot even ensure my own constancy, and I constantly fear that my heavy past karma will cause me to fall into hell, let alone transform them into lotus flowers;
if I cannot even know what is happening in the next room, how much less can I see the infinite worlds? This is what is called "the Amitābha of one's own nature" (svabhāva-amitābha).
Truly, it is not easy to reach [the Pure Land]. Nevertheless, while my mind can be the Pure Land, I have not yet suddenly become the Pure Land;
while my nature can be Amitābha, I have not yet suddenly become Amitābha.
How could I neglect the Pure Land without cultivating it, or abandon the desire to see Amitābha? Therefore, by cultivating the Western Paradise and beholding the Buddha, one attains the Way.
This is exceedingly easy; however, if one remains in this world alone, wishing to practice Chan to awaken the nature and transcend the Buddhas and Patriarchs, it is exceedingly difficult.
Moreover, for those who cultivate the Pure Land, there is no obstruction to practicing Chan. Why then do those who practice Chan disparage the Pure Land and fail to cultivate it?
The *Great Amitābha Sūtra* states: "In the ten directions, there are immeasurable Bodhisattvas who have attained rebirth in the land of Amitābha..."
If even those Bodhisattvas in that Land of Amitābha Buddha still desire to be reborn there, what person am I that I would not wish to be born there?

Is my fruit then superior to that of all those Bodhisattvas? To speak from this perspective, the doctrines of "the Pure Land is but the pure mind" and "Amitābha is one's own nature" are grand but not essential, lofty but not practical;
those who have not yet reached the stage of cultivation have misled many. It is better to simply set foot upon [the path].
If one practices the recitation and cultivation based on the actual ground, every person will surely be born in the Pure Land and directly escape the cycle of saṃsāra;
this is worlds apart from those who speak empty words without substance.
That the Pure Land cannot be compared to the realm of immortals is something one must not fail to believe.
With the Buddha-eye, he perceives the events of immeasurable kalpas; from antiquity to the present, there is nothing he does not see.

Furthermore, one who observes the precept against false speech will certainly not speak falsely to deceive others. Moreover, one who observes the precept against the conceit of self will certainly not harbor a sense of self to boast before others.
Therefore, his words are truly worthy of being taken as a model for study. According to the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, there are ten kinds of immortals (*ṛṣi*), all of whom possess longevity.
When the count of ten million kalpas is exhausted, one enters the cycle of rebirth once more because one has never fully realized the true nature;
thus, one shares the same name as the beings of the six realms—these are all people within the wheel of saṃsāra. Among the worldly seekers of immortality, not even one in ten thousand succeeds;
and even if they do attain it, they cannot escape saṃsāra because they remain attached to the physical form and spirit and are unable to relinquish them.
As for the body and spirit, they are merely delusions manifested within the true nature and are not ultimate reality.
Thus, Hanshan’s poem says: "Even if you were to become an immortal, you would be no different from a corpse-guarding ghost.

This is unlike the Buddhist approach to life and death, which is spontaneous and free from all constraints. In the recent few centuries, those who attained immortality have been none other than Zhongli and Lü.
Among those who studied under Master Zhongli, including your own relatives and acquaintances, there were surely many thousands;
yet their number was not small, and in the end, they all died and were buried beneath the earth—thus, their lifelong efforts were spent in vain.
If you wish to seek long life, nothing compares to the Pure Land. Those born in the Pure Land enjoy an immeasurable lifespan; how great indeed is such longevity! Is it not so?

To know that one must study the methods of the immortals while practicing this Dharma-gate is like discarding a beautiful jade present before one’s eyes to seek a phytokiesel (wu-fu) stone whose acquisition is uncertain—is this not delusion?
Moreover, those who attain the state of an immortal keep their gains extremely secret and do not transmit them, claiming that to reveal the celestial mechanism (*tianji*) is a sin;
yet the Buddha’s Dharma-gate fears nothing more than its transmission not being widespread, desiring instead—
To exhaustively deliver all sentient beings before finally attaining completion—this is the vastness of his compassion, immeasurable and beyond comparison with that of immortals.
The cause and effect of the Pure Land are not false; they must be believed.
There are those who do not believe in cause and effect, and consequently do not believe in the Pure Land. How can one possibly disbelieve in cause and effect? A sutra states:
"If you wish to know the causes of your previous life, look at what you receive in this life; if you wish to know the effects of your future life, look at what you create in this life.
If you do not believe these words, why not observe the matters before your very eyes? When a person is born...
Thus there arise differences in wealth and poverty, nobility and lowliness, suffering and joy, toil and ease, honor and disgrace, longevity and early death;
these various misfortunes and blessings differ from one another. Although this is called the mandate of Heaven (*tianming*), how could Heaven show partiality toward individuals?

It is simply because the good and evil deeds performed by people in their previous lives were not the same, and thus the retributions they receive in this life—whether fortune or calamity—are likewise different. Heaven merely presides over this.
It is simply this: for this reason, this body is called the "retribution body" (*vipākakāya*). A retribution body is so named because it arises as a result of what one did in previous lives.
Since the deeds performed in previous lives could not be purely virtuous, one does not receive purely auspicious rewards;
thus, there are those who are wealthy and noble yet suffer from misery and an early death, those who are poor and lowly yet enjoy longevity and happiness, and those who possess honor and favor.
As for those who suffer humiliation and distress, their retributions follow each according to what they have done, just as a shadow follows a form without the slightest discrepancy;

thus it is said that by planting peach one obtains peaches, and by planting apricot one obtains apricots. There has never been a case of planting hemp and obtaining beans, or planting wheat and obtaining millet.
It is only because the time of sowing is brief while the time of harvest is vast that the acts of good and evil performed are very small, yet the results received are great.
The retribution for misfortune and fortune is so immense that it is said: "In spring one sows a single grain of millet; in autumn one harvests ten thousand grains.
For a person in life, the karmic fruition of good and evil is just like this; it is the natural principle of the creative transformation (*zaohua*).

If this principle can be trusted, then the doctrine of the Pure Land must necessarily be trusted. Yet, there are people who observe that good and evil deeds do not immediately yield their retribution in the present.
Consequently, they do not believe in cause and effect, and because of this, they fail to believe in the Pure Land;
yet they do not realize that there is no one who lacks retribution—it is simply a matter of whether it is sooner or later. The Buddha said to Ānanda:

"There are those who perform good deeds in this life but fall into hell after death, and those who commit evil deeds in this life but are born in heaven after death. Ānanda asked why this was so, and the Buddha replied: "In this life..."
Those who perform good deeds in this life yet fall into hell upon death do so because the goodness of their present life has not yet ripened, while the evil of their past lives has already ripened.
Those who commit evil in this life yet are born in heaven upon death do so because the evil of their present life has not yet ripened, while the goodness of their past lives has already ripened.

Where that which has ripened is present, one first receives the retribution; it is like a debt, where what is most urgent is repaid first. As the Master of the Left (Zuo Zhuan) said regarding [the case of] Luan...
Wuzi possessed such virtue that it could protect his son; thus, although his son Yan committed evil, he was able to escape calamity.
Yet when Yan’s son Ying practiced goodness, he was instead burdened by Yan’s past transgressions. Consequently, although Ying was virtuous, he met with misfortune.
If the retribution for good and evil is already like this when observed within a single lifetime, how much more so across different generations? Thus it is written in the Book.
It is said that "The Way of Heaven brings blessings to the good and calamity to the licentious," and Laozi says, "The net of Heaven is vast; it is wide-meshed, yet nothing escapes.
Since these three teachings all speak this principle, how can one fail to believe in cause and effect simply because the retribution is not yet visible before one's eyes?
And on account of such disbelief, could one then fail to believe in the Pure Land?
The Pure Land is like a bright mirror; one cannot but believe in the sun and moon. Some may ask:
"If a person here in this world recites the Buddha’s name, how can a lotus flower immediately arise in the Western Seven-Jeweled Pond?
I tell them: "This is not difficult to understand. It is, for example, like a great bright mirror: whenever an object comes before it, its reflection appears."

How could the reflection in a mirror ever admit the intervention of the mind? In the land of Amitābha Buddha, which is pure, clear, and bright, the ten directions of the world are naturally reflected as clearly as one’s own face seen in a bright mirror.

For this reason, there is no room for doubt that when one recites the name of the Buddha here, a single lotus flower will naturally arise in the western seven-jeweled pond. Or, it is further said: "Recite..."
Regarding the mantra for rebirth: it is said that Amitābha Buddha constantly dwells upon the crown of one's head to protect that person.
One might ask, "If this is so, how can the Buddha dwell upon the crowns of every single sentient being throughout the infinite worlds? The answer is:
it is like the single moon in the sky, which naturally appears reflected in all bodies of water. Or again, it is said that through the power of cultivation...
Regarding the question: "When one who practices with diligence is at the point of death, the Buddha and Bodhisattvas come to welcome them.
If there are immeasurable sentient beings throughout the worlds of the ten directions, how could the Buddha know the time of each of their deaths and go to welcome them all?

The answer is: It is like the sun in the heavens, which illuminates immeasurable realms in a single day; this occurs spontaneously. How much more so the majestic spiritual power (*vīrya*) of the Buddha, which far exceeds that of the sun!
If the moon dwells entirely upon one’s crown and its timing is fully known, how can there be any cause for doubt? (The above is from the *Lungshu wen*).
Taking correct faith in the Pure Land as essential, one must not fail to believe.
For all who wish to practice nianfo, it is necessary to give rise to faith; without faith, one gains nothing at all. Master Sengzhao said:
That "it is thus" is the characteristic of faith; that "it is not thus" is the characteristic of lack of faith.
Indeed, faith is the primary principle for entering the Way, while wisdom is the profound art of ultimate realization. The opening words of various sutras, "Thus have I heard," refer to faith;
the subsequent mention of "practitioners" refers to wisdom. Furthermore, it is said that "faith" is a term for compliance; when one has faith, [one acts accordingly].
The principle of what is being taught is consistent; thus, the way of teacher and disciple is established. Whether a scripture is extensive or concise, it is not transmitted without faith.
Therefore, the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra* states: "If there are those who have faith, they should make a vow to be born in that land.
This is the point where our original teacher, Śākyamuni, exhorts us to have faith. You all should believe this praise of inconceivable merit.
This is the point where the Buddhas of the ten directions exhort one to have faith. For those whose mind of faith is pure, the flowers bloom and they immediately behold the Buddha;

this is the point where the *Treatise on Rebirth* exhorts one to have faith. That which is called "faith" refers to: faith that the Buddha’s teaching in the sutras—that mindfulness of the Buddha (nien-fo) definitely leads to birth in the Pure Land;

faith that mindfulness of the Buddha definitely extinguishes all transgressions; faith that mindfulness of the Buddha definitely receives the protection of the Buddhas; and faith that mindfulness of the Buddha definitely attains [enlightenment].
The Buddha’s testimony that those who practice nianfo will certainly be met by the Buddha at the moment of death;

the conviction that through nianfo, all sentient beings who share this faith will attain rebirth in the Pure Land; the certainty that those who practice nianfo and attain rebirth will surely reach the stage of non-retrogression;

and the assurance that those born in the Pure Land through nianfo will certainly not fall into the three evil realms. If one receives this Dharma and maintains this mindfulness, one shall attain rebirth in the Pure Land.

It is certain that Master Daxing encouraged those who practice *nianfo* (Buddha-recitation) with these principles: the mind should only believe in the Buddha, for the Buddha knows it through his power of knowing others' minds (*paracittajñāna*);

the mouth should only recite the name of the Buddha, for the Buddha hears it through his divine ear (*divyaśrotra*); and the body should only prostrate to the Buddha, for the Buddha sees it through his divine eye (*divyacakṣus*).
Furthermore, he used this analogy: one whose faith is sincere is like a fruit tree deeply planted, its roots firmly established.
Because it is deep, the wind cannot move it, and later it bears fruit to relieve the hunger and thirst of others. It is the same for those who practice mindfulness of the Buddha (*buddhānusmṛti*):

once a Bodhisattva of the Ten Stages (*daśabhūmi*) has given rise to faith and practiced mindfulness of the Buddha, even if they encounter adverse conditions, they would rather sacrifice their own body and life than retreat from that faith.
As the *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa-sūtra* says: "Deep faith is firm and solid, like a diamond (*vajra*); it is a treasure of the Dharma."
Universally illuminating like rain upon nectar: all you who share this same aspiration must have deep faith that what the Buddhas have spoken is true and not false.
Within the sea of birth and death, mindfulness of the Buddha is supreme; cultivate pure karma with single-minded devotion, vowing to escape the cycle of rebirth.
Time does not wait for man—be careful not to harbor doubt or regret. As the Verse on Right Faith in Rebirth by the Chan Master Ciyun of India states: "I prostrate..."

In the Western Land of Bliss, Amitābha, the World-Honored One and Great Compassionate Honored One, is the sovereign lord. Relying on various *sūtras*, I have established the definitive faith for rebirth therein.
For those who abide in the Mahāyāna with a pure mind, ten moments of mindfulness directed toward that Amitāyus will ensure rebirth;
at the end of life, they will surely see the Buddha in a dream and attain birth there. Thus it is said in the *Mahāratnakūṭa Sūtra*: "The fires of the hell of the five heinous crimes..."

The *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra* (Sixteen Contemplations) states: "If one encounters a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*) and arouses a fierce resolve, reciting the Buddha’s name ten times, one will immediately attain rebirth.
It further says: "If one possesses a heart of joy and delight, even as few as ten recitations will lead to rebirth;

otherwise, Buddhahood will not be achieved. The *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra* (Forty-eight Vows) likewise states: "All who hear my name and give rise to a sincere heart, turning back [from delusion] in a single thought..."
Regarding rebirth in that land, it is excluded only for those who have committed the five heinous crimes or slandered the True Dharma; thus says the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra*.

As for those who at the time of death are unable to practice visualization or mindfulness, but merely form the thought of knowing that the Buddha exists, such persons will attain rebirth upon the cessation of their breath;

thus says the *Mahābherīhāraka Sūtra*. Furthermore, if one for a day and a night suspends silk canopies and banners while single-mindedly recollecting rebirth without interruption of the mind, one shall likewise attain rebirth.
While lying down in sleep, one dreams of the Buddha; thus it is said in the *Sukhāvatīvyūha-sūtra*.

If one recites the name of the Buddha day and night for a single day with earnest diligence and without interruption, exhorting others in turn to be reborn together [in the Pure Land], as stated in the *Mahākaruṇā-puṇḍarīka-sūtra*, then after one day, two days, up to seven days of upholding the name with an undistracted mind, the Buddha will appear before that person.
The *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra* states that if a person hears of that Amitābha for one day, two days, or more, and maintains focused mindfulness before them, they will be reborn there.

The *Pratyutpanna Samādhi Sūtra* likewise states that if one performs prostrations with the five limbs to the Buddha during the six periods of the day and night, maintaining uninterrupted mindfulness so as to see that Buddha directly, one will be reborn there. The *Drum* [Sūtra]... [text fragment ends].

The *Ghoṣarāja-sūtra* states thus: "If one observes the fast and precepts for ten days and ten nights, suspends silk banners and canopies, burns incense and lamps, and maintains mindfulness without interruption, one will attain rebirth. The *Great Amitābha Sūtra* states thus:

"If a person single-mindedly recollects a Buddha of a particular direction, whether walking or sitting, after seven weeks they shall see that Buddha in person and immediately attain rebirth. As stated in the *Mahāsannipāta-sūtra*:
This explains that if a person makes a vow to constantly practice walking meditation for ninety days, without sitting or lying down, they will see Amitābha Buddha within samādhi;

it is stated thus in the *Sūtra on the Standing Practice*. Furthermore, if a person sits upright facing due west for ninety days and constantly recollects the Buddha, they can achieve samādhi and be born before the Buddha; this is stated in the *Mañjuśrī-prajñā-sūtra*. Regarding myself...
The verses from various sutras are thus spoken in brief, yet they are inexhaustible; may those who hear them together give rise to right faith that the Buddha’s words are true and not deceptive.
Since the Buddha has clearly declared that rebirth [in the Pure Land] is easy, may each of you maintain right faith without doubt.
(From the *Lianzong baojian*)
The Pure Land encompasses precept, concentration, and wisdom; one must truly believe this.

Everyone says that practicing the Pure Land is not equal to the methods of Chan, Teaching, and Vinaya, yet I alone maintain that among the dharma-gates of Chan, Teaching, and Vinaya, none is equal to the practice of the Pure Land.
For true purity, clarity, wondrousness, emptiness, penetration, and spiritual responsiveness are inherent in all beings, whether wise or foolish.

Because the fundamental nature, the faculties, the sense objects, and the illusory appearances of the environment all sink together into the cycle of birth and death, continuing uninterrupted through kalpas, the Śākya clan established the expedient means of Chan, Teaching, and Vinaya to lead practitioners through these gates so that they might all attain transcendent awakening.
Only Amitābha Buddha has uniquely opened a single gate called the Practice of the Pure Land; it is like a singular prescription for curing disease—simple, direct, and essential.
To cut off a single thought of single-mindedness is to reach the other shore; regardless of whether one is a monk or a layperson, all may practice this.
While it is known as a shallow teaching for the sake of transforming the ignorant and the common, in reality, it is the swift path to attaining Buddhahood.

Among those who study Buddhism today—be they in Chan, Teaching, or Vinaya—nothing surpasses Chan for its ultimate, sudden, and perfect realization; yet it is not for those of dull faculties or inferior capacity, but only for those of divine and superior endowment.
Those who merely grasp at intellectual understanding cannot avoid the error of falling into a stagnant void; for those who study the Three Vehicles, nothing is equal to the Teaching.

To forget the trap once the fish is caught, and to see the moon through the pointing finger—yet even these do not avoid the ailment of poring over old paper. For protecting the good and warding off evil, nothing is equal to the Vinaya.
Unless one’s body and mind are pure and internal and external are as one, one cannot avoid the suffering of many entanglements. In sum, [the path lies here].
If one examines this discourse regarding its entryway, it consists of Chan, Teaching, and Vinaya; if one considers its ultimate destination, it is Precept, Concentration, and Wisdom.

Is there any way to attain Precept, Concentration, and Wisdom other than through the single gateway of the Pure Land? When reciting the Buddha's name, one chants with the mouth and contemplates with the mind that "all evils shall not be committed"—is this not the binding of the precepts?
When mindfulness is fixed upon the pure realm, illusory dusts are extinguished together—is this not concentration? Is this not wisdom?
It is not fixed mindfulness; in reality, there is no mind of mindfulness. When the mental flowers are serene and still, is this not the wisdom of one who can screen away myriad anxieties?
With a single intent directed toward the West, one awakens to the sudden and perfect capacity without the need for blows or shouts.

One attains the true Dharma-eye without reading the Great Canon, achieves great sovereignty without maintaining the four dignified postures, and remains neither defiled nor pure, free from all entanglements.
At such a time as this, when there is no liberation [from the cycle of birth and death], what are precept, concentration, and wisdom? What are meditation, doctrine, and discipline?
My mind and the Buddha-mind are entirely without distinction; this is the ultimate realization of the Pure Land path.
As for the water of eight virtues and the golden lotus pedestals, why should one harbor any doubt? (From "An Exhortation to Practice the Pure Land," by Zheng Qingzhi)
When it comes to the Pure Land, Amitābha alone is uniquely recommended;
one must believe this. Among the Tathāgatas of the ten directions, all may be approached, yet Amitābha is uniquely recommended for three reasons:

first, the profundity of his vows; second, the affinity with those in the Sahā world; and third, the correspondence of his transformative path. Regarding the weight of his vows: Amitābha made vast and great...

His vow states: "If, since my attainment of Buddhahood, there should be sentient beings who wish to be born in my land, or who hear my name and cultivate various roots of goodness while reciting my name even ten times, yet should not be born therein, I vow not to attain perfect enlightenment.
Furthermore, once born in my land, if there should be any regression or lack of certainty regarding their attainment of Buddhahood, I vow not to attain perfect enlightenment."
The *Huayan chao* states that Amitābha’s vows are profound and universally embrace the sentient beings of this Sahā world.

Those with the karmic affinity—be they monks or laypeople, men or women, noble or humble, rich or poor—who heard the Buddha’s teachings during Śākyamuni’s lifetime and took refuge in Amitābha were already numerous.
Even after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, anyone who heard even a little of the Buddhist teachings understood [this truth].

Even those who are stubborn, foolish, violent, evil, or devoid of faith—whether they encounter calamities and perils, or involuntarily utter sounds of praise or lamentation—may find themselves spontaneously calling upon the name of Amitābha Buddha.
This extends even to children and women who, using sand or clods of earth, or by drawing on walls, fashion images of Amitābha Buddha. Even so...

Those whose practice is not yet stable and whose mastery of speech is not yet perfected can naturally chant the name of Amitābha Buddha; all of this arises without exhortation and occurs without instruction—how could it be anything other than the presence of a karmic affinity? It is said that after this sutra has passed away, the Buddha-dharma will be entirely absent, except for the four-character name of Amitābha Buddha, which remains to save and deliver sentient beings;
thus, Tiantai said, "One should know that that Buddha has a particular affinity with this degenerate world.

Regarding this connection, the former sages maintained that the holy ones of the two lands manifest their residence in either the pure or the defiled realms in order to subdue beings through the two gates of *zhè* (subduing) and *shè* (gathering).
Sentient beings are broken by this world through its impurity, suffering, brevity, and manifold demonic afflictions, so that they may come to know what to loathe;
they are gathered by means of purity, bliss, longevity, and non-retrogression, so that they may know what to rejoice in.
Once they both loathe and rejoice, the path of transformation proceeds. Furthermore, beyond the bestowal of the Way through the Three Vehicles, Śākyamuni has those who are to be saved...

Because those who have not yet exhausted their afflictions rely on Amitābha for deliverance, he repeatedly and earnestly praises and exhorts them to go [to the Pure Land] throughout the Mahāyāna sūtras;
this is because it is a matter of mutual relevance within the path of transformation. For these three reasons, he alone is thus extolled (*Jingtu huo wen*).
One cannot fail to believe that the suffering and happiness of the Pure Land are comparable;
as the sutra says, "The sentient beings of that land have no manifold sufferings and experience only various joys," and for this reason it is called the Land of Ultimate Bliss (*Sukhāvatī*).
Now, if we contrast this with the Sahā world: here, all who are born with bodies of flesh and blood experience nothing but suffering, whereas there, they are transformed from lotus blossoms.
Here, there is the suffering of birth and non-birth, for the succession of seasons brings about the daily encroachment of senescence;
there, however, there is no suffering of aging, for cold and heat do not shift and there is no decay. Here, the four great elements are difficult to harmonize and many illnesses arise;

there, however, there is no suffering of illness, for the transformed body is fragrant and pure. Here, those who reach seventy are rare and impermanence is swift; there, however, there is no [suffering of] the end of life.

There is no suffering of death; this is because they possess affectionate attachments, whereas those who have such attachments must inevitably part. There is no suffering of being separated from loved ones;

this is because they have no parents, wives, or children, whereas others do. There is no suffering of meeting with enemies; this is because they have no foes or adversaries, whereas those who have enemies must inevitably encounter them.

There is no suffering of encountering the hateful; this is because they are gathered with the most virtuous, whereas others are not. There is no suffering of hardship, hunger, cold, or insatiable craving; this is because they... [the text continues].

This [life] provides clothing, food, and precious jewels for enjoyment as they appear; that [state], however, has a form and appearance that is humble and coarse, with many of the six sense faculties impaired.

This [life] possesses a dignified and majestic countenance, and the body is endowed with radiance; that [state], however, is subject to the cycle of birth and death, while that [state] has forever realized the non-arising of phenomena.

This [life] contains the sufferings of the four realms of existence; that [state] does not even have the name of the three evil paths. This [life] is filled with thorns, pits, and uneven ground; that [state] is free from such obstacles.

That realm is filled with uneven earth, stones, sand, and mud; this one is a ground of pure gold, where jewel-trees reach the heavens and seven-jeweled towers soar aloft, with flowers of four colors in full bloom.
That realm belongs to the time when the Twin Trees have already passed away and the Dragon Flower has not yet appeared;

this one is where the Honored One of Immeasurable Life currently dwells and preaches the Dharma. In that realm, Avalokiteśvara and Mahāsthāmaprāpta are revered only by their illustrious names; here, however, they are present in person. That realm...
In this [world], one has two superior persons as close and eminent friends; yet there, the various māras and non-Buddhists disturb and confuse right practice.

Exhorting to World-transcending Filial Piety:
Exhorting one’s two parents to practice worldly filial piety has three aspects, while world-transcending filial piety has one. The three aspects of worldly filial piety are:
first, nourishing one’s parents with delicious food; second, honoring one’s parents through rank and emolument; third, cultivating virtue and exerting conduct to become a sage or a worthy.
To manifest one's filial devotion in this manner is what is called "filial piety" in the world.

Filial piety that transcends the world, however, consists in exhorting one’s parents to observe the precepts, uphold the Way, single-mindedly recite the Buddha’s name, and aspire for rebirth in the Pure Land to behold Amitābha and attain non-retrogression;
for a child, repaying their parents is greatest in this way. I was born late and have only recently heard the Buddha-Dharma, yet my parents have already passed away like the withered wind-blown tree.

Exhortation to Practice True Buddha-Recitation:
Those who study the Buddha-dharma need not concern themselves with external adornments or formal appearances; they value only genuine practice.

Lay practitioners do not necessarily require black robes or clerical caps; those who wear their hair may simply maintain their ordinary attire while constantly reciting the Buddha’s name. It is not required that they change their dress.

Those who desire stillness need not insist on striking fish-bells and beating drums; they may silently recite the Buddha’s name in quietude. Those who fear involvement need not insist on joining large assemblies;
they may recite the Buddha’s name with their doors closed. Those who can read need not insist on entering monasteries to listen to sutras;
they may recite the Buddha’s name according to the teachings. Rather than burning incense for a thousand miles, it is better to sit peacefully at home.
Reciting the Buddha’s name while maintaining a domestic shrine and serving false teachers is not as good as reciting the Buddha’s name with filial piety toward one’s parents;

making extensive friends who are demonic obstacles is not as good as reciting the Buddha’s name in solitary purity; making offerings to a storehouse for the sake of future lives is not as good as reciting the Buddha’s name by performing meritorious deeds in the present;

making vows for protection and averting calamities is not as good as reciting the Buddha’s name while repenting and reforming oneself; and studying the texts of external paths is not as good as [reciting the Buddha’s name].
If you do not recognize a single character, it is better to recite the Buddha’s name than to speak recklessly of Chan principles out of ignorance;

if you seek supernatural powers from spirits and ghosts, it is better to sincerely uphold the precepts and recite the Buddha’s name; if you lack right faith in cause and effect, it is better to recite the Buddha’s name. To state the essentials:

to rectify the mind and extinguish evil while reciting the Buddha’s name is called being a "good person"; to collect the mind and eliminate distraction while reciting the Buddha’s name is called... [being a good person].

Out of great compassion, the Great Sage directly exhorted them to single-mindedly hold the Name, precisely because holding the Name is easy. If one holds the Name while deeply penetrating the true mark (*dharmatā*), its merit will equal that of the sublime contemplation (*prajñā-vipaśyanā*);
there is no doubt that one will attain the highest grade of the highest level. Therefore, the commentaries and sub-commentaries focus exclusively [on this].
The *Gandhu-śāstra* on the Single Gate of Upholding the Name also states that there are seven kinds of excellence in the practice of *nienfo* (Buddha-recollection).
First is the excellence of being few in words and easy to practice; because one merely recites the single phrase "Namo Amitābha Buddha," it can be practiced by all people.
Observing this, we know that upholding the Name is a dharma accessible to the masses, and for this reason, it is listed first, while visualization (*guan*) follows.

The Dharma continues here: those who practice according to their capacity and lot may either maintain the Name while simultaneously engaging in visualization, or engage in visualization while simultaneously maintaining the Name.

In total, this is one Buddha; there is no need for the concern of "lifting one and letting go of another. If one is unable to cultivate visualization, one may simply and exclusively maintain the single method of reciting the Name.
As it is said: "The principle of returning to the source is non-dual, yet the expedient means are manifold."
The gateway and its successful fulfillment are one and the same. This concludes the fourth section: the Dharma-gate of Recollecting the Buddha.
Regarding the Dharma-gate of Reciting Verses with Ten Recitations of the Buddha’s Name:
the Original Vow of Amitābha Buddha states that if sentient beings, with a sincere heart, believe and rejoice, desiring to be born in my land, they shall recite the name ten times.
If my name were not to arise, I would not have become a Buddha. Therefore, every morning at dawn, you should join your palms, face west, and prostrate yourself, reciting ten times:
"Namo Amitābha Buddha; Namo Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva; Namo Mahāsthāmaprāpta Bodhisattva;
Namo all Bodhisattvas, Śrāvakas, and other supreme virtuous ones. Then, prostrate once more.
Recite the entire verse for the Ritual of Mindfulness of the Bodhisattva of Great Compassion, Praising the Buddha and Repenting of Sins with Dedication and Aspiration once:
"The Buddhas of the ten directions and three periods of time, Amitābha is foremost; He delivers sentient beings through the nine grades, his majestic virtue is infinite.
I now take full refuge and repent for the sins of the three karmas; Whatever merits and virtues I possess, I dedicate them with a sincere heart. May [all beings]..."
For fellow practitioners of nianfo, the response of the Buddha manifests at all times; at the moment of death, the realm of the Western Paradise appears clearly before one’s eyes.

All who see or hear this shall exert themselves with diligence and together be born in the Land of Ultimate Bliss. Having seen the Buddha, they will transcend birth and death, and like the Buddha, they shall deliver all beings.
Then, having prostrated once more, they withdrew. This verse possesses great majestic power; it can extinguish all transgressions and increase all merit. It is the crown of the head.
It is especially virtuous to burn incense and perform prostrations at the prescribed times; if one does so with a sincere heart every day, one will certainly be reborn in the Middle Grade.

If one is illiterate and unable to perform the aforementioned rites and recitations, one should join one’s palms each morning, face west, and with utmost sincerity, pay homage and recite the Buddha’s name ten times, followed by the four-line verse for making vows to the Bodhisattvas, which says:
"May I, together with those who recite the Buddha’s name, be born together in the Ultimate [Pure Land]."
Rejoicing in the Pure Land, one beholds the Buddha and realizes the nature of birth and death; like the Buddha, one delivers all beings. Then, prostrating once more, one withdraws.
In this way, there is none who does not attain rebirth. (From *Longshu Wenzhang*).
The Dharma Gate of Ten Breaths and Ten Recitations.

For laypeople busy with worldly affairs, every morning after dressing, they should face west and join their palms to recite "Namo Amitābha Buddha" in a single breath as one invocation. Ten such breaths constitute ten invocations (*daśanāma*).

This is not limited by a specific number of Buddhas, but follows the length of each breath, taking the exhaustion of the breath as the measure. The sound of the recitation should be neither too loud nor too soft.
To recite these ten invocations continuously and without interruption while maintaining a low profile is intended to prevent the mind from scattering;

this focused application of effort relies on using the breath to bind the mind. One should dedicate the merit of these ten invocations with the vow to seek rebirth in the Western Land, ensuring that throughout this single lifetime there is no interruption, so that rebirth will be certain (Master Ciyun).

Regarding the Dharma-gate of recollecting the Buddha during the six periods of the day and night, Master Huiyuan established the Donglin Society to practice the worship of the Pure Land during these six periods. As a Tang poem states:

"Master Huiyuan alone carved a lotus water-clock, yet he still performed his devotions toward the mountains during the six periods. All who practice this should first establish themselves in a pure room.
Place an image of the Buddha and offer incense, lamps, and other offerings according to one's means.

Bathe to remove dust and grime, put on clean garments, and at the time of sunrise, midday, sunset, the first watch of the night, midnight, and the final watch of the night, stand before the Triple Gem with body upright and palms joined in faith.
Bow in worship toward the West, gaze upon the compassionate countenance, and recite "Namo Amitābha Buddha" a thousand times.
Chanting the liturgy for bowing to the Buddha forty-eight times, recite the text for the Western Pure Land, make vows, and dedicate the merit.

Practice the Way with single-minded devotion during the six periods of the day without weariness; when pure karma is perfected, you will surely attain rebirth in the highest grade of the highest level.

Furthermore, according to the Yunqi Rituals for Morning and Evening, add the recitation of one scroll of the *Amitābha Sūtra*, three recitations of the *Wǎngshēng Zhòu* (Dharani for Rebirth), and one thousand recitations of the Buddha’s name. South.
Recite "Homage to Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva," "Homage to Mahāsthāmaprāpta Bodhisattva," and "Homage to the Assembly of Bodhisattvas of the Pure Great Ocean" ten times each;
perform prostrations according to one's physical capacity and recite the Great and Small Vows as much as possible before dedicating the merit.
This format is simple, convenient, and authentic; it may be practiced three times daily, or at dawn and dusk by the entire assembly, and is most worthy of emulation.
If one is entangled by worldly affairs and unable to follow the prescribed form, one must rise early to burn incense, pay homage to the Buddha, and recite his name;
the same applies at dusk. Such acts of worship and recitation must not be omitted.
Should one occasionally have public business that causes the omission of these rites, one must immediately repent before the Buddha the following morning (from the *Hezuan*).
Regarding the Dharma Gate of Repenting Sins and Mindfulness of the Buddha,
the *Great Amitābha Sūtra* states: "If the devas and people of the ten directions hear my name, maintain purity through fasting and precepts, further perform various good deeds,
and single-mindedly fix their mindfulness upon me— even for as little as one day and night without interruption— they will certainly be born in my land."
Furthermore, it is said that those who committed evil in previous lives, upon hearing my name, shall immediately repent and perform good deeds, vowing to be born in my land;
at the end of their lives, they shall all bypass the three evil realms and come directly to be reborn there.

Those who practice and uphold this path should first purify the altar and set out offerings of incense and lamps, inviting bhikṣus and other virtuous persons to petition the Buddha on their behalf, and must not involve themselves in worldly household affairs.

Do not approach women; observe the precepts and maintain your practice by reciting the Buddha’s name day and night—one thousand times for each Buddha—and recite one scroll of the Amitābha Sūtra three times in this manner, repenting with a sincere heart and dedicating the merit.
The Dharma Gate of the Samādhi of Mindfulness of the Buddha through the Single Characteristic.
The Buddha said: "A bodhisattva who can correctly practice the Samādhi of the Adornment of the Single Characteristic will swiftly realize Bodhi.

Those who cultivate this practice should distance themselves from clamor and distraction, refrain from contemplating manifold characteristics, and focus their minds with single-minded devotion upon the One."

The Tathāgata carefully adopts a name and skillfully contemplates his appearance and demeanor; this constitutes a universal contemplation of all Buddhas of the three periods of time, whereby one immediately attains the omniscient wisdom (*sarvajñajñāna*) of all Buddhas.
The *Ten Doubts Treatise* of the Tiantai school states: "All Buddhas are entirely equal;

however, because sentient beings have dull faculties and are mostly turbid and distracted, if one does not single-mindedly bind one's mindfulness to a single Buddha, [then one will not attain realization]."

Because samādhi is difficult to achieve when the mind is distracted, one should focus exclusively on mindfulness of Amitābha Buddha; this is the practice of the *ekalakṣaṇa-samādhi* (one-characteristic samādhi).
The practitioner should maintain single-minded, exclusive mindfulness, never forgetting it whether dreaming or awake.

One must not interrupt it with other activities, nor separate it with greed, anger, or other afflictions. Whenever a transgression occurs, one should immediately repent, ensuring there is no gap between thoughts, no gap of days, and no gap of time.

If, in every thought-moment, one never departs from the Buddha and every thought-moment is pure, luminous, and perfect, one immediately attains the Samādhi of the Single Characteristic (*ekalakṣaṇa-samādhi*).

Regarding the Dharma-gate of the Samādhi of Mindfulness of the Buddha through Gathering the Mind and Regulating the Breath, the *Mahāsaṃnipāta Sūtra* states: "Those who seek unsurpassed Bodhi should practice the dhyāna-samādhi of mindfulness of the Buddha. A verse therein says: "If..."
If a person focuses their mind exclusively on reciting the name of Amitābha Buddha, this is called the unsurpassed, profound, and wondrous dhyāna.

When one perceives the Buddha through the visualization of the ultimate mind, this is precisely the Dharma of non-arising and non-extinction. The *Sūtra on the Samādhi of Sitting Meditation* states: "When a Bodhisattva practices sitting meditation, they do not contemplate anything else but contemplate only a single Buddha;
thus they immediately attain samādhi. For beginners practicing this, it is unavoidable to encounter the two afflictions of dullness and distraction; therefore, one must...

From the *Ji duizhi rentian baojian* (The Precious Mirror for Humans and Devas as a Countermeasure): "Whenever one cultivates meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), one enters a quiet chamber and sits upright with the body straight.
One counts the inhalations and exhalations, counting from one to ten, from ten to a hundred, and up to a thousand or ten thousand.
When this breath becomes still and this mind becomes tranquil, they are equal to empty space. Without the need for forced restraint, after a long time, a single breath will abide of its own accord."
When exhaling and not inhaling, one perceives that these breaths emerge from the eighty-four thousand pores like rising clouds and mist;
all illnesses from beginningless time are spontaneously eliminated, and all obstacles are naturally extinguished.

One attains spontaneous, clear awakening, like a blind person suddenly gaining sight—seeing through clearly at that moment without needing someone else to point out the way. Now, this practice of concentrating the mind to recite the Buddha’s name...
To achieve the samādhi that counteracts dullness and agitation, the method of counting the breath is most essential.
Whenever sitting, first visualize your own body within a circle of light and silently observe the tip of the nose. With each inhalation and exhalation, silently recite "Namo Amitābha Buddha" once.
Skillfully regulate the breath—neither too slow nor too fast—so that the mind and the breath rely upon one another, following the breath as it goes out.
Whether entering, walking, standing, sitting, or reclining, one should practice this at all times without interruption, constantly maintaining it in secret.
Eventually, when one enters deeply into meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) such that both breath and thought are forgotten, this very body and mind become equal to empty space.

Through long-term cultivation until it reaches full maturity, the eyes and mind open and penetrate, and *samādhi* suddenly manifests before one; this is precisely the Pure Land of Mind-Only. (From the *Lianzong baojian*).
While people of the world mostly use precious gems, diamonds, bodhi wood, or *mukta* seeds as prayer beads, I take the inhalation and exhalation of breath as my rosary.
Reciting the Buddha’s name in accordance with the breath provides great reliance; it brings peace to fear, for if even one breath does not return, one belongs to the next life.
Whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, I constantly use this rosary, even when falling into deep sleep.

If one sets aside the Buddha [image] and sleeps, then upon waking continues the practice, one will surely see that Buddha within a dream—just as smoke rising before fire appears when drilling for fire.

If the dreaming does not cease, the samādhi will be accomplished; beholding the *ūrṇā-kośa* (the white tuft of hair) face-to-face, one will personally receive a prediction of enlightenment (*vyākaraṇa*).
There is not even a one-in-ten-thousand chance of failure. (From the *Bao Wang Lun* by Master Caotang).
Regarding the Dharma-gate of the Samādhi of Chan and Nianfo, the distant patriarchs have said:
"Without wisdom (prajñā), Chan cannot exhaust its stillness; without Chan, wisdom cannot deepen its illumination.

Chan and wisdom are the terms for illuminating while being still; they assist one another. Illumination does not depart from stillness, and stillness does not depart from illumination—this is mindfulness.
If a person who follows the Buddha wishes to practice Chan to see their true nature, they should simply rely on this method:

sitting upright in a quiet room, clearing away distracting burdens, severing the dust of worldly emotions, and staring wide-eyed. With the mind neither clinging to external objects nor dwelling in internal concentration, one turns the light back to shine upon oneself;
when both internal and external are stilled, one then silently and continuously raises the thought "Namo Amitābha Buddha" three or five times, and then returns [to stillness].
Guang looked at the clouds himself and said, "If one sees one's nature, one attains Buddhahood. Ultimately, what is this original nature of mine?
Amitābha then examined him closely: "Right now, from where does this single thought that you have raised arise?
Having seen through this thought, look again—who is it that is looking? After reflecting for a long time, he again raised the thought: "Amitābha Buddha."
Furthermore, gaze thus and investigate thus, applying yourself with urgency and diligence without allowing for interruption;
remain alert and unclouded, like a hen brooding over her eggs, maintaining this practice regardless of the four modes of deportment. Gaze thus, look thus, and investigate thus;
suddenly, while walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, upon hearing a sound or seeing a form, you will awaken to clarity and personally behold your own original nature.
When Amitābha’s internal and external, body and mind, are simultaneously and completely transcended, the entire earth is this very Western Pure Land;
the myriad phenomena are none other than one's own self. In stillness, there is no lack of illumination; in movement, one does not depart from quiescence.
Thereafter, through the perfect integration of compassion and wisdom, one guides those who have not yet awakened, attaining birth in the highest grade within the Land of Adorned Retribution.
Chan Master Tushou Yue addressed the assembly on the Three Barriers: 1. "Plucking the grass to investigate the profound is intended solely for the realization of one's nature.
Right now, where does this person’s nature reside? 2. "Having recognized one's original nature, one seeks to escape birth and death.
When birth and death arrive, how will you escape them? 3. "Having escaped birth and death, one must know the destination. When the four elements separate, where will you go?"
If you pass through this barrier, you will be neither bound by birth and death nor hindered by going, coming, or the present.

A person who recites the Buddha’s name throughout the twelve periods of the day should single-mindedly hold the phrase "Namu Amida Butsu" and contemplate it with profound stillness. Furthermore, they should turn the light back upon themselves to examine:
"What is my original nature? When the four elements separate, where shall I go? By constantly harboring such doubt, one may suddenly realize the truth.
One immediately knows where it lands: this is precisely the direct and straightforward path of cultivation (from the *Lianzong baojian*).

In general discussion, among the multitudes of bodhisattvas who practice the recitation of the Buddha’s name, there are those who, throughout kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, have been unable to fulfill the six perfections and myriad practices even now.

When the mind recollects the Buddha, all myriad conditions are naturally relinquished; this is the perfection of giving (*dāna-pāramitā*). When the mind single-mindedly recollects the Buddha, all evils are naturally blocked;
this is the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīla-pāramitā*). When the mind single-mindedly recollects the Buddha, the mind becomes naturally supple;

this is the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*). When the mind single-mindedly recollects the Buddha, one never again falls back; this is the perfection of diligence (*vīrya-pāramitā*). When the mind single-mindedly recollects the Buddha, as for other [matters]...

The non-arising of conceptualization is the perfection of meditative concentration (*dhyāna-pāramitā*); mindfulness of the Buddha with single-mindedness and clear right mindfulness is the perfection of wisdom (*prajñā-pāramitā*).
When one pursues this to its ultimate limit, it does not transcend the single mind, yet all myriad practices are fully present;
abiding thus in unsurpassed *bodhi* constitutes the most supreme skillful means (*upāya*). (From the *Sūcāo*)
The method for holding the name has no fixed rules: one may recite it aloud, or in a low voice;
one may recite it like flowing water, or while prostrating; one may recite it while counting, or without counting;
one may recite it while walking, or while standing, or while sitting quietly, or while lying on one’s side; one may recite it silently, or clearly, or with the lips and tongue moving slightly.
One may recite with a single breath or a certain number of sounds; one may recite according to the breath when ill or timid;
one may recite alone or together with a multitude. The essential point is simply to ensure that the mind does not become distracted.

Some advise that if one recites the Buddha’s name with a forceful voice, the Samādhi will be easily accomplished, whereas if one recites in a low voice, the mind will often wander and disperse. For this reason, the key to dispelling distraction lies especially in the sound.

It is about being fierce and earnest. Furthermore, there are several ways of reciting the Buddha’s name with such intensity: first, "courageous recitation. If one is too weak-willed, it will not suffice.

It is like a filial son seeking to avenge a deep grievance against his parents; even if he must go to a high precipice, a deep ravine, a path of glowing spirits, or a tiger’s den, he goes without fear. Therefore, [one must be fierce].

First, the thought of sorrow is so overwhelming that it cannot be contained; every time I contemplate the Buddha, my hair stands on end and my inner organs feel as if they are being torn asunder, for I remember my late mother, who was compassionate toward her child, and my deceased son, who possessed great wisdom. Thus, I am moved to indignation. Second, the thought of resentment is so profound that it cannot be pacified;
like a failed candidate who is destitute yet burdened by talent, or one who is silent and neglected, whenever I bring this to mind, I am nearly overcome with distress.
First, because one does not wish for [unwholesome] states to arise, there is a single thought of longing and attachment that is so profound it cannot be expressed;

it is like a deeply cherished object that haunts one’s soul and dreams, fearing only its loss. Second, when pleasant things appear before one, there is a surge of exultation and joy, like one who, cold, finds clothing, or one who, hungry, finds food.
Third, when adverse conditions confront one, there is a piercing sense of regret and remorse, as if one had emerged from the dead.
To escape [suffering], one must unify the mind and mouth so that every single syllable flows forth from the very marrow of the liver;
only then is this the true realm of *nianfo* (Buddha-recitation). This is a general discussion of the principle and practice of *nianfo*, focusing on a single thought-moment.
"One mind without distraction" (*ekacitta-avikṣipta*) refers to the ultimate state of upholding [the name]. This constitutes the essential purport of this sutra.
"One mind" (*ekacitta*) excludes mere verbal recitation while the mind does not contemplate;

"without distraction" (*avikṣipta*) excludes cases where the mind contemplates but the contemplation is not unified, or where the contemplation is unified but at times becomes distracted. "One mind without distraction" is the consummation of the practice of pure karma.
This is complete. To maintain the center through mindfulness and investigate its essence can be briefly divided into two types of mindfulness. First, regarding mindfulness:

one constantly remembers and constantly recollects the Buddha’s name, using the mind to trace each syllable until they are distinct; the preceding phrase and the succeeding phrase continue in succession without interruption.
Whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, there is only this single thought and no second thought, just as in the Samādhi of Perfect Radiance.

This refers to what the Sūtra means by "making the mind one amidst the silence of space," "making the mind one amidst the various afflictions," and so forth, up to "making the mind one in all circumstances—whether praised or reviled, gain or loss, good or evil.
While this constitutes unity on the level of phenomena (*dharma*), it has not yet reached penetration on the level of principle (*tattva*).

Because one possesses only the power of faith and has not yet seen the Path, it is called "unity of mind in terms of phenomena" (*śamatha-ekāgratā*)—a state of concentration (*samādhi*) without wisdom (*prajñā*).
It is also called "concentration" (*samādhi*) because it subdues delusion; it is called "without wisdom" because one has not yet been able to shatter delusion. As for "investigating the essence":

upon hearing the name of the Buddha, one does not merely recollect it, but extends that mindfulness into contemplation to investigate the source of its origin. When this investigation reaches its ultimate point, there is a sudden realization and accord with the two meanings within one's own fundamental mind.
The first [meaning] is that the object of cognition and the wisdom that cognizes are non-dual, such that the mind capable of recollection is not external to [the Buddha].

There is no Buddha who is the object of my thought; this wisdom is not external to the Buddha as he is contemplated, nor is there a mind capable of contemplating the Buddha that exists apart from him.

Since there is no wisdom outside of suchness (*tathatā*), and neither suchness nor wisdom exists independently, there is only the single mind. These two—suchness and wisdom—are simultaneously quiescent and luminous, beyond conceptualization.
If one speaks of their existence, the very essence of the mind that contemplates is itself empty, and the Buddha who is contemplated is realized as such.
It cannot be apprehended. If one says it is non-existent, the mind that contemplates is vividly lucid and unclouded, and the Buddha who is contemplated is distinct and clear.
If one says it is both existent and non-existent, then both the state of having thoughts and the state of being without thoughts are extinguished.

If one says it is neither existent nor non-existent, then both the state of having thoughts and the state of being without thoughts are preserved: "neither existent" means it is eternally quiescent, and "not non-existent" means it is eternally illuminating.
Neither dual nor non-dual, it is neither quiescent nor illuminating; yet it illuminates while being quiescent. Beyond the reach of thought and speech, it is ineffable and indescribable;
thus, there is only the single mind. Herein, the duality of subject and object dissolves and the views of existence and non-existence are exhausted.

Within this fundamentally pure essence, what further phenomena could there be to cause confusion? Because one perceives the truth, wisdom is conjoined with meditative concentration—this is what is meant by the name [of the Samādhi].

The principle is the one mind. When we speak of "wisdom" (*prajñā*), it is because wisdom can illuminate delusion; when combined with "concentration" (*samādhi*), it is because concentration illuminates that delusion is fundamentally empty, whereby delusion is naturally subdued.

Furthermore, illumination can destroy delusion, not merely subdue it. Although phenomena and principle are distinguished, their capacities are mutually interpenetrating; one need not harbor doubts or obstructions.
Regarding "phenomenal mindfulness," one may doubt for oneself that the rational nature is not clear, rendering one's actions fruitless. One should know that regarding phenomena...

To attain penetration of principle is as described in the "Chapter on Great Power" regarding perfect penetration: "Without relying on expedient means, one spontaneously attains the opening of the mind.

Master Konggu said: "If one does not investigate 'Who is it that recites the Buddha's name? but simply proceeds with pure, single-minded recitation, there will also be a day of awakening. This refers to the "attainment of principle through conceptualization.

One should be wary that if the recitation of the Buddha's name is infrequent, one may fall into emptiness; therefore, one must know that while principle is attained through penetration, practice is maintained through the recitation of events.
To contemplate the principle of oneness is to be mindful of Amitābha in every thought-moment; is it not therefore great to recite his name?

For this reason, the two modes of mindfulness—concentrating the mind and embodying the mind—are mutually permeated in both practice and principle, for they are fundamentally non-dual (from the *Shuchao*).

The *Commentary on the Ritual for Visualizing the Dharma-Gate* (*Limenianxiangfa-men shuchao*) states: "When prostrating to the Buddha, one should visualize oneself within a lotus flower, performing the prostration with reverent devotion while the Buddha sits upon a lotus flower receiving one's veneration.
When reciting the Buddha’s name, one should visualize oneself within a lotus flower."
Sitting in the full lotus posture upon a lotus flower, the Buddha receives me; thereafter, one should single-mindedly hold his name.

Formerly, there were two monks who visualized the opening and closing of a lotus flower and thereby attained rebirth in the Pure Land. How much more so for those who add the practice of holding the name—could there be anyone who does not attain rebirth?
Longshu Wen said: "When reciting the Buddha’s name, one should visualize one's own body standing before the Buddha in the Pure Land with palms joined."
With a sincere mind, one should recollect the Buddha; the same applies to recollecting the Bodhisattvas.

One should also recollect all Bodhisattvas, Śrāvakas, and other superior virtuous persons, visualizing their minds and bodies within the Pure Land. When chanting, one should imagine that the sound reaches before all the Bodhisattvas and virtuous persons.

When prostrating, one should likewise visualize performing the prostration in the Pure Land. When reciting verses, one should also visualize being reverently present before the Buddhas in the Pure Land.
When reciting gāthās, it is sufficient to have images of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas; there is no need to visualize them in such detail.
Nevertheless, one must imagine those images as the actual presence of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas appearing here to receive one’s prostrations and listen to one’s recitation.
With single-minded devotion, one will surely attain a high rank in the Pure Land. This method of visualization for teaching and contemplation is a practice accessible to all (from the *Hezuan*).
The Dharma Gate of Visualizing the Buddha’s Ūrṇā-kośa:
Purify yourself through fasting and precepts, clarify the mind, and sit silently facing west with eyes closed.
Visualize Amitābha Buddha, of true golden hue, seated upon a great lotus flower in the midst of a pond of seven treasures in the Western Quarter; his body is one zhang in height.
Between the two eyebrows, rising upward, there is a single white tuft of hair (*ūrṇā-kośa*), eight-sided and hollow within, which spirals to the right five times;

its radiance is brilliant and pure, illuminating the golden countenance. Next, settle the mind and focus one’s thoughts upon this white tuft, ensuring that not even the slightest extraneous thought arises.
Whether closing or opening the eyes, one should see it clearly. By practicing this for a long time, the mind will become perfected through recollection.
When one becomes matured through natural resonance, one beholds the entire body of the Buddha; this method is the most supreme.

It is said that when one contemplates the Buddha with the mind, this very mind is itself the Buddha—this surpasses even oral recitation. After death, one will certainly be reborn in the highest grade of the highest level.

Tang Qifang and Yuanguo, these two, practiced the visualization method for only five months and personally realized that their bodies had reached the Pure Land, where they saw the Buddha and heard [the Dharma].
The remaining details of the Dharma are recorded extensively in the *Sixteen Contemplations Sutra* (Longshu Edition).

I have observed that in recent years, while the periods for Chan meditation, Vinaya study, and doctrinal lectures are being propagated everywhere, the gateway of Pure Land contemplation has been neglected and rarely taught.
This is why, although there are not few people in the world who recite the Buddha’s name with their mouths, those who are born in the Pure Land are not many.
Because they do not cultivate the gates of contemplation (*vipaśyanā*), those who would otherwise be reborn find that while their minds can go there, their mouths cannot utter the name.

If those who practice contemplation continue in an unbroken stream—whether eating and drinking or dressing themselves—remaining constantly within the state of contemplation; or if they travel spiritually through the sea of lotuses to pay homage to the Buddha;
or sit gazing at the golden countenance with its radiance shining in the four directions; or behold Amitābha face-to-face, his body filling the void.
Whether it be emptiness or the vision of stillness, one’s companions arrive together at the waters of virtue;
as the ancients said, "If one maintains this single contemplation, one may hope to reach its peak"—this is something that must not be unknown (Tang Yizhi).
Regarding the Dharma-gate of the Samādhi of Buddha-Recollection through the Three Contemplations in One Mind, Master Zhiyi stated:
"Since the teachings and principles of all Buddhas are already clear, there is no way to restore one's nature except through contemplative practice (*guanxing*).

Thus, based on the principle of the three truths within one mind, he demonstrated the three cessations (*san zhi*) and the three contemplations (*san guan*), wherein each moment of contemplating the mind finds that it is ungraspable in every thought-instant."

"First emptiness, next the provisional, and finally the Middle—observing a single thought-moment as being like the moon beyond the clouds—is the practice-pattern (*lakṣaṇa*) of the Distinct Teaching (*pratyekavyavasthāna-yāna*).
It further states: "In destroying all delusions, nothing surpasses emptiness; in establishing all phenomena, nothing surpasses the provisional;
in realizing the ultimate nature of all things, nothing is greater than the Middle. Therefore, within one there is all, and within the Middle there is no Middle."
If there is no emptiness, there is no non-emptiness; the same applies to the provisional. This is precisely the characteristic of practice in the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*).

As the Bodhisattva Nāgārjuna stated in verse: "The phenomena produced by causes and conditions, I say, are empty; they are also called provisional names, and they are also called the meaning of the Middle Way.
Regarding the Three Truths: the Middle Truth subsumes all phenomena, the True Truth (*zhendi*) negates all phenomena, and the Conventional Truth (*sudì*) [establishes them].
In establishing all dharmas, taking up one is to manifest all three; they are not sequential.
These are all inherently possessed by sentient beings and are not obtained through artificial effort. Yet they remain hidden and unmanifest because they are shrouded by the three delusions:

ignorance clouds the *dharmatā*, the "dust-sand" afflictions obstruct the transformative guidance, and the views and thoughts hinder emptiness and stillness. Therefore, the Three Contemplations are established to shatter these three [delusions].

The delusions are subverted and the three wisdoms are realized to achieve the three virtues: through the contemplation of emptiness (*śūnyatā*), one subverts the delusions of views and thoughts (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*) to realize all-encompassing wisdom (*sarvajñā*) and achieve the virtue of prajñā;

through the contemplation of the provisional (*prajñapti*), one subverts the delusions of the sands of the Ganges (*rajas-kleśa*) to realize the wisdom of the modes of the path (*mārgākārajñatā*) and achieve the virtue of liberation (*vimukti*);

and through the contemplation of the middle (*madhyamā*), one subverts the delusion of ignorance (*avidyā-kleśa*) to realize the wisdom of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*) and achieve the virtue of the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*). Now, as for the nature of these three truths:
Because it exhausts principle and fully realizes nature, it differs from the Chan school and yet is not different.

When a practitioner recollects the Buddha, the mental faculty (*manas*) serves as the cause and the white tuft of hair and circular halo serve as the conditions; the mindfulness thus aroused is the "dharma produced.
By contemplating this with truthfulness, the mind of recollection arises as a provisional name. Its essence is empty and void; seeing this mind is seeing the *tathāgatagarbha*.
This is the manifestation of the Middle by departing from extremes; whether it be the sense faculties or their objects, all are the Dharma-realm.
That all Buddhas and sentient beings universally respond in a single thought-moment is precisely the Middle within the extremes. Herein there is neither Buddha nor thought;

this is the perfect cultivation of the three modes of mindfulness of the Buddha in the Mahāyāna. Therefore it is said: "Without marks, without emptiness, and not without emptiness—this is the true mark of the Tathāgata" (*Lianzong baojian*).

Regarding the contemplation of the Buddha according to the *Sūtra on the Visualization of the Buddha of Infinite Life*, it says: "If one wishes to give rise to the aspiration for rebirth in the Western Land, one should first visualize a sixteen-foot golden image upon the waters of the pond, as previously described.
[However,] the boundless dimensions of the body are not within the mental capacity of ordinary beings."
As for what is reached [by this practice], it is that the eighty thousand marks and signs can only be seen by those at the stage of the ten faiths;
they are not the objects of contemplation accessible to ordinary beings through their own minds. Therefore, one is led to contemplate the body of sixteen feet, which possesses thirty-two marks.

Since these cannot be contemplated all at once, one must enter through a single mark or sign. One need only contemplate the white tuft of hair between the eyebrows, and the thirty-two marks will manifest of themselves.
However, when one wishes to contemplate this correspondence in the present, one must first realize that all phenomena are mind-only and that everything is consciousness-only. Thus, a sutra states:
"The mind encompasses the great void, its measure pervading the sands of the world. It further states:

"The mind is like a skilled painter, creating the various five aggregates (the five aggregates being form, sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness). Within all worlds, there is nothing that is not created from the mind. This is the environment of Ultimate Bliss.

The land, the jewel trees, the jewel ground, and the jewel ponds of the Reward Land, as well as the bodies of the ocean-like assembly of Amitābha—their primary retributive marks such as the thirty-two signs—are all inherently possessed within my own mind and created by my own mind; they do not come from outside.
Only one who can realize this may discuss "contemplating the Buddha through the very mind" and attain what is called "the Pure Land of Mind-Only and the Original Nature Amitābha. Thus it is said.

The Great Master Tiantai explains the two phrases "this mind makes the Buddha" and "this mind is the Buddha" from the perspective of the cultivation of contemplation as "the mind making [the Buddha]," and from the perspective of original endowment as "the mind being [the Buddha].
Thus, contemplating the Buddha by means of the mind is also called "contemplating the Buddha in relation to the mind.

This is explained by taking the side of entrusting oneself to the Buddha when focusing on the mind, and by taking the side of original endowment when focusing on the mind; each of these mentions only one aspect.
The meaning and the intent must both be contained therein. Why? Because Amitābha’s Pure Land is already inherently possessed within my own mind;

therefore, by relying upon the thirty-two marks of that Buddha of fruition, one perfumes the nature-body (*dharmakāya*) and the essence of the fundamental nature inherently possessed within one's own mind.

When contemplative wisdom is perfected, it naturally manifests. The *Miaozongchao* states: "By relying upon that [Pure Land]—both its environment and its inhabitants—one perfumes the mind-nature; thus, the mind-nature is easily transformed."

"Generating [the aspiration]" refers precisely to this meaning. The Buddha provides an analogy, saying: "It is like holding a bright mirror and seeing the reflection of one's own face. The mirror is a metaphor for contemplating the Dharma;
'holding' is a metaphor for practicing contemplation; and 'seeing the reflection' is a metaphor for the completion of contemplation, which is none other than the Buddha of the original nature."

The treatise on the three contemplations within a single mind states that when contemplating the Buddha by means of the mind, one must employ the three contemplations to realize him; only when the contemplation is perfected does the true Buddha manifest.

The three contemplations—emptiness, provisional existence, and the middle—are discussed from the perspective of the contemplating subject as the "three truths," while they are spoken of as "truths" from the perspective of what is manifested. Thus, the contemplation and its object are non-dual, being neither subject nor object.
It is just as our former patriarchs said: "The three truths and the three contemplations are neither three nor three; they are one, one, and one, with nothing to which they can be attached.
Thus, while the names of truth and contemplation differ, their substance is the same. This is what is meant by saying that the subject and object are non-dual.
To illuminate this white curl is precisely my own mind; outside the mind there are no dharmas, and since every dharma cannot be apprehended, its characteristic is emptiness.

It is manifestly provisional; the provisional is itself the object, and emptiness is the contemplation. When one clearly penetrates this, one is not defiled by the object—this is the "forgetting of the provisional.
When one clearly penetrates this, one is not purified by wisdom—this is the "forgetting of emptiness.
Since the object contemplated is empty, the contemplating contemplation is also quiescent. Being neither defiled nor pure, subject and object are simultaneously extinguished; this is the Middle Way.

If one discusses the contemplation of the provisional (假觀), it is likewise thus: the white tuft of hair is manifestly present, yet as when a bhikṣu contemplates the rising of various lights from a skeleton, this is the provisional;
its marks cannot be apprehended, which is the empty (空). This has no one who brings it here, nor does this skeleton exist—this is the middle (中).
If one discusses the contemplation of the middle (中觀), one realizes that this white tuft of hair is neither empty nor provisional; if the mind harbors conceptualization, then...
Delusion and non-conception are nirvana; this Dharma cannot be demonstrated, for it is all produced by mental conception and transcends the two extremes.

Since both are extinguished, there must be simultaneous illumination. Because of this simultaneous illumination, emptiness and the provisional are distinct yet complete; extinction and illumination occur at the same time and cannot be sequential.
Thus, when one is empty, all are empty—the three contemplations are simultaneously empty; when one is provisional, all are provisional.
The three contemplations are simultaneously provisional, within the one there is all, and within the three contemplations there is the middle;
the single mind encompasses the three contemplations and the three truths are a single realm, neither before nor after, transcending all discussion—this is called the Perfect and Sudden Samādhi.

Regarding the sixteen sublime objects, all are contemplated with the single mind through the threefold contemplation (*san-guan*) upon the three truths (*san-di*). As for attaining the ultimate destination and the direct shortcut regarding these objects, none is more so than Master Huaize.
Quoting the *Guanfo sanmei jing xuanyi shu* (Commentary on the Profound Meaning of the Sutra on the Samādhi of Contemplating the Buddha), he says:

"To realize that the nature of a single thought inherently possesses the wondrous realm of the three thousand [realms]—this 'realm' is precisely the conventional (*jia*). That it is from the beginning empty and quiescent—this 'emptiness' is precisely the contemplation (*guan*). This constitutes the simultaneous illumination of both emptiness and the conventional. There is no one who can contemplate this emptiness [as an object], nor is there anything that can be contemplated by wisdom..."
