Purity means the extinction of emptiness; the absence of an object of contemplation means not being defiled by objects, which is the extinction of the provisional. When both object and contemplation are simultaneously severed, subject and object are instantly extinguished.

This simultaneous extinction of the two extremes constitutes the Middle Way. This is the single mind and three contemplations within daily life, wherein there is no sequence of before or after. Furthermore, the verse says: The object is wondrous provisionality; contemplation is emptiness.
When both object and contemplation are extinguished, this is the Middle. How could there ever be before or after in this extinction and illumination? One.
When the mind is harmonized and completely severed [of delusion], there is no longer any fruit to be pursued;

if one can practice and contemplate in this manner—namely, that the Pure Land is solely the mind and Amitābha is one's own original nature—he will be present within the practitioner’s heart and eyes at all times. The *Miaozong* states:

"Initially, when the five turbidities are light, it is the 'Pure Land of Co-residence. For those who possess the precepts and good roots, those in the ordinary stages of the four teachings are all able to cause the five turbidities to become light."
Those with inferior affinity for the Shared Land perceive it as pure, while those with superior affinity perceive both the environment and its inhabitants (*āśraya-vijñapti*) as most pure;
this is the Pure Land of Expedient Means, which is also perfectly round because its inhabitants are most pure.

Therefore, those who desire rebirth in the Land of Ultimate Bliss through the highest grade of birth must investigate the profound principle of the single mind and threefold contemplation. (The above is from Master Zhanran’s *Jingguan Yaomen*).
The treatise explains that the perfect cultivation of the three contemplations gives rise to the four pure lands.
The five aggregates, six sense organs, six sense objects, and six consciousnesses constitute the mundane truth (saṃvṛti-satya) of the realm of the six classes of ordinary beings.

The twelve links of dependent origination and the four noble truths constitute the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya) of the realm of the Dharma for the Two Vehicles. The six pāramitās, the three titles, and the four virtues constitute the Buddha’s Bodhi.

Within the *dharmadhātu*, by invoking the true emptiness of the Tathāgatagarbha, the perfectly interfused ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), the three truths of the ten realms are all [encompassed];

this is what Tiantai calls "one is truly all, all is true," wherein there is no conventional (*saṃvṛti*) or middle (*madhyama*) that is not true, and the three truths are all present, functioning to dissolve all phenomena.
By invoking the non-empty Tathāgatagarbha, the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), the three truths of the ten realms are all...
This refers to what is called "the one mundane is all mundane," wherein there is nothing that is not mundane within the True and the Middle;

thus, the three truths all possess the function of establishing phenomena. When one takes up the truth within the empty and non-empty *tathāgatagarbha*, the three truths of the ten realms are simultaneously transcended;
this "simultaneous transcendence" is neither "is" nor "is-not. This is what is meant by "the one middle is all middle," wherein there is nothing that is not mundane or true.

The middle three truths all possess the capacity to encompass the Dharma; in reality, these three truths exist within a single mind—wherein negation is simultaneously affirmation, and affirmation is simultaneously negation;

it is neither negation nor affirmation, yet through negation there is affirmation. This is the nature of the Tathāgatagarbha, the eternally abiding true mind; such is the fundamental nature of phenomena.
In the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, this is called the "true aspect of all phenomena" (*dharmatā-lakṣaṇa*); in the *Śūraṅgama-samādhi-sūtra*, it is called...
Pounding ten thousand kinds of incense to create the "Ninefold Flower Adornment" is called "a single mote of dust containing a great chiliocosm of sutra scrolls.
The *Contemplation Sutra* is called "the Tathāgata’s Dharma-realm body. All these are the inconceivable, perfectly interfused Three Truths.

The Three Truths are the objects of contemplation; the Three Contemplations are the means of contemplation. To contemplate in accordance with the nature of reality is to contemplate beyond all relative distinctions.
Illuminating the ordinary and illuminating the single realm: in terms of practice and conduct, it is three while being one; in terms of perfect fusion, it is one while being three.
When one contemplates emptiness through the contemplation of emptiness, the *tathāgatagarbha* is the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), and thus all three truths are empty.

When the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) is empty, this contemplation can empty the views and afflictions (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*) to reveal the principle of the ultimate truth. When the ultimate truth is empty, this contemplation can empty the objects of the senses (*viṣaya*).

When the *sa* [of *sāṃvṛti*] manifests the principle of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) and the middle truth (*madhyama-satya*) as empty, this contemplation can empty the unmanifest middle truth;

by means of the contemplation of the provisional (*prajñapti*), one contemplates the non-empty Tathāgatagarbha. Regarding conventional truth, all three truths are established: conventional truth establishes that which can shatter the "dust-like" afflictions (*pāramitā-śata-sahasra*);

true truth establishes that which can shatter the views and thoughts (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*); and middle truth establishes that which can shatter ignorance (*avidyā*). This is observed through the contemplation of the middle way (*madhyamaka*).
Within the Tathāgatagarbha of emptiness and non-emptiness, according to the principle of the Three Truths as the Middle, the raising of any single contemplation immediately encompasses the other two.
When one raises the contemplation of emptiness, both the provisional and the middle are also empty, for all three contemplations are able to sweep away attachment to marks.

When one raises the contemplation of the provisional, both emptiness and the middle are also provisional, for all three contemplations possess the meaning of establishing dharmas. When one raises the contemplation of the middle, both emptiness and the provisional are likewise [the middle].

In the three contemplations of the middle [stage], each point is absolute and without dependence; therefore, when a person of the Perfect Teaching (yuanren) seeks rebirth in Sukhāvatī, they set out by means of the single mind and the three contemplations to contemplate the environment and inhabitants of the Western Land as a single realm that is simultaneously the Three Truths.

This is the contemplation of the Land of Common Abode for Ordinary Beings and Sages. These three contemplations are precisely the same three contemplations used to observe the three higher lands. This is because the six classes of ordinary beings perceive only existence.

Because views and afflictions (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*) act as its decay, the Two Vehicles perceive emptiness; because the "dust-sands" of ignorance act as its ailment, the Bodhisattva cannot find ease within the Middle Way between the two extremes;
and because ignorance acts as its cataract, one accords with the nature of reality to cultivate the three contemplations.
Thus, by lightening the five turbidities, one destroys the three delusions of views and afflictions, dust-sands, and ignorance. Once these three delusions are exhausted, the ten realms...
The three virtues of the environment and its inhabitants are further manifested through the wisdom of the three contemplations:

by regarding the five turbidities as light, the environment and inhabitants of the six realms of ordinary beings are revealed, whereby one attains birth in the superior pure land of the Shared Pure Land (*sāṃbhogika-kṣetra*).

By using the wisdom of the three contemplations to destroy the afflictions of views and thoughts (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*), the environment and inhabitants of the two vehicles are revealed, whereby one attains birth in the superior pure land of the Land of Expedient Means (*upāya-kṣetra*). Through the wisdom of the three contemplations...
When ignorance is severed, the environment and inhabitants of the Bodhisattva stage manifest as the Pure Land of True Reward of the Superior Grade;
when ignorance is completely destroyed by the wisdom of the three contemplations, the environment and inhabitants of the Buddha-realm manifest as the Pure Land of Tranquil Light.
(From the *Compilation of Explanations for the Diagram of Infinite Pure Lands*).
Morning Bell of the Pure Land, Scroll Four;
Morning Bell of the Pure Land, Scroll Five; Section Five:
The Dharma Gate of Meritorious Practice.
The essential principle of pure karma and great meritorious practice is to take goodness as one's ultimate refuge.

It is said that the six perfections and myriad practices do not transcend the single mind, and that the eighty-four thousand dharma-gates—wisdom and merit alike—are all produced from a single thought of mindfulness of the Buddha.
Thus, the Dharma-gate of the Pure Land is encompassed by this single mindfulness of the Buddha; why seek more?
Although the Sixth Patriarch said, "If there is no unwholesome thought in the mind, the Western Pure Land is not far from here;
if one harbors an unwholesome mind, it will be difficult to reach it even while reciting the Buddha’s name and seeking rebirth," this is indeed the ultimate discourse of all time.
Master Cizhao of the White Lotus Society also instructed his disciples, saying: "If you focus single-mindedly on Amitābha but do not uphold the precepts, then [there will be obstacles]."
If one commits offenses and fails to practice giving, the karma of greed and avarice will increase; if one does not show respect to all, the karma of arrogance and contempt will arise.
With such evil karmas obscuring one’s path, how could it be possible to be born in the Pure Land?

Examining the original practices of Amitābha, we see that he well protected the three types of action, cultivating both merit and wisdom. Thus we know that the ultimate limit of goodness is precisely Buddhahood.
Goodness is the foundation for becoming a Buddha, and a Buddha is the teacher who cultivates goodness.

Although the sutras state that even an extremely evil person can attain rebirth through ten recitations, this too is simply a matter of a single thread of sincere, wholesome mind being met with a corresponding response;
there is no other path outside of this. Someone might say: "Merit and practice are matters of worldly convention; how can they be relevant to the Dharma? To this I reply:

If even provisional teachings on the Buddha-dharma are not equal to the true conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), how much less so could the minute dust motes of the world—which are all universally encompassed by the Buddha-dharma—not be included within the conventional truth?
The *Vimalakīrti Sūtra* states: "The non-arising of the unwholesome and the non-extinction of wholesome dharmas constitute the Buddha-nature.
This non-arising and non-extinction is precisely the direct path to Nirvana, which severs the three types of unwholesomeness.

Karma is precisely what is meant by closing the gates to the evil realms; if one wishes to empty it along with conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), that is a vacuous emptiness and not true emptiness (*bhūta-śūnyatā*).
Master Lianchi’s preface to the *Chongxing lu* states: "In practicing the Way, maturity is fundamental, and virtuous conduct is fundamental.
To listen to their words, they seem to surpass the Buddhas and Patriarchs; yet when their conduct is examined, they fall behind ordinary people."
This is a malady of the Dharma-ending age and is what the great virtuous ones with clear eyes have rebuked.

Therefore, when practicing the nianfo (recollection of the Buddha) of the Pure Land path, one must cultivate a wholesome mind and perform wholesome deeds. When one’s mental activity accords with the Buddha, the mind naturally becomes pure and the land naturally becomes pure;
this is what is meant by "the Pure Land of the Mind" and the "Amitābha Buddha of Original Nature. Thus, the Buddha and goodness are non-dual.
The Mindfulness of the Buddha and Meritorious Practice are not two separate gates; practitioners must by no means view them as two distinct poles.
This concludes the fifth section, the Dharma Gate of Describing Meritorious Practice:
The True Cause for Filial Support of One’s Parents.
I deeply reproach those among the conditioned Sangha who are unfilial toward their parents. Someone may say:

"Since those who have left the household life have already bid farewell to their kin and severed their attachments, to reproach them would only stir up feelings of affection and love. I reply: How can you speak such evil words?

Great filial piety was practiced by the World-Honored One Śākyamuni, who requited his parents' kindness over successive kalpas and accumulated causes to achieve Perfect Enlightenment. Furthermore, the *Brahmajāla Sūtra* states that although the precepts encompass ten thousand practices...
Taking filial piety as the fundamental principle, the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra* states that "filially supporting one's parents is the primary cause for pure karma.
In antiquity, there were those who built halls to honor their mothers and others who carried their mothers while begging for food; yet they never allowed such affection to become a burden.

How is it that you sever your love for your own kin to form close ties with patrons, never ceasing to accept their gifts, and even raising disciples more dearly than your own flesh and blood? This is improper.
To have parents and yet treat them as mere parents—emerging from one act of love only to enter back into another—is such perversity!
Furthermore, while you yourself receive offerings from the ten directions, remaining well-fed, warm, and securely settled, you sit by idly watching your parents suffer hunger, cold, and desolation.
If you find peace in this, then do it so (from *Zhuchuang Sanbi*).
Those who wish to leave the household life may, due to various circumstances, find that their parents do not permit it;

in such cases, they should exhaust their filial duty within the home while encouraging the cultivation of causes for transcending the world. If one can realize the truth while remaining in secular life, there is likewise a path to attaining Buddhahood (*Lianzong baojian*).
During the Taihe era, Yang Fu took leave of his parents to travel to Shu to visit the Great Being Wujie. On the road, he encountered an old monk who asked where he was going.
Fu replied, "To visit Wujie. The monk said, "If you see Wujie, you will not see the Buddha.
Fu asked, "Where is the Buddha? The monk said, "Return quickly; whoever is wearing robes and shoes of a certain color is he. Fu then returned home, arriving at night.
When she knocked at the door, her mother heard the sound and was overjoyed; she threw off her robe and opened the door, and it was exactly as the old monk had described—the form of the Buddha.
From then on, Fǔ served her parents with all her might, expressing love and reverence. She annotated the *Classic of Filial Piety* (*Xiàojīng*) by several tens of thousands of words.

Once, when her inkstone was exhausted and she wished to fetch water, the water suddenly filled the basin. Zōngqǐ remarked, "The Six Dynasties held the *Classic of Filial Piety* in high esteem; eminent monks and scholars of that era..."

Some used [the *Xiaojing*] for burial with the deceased or to offer to the spirits; those suffering from illness recovered by reciting it, and those bound by difficulties were released by its recitation.

Thus, Emperor Huang Xuan recited the *Xiaojing* twenty times daily, modeling his practice after the *Guanyin Jing*. Therefore, the Buddha in the hall is no different from the Buddha on the sacred mountain;
the Confucian *Xiaojing* is likewise no different from the various sutras spoken by the Buddha. Master Yang annotated this scripture.
Such is the spiritual response; why doubt that one will be reborn in the highest grade? (According to the *Ganying Shu*).

Regarding the primary cause of the compassionate mind and non-killing, it is said that Avalokiteśvara is born from all manner of goodness. This is because compassion loves people and compassion loves all things; therefore, [to lack compassion is to] kill.
Birth is the foremost of all precepts; abstaining from killing is a great good, while killing is a great evil. Therefore it is said:
"For anyone who wishes to kill, they should regard themselves as no different from the life of the creature they would kill. Thus, by not killing, one receives the retribution of longevity;
by killing, one receives the retribution of a short life. This is because what one desires for oneself, other beings also desire for themselves.
To wish for one's own life to be long while killing the lives of other beings—where could such a principle exist?
To kill living beings merely to provide for one’s palate means that once the chopsticks are laid down, the flavor is already gone, yet the karma of killing remains.

If one kills to provide for guests, since one has habitually observed the precept against killing, they certainly would not blame me; moreover, as the perpetrator of the act must themselves bear the karma, why should I be held responsible?
Yet you have forgotten yourself. If it is for the sacrifice to the ancestors, Confucius himself performed sacrifices with simple vegetables and vegetable soup.
If it is for the sacrifice to the deities, the spirits value purity, clarity, and integrity; they do not partake of offerings of blood. As the *Book of Changes* states:
"The ox slaughtered by the neighbor in the east is not as good as the *yue*-sacrifice of the neighbor in the west. One can cultivate the Pure Land by observing this precept of non-killing.

Having already attained rebirth, one is certainly not of the lower grade. However, for those who are deeply attached to worldly flavors and unable to maintain a perpetual fast, they should at least observe the six monthly fasts, the ten monthly fasts, and the fasts on the first, fifteenth, ninth, and ninth days of each month. As for the flesh of sentient beings, it is fundamentally not a substance that ought to be eaten;

because one has become accustomed to hearing and seeing it, one fails to recognize its impropriety. Those who sincerely cultivate the Pure Land must resolve to abstain from meat and adopt a permanent vegetarian diet.

If one is unable to sever [the killing] at the highest level, one should at least eat the three kinds of pure meat (namely, not having seen the killing, not having heard of the killing, and not suspecting it was for oneself), while reducing their quantity.
If eating with various flavors, eliminate one; if every meal consists of meat, intersperse them with vegetarian food.

Since the provisions of a person's worldly fortune are limited, by acting in this way one can naturally extend one's life. By accumulating merit through compassion, one will gradually enter an excellent state. As the saying goes: "In the world..."
If one wishes for the upper realm to be free from the kalpa of war, sentient beings must not eat meat; yet even those who do not avoid eating the three kinds of "pure" meat should,
on the day following [the consumption], recite the names of the Four Sages of the Western Paradise along with their mantras for the sake of the sentient beings whose flesh was eaten,
thereby aiding them toward rebirth there (compiled from *Lungshu Wenzhang*).
Lianchi said: "Heaven and Earth produce things to provide for human sustenance—various grains, various fruits, various vegetables, and various delicacies from both water and land.
Humans further employ their ingenuity to bake, feed, salt, sour, boil, and roast them;
one might say they are already fully and abundantly satisfied. Why, then, must we go to the trouble of taking that which shares our own vital breath?"
To kill and eat those who share one's own nature as a parent and child, who possess consciousness and awareness, and who experience pain, itching, birth, and death—is this not contrary to reason?
It is commonly said that what matters is the goodness of the heart and not vegetarianism;
yet alas, to slaughter a body and devour its flesh is the ultimate maturation of the world’s most cruel, poisonous, and evil hearts—how could it ever be a good heart?
At that time, Cheng Luan spoke in a mild tone, saying: "Some may say that good intentions and good deeds do not lie solely in sparing the lives of birds and beasts;
it is sufficient simply to have no heart of deception toward others and no deeds of harm toward them.

Yet, do you realize that in the practice of 'loving one's kin' and 'benefiting others,' there is a distinction of priority between humans and things, though not a distinction of partiality? If you can already bear to be cruel toward things..."
If one deceives and harms others, there will inevitably be those who deceive and harm them in return; why is this so? It is because human beings possess only this single thought of forbearance.
How could one be patient toward animals alone while lacking patience toward humans? Now, when animals see a person wielding a blade, they never fail to tremble with fear and cry out in grief;
yet, because their wisdom and strength cannot match that of man, they are ultimately slaughtered by him. This is the law of cause and effect.
The principle that those who harbor grievances seek retribution for their lives is necessarily so. Huang Tingjian (Huang Luzu) wrote in a poem:
"My flesh and the flesh of sentient beings differ in name but not in substance; they originally share the same nature, differing only in physical form.
Let them suffer the bitterness while you enjoy the rich flavors; do not wait for Old Yan to pass judgment—examine yourself now, for the current of slaughter is just beginning."

Soldiers and bandits fill the land, and those who encounter them often meet with slaughter. I have frequently seen those fleeing chaos who, by some twist of fate, run directly into the very villains they seek to avoid.

The Buddha said that when causes and conditions converge, the retribution of karma is difficult to escape; it is precisely this which is meant when one says that those who commit acts of killing will inevitably suffer the retribution of being killed themselves.
To turn back the wheel of calamity, one must release living beings, observe the precept against killing, and seek rebirth in the Pure Land. (From *Hezuan*)
Regarding the true cause of upholding the precepts and the ten wholesome paths leading to Nirvana:
the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states that while the Buddha is in the world, one takes the Buddha as teacher; after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, one takes the precepts as teacher.

The *Brahmajāla Sūtra* states: "The precepts are like the sun and moon, and also like a string of pearls; by means of them, the multitude of bodhisattvas, as numerous as motes of dust, achieve perfection."
Because he has attained perfect enlightenment, the Buddha established the precepts as the foundation for cultivating the Way.

He ordained five precepts for lay followers (*upāsaka*), ten precepts for novices (*śrāmaṇera*), and two hundred and fifty precepts for fully ordained monks (*bhikṣu*). For Bodhisattvas, there are the ten grave and forty-eight light precepts;

all of these are fundamentally based upon the five precepts—namely, the prohibitions against killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, false speech, and drinking alcohol. As for the abstention from eating meat, this is subsumed within the precept against killing.

Furthermore, killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct constitute the three karmas of the body; false speech, frivolous speech, divisive speech, and harsh speech constitute the four karmas of the mouth;
and covetousness, anger, and wrong views constitute the three karmas of the mind. These combined form the ten precepts.

To violate them and fail to maintain them is called the ten unwholesome actions. Not drinking alcohol, not eating meat, not engaging in sexual desire, and not eating the five pungent herbs are what is termed—
By observing the ten precepts while maintaining the fast, one attains rebirth in the heavens; by observing the five precepts, one does not lose the human form.

If one fully maintains the fast and the precepts, cultivates the ten wholesome karmas, pays homage to the Buddha, recites the Buddha’s name, reads and recites the Mahāyāna sutras, and thereby understands the primary meaning [of reality], dedicating these merits toward rebirth in the Western Land, one will certainly attain the highest grade of the highest birth (*śreṣṭha-uttama-upapatti*). Even if one merely maintains the five precepts while cultivating the Pure Land, it is likewise so.
One shall not fail to be reborn in the Middle Grade, Superior Birth.
The Buddha takes greed, anger, and delusion as the three poisons. When the poison of greed resides in the mind and manifests in the body, it becomes theft.
Whether in light or in darkness, all such acts are called the seizing of the five sensory desires; form is considered the foremost. The Tathāgata has said that he causes the world—
Furthermore, there is one matter that is like sexual desire—few indeed are those who attain the Way through it. The *Sūtra of Perfect Enlightenment* states:

"All sentient beings, because of sexual desire, establish their very nature and life; through thousands of births and ten thousand kalpas, they have come from within this. Thus, sexual desire is particularly heavy;
the eight difficulties and the three miserable realms are where one goes because of it. Moreover, among all calamities, the disaster of lust is the most惨烈 (catastrophic).
The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* states: "In your cultivation of samādhi, you originally set out to transcend worldly toil; yet if the lustful mind is not eliminated, you cannot escape from defilement.
Even if you possess great wisdom and various forms of meditative concentration manifest before you, if you do not sever lust, you will inevitably fall into the paths of Māra. It further states:

"If you seek the Buddha’s wondrous fruit with a lustful mind, even if you attain wondrous enlightenment, it will all be rooted in lust. With lust as its fundamental cause, one revolves through the three realms of existence."
The path must inevitably emerge from this; at the very outset of this sutra, the discourse is established by borrowing the context of the brothel.

This is because it directly takes the fundamental ignorance (*avidyā*) of sentient beings as its primary point of reference, and only thereafter does it provide the karmic conditions for the Way. This is truly the "needle-method" of the Tathāgata’s crown-school.
Furthermore, the *Sutra of Forty-two Sections* states: The Buddha told the śramaṇas, "Be careful not to look at women; if you see them, do not..."
Upon seeing such a person, be careful not to speak with them; if you must speak, then admonish your mind and rectify your conduct, saying:
"I am a śramaṇa dwelling in a turbid world; I should be like a lotus flower, unsullied by the mud. To the elderly, treat them as a mother; to those of middle age, as an elder sister;
to the young, as a younger sister; and to the very young, as a daughter. Honor them with propriety and sincerity, and contemplate this with focused attention. Observe yourself.
From head to foot, one should inwardly contemplate that body: what is there within it but a profusion of foul secretions and various impure substances?

By means of this, one should clarify the mind. According to the words of this sutra, this is truly the most fundamental instruction of the Śākya; it is not only for śramaṇas to follow, but is appropriate for all.
The *Yuling Jing Zhu* states: "Among the three karmas of killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct, the root of lust is the most difficult to uproot.
Even when a blade is held to one's chest, one still feels compassion; yet when it comes to breaking through walls and windows (theft), people consider it a minor matter and do not refrain from it.

Once one is submerged in the waves of desire, one sinks to the very bottom and willingly accepts this state, which is the easiest to lose. This is especially so when confronted by objects of exquisite beauty, where the impulse arises suddenly and is difficult to restrain."
One moment of this [lust] diminishes one's merit; by it, one’s life-span is snatched away; by it, one’s body is destroyed; by it, one falls into the kalpas of suffering.
What bitterness is there in trading the pleasures of a fleeting instant for the poisonous harms of birth and death?

Since the retribution for lust is grave, the karmic retribution for the act of inciting lust is naturally no light either. Nowadays, when people see the beauty of women, they habitually address them as "Avalokiteśvara."
The words of the *zhizhi* (jesters) and performers likewise reach the height of caricature and mockery; such ways of misleading people through their customs are beyond counting.
Therefore, the two precepts against frivolous speech (*sambhinna-pralāpa*) and sexual misconduct (*kāma-mithyā-cāra*) are equally weighty.
King Longshu said: The sutras state that karmic retribution often stems from verbal karma, for the mouth is easily provoked.
What is called "harsh speech" (*pāruṣya*) refers merely to a mouth of malice and anger, where one's words are not gentle; nowadays, people go so far as to use foul language (*durbhāṣita*).
While the retribution for harsh speech is already fearsome, the retribution for foul language is that of the hells and the animal realm. People—
One should diligently restrain oneself and constantly recite the name of Amitābha Buddha to cleanse the defilements of oral karma;
even when hearing others speak evil words or foul language, one should likewise constantly recite the Buddha’s name to cleanse the defilements of the auditory faculty.

Wang Longshu said: "When people frequently give way to anger, let us set aside for a moment the fact that it harms things and invites calamity; first, it injures one's own harmony and damages one's vital energy (*qi*).
If a person can reach the state of compassion and benevolence, they will realize that anger is not good.

However, while in the midst of anger, one does not perceive this oneself. One must simply endure it again and again; if one practices this for a long time, there will naturally come a point where one gains mastery."

When encountering those who are poor and lowly, servants and slaves, or those who treat one with contempt and defiance, it is easy to give rise to anger; therefore, one must be especially cautious and restrained.
Even if all sentient beings were to commit great evils against me, I would not give rise to anger that would defile my pure mind.
Considering their ignorance, I should instead give rise to compassion. The Buddha said: "People are foolish and regard me as unwholesome, but I [regard them] through the four..."
When one responds with gravity to the gravity of equal compassion, protection, and salvation, meeting evil with goodness, the vital energy of merit and virtue always resides here;
the harmful energy and heavy calamities, conversely, fall upon the other. There was a foolish man who reviled the Buddha, but the Buddha remained silent and did not answer.
When the reviling ceased, the Buddha asked with pity: "If a person offers a gift with propriety and that person does not accept it, to whom does the gift belong?"
[The man] said, "I am taking this back to the Buddha myself. The Buddha said, "Now you revile me, yet I do not accept it; you are merely bringing misfortune back upon your own person.
It is like an echo responding to a sound or a shadow following a form; there is ultimately no escaping it. Be cautious in committing evil!
O you who are prone to anger, why do you not take the Buddha as your Dharma? (The above is from the *Hezuan*).

Those who have left the household life must forever sever lustful desire; lay practitioners (*gṛhapati*) should refrain from sexual misconduct. However, even for those studying the Path, one must be cautious regarding even "proper" sexual relations;

all women other than one's own wives and concubines are termed "improper. Even if not within one’s own chamber, engaging in improper places such as external residences or separate estates constitutes transgression.
On the first and fifteenth days of the month, on one’s birthday, and during the eight gates and six fasts of spring and autumn, one must observe these precepts.
If one commits a transgression on such a day, whether by night or by day, it is an improper time;
even for wives and concubines, this is called "deviant practice," and practitioners must not fail to exercise restraint. The Buddha said: "Observing the fast for a single day brings five blessings:
little illness and physical ease, little lust and little sleep, rebirth in heaven, and knowledge of past lives. The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* states that these various assemblies...
One who seeks samādhi should sever the five pungent roots (*pañca-gandha*). When consumed cooked, they arouse lust; when eaten raw, they increase anger.

(The five pungent roots are scallion, garlic, leek, onion, and *hingukhu*; *hingukhu* is found in the Western Regions. Regarding verbal karma, false speech arises easily but is difficult to eliminate.
Because worldly people are habituated to defilement, delusive thoughts fly about; thus, false speech is readily emitted whenever one wishes to deceive, mislead, or conceal from others.
Whatever is not beneficial to others may sometimes achieve its purpose through slight adaptation to circumstances;

however, that which benefits oneself while harming others cannot be called anything other than false speech (*mṛṣāvāda*). Even if one does not harm others, if one generally lacks truthful speech, this too is a deluded mind that must be guarded against.
As for frivolous speech (*saṃbhinnapralāpa*), it is easy for all words that form a literary composition to enter into this category.
Listening to words as licentious as those concerning desire is a profound defilement;

yet people adorn themselves with flowery and moon-like seductive phrases, and because they cherish such finery, they gradually sink into the midst of lustful passion without realizing it. Extending this principle broadly, there are many such categories.
This includes malicious speech, such as reviling others, speaking of others' shortcomings, delighting in jesting, and uttering foul language—such are the "dragon-flapping" mouths.

The *Karmic Exhortation Diagram* states: "In this present age, there is a single word that praises another, and that person receives blessings for the rest of their life, extending even to their descendants;
yet there is a single word that ruins another, and that person suffers harm for the rest of their life, affecting even their descendants.

Is the karma of speech not, therefore, grave? What goes out from you returns to you; since it is already fearsome when directed at others, how much more so when it falls upon oneself? However, as for [the matter of] being...
Those who resent Heaven are impoverished; those who resent others lack wisdom. One should simply exercise self-restraint and vigilance. As for double-tongued speech:
speaking of this person to that person, and speaking of that person to this person, can cause mutual resentment and lead to ruin;
its evil is no small matter. Greed may be compared to the ocean: though all streams flow into it, it is never filled. Thus, the various evils produced by human beings all [originate from greed].
It begins with greed; greed is the root of all evils. Those who harbor hatred desire to harm others, yet they instead harm themselves.
When one inflicts evil upon others through body or speech, one receives back a hundred-thousandfold more evil in return.
Thus, one knows that hatred is a great self-destruction. Precisely when anger is about to arise, one must quickly recite the Buddha’s name several dozen times.

Later, when examining this matter, one considers whether anger is appropriate or inappropriate; yet the wisdom of *prajñā* lacks any illumination, leaving one in a state of bewildered ignorance, not knowing what the nature and life-force (*xing-ming*) truly are—this is called delusion.

Even if one possesses worldly intelligence, discernment, and a talent that radiates in all directions, and cannot believe or accept the wondrous, luminous true nature or the laws of cause, effect, and retribution—this too is called delusion. (Compiled by Ding Lianlü Jiěhuǒ)
The Buddha said: "Those who commit evil in bodily conduct, speak evil with their mouths, and harbor evil thoughts in their minds are people of this hell.
Generally, the good and evil of human life do not exceed the three karmas of body, speech, and mind. When all three karmas are evil, it constitutes purely black karma, for which one enters hell.
If all three karmas are good, it constitutes purely white karma, whereby one is born in heaven. Among these three karmas..."

If even a single act of merit—such as a mixed karma that nonetheless does not lead to rebirth in hell—is sufficient for this, then how much more so when one recites the Buddha’s name with the mouth despite the corruption of body and mind?
Furthermore, if while reciting the Buddha’s name with the mouth one can also visualize the Buddha’s form with the mind, then the mental karma is virtuous;
if one straightens the body and holds a rosary in the hand, then the physical karma is virtuous. Thus, all Buddhas have revealed this method of recitation.

The purpose of this gate is precisely to guide sentient beings toward the excellence of their verbal karma (*vākkarma*), so that they may gradually cultivate the excellence of their physical and mental karma.

If one can constantly bring these three karmas into excellence to cultivate the Pure Land, one will certainly attain birth in the highest grade. Once, while in Zhenjiang, I heard a shrimp seller shout "shrimp!
once; from this, I knew that his three karmas were all evil. His physical karma was evil because he bore a load of shrimp upon his body, and his mental karma... [was likewise evil].
If one intends to sell shrimp, the mental karma is evil; if one shouts while selling shrimp, the verbal karma is evil.
These are what the Buddha calls people destined for hell. Observing this, there are many such "hell-beings" right before our eyes; how can we not stand in awe?
The Buddha takes killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct as the three karmas of the body;

yet Confucius spoke of "overcoming the remnants and abolishing killing," and the *Shijing* states that King Wen’s virtue reached even the birds, beasts, and insects—was this not a warning against killing? As for stealing, it hardly needs further mention.
Confucius said, "I have never seen one who loves virtue as much as they love beauty," and the poets of the *Shijing* censured those who do not love virtue.

To take pleasure in beautiful forms—is this not refraining from sexual misconduct? The Buddha regards false speech, frivolous talk, double-tongued speech, and harsh words as the four karmas of the mouth.
Confucius said, "If a person lacks trustworthiness, I do not know how they can function"—this was not a failure to refrain from false speech.

He said, "Those who are artful in speech and possess a pleasing countenance have little benevolence"—this was not a failure to refrain from frivolous talk. The Book of Documents says, "You must not..."

To follow one's face in compliance yet speak with malice behind one’s back is not failing to guard against double-tongued speech. King Wu’s Inscription on the Mirror says: "The mouth breeds filth; the mouth destroys the mouth.
This shows that he never failed to guard against harsh speech. Furthermore, the Buddha identifies greed, anger, and delusion as the three karmas of the mind.
Confucius said, "When one sees gain, think of righteousness," which is precisely guarding against greed. He also spoke of Boyi and Shu Qi, who did not harbor [malicious thoughts].
"To abandon past evils is to guard against anger; to say that those who are distressed yet do not study are the lowest of the people is to guard against delusion.
From this it may be seen that Confucianism and Buddhism have never been different. (From the *Long zuan wen*).

Regarding the primary cause for generating the bodhicitta, the *Jingtu zongyao* (Essentials of the Pure Land School) states: "The unsurpassed fruit of Buddhahood is called 'Bodhisattva'; if one generates this mind, one will certainly attain Buddhahood.
The *Jingxing famen* (Dharma Gate of Pure Conduct) states: "In practicing the Pure Land, one must skillfully generate the resolve; if it is for oneself [to escape] the five [desires]..."
If one rejoices in the nine grades of rebirth with a defiled mind, this contradicts the bodhicitta and constitutes the practice of a śrāvaka.

However, if one gives rise to great compassion for sentient beings, seeking birth in that land in order to swiftly perfect the power of the Way and spiritual penetrations (*abhijñā*), traveling throughout the ten directions to rescue and deliver all beings so that they may attain Buddhahood, then this accords with the bodhicitta and constitutes the practice of a Bodhisattva. Before the Triple Gem, one should resolve the mind with sincerity.

The vow was made as follows: "I, disciple [Name], from this day forth, shall give rise to this great resolve not for the sake of seeking for myself the blessings and rewards of the human or celestial realms, nor those of the Pratyekabuddhas, Śrāvakas, or even the various stages of Bodhisattvas belonging to the provisional vehicles;

rather, relying solely upon the teachings of the Supreme Vehicle, I shall give rise to the Bodhicitta and vow that my present parents, my parents of many lifetimes, and all sentient beings of the Dharma-realm [shall likewise attain it]."
"May all enemies and kin be reborn together in the Pure Land and all attain non-retrogression from Anuttara-samyak-sambodhi.
Thus it is said three times. At all times, one must generate this mind with the utmost urgency. Master Lianchi said:
"The third of the Three Blessings in the *Amitābha Sūtra* is the generation of the Bodhicitta; this is as [indescribable] as space in the *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtras*."
The merit of such contemplation is not the tainted merit of humans or devas (from the *Hezuan*).

To read and recite the Mahāyāna *zhengyin* (the true cause)—wherein the "true cause" includes items such as deep faith in cause and effect and exhorting practitioners to have faith, as already seen previously and thus not listed again here—the *Jingtu Zhigui* states:
"The Mahāyāna sūtras are that which all Buddhas take as their teacher; the Buddha-fruit of Bodhi arises entirely from within them."

The *Chūkan-kyō* (Sutra on Emerging from Meditation) states that the three types of pure karma, as well as the highest grade of the highest birth (*jō-hon-jō*), all declare the reading and recitation of Mahāyāna sutras to be the primary practice for rebirth in the Pure Land.

Thus, those who cultivate pure karma should uphold, read, and recite Mahāyāna sutras such as the *Lotus Sutra*, the *Avataṃsaka*, the *Prajñāpāramitā*, and the *Nirvāṇa*, which specifically discuss the Pure Land;
relying on the power of these Mahāyāna teachings, they shall certainly attain rebirth. Therefore, one should resolve to do so.
Yin said: "Recitation means externally relying on the permeation of hearing while internally supporting it with contemplation of principle; it does not refer merely to words, texts, mouth, or ears.

If one is biasedly addicted to scrolls and volumes, one will spend a lifetime vainly counting another's treasures. The Sixth Patriarch said: "To recite with the mouth and practice with the mind is to turn the sutra;
to recite with the mouth but not practice with the mind is to be turned by the sutra. Can those who recite not know this?"
(Provisions for the Pure Land). Question:
In the past, it was said that taking "contemplation of the mind" as the primary goal and the sutras and teachings as the daily light of the sun allows one to see further;

it was also said that "withered meditation lacks wisdom. Now, if one focuses solely on the practice of nianfo (reciting the Buddha's name), can wisdom still be generated? Answer: Studying the teachings is like reading medical texts.
To employ skill in the mind-ground is like taking medicine: first clarify the teachings, for this is the correct principle.

For those who study the Way, what is precious lies in discerning the false from the true, the great from the small, and the partial from the perfect. There is no time to read everything exhaustively; you may simply look at the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*.
Once you have cultivated the Pure Land, you must read through all the various texts concerning the Pure Land, and then set aside the written words and single-mindedly recite the Buddha’s name.

What is called "wisdom" (prajñā) refers to one who thoroughly understands the scriptural teachings and excels at expounding them; however, to engage in empty talk with the mouth while attaining nothing in the heart is "mad wisdom.

Only when there is true investigation and actual realization is it termed "right wisdom. After clarifying the teachings, one should single-mindedly recite the Buddha’s name and give rise to this wisdom (from *Lianchi Yigao*).

The *Vimalakīrti Sūtra* states that the pure mind practicing goodness is the true cause [of Buddhahood], and the Buddha further says: "Know that the direct mind, the profound mind, and the Mahāyāna mind are the pure land of the bodhisattva.
Master Zhaolun remarked: "The purity of a land must necessarily arise from sentient beings."

The purification of sentient beings necessarily depends on the purification of their various practices; when practices are purified, sentient beings are purified; when sentient beings are purified, the Buddha-land is purified. This is an inevitable principle.
Since the land is free from defilement and crookedness, it arises from the straightforward mind (*ṛju-citta*). Therefore, it is said that the straightforward mind is the pure land of a bodhisattva.
"Straightforward mind" means being honest and upright without guile; this mind is the root of all myriad practices and the foundation for planting [wholesome] seeds.

To plant roots of virtue that are deep and firm so they are difficult to uproot is the profound mind (*gambhīra-citta*). To mount the eighty thousand practices and carry all under heaven, not omitting a single person, is the Mahāyāna mind (*mahāyāna-citta*).
To desire to propagate the Great Way, one must first make the mind upright; once the mind is truly upright, one may then enter into practice, which can then become profound.
When practice is profound, its vast application becomes boundless. Having equipped oneself with these three minds, one next cultivates the six perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*).

Regarding the myriad practices (the six pāramitās—namely, giving, precept-keeping, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom; these "myriad practices" refer to what is cultivated and accumulated within these six perfections, which, when summarized, constitute them):
yet this pure mind exists in all sentient beings—who does not possess it? It is mostly because they are deluded and do not realize it that the Great Master, the Sixth Patriarch, said:
"A single thought of level and straightforwardness is Amitābha; a single thought of crookedness and danger is a sentient being. This is because...

People dwelling in a defiled world manifest ignorance in their conduct; though they speak with a straightforward mind, their actions are full of flattery and crookedness. Sunk in the ocean of suffering, they are unable to emerge.

Out of compassion for them, the Buddha guides them by means of mindfulness of the Buddha (*buddhānusmṛti*), subduing their distracted minds, causing them to abandon what is perverse and treacherous and return to uprightness.
Thus, from among sentient beings, they are born in the Pure Land. Therefore, the *Ratnarāja-sūtra-śāstra* says: "When a pure pearl is cast down..."
Just as turbid water cannot become clear without purification, so too, when one directs the thought of the Buddha toward a distracted mind, that mind cannot fail to become the Buddha.

Thus, it is by recollecting the Buddha that the direct mind is revealed; it is by means of the direct mind that one performs various wholesome deeds; and it is through these wholesome deeds that one attains the pure land of the Buddha.
Therefore, it is said: "If you wish to attain the pure land, you must purify your mind."

For a person who practices the recitation of the Buddha's name, even if their defilements have not yet been purified, they must examine themselves whenever a thought arises. Whether it be a mind of stinginess and greed,
anger and resentment, deluded attachment, fame-seeking, profit-seeking, jealousy, deceit, pride, arrogance, flattery, false views, discursive thought, the duality of subject and object,
or any of the various favorable or adverse circumstances that follow— [in all these cases, one must self-examine].
When a single mind produced by defilement—that is, a worldly mind—should arise, one must immediately and urgently recite the Buddha’s name with a loud voice.
Composing the mind and returning to correctness, do not allow evil thoughts to continue; strike them down directly until they are completely purified and exhausted.

Then, cultivate a mind of deep faith, a mind of utmost sincerity, a mind of aspiration and dedication, a mind of compassion and loving-kindness, a mind of humility, a mind of equanimity, and a mind of skillful means.

One should always protect all wholesome qualities; one should know that the various superior and virtuous people of the Land of Ultimate Bliss attain rebirth there and do not regress from Bodhi precisely because they have severed evil and practiced goodness.
To rely upon this for cultivation and practice constitutes the correct practice of the Pure Land.
(Above from *The Jewel Mirror of the Lotus School*)

"Practicing all manner of good is the primary cause" (the preceding two phrases are categorized as the primary cause by inferring from the three blessings and nine grades of the *Contemplation Sutra*).
Master Niaoke said: "Commit no evil; practice all manner of good. A three-year-old child can recite this, yet an eighty-year-old cannot fulfill it.
Those who cultivate the Pure Land through mindfulness of the Buddha must not fail to take these words to heart. Excluding [other practices], [this is the essential].

In all matters, he was filial in his support and compassionate in his heart; outwardly, he was as loyal as a minister serving his sovereign, honoring his teachers and elders, and showing kindness toward his brothers and friends.

His domestic life was harmonious and solemn, and he maintained close ties with his kinsmen while reverently attending to his seniors—adhering to these great principles of human relations without allowing even the slightest deficiency.
Regarding the veneration of the Triple Gem, he repaired temples, swept the halls, made offerings to the Buddhas, provided meals for the Sangha, and expounded the True Dharma.
The supreme undertaking of all Buddhist gates—the carving and printing of the scriptures—does not require one to be servilely bound by worldly entanglements;

rather, one should act according to one's lot and capacity, lest one miss the opportunity before one’s very eyes. Furthermore, if serving as an official, one should be benevolent and benefit the people; if leading troops, one must strictly prohibit slaughter and plunder;
if acting as a leader, one should instruct others with goodness; and if in a subordinate position, one should serve superiors with diligence. This extends even to one's gaze...

Caring for the elderly and infirm, nurturing the orphaned and young, relieving hunger and cold during years of famine, providing aid to those freezing from the elements, supporting the three classes of kin,
showing compassion to the four types of destitute, distributing medicine, assisting with coffins, repairing bridges and roads, encouraging the cessation of litigation, remitting debts,

reverently sparing the characters on discarded paper, extensively practicing expedient means, refraining from killing and releasing captive creatures, and burying stray cattle and dogs— those who perform such deeds as these [shall not...].
One must be able to fully recount all virtuous deeds and ensure they are put into practice, while strictly forbidding and refraining from all evil acts.
Even if others should encroach upon, oppress, or insult one, and if the situation makes it difficult to endure, one should simply turn inward and reflect:
"I am a person who cultivates the pure karma; how could I deign to engage in petty comparisons with such as these? Through this, peace and harmony will naturally prevail in the present moment.

The essence of the mind is pure; by dedicating the merit of all good deeds performed on this basis toward rebirth in the Western Land, with uninterrupted mindfulness in every thought, one will certainly attain birth in the highest grade.
Master Lianchi constantly used the *Daishō Ōkan-hen* (The Supreme Response Chapter) as a manual for his students; he once replied to Zhou Haimen, saying:
"The two phrases 'Commit not a single evil' and 'Practice all manner of goodness' penetrate from the highest to the lowest.

To speak of them in shallow terms, they merely involve avoiding evil and performing good—the conduct of a decent citizen observing the bounds of propriety in a common village. To speak of them in profound terms, they entail the total eradication of even the slightest evil and the..."
The Tathāgata, World-Honored One—the Perfectly Complete One, God among Gods, Sage among Sages—is likewise so.

The *Ganying pian* (Tract on Resonance and Response) is also said to be entirely plain and substantial; though its traces may appear superficial, one must verify every matter against the mind and examine each sentence with care before one can attain [its truth].
The praises, transmissions, and commentaries of former sages are not few. In recent years, I have once again compiled and edited [this work], for which there is a preface.

According to one book, if a person can uphold and recite [this text] and embody it in their conduct, using this to turn their aspirations toward rebirth in the Pure Land, how could they be limited to merely the middle grade?
Furthermore, the preface to the *Record of Self-Knowledge* by Master Lianchi states: "In my youth, I saw the *Code of Merits and Faults of the Taimei Immortal Lord* and was greatly delighted;

I immediately had it carved into printing blocks to distribute. The Immortal Lord said that ordinary people should place this register at their bedside so that every time they face the darkness of night and enter [their chambers],"
I have recorded my daily deeds in a register, accumulating them day by day, month by month, and year by year. Sometimes I balance merit against demerit, or demerit against merit;
as these quantities offset one another, I personally recognize my transgressions and blessings, rather than relying solely on external signs of fortune or misfortune.

I have previously composed the "Explanatory Preface to the Diagram for Encouraging Cultivation, Merit-Making, and Buddha-Recitation" and the "Explanatory Preface to the Diagram for Returning to the Precepts," encouraging others to receive and uphold them; however, I shall only practice this myself each day.

For each "Fú" (福) character, place one dot; for every thousand recitations of the Buddha’s name, fill in one circle. Regardless of how many [recitations] are performed, hold this toward the Buddha before you as a witness.
This may be practiced by both those who have left the household life and those who remain at home (*Hezuan*).
Giving is the True Cause (as giving stands at the head of the Six Perfections, it is undoubtedly the True Cause).
The Buddha said: "If you wish to obtain grain, you must diligently plow and sow; if you wish to obtain wisdom, you must diligently study and inquire;

if you wish to obtain long life, you must diligently refrain from killing; if you wish to obtain wealth and honor, you must diligently practice giving. There are four kinds of giving, the first of which is:
The four types of giving are: first, the gift of material wealth; second, the gift of the Dharma; third, the gift of fearlessness; and fourth, the gift of the mind.
The gift of material wealth consists of bestowing riches upon others. The gift of the Dharma consists of instructing others in the teachings of goodness.

The gift of fearlessness refers to comforting humans and sentient beings when they are in a state of dread, or teaching them how to escape such dread so that they possess a heart free from fear. The gift of the mind...
Although one's power may not be sufficient to save others, one must always maintain the heart that seeks to save them. An ancient proverb says:
"If everyone knew there would be a coming year, every household would plant next year's grain; if everyone knew there was a future life, why would they not cultivate the merit of that future life?
One cannot sow grain in the morning and eat it in the evening; likewise, one cannot perform acts of giving and cultivate merit, and then expect immediate results.

The reason why receiving grain [as a reward] must necessarily occur within half a year, while the merit [of spiritual cultivation] must necessarily be separated by a lifetime, is that both the Confucian and Daoist teachings speak of giving and its retribution, yet they do not mention the separation by a lifetime.
What is meant by "he who loves others will always be loved by others; he who respects others will always be respected by others;
he who harms others will surely be harmed in return"—these are all instances of giving and retribution within the present life. The Buddha, moreover, says:
If a person, having given a gift, later feels regret; or if one takes another's property by force and uses it for giving;

or if a person first fails to support their parents and torments their wife, children, servants, and slaves, yet gives a gift because of that suffering—such a person is called an evil person whose giving is merely nominal.
Although such a person may obtain wealth in the future, it will always be depleted and never accumulate. If a person... [the text continues].

One who acquires wealth and treasures constantly loses them and fails to accumulate them; unable to utilize them, the body suffers from many ailments and pains. The *Compendium of Essential Passages from Various Sutras* states:

"If there is a poor person who has no wealth to give, yet gives rise to a mind of sympathetic joy (*anumodana*) when seeing others practice giving, the karmic reward of that sympathetic joy is equal to that of the actual giver, without any difference. *Dinglianlujiehuo* says: "The single dharma of giving..."
Compassion (*karuṇā*) and reverence (*gaurava*) differ: compassion is the relief of poverty and the alleviation of suffering, while reverence is the making of offerings to the Triple Gem.
To have reverence without compassion is called a perverted mind; to be free from stinginess, where compassion and reverence are one, is [the correct state]. (From the *Hezuan*).

While a certain scholar was assisting in the construction of a grand pavilion as a skillful means to benefit others, he purchased a pair of boots in the marketplace of the capital. He saw a pair of boots that were exceptionally large, resembling those worn by his father for funeral processions.
Upon asking where they had come from, the seller replied, "An official brought them here to have them repaired; he will likely return shortly."
He went to visit him and indeed saw his father dismounting from his horse, taking off his boots, and bowing; yet [the father] departed without looking back.

He pursued him for several *li*, but as he was about to lose him, he called out, "We are father and son in this life; why do you not say a single word to instruct me? His father replied, "Study with Ge Fan.
He asked who Ge was, and [his father] said, "A man of the world. He then inquired after his whereabouts. At that time, Ge was...
The Governor of Zhenjiang went to see him and told him of these matters, asking why he was so highly regarded by the world of the unseen.
Ge said, "In the beginning, I performed one beneficial act for others each day; gradually it increased to two, three, or even ten acts.
To this day, forty years have passed as if they were but a single day. When asked what constituted these beneficial acts for others, Ge pointed to the footstool beside his seat.
He said, "If an object is placed improperly, it may cause someone's foot to stumble; I shall set it right.
Furthermore, if a person is thirsty and is given a cup of water to drink, these are all matters that benefit others. One should act according to the skillful means of each situation.
From high officials and ministers down to beggars, this can be practiced by all; it depends solely on doing so for a long time without ceasing. The son bowed and withdrew.
Later, Ge passed away at a high age while sitting in meditation. Observing this, one should strive in deeds that benefit others;
how could one ever engage in deeds that harm them? Furthermore, Ge concurrently cultivated the Pure Land practice; later, a monk who traveled spiritually to the Pure Land saw Ge there.
Frugality and simplicity assist in cultivation;

I have heard the Perfect One say that for human beings, clothing, food, wealth, and official rank are all fixed by destiny in the underworld. If one is frugal and does not covet, one’s lifespan may be extended;
if one is extravagant and seeks beyond what is due, one’s allotment will be exhausted and life will end. It is like a person who possesses a single coin.
If one uses one hundred days' worth in a single day, it may suffice for ten days; if one uses fifty days' worth in a single day, it may suffice for twenty days.
Yet if one gives rein to greed and extravagance, ruin and death will be seen immediately. If one spends a thousand days' worth in a single day, will there still be any remainder? Someone might ask:
"Why is it that some people are frugal and modest yet have short lives, while others are greedy and extravagant yet live long? I say: regarding those who are frugal and modest...
A short life means that one's allotted number of births is small; if one is further greedy and extravagant, it will become even shorter.
A long life despite greed and extravagance means that one's allotted number of births is large; if one is further frugal and modest, it will become even longer.

Furthermore, Heaven and Earth are impartial toward humanity—how could there be such differences in the allotted number of births? [The answer is: Those who receive their lot in this life are all [the result of] what was done in the past.
In this world, for those who cultivate the Pure Land through the faculty of hearing, it is certainly not a matter of having great merit or long life;

however, one must refrain from actions that diminish merit and shorten life, as these constitute a lack of virtue, while one must strive to increase merit and prolong life, as these constitute the cultivation of profound virtue.
(The above is compiled from the *Lungshu Wencun*).

From the time he was a common scholar until his attainment of the jinshi degree and his rise to the pivotal positions of the imperial secretariat, Zhang Zishao wore coarse clothing, ate simple food, and possessed no articles of luxury;

even his writing brushes were those that had been worn down to the handle. Hu Keren lived an official life while consuming only vegetables for his entire career and slept within a single paper curtain.
If such men as these, while manifesting in the bodies of lay officials, practiced the conduct of bhikṣus, how much more so should one who is already a bhikṣu by body?
The Buddha ordained that *dhūta* monks should beg for food, wear robes made of discarded rags, and dwell among cemeteries or under trees.

Now, while staying here among the assembly, we have sufficient offerings of clothing and food provided by donors; our summer retreat is at a forest hermitage (*āraṇya*). Is it appropriate to seek further comforts?
With a single alms bowl with four patches and a pair of sandals, the noble tradition of the ancient worthies remains undiminished after thirty years.

Thus, I feel shame and self-reproach for this, and I report it together with my fellow practitioners (from *Lianchi Sanbi*). Two men who sought official careers took wealth not given to them to assist their studies;
while traveling to the capital, they sought a dream at the temple of the Two Prime Ministers (*Erxiang Miao*). One of them dreamed that an official appeared.
He held up one leaf of a register and pointed to a wooden board, saying, "This is the future career of those who came with you.
Upon examining it, he saw that they were ranked from minor officials up to the Prime Minister, yet some still had a mark of deletion beside them. He asked, "What does this mark of deletion mean?

The one holding the register replied, "If these officials love wealth and take what is unjustly obtained in the world by even one *qǐng* [of land], then one *qǐng* here shall be deleted—if they are in a hurry."
It is still possible to reform one's faults; when that man heard this, he repented his transgressions and did not dare to take what was not rightfully his.

Later, he indeed attained the position of a Surveillance Commissioner (Jiansi). Observing this, one sees that wealth acquired through unrighteous means is truly to be feared. Knowing this, cultivate the wholesome conditions for the Pure Land, and they will naturally ripen. (From *Longshu Wenzhang*)

The ancient monastery at Jiagangjing in Jiaxing was on the verge of collapse, and a monk wished to repair it. Furthermore, because the Juchiao Tongji Bridge was used by many travelers and residents, it had fallen into ruin;
a layman offered one thousand *jin* of silver for its reconstruction. This monk was also a man of integrity, yet he diverted the funds intended for the bridge to repair the temple.
Not long after, the monk passed away and appeared in a dream to his disciples, saying: "Because of my error regarding cause and effect, I am suffering..."
A divine retribution manifested: a pig in a certain household was born with white hair on its hind hooves as a sign that it would be born the following day.
[The owner] thought, "You must redeem me; I repent. After the fundraising for the bridge construction was completed, he went to inquire and found it was indeed so, and he told everyone everywhere.

The bridge was eventually finished, and the pig subsequently died. Now, when lay donors' offerings for the *caitya* (monastery) are used interchangeably, this occurs everywhere; who knows of such errors?
If the retribution for such offenses is as described, what need is there to mention those who embezzle the permanent endowment or conceal offerings of faith?
An ancient verse says: "A single grain of rice from a donor is as large as Mount Sumeru; if one does not realize the Way upon its return, one shall be reborn with fur and horns. It further says:
"On that day when Old Yama settles your account for the cost of your meals, see what you will have to offer in exchange. This applies to all who have left the household life.
Why do you not vigorously reflect upon these words? To curb the mouth and belly and to restrain lust is to assist in cultivation;
for food, drink, and sexual intercourse are among the great desires of human beings. To regulate them as if they did not exist is to be a sage; to moderate them is [the way of the wise].
To refrain from indulgence is to be a worthy person; to indulge without moderation is to be among the most ignorant.
Indeed, taking life to provide for one’s palate and succumbing to lust to lose one’s true nature are both ways of creating karma. Moreover, these two reinforce each other:
when fine food and drink cause the blood and qi to flourish, the blood and qi flourishing leads to increased lust; and with increased lust, the blood and qi are, in turn, depleted.
When the blood and qi are depleted, one must rely on food and drink for nourishment; thus, these two mutually create conditions for transgression.
If one wishes to reduce the consumption of food and drink, one must first restrain sexual desire; if one can restrain sexual desire, then one can reduce the intake of food.
This is truly the way to secure the body and prolong life. As Master Cijue said: "Food and drink are to humans what the sun and moon are to the long-term essence."
This coarse thing merely serves to plug the wound of hunger; once it has passed three inches [into the body], what does it become? There is no need to scrutinize it with such fine discernment.
If you can reflect in this way, you will naturally be able to restrain your appetite. The Rustic Devoted to Reality said:

"Skin wrapping bone, flesh, urine, and excrement—yet people forcibly feign coquettish charm to deceive others. All heroes of the ages have been undone by this; for a hundred years, we share the same fate."
If one can reflect and contemplate in this way when creating a single pit of dust, one will naturally be able to restrain sexual desire.
Indeed, if these two matters are thoroughly understood, how could there be illness or premature death during one's lifetime? And after death, how could there be rebirth in the hells or as an animal?
Those who cultivate the superior grade must not fail to observe these precepts.

One who assists others in their cultivation through both merit and wisdom must not fail to cultivate both merit and wisdom. Constantly performing various deeds that benefit sentient beings and practicing skillful means constitute the cultivation of all manner of goodness;

this is what is meant by "cultivating merit. To understand cause and effect, to recognize transgression and blessing, and to contemplate the scriptures of the Śākya clan within—this is what is meant by "wisdom."
Beyond the Confucian texts of those who contemplate the nature of principle (*xingli*), there is what is called the cultivation of wisdom (*prajñā*) through the understanding of worldly affairs.
Cultivating merit brings wealth and status; cultivating wisdom brings clarity and understanding. If one cultivates wisdom but not merit, one may possess clarity yet remain impoverished.

If one cultivates merit but not wisdom, one may possess wealth and status yet remain ignorant. If one cultivates both merit and wisdom, one will possess both wealth and status as well as clarity; these two [results] will never be lacking.

To cultivate only ignorance leads to poverty; because the Buddha cultivated both merit and wisdom, he is called the Honored One with Two Feet (*dvipadottama*), for he was fully endowed with both merit and wisdom.
It is better that wisdom surpasses merit than that merit surpasses wisdom; as the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* says:
"To experience happiness in the present while sowing the seeds of suffering for the future. A verse states: "Cultivate both merit and wisdom. Furthermore, contemplate Amitābha nine times.

In the *Lotus Sūtra*, in the first chapter, what further doubt could there be? For those who clearly understand the precepts and practice them will certainly attain birth in the highest grade of the highest level.

Furthermore, a verse states: "Though one may cultivate merit and wisdom, if one does not know to recite the name of Amitābha, even if one attains the fruit of Arhatship in this world, the cycle of saṃsāra will have no end.
Only by attaining the fruit of Arhatship while practicing in this world can one finally escape saṃsāra.
This is because of their worldly attachments (the above is compiled from the *Longshu Wenzhang*).
They do not aspire to honor and glory, nor do they shrink from contempt;
yet when assisting those who cultivate the Way through great indignation or great humiliation, they may only manage to endure with effort, failing to remain free from a longing for the world.
To be unable to forget one's feelings because of honor and prestige when others slight one is truly not right. Honor and prestige diminish blessings and summon calamity;

while being slighted removes transgressions and eliminates karma. This is like National Teacher Wudao (who in a previous life was the Han official Yuan Ang), whose karmic enemy, Chao Cuo, sought for ten generations to take revenge but could not do so because the Master’s precepts were so pure and strict. Emperor Yizong heard of the Master’s Way.

Dezhao had inscribed [the scripture] and was granted a precious sandalwood throne; that he met with misfortune and developed sores on his face—how could this be anything other than a calamity summoned because he failed to cultivate merit?

The *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states: "If a person’s transgressions from previous lives should cause them to fall into the evil realms, yet they are now treated with contempt by others in this life, their transgressions from previous lives will be immediately extinguished. Indeed, even by the spiritual power of this sutra...
If one must wait for others to treat one with contempt before one's transgressions are extinguished, then such contempt is actually a subtle method for transforming heavy sins into light retribution;
one ought to accept it as sweet as honey, so why be angry? Thus, between honor and prosperity on the one hand and contempt on the other, who is fortunate and who is unfortunate?
Formerly, when Tan Zixiao was struck by a beggar and two of his teeth were broken, he thanked the benefactor, saying: "Wang, you have increased my merit."
Yiyang believed that this was the exhaustion of his lifelong practice. Regarding Master Qing, people slandered him for being intimate with nuns and novices;

when someone questioned him about this, the Master smiled and said, "It is indeed as it has been reported. (After the Master passed away, there were five-colored śarīra relics. Alas! In the vast and murky five turbidities, who can truly fathom such a person?
(Below: The Lotus Companions Enter the World like a Mustard Seed in Fire).
Regarding the practice of ritual repentance as an aid to cultivation, Master Lianchi said: "A single-minded purity constitutes the internal illumination of principle-contemplation (*li-guan*);

the diligent application of the five limbs is called the external assistance of ritual repentance (*shi-chan*). Directly contemplating the fundamental mind is indeed a direct and essential path, yet sentient beings in the Dharma-ending age possess meager wisdom."

When defilements are heavy, one must necessarily employ both rational contemplation (*yoniśomanasikāra*) and ritual repentance (*vastu-pratikramaṇa*), bringing them together internally and externally; only then can concentration (*samādhi*) be stabilized and wisdom (*prajñā*) perfected, allowing for swift liberation from birth and death. Yet nowadays, people maintain only ritual repentance while rational contemplation is utterly neglected—how much more so when they merely adorn themselves with empty words, lacking any genuine remorse within? Master Guānlián’s statement implies that only when both principle and practice are cultivated together can it truly be called repentance.
