When the mind of mindfulness of the Buddha arises from hearing the names of the Buddha’s pure and true merits, it takes as its object the mind directed toward unsurpassed bodhi.
How can one true and one false be compared? It is like comparing a person [to a reflection].

When struck by a poisoned arrow such that the flesh was pierced and the bone broken, as soon as he heard the drum of the "Extinction of Defilements" medicine, the arrow was extracted and the poison removed.

For one who is resolute, at the moment of committing a sin, there is an interrupted mind with a subsequent thought; yet at the moment of recollecting the Buddha, there is an uninterrupted mind without a subsequent thought.
Consequently, when life is about to end, because the wholesome mind is so intense and powerful, one is reborn immediately—just as, for example, [a fire from] ten spans of...
A thousand men could not restrain him, yet a youth brandished his sword and in an instant split [the mountain] in two.
It is like a pile of firewood accumulated over a thousand years that is consumed in a short time by a single grain of fire.

Or it is like a person who, having cultivated the ten wholesome deeds throughout their entire life and thus ought to be reborn in heaven, falls into the Avīci Hell at the moment of death because of a single thought of resolute wrong view.
Because evil karma is so fierce and delusory, it can even displace the wholesome karma of an entire lifetime and cause one to fall into the evil realms;

how much more so, then, could the true and uninterrupted wholesome karma of mindfully reciting the Buddha’s name with a fierce resolve at the moment of death fail to displace beginningless evil karma and enable rebirth in the Pure Land?
Such a thing is impossible (from the *Ten Doubts of the Wise Man*).
Question: Since it is said that one may attain rebirth through ten recitations at the moment of death—even in a brief instant after seven days—how is this possible?

Answer: It is precisely because of single-mindedness, as explained in the *Jñānaprasthāna-śāstra* (Treatise on Wisdom). Furthermore, it is due to the power of both self-effort and the power of others, as explained in the *Nāgasena-bhikṣu-sūtra*.

The *Jñānaprasthāna-śāstra* states: "Although the duration of time is short, the power of the mind is fierce and sharp; this final thought is called the 'Great Mind. One should know that this is indeed so."
Because of single-mindedness without distraction, the *Nāgasena Bhikṣu Sūtra* states: "It is like placing a large stone upon a boat;
because of this, it does not sink. When an evil person recollects the Buddha, they do not fall into hell but instead attain rebirth [in heaven]. It is just like this:
the power of one's own mind and the power of the Buddha's vow mutually accomplish each other" (*Shuchao*).

Regarding the filial duties of a child toward their parents for the purpose of ensuring their rebirth in the Pure Land: when one perceives that the time for their rebirth has arrived, they should compile a record of all the various good deeds performed by their parents throughout their lives into a single document.
This should be read from time to time to inspire joy in the hearts of the parents. Furthermore, one should request the parents to sit or lie down facing west and recite [the Buddha’s name].

Recite the name of Amitābha and set up an image to welcome him as he approaches the Pure Land; at the moment his life comes to an end, you must further apply your mind, refraining from wailing and weeping that might disturb his right resolve.
Recite the Buddha’s name with one voice to assist him in proceeding to the West, so that he may personally attain birth in the Pure Land and receive all manner of bliss—is this not excellent?
The filial care you have provided throughout your life reaches its true fulfillment at this very hour. Send these words to those who practice filial piety.
"May you, son and grandson, never forget this matter (exhorting Emperor Wen).
Admonish your kinsmen to be reborn in the Great Way;
though there is no emotion, there is equality between enemies and kin. Yet for ordinary people who are attached to their kin, speaking of equality seems [difficult]."
For those who have not yet attained realization and whose passions and attachments remain unextinguished, the only way is to cultivate pure karma together with companions bound for the Western Land;
thus, their emotions will return to the state beyond emotion, and their attachments will be forgotten as a unity.

In this, the mental characteristics of ordinary beings are not destroyed, and they are universally delivered to rebirth—surely this is no less equal than the act of shedding tears and bidding farewell at the brink of peril.
"Rather than waiting for the body to decompose before exhausting one's resources for a lavish burial, how can one say that the latter’s love is greater?
Those with clear eyes will surely discern this for themselves. (From *Cuan guxiang xiaoxi*)
The "Chapter on the Worthy Head" (*Bhadrapāla-parivarta*) of the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* states: Furthermore, it emits a light named "Beholding the Buddha.
This light awakens those whose lives are about to end, causing them to see the Tathāgata according to their thoughts; at the moment of death, they attain rebirth in that Pure Land.

Seeing those who are approaching the end of life, it exhorts them to practice mindfulness of the Buddha and manifests sacred images for them to behold and revere, so that they may develop deep faith and aspiration toward the Buddha. It is for this reason that this [light] is accomplished.
Whenever one encounters a kinsman or any person facing the end of life, first place a standing image of the Buddha in the bedroom on the bedside table, facing east.
The patient should face west, opposite the Buddha. Those attending the patient should burn incense, scatter flowers, strike the chime, and assist in chanting the Buddha’s name;
even if the patient has not previously practiced mindfulness of the Buddha, they must employ various skillful means to do so.
One should encourage them to invoke the Buddha's name; if they have an illness or leave behind impurities, these should be immediately removed without incurring any fault.
Because the Buddha’s mind is compassionate, he only hopes for their sincere devotion and harbors no hatred (from the *Wujinding*).
For those who attend to the sick and cultivate pure karma, it is not easy to exert themselves when the dying person is heavily obstructed by delusion and confusion at the time of death;

thus, the responsibility of the caregiver is no small matter and must be planned for in advance. At the moment of death, one must avoid provoking anger or attachment, lest these lead to an erroneous rebirth.
It is especially to be feared when one enters the path of others. The *Saṃyukta-avadāna-sūtra* (*Za piyu jing*) states that King Ajātaśatru erected a stūpa and temple for the Buddha;
his merit was so magnificent that at the moment of his death, an attendant dropped a fan onto the king’s face, causing him to become enraged and immediately take the body of a snake.
A śramaṇa preached the sūtra to him, and upon hearing the Dharma, he was reborn in heaven. Therefore, one must not fail to attend to those who serve one at the time of death.
This is to protect the mind of the sick person (Zuan Dinglianlu).

Adorning oneself with mindfulness of the Buddha to deliver both enemies and kin and to recommend the deceased for rebirth is not as effective as the merit one has personally cultivated during one's lifetime; what is called the "ten recitations" refers precisely to this personal cultivation prior to death.

Reciting the Buddha’s name does not mean requesting others to recite it on your behalf after death. As the sutras state: "After death, if one has merit performed by others, one receives seven parts of the reward;

if one performs it oneself before death, one receives a thousand- or ten-thousand-fold retribution. Therefore, for those who recite the Buddha’s name, relying on others is not as good as seeking [merit] within oneself.

Even if you have committed evil deeds, though it may be difficult to attain rebirth in the Pure Land through recitation alone, if you simply give rise to the aspiration to see the Buddha and attain the Way, you will subsequently deliver others.
The minds of all enemies and kin will thus not fail to arise [in compassion]. Someone may ask:

"If a person has committed evil throughout their life and harmed sentient beings, yet recites the Buddha’s name at the moment of death and is reborn in the Pure Land, when can the enmity between sentient beings be resolved? The answer is:
"Once one is reborn in the Pure Land and attains the Way, one delivers all enemies and kin; is this not far superior to the mutual vengeance of enmity?"
Is this not a karmic retribution from which there is no time of escape? (From the *Zuan Longshu Wen*).

One who prepares for the end by inviting others to recite the Buddha’s name should, while in good health, invite others to recite the Buddha’s name, repent of their transgressions, and resolve their grievances; how much more so when one is at the point of death—should one not be courageous?
It is of particular importance to vigorously resolve to invite those who have long cultivated pure karma to perform great Buddhist services (*buddhakārya*) to assist in the journey to the West.

The *Precious Pearl Collection* records that when the *karmadāna* was near death, he used his remaining assets twice to invite the assembly to recite the Buddha’s name, thereby attaining rebirth in the Pure Land.
This recalls how the Dharma Master Daoyin said to Emperor Minghuang: "The power of the Buddha, the power of the Dharma, the three sages, and the ten [stages]..."
Even the Sages cannot fathom it; one should simply believe in and practice it. Observing this, it serves as a crimson banner for those who cultivate the Pure Land (from the *Zuan lebang wenlei*).
If one has not yet finished preparing for death, one should contemplate the end by reciting the Buddha’s name.

Someone may ask: "If it is said that those who have committed evil throughout their lives can still be reborn by reciting the Buddha’s name at the moment of death while carrying their karmic burdens, then may I simply attend to worldly affairs during my lifetime and wait until the very end to begin reciting the Buddha’s name? The answer is: This is what is called "adverse evil."
Ordinary people who recite the Buddha's name at the moment of death must have possessed roots of goodness and the causes and conditions of merit from previous lives;

only then do they encounter a spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra) and attain the practice of nianfo. Such fortunate occurrences are as rare as one in ten thousand. Have you not seen what the *Qunyi lun* says?
"In this world, there are ten kinds of people who cannot recite the Buddha’s name at the time of death: first, those who have not yet encountered a virtuous friend..."
There are ten common ways in which the body is afflicted by the suffering of karma: first, being bound by karmic pain; second, losing the power of speech due to wind-disorders;

third, becoming deranged and losing one's mind; fourth, encountering water or fire; fifth, meeting tigers or wolves; sixth, facing evil associates at the time of death; seventh, dying in a state of stupor and delusion;
eighth, being killed in military arrays and battles; ninth, losing one's life on high cliffs; and tenth, [the aforementioned sufferings]. These ten types of circumstances are frequently encountered.
Whether summoned by past conditions or retributed for present karma, it may suddenly manifest before you, leaving no room for avoidance;
you must then undergo the retribution according to your karma, suffering pain and incurring guilt within the three miserable realms and the eight difficult states.

Even if you were free from such evil conditions, you would still inevitably suffer the agony of illness, dying of natural causes, and experiencing the wind-blade dismemberment of the body as the four elements separate—this is the suffering of sickness.
Pressed by distress, frantic with fear and agitation, one cannot even manage to recite the Buddha’s name; it would be better for you to die while free from illness.
Or perhaps your worldly affairs are not yet finished and your attachments to the world have not ceased; greed for life and fear of death disturb your breast.

If you are a layperson, furthermore, your private estate is not settled and your final arrangements are not decided; with your wife wailing and children crying, you are tormented by a hundred kinds of anxieties—how can you recite?
Even if you cannot recite the Buddha’s name, I will further grant you grace: consider the time before you fell ill, when you merely had some slight ailment in your body;
you endured pain and suffering, crying out and groaning, seeking medicine and doctors, praying and repenting, as your various thoughts flew about like birds.
Even if you cannot recite the Buddha’s name, I will further grant you grace: consider the time before you were ill, when you were simply old and decrepit.
When these signs manifest before you, you are suddenly struck with decrepitude, sighing in sorrow and filled with distress;

you can only direct your efforts toward this aging body, yet even then, reciting the Buddha’s name becomes impossible. Furthermore, even while you have not yet died—precisely when you are in the prime of youth and vigor—it is the very time to recite the Buddha’s name.
If your wild mind has not yet ceased and you remain entangled in worldly affairs, reaching out to this and that in pursuit of various attachments, how can you hope for anything else?
When thoughts are in turmoil and the karmic consciousness is vast and wandering, even the practice of mindfulness of the Buddha will not suffice. Furthermore,

even if you possess leisure and independence and have the resolve to cultivate the Way, if within the midst of worldly phenomena you cannot reflect upon them clearly, cannot let go of them, cannot hold yourself steady, and cannot remain seated in stillness— suddenly,
when some slight境 (object-condition) appears before you, the "host" follows it into delusion, and your mindfulness of the Buddha falters.

How extraordinary! Consider this: when one is old and infirm, or even during the days of youth and leisure, if there is even the slightest matter weighing on the mind, it already makes it difficult to recite the Buddha's name;
how much more so when facing the time of death? Furthermore, you say, "I will attend to worldly affairs for now.
But worldly affairs are like dreams, like illusions, like shadows, like echoes—what single thing among them has any real substance?

That one thing can substitute for [escaping] birth and death; yet, even if you were to extensively construct monasteries and greatly increase the permanent endowments, thinking you have performed many good deeds, you would instead be violating the Tathāgata’s precepts against constructing monasteries without embodying the fundamental essence of the Way.
How could you know that the merits of conditioned phenomena harbor many faults? Before heaven is attained, hell is already established; before life and death are clarified, they remain unresolved.

All these are the roots of suffering. Only when the light of the eyes falls to the ground and one undergoes suffering will one realize that all that was done throughout one's life was merely adding shackles to shackles and chains to chains;
having lost this human body, it will be difficult to recover for ten thousand kalpas. Even an iron-hearted man must shed tears upon hearing this.
The Patriarch spoke thus with such bitter words to exhort people; did he ever permit you to continue engaging in worldly affairs?
Do you wait until the moment of death before reciting the Buddha’s name? Furthermore, have you not seen Chan Master Sishin say:
"People in this world possess wealth and treasures as vast as mountains, with wives and concubines surrounding them, enjoying themselves day and night. Do they not desire to live long in this world?

Yet how can they resist the fact that their future is limited and imperceptibly hastens toward its end? When the summons arrives, one must comply; there is no room for delay. Now, consider this for yourselves.
What we see with our eyes and hear with our ears is that, despite being in the prime of youth, how many people have already passed through birth and death?

Yet most people say they will wait until old age before they have the leisure to recite the Buddha’s name. They do not realize that on the road to the Yellow Springs, no matter whether one is young or old, how many can actually reach old age?
As the ancients said: "Do not wait until you are old to recite the Buddha’s name; for among the solitary graves, most belong to the young. Furthermore—
It is said that since early years, one has sought a wife, raised children, and managed the household affairs, enduring myriad hardships;
yet suddenly, when the three-inch breath is severed, all must inevitably cease at once. If there are filial sons and grandsons, they may still remember their parents;
but if there are unworthy children, even while the bones of the parents are not yet cold after death, they will seize and divide the property.

To indulge in pleasure at will—when compared to this, what is of such vital importance? To compose "thousand-year melodies" (long-term schemes), one’s descendants shall surely have their own blessings;
do not act as a beast of burden for your descendants. The ancient masters thus spoke with bitter urgency to exhort people:
did they ever permit you to merely attend to worldly affairs while waiting until the moment of death to recite the Buddha's name? You should reflect that while living in this world, one can...

How many times have I, while still free from illness and old age, stirred my body and mind and set aside worldly affairs to gain a single day’s time to recite the name of Amitābha, or to gain a single session’s effort to cultivate pure karma?
As for whether one meets a "good death" or a "bad death" at the moment of life's end, I have already prepared my provisions; my future path is thus secured.
If you do not achieve stability in this way, repentance will be difficult to pursue later. Reflect on this, reflect on it!
(Master Tianru’s *Questions on the Pure Land*).
*The Morning Bell of the Pure Land*, Fascicle Seven.
The Morning Bell of the Pure Land, Volume Eight:

The Correct Discernment of the Principles of the Lotus School. Having fully analyzed the teachings of past and present, both principle and phenomena are harmoniously integrated, and the shallow and the deep are complete therein.

I fear that those of brilliant intellect and superior talent, whose haughty spirits are not easily subdued, often speak in grandiloquent terms of profound understanding, yet their arguments become fragmented and diverge in a hundred directions.
Their maladies are threefold: first, they are biased and cling to their own views; second, they misinterpret the intended meaning;
third, they merely follow in the footsteps of others. This is called "petty wisdom," but it is in fact great folly; nothing else leads to such self-delusion and the delusion of others.
Furthermore, the finest clarified butter (*sarpis*) and poison are of one and the same flavor; right knowledge and vision constitute the clarified butter, while perverse understanding is the poison.
Once it has entered the mouth, there is no remedy. A person of clear eyes should first [discern this]. Master Lien said:
"The teaching of the Pure Land focuses the single mind on the direction of the West to transcend the three realms horizontally; it realizes that there is no land outside of the mind."
When the one true reality is limpid and still, the myriad dharmas vanish; who then is outside the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss?

When the mind is non-existent, the seven jewels adorn the land and the nine lotuses bloom; how could this hinder primordial stillness? Those of superior capacity realize the principle through phenomena, remaining firm in their conviction without wavering;
even those of inferior capacity follow upon hearing this teaching, never giving rise to delusion. Thus, there is neither "not superior" nor "not [inferior]."
When one’s lower station reaches the middle stream, yet one still follows desires and opposes one’s own will, there is no fixed direction.
For this reason, the ten doubts pervade even the wise. Someone asked Master Ze, who replied: "The celestial drum resounds repeatedly and the compassionate heart is lingering;
how could these be called many words? They are words that cannot be avoided. Furthermore, as the sun sinks and oil-fed lamps are lit, the illness grows severe and medicine increases in dose.
These two treatises are able to demonstrate that disputation cannot be ceased; such is the eighth section, "Establishing the Correct Disputation.
This section establishes that generating birth in the Pure Land and saving sentient beings constitutes an easy path of practice.

Question: Since Buddhas and Bodhisattvas take great compassion as their primary vocation, they ought only to vow to be born within the triple world to rescue and deliver sentient beings amidst the five turbidities and the three miserable realms.
Why, then, do they seek birth in a pure land, focusing solely on self-benefit? If so, does this not constitute a lack of great compassion and an obstacle to the path to Bodhi?
Answer: There are two types of bodhisattvas. The first are those who have long practiced the bodhisattva path.
Those who have attained the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) truly deserve this responsibility.

As for the second type—those who have not yet attained it but have returned [to the path], as well as ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) who have first resolved their minds [on enlightenment]—these ordinary beings and bodhisattvas must always remain inseparable from the Buddha.

Only when they have perfected the power of patience are they fit to dwell within the triple world and rescue suffering sentient beings amidst evil ages. Why is this? Because in evil worlds, afflictions (*kleśa*) are powerful, and one possesses nothing of one's own.

With the power of patience lacking, their minds follow after sensory objects; bound by sounds and forms, they fall of their own accord into the three miserable realms—how then could they save sentient beings?

Even if they should be born among humans, the Path of the Sages is difficult to attain. Should they, perhaps through upholding the precepts or cultivating merit, become kings, ministers, or those of great wealth and power, yet encounter a virtuous friend (kalyāṇamitra), they refuse to trust or accept them; instead, they remain greedily deluded and negligent, riding upon these very habits.
Those who commit evil deeds enter the three miserable realms and, after passing through immeasurable kalpas, emerge from hell only to receive the body of a poor and lowly person.
Such is this cycle of rebirth that continues until this very day; every person is like this, and this is called the "difficult path. Thus, the *Vimalakīrti Sūtra* says:
"If one cannot even save oneself when ill, how can one save those who are sick? And the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Śāstra* says: "It is, for example, like two people..."

Each had relatives who were being swept away by the water; one person, driven by urgency, entered the water directly to rescue them, but because he lacked skillful means (*upāya*), both he and the others drowned.
Another person, possessing skillful means, went to fetch a boat or raft and, by boarding it, rescued and received them all, so that they were entirely freed from the peril of drowning.
A bodhisattva who has newly resolved [to attain enlightenment] is also like this: having not yet attained the power of patience (*kṣānti*), he must always...
Only after approaching the Buddha and attaining the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) can one save sentient beings, just as one who has obtained a boat [can cross the sea].
Furthermore, the treatise states: "For example, an infant cannot be separated from its mother; likewise, a fledgling bird, relying on the tree and clinging to the branches, cannot travel far.

Only when its wings and feathers are fully developed can it fly through the air without obstruction. Ordinary beings lack such power; they must simply focus their mindfulness exclusively upon Amitābha Buddha."
By accomplishing samādhi through the perfection of karma, one focuses the mind at the time of death and attains rebirth with certainty, free from doubt.
Having beheld Amitābha Buddha and realized the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), one returns to the realm of birth and death within the triple world.

Riding the ship of non-arising patience, one extensively performs Buddha-activities with sovereign ease, teaching and transforming those in the hells to rescue suffering sentient beings; it is for this reason.
Because they seek birth in the Pure Land, the *Daśabhūmivibhāṣā-śāstra* calls it the "Easy Path" (Tiantai Master Zhiyi).
To distinguish between seeing one's nature and awakening to the Way, do not disparage the Pure Land.

Question: If seeing one's nature and awakening to the Way allow one to transcend birth and death, what need is there to fix the mind on that Buddha and seek birth in another realm? Answer: [See following text]

It is said: "A true practitioner of the Way should examine themselves, for as the saying goes, 'When a person drinks water, they know its temperature for themselves. You virtuous ones, observe your own conduct and understanding:
have you seen your nature and awakened to the Way? Have you received the prediction of the Tathāgata and succeeded to the rank of the Patriarchs, being able to equal Vasubandhu and Nāgārjuna?
Have you attained unimpeded eloquence and realized the Samādhi of the Lotus Sūtra, being able to equal the Tiantai Master Zhiyi?"
Are the teachings of the various schools not all widely practiced? Can one truly practice both [this life and the Pure Land] as did Master Guoqing Zhong?

These great beings all clearly bestowed verbal instructions, deeply exhorting us toward rebirth; this is surely for the sake of benefiting oneself and others. How could they ever intend to mislead others or themselves?

Furthermore, the Great Hero (the Buddha) praised it and exhorted us with his golden mouth; we should respectfully follow the examples of past sages and reverently obey the Buddha’s decree—it is certainly not erroneous.

This is an error; nevertheless, the accounts of ancient and modern deeds recorded in the *Wangsheng zhuan* (Biographies of Those Reborn) are numerous and manifest, and one should diligently study them to reflect upon oneself.
Furthermore, one must consider for oneself: at the time of death, will one certainly attain mastery over life and death, departure and remaining?
Since beginningless time, have one's heavy karmic obstructions certainly not manifested before one? Will this retribution-body certainly escape the cycle of saṃsāra?
Do you have the freedom to appear and disappear at will while traveling through the three miserable realms and the evil paths, and are you certain that there is no suffering?
Do you have the certainty that you can dwell as you please throughout the ten directions of the heavens and the human world without any obstruction?

If you have attained such clear self-confidence, what could be more auspicious than this? If you have not yet reached it, do not be arrogant for a moment, lest you cause yourself to sink into eternal oblivion.

Having lost the opportunity for spiritual benefit, whom shall one blame? Alas, how tragic! What lamentation can avail now? (Master Yongming Shouchan). To take thought as thought and birth as birth is the error of those with the view of permanence (*śāśvata-dṛṣṭi*). To take non-thought as... [the error of those with the view of annihilationism (*uccheda-dṛṣṭi*)]. Five delusions regarding the failure to cultivate the Pure Land. For those who regard thought as thought and birth as birth, this is what is lost through the view of permanence. To regard non-thought as... [is what is lost through the view of annihilationism]. [The text continues: ...to regard non-birth as birth is the error of those with the view of permanence. To regard birth as non-birth is the error of those with the view of annihilationism. To regard non-thought as thought is the error of those with the view of permanence. To regard thought as non-thought is the error of those with the view of annihilationism. To regard non-birth as birth is the error of those with the view of permanence. To regard birth as non-birth is the error of those with the view of annihilationism. These five types of people do not understand that the nature of the mind is originally pure and that the nature of phenomena is originally empty. They do not realize that the mind-ground is originally tranquil and that the dharma-realm is originally still. Because they do not know this, they fail to cultivate the Pure Land. This is called the first delusion: the delusion of dualistic grasping. Furthermore, there are those who, having heard that the Buddha-lands are all empty and that the Buddhas are all like illusions, say: "If all lands are empty, then there is no land of the Western Paradise; if all Buddhas are illusory, then there is no Amitābha Buddha. Because they hold such views, they do not cultivate the Pure Land. This is called the second delusion: the delusion of nihilistic emptiness. Furthermore, there are those who, having heard that the Pure Land is a place of reward for the practice of merit, say: "If one cultivates the Pure Land, one will surely attain rebirth there. But if one attains rebirth there, one will remain subject to birth and death. Since birth and death are suffering, why should I seek it? Because they hold such views, they do not cultivate the Pure Land. This is called the third delusion: the delusion of attachment to the Lesser Vehicle. Furthermore, there are those who, having heard that the Pure Land is a realm of form, say: "Form is an obstruction; how can one escape it? Emptiness is liberation; I should dwell therein. Because they hold such views, they do not cultivate the Pure Land. This is called the fourth delusion: the delusion of attachment to emptiness. Furthermore, there are those who, having heard that the Pure Land is a realm of mind-only, say: "Mind is originally empty; there is no land outside of mind. Why should I labor to go there? Because they hold such views, they do not cultivate the Pure Land. This is called the fifth delusion: the delusion of clinging to the principle of mind-only. One who wishes to transcend these five delusions and attain rebirth in the Pure Land must first abandon the view of permanence and the view of annihilationism, and then cultivate the practice of the Pure Land. Only then will one be able to depart from the three realms and be born in the Land of Ultimate Bliss. Thus it is said: "If you wish to be born in the Land of Ultimate Bliss, you must first abandon the two extremes of existence and non-existence. This is the essential meaning. Therefore, one should diligently cultivate the practice of the Pure Land. Do not let the opportunity pass. Once lost, it is difficult to regain. This is the instruction of the Great Master. It is said: "When the time of death arrives, what shall one rely upon? If one has cultivated the Pure Land during life, one will certainly attain rebirth there. How could one afford to be negligent? One must strive with all one's heart. This is the final exhortation. May all beings hear this and awaken to it. May they all together cultivate the path and be born in the Land of Ultimate Bliss. Thus ends this brief explanation of the five delusions regarding the failure to cultivate the Pure Land. May it serve as a mirror for future generations.
