Today there are many who are stung by venomous snakes; there are also many who, having been stung, feel no regret and yet suffer its sting once more.

How could it be merely a single plowman? (The Parable of the Snake) To illustrate this for people regarding the worldly objects of wealth, form, fame, and profit, there is a metaphor: suppose a mass of fire is here, and these five things are beside it;
they are just like dry grass that ignites as soon as it is touched. The second is like wood: if one blows upon it, it [blazes].
The first is like iron: it cannot be ignited, yet it can still be melted. The second is like water:
not only does it not burn, it can even extinguish fire; yet if one separates it from a cauldron or jar, it can still boil.
The third is like empty space: it then permits burning and scorching, yet its essence remains as it was, requiring no further effort.

The practice of cessation will itself cease; initially, while one is still among ordinary beings practicing and studying, it is only at the very end that one is named a Great Sage, a Tathāgata (the object of perception; above, from the Lotus Pond).
Past events are empty; present events are empty before one's eyes; and the future is definitively empty.

All worldly conditions—whether pleasant, like clusters of brilliant colored clouds, or unpleasant, like turbid mist obscuring the sky—are but illusions. When people encounter what accords with their desires, they give rise to attachment;

when things go against their wishes, they harbor resentment. Thus, they only increase their dark karma (*kṛṣṇa-karman*); where is the true reality (*bhūta-lakṣaṇa*)? One must simply, from time to time, [contemplate this].
When one contemplates emptiness, one must not grasp at it as being existent, for that would obstruct the Vajra-like mind within oneself.

What the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* refers to as "no mark of self, no mark of person, no mark of sentient beings, and no mark of a life-span" is precisely what is called the "true emptiness" (*bhūtakoṭi-śūnyatā*)—the foremost, most urgent practice for transcending the world. (True Emptiness; from the *Hezuan*).
The world universally claims that none are more wretched or more pitiable than widowers, widows, orphans, and the solitary;
yet I privately hold that none in the world are more refined or more joyful than these four kinds of people.
It is a pity they do not know to take refuge in the Pure Land; for while they have no one to rely upon in this life, after death they will surely fall into the cycle of rebirth.

If things turn out this way, it would indeed be truly bitter. However, if one hears the Buddha-dharma, gives rise to faith and joy, and focuses the mind on the Western Land, then one will have no attachments at birth and no fetters at death;
attaining the stage of non-retrogression, one will forever leave behind the defiled and turbid world.
Who could be more fortunate than you? Yet, while you yourself are like a person who has attained such liberation, you instead say that you are worthy of pity.
Alas! People today merely recognize their own bodies and households as too real and their kin as too heavy;

thus, even those who are virtuous and wise may be able to treat fame and office lightly and remain content in poverty and low station, yet when it comes to children and grandchildren, they absolutely cannot break free from them.
Those without children do not know the joy of being childless, while those with children willingly endure the suffering of oxen and horses. This matter of the eldest son remains unresolved.
A young girl comes again, and when the man is fortunate enough to marry her, she is urged to wed once more;

in this constant turmoil and haste, where is there room for him to have time to recite the Buddha’s name? He does not consider at all how much trouble he has caused others—what business is it of yours?
It would be better to be like those four types of people who are pure and resolute, living freely and at ease, without burdening anyone else.
Because this person does not come to collect debts, his creditors are few;

because this person does not come to repay debts, he can take advantage of this opportune moment to focus single-mindedly on cultivation, transcending birth and death. He is truly the most joyful person in the world.
Generally speaking, for a human being, the less attachment there is, the less bondage there is; the less [attachment], the more [freedom].
When the fetters are thus diminished by even one part, karmic obstructions are lightened and worldly conditions become shallow, while the affinity with the Buddha deepens;
quickly and constantly recite the Buddha’s name to seek rebirth in the Pure Land. (From *The Collected Works on the Plain Discourse of Chengluan*, Section on the Four Poor People).
In our city of Hangzhou, there was a man named Luma who, having reached middle age, said to his son:

"My affairs of marriage and settling my family are now complete, and you children are also capable of supporting yourselves. I shall seek an opportunity to depart. Thereupon, he prepared a coffin and outer casing;

he fully provided for the soul-palanquin, the bright banner, the drum and music, and had his sons don mourning dress and carry staffs to lead the coffin. He himself followed behind in a sedan chair until they reached West Lake to bid farewell.

He placed his coffin in the courtyard of his villa and sent his son back home, posting a notice on his gate that read: "Only today am I truly at leisure; until death, I shall not enter the city. Alas! How enlightened he was!
Worldly men possess domestic ties, so it is only natural that they should be busy. To claim one is "only today at leisure" after having escaped such busyness is appropriate;
yet for those who have left the household life—whose nature is fundamentally at leisure—to instead exhaust their bodies and weary their wills in pursuit of profit and status is a contradiction.
To claim a name and not know when to rest—this should be titled: "Only Today Am I Busy. Beneath the *kāṣāya* one loses the human body, losing it again and again.
The Buddha said: "Constantly rub your own head to cast off finery and ornamentation. But surely this applies not only to finery;
constantly rubbing one's own head means: "I am a monk; I suddenly abandon all worldly conditions and single-mindedly contemplate the Way" (only today am I free).
Nowadays, people shave their heads and dye their robes, claiming this constitutes leaving the household life;
alas, this is merely leaving behind one's own great family home, not leaving the burning house of the triple world. Whenever I see someone newly ordained, they invariably possess a sincere heart;
yet after some time, they become defiled by worldly conditions, fame, and profit, eventually returning to adorn themselves with fine garments and acquiring fields.
They raise livestock and maintain large households, accumulating vast amounts of gold and silk; they are diligent in building worldly connections, no different from the laity.
The Sutras state that when a single person leaves the household life, Pāpīyān is struck with fear; if this is now the case, Pāpīyān may pour out wine to celebrate!
Those who leave home with a sincere heart must watch keenly and see through [the truth]: I have seen ascetic monks practicing austerities in deep mountains, yet once they step out of the mountains...
If one is buried for a lifetime by the refuge and offerings of even dozens of faithful men and women, how much more so for those of greater stature?
The ancients said that one must once again leave the home of afflictions and sever the net of worldly toil;
this is "leaving home" after having already left home. It is easy to leave the home one was born into, but difficult to leave the home one has subsequently entered. I offer this as an admonition.
At night, he was filled with trepidation. (Regarding "after leaving home" [and so forth], this is from the *Zuanlian Chi*). The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* states:

"Principle is realized through sudden awakening, and by virtue of that awakening, it is simultaneously eliminated; however, phenomena are not suddenly removed, as they are exhausted only through gradual stages.

Thus, even after awakening, there remains further cultivation and study; one does not reach completion through a single awakening alone. Ancient Buddhas and Bodhisattvas [practiced] for three great kalpas.

He replied, "Even before the three kalpas of cultivation were completed, [the truth] was already realized. [The questioner asked: "If awakening is already complete through sudden enlightenment, why is there still the need for gradual cultivation?
Chan Master Yuanzhi said, "One suddenly clarifies that one's own nature is no different from that of the Buddha.

However, because of the defiled habits accumulated since beginningless time, one must employ gradual cultivation as an antidote to cause clarity to arise in accordance with that nature. It is like a person eating a meal: they are not satisfied by a single mouthful."

Chan Master Lingyou said: "Nowadays, although those with a beginner's mind may, through conditions, attain sudden enlightenment into the fundamental principle in a single thought-moment, they still possess habitual tendencies from beginningless kalpas that have not yet been suddenly purified. One must teach them to cleanse and eliminate the flowing consciousness of present karma;
this is cultivation. It is not said that there is some other dharma to teach them to practice and pursue—this statement does not penetrate the ultimate Dharma."
Those who have not reached the ultimate source cannot speak of it; why is it that those who have only a slight degree of awakening immediately claim that their lifelong study of Zen is finished?
(This refers to the fact that there is cultivation even after awakening; see *Hezuan*).
One realizes that wealth and honor are illusory;
viewing them from the perspective of poverty and low station, one sees their blazing aura and cannot help but covet them with longing.
Yet, those who actually possess them do not necessarily find true happiness therein. Huangfu Mi said: "Wealth and honor disturb the spirit and exhaust the essence, as if [carrying] a single load."
If a person’s joys and angers are unpredictable, the anxiety lies with their superior; if those in the same rank harbor divergent intentions, the anxiety lies with the collective sentiment.

Because of greed for office, one suffers from the fear of gain and loss; because of strife for power, factions differ and align themselves. The higher the position, the heavier the burden of nobility;
the more exalted the favor, the greater the number of those who harbor resentment. At midday, the sun begins to decline; when the moon is full, it immediately wanes. When the granary is full—*cāng*.
When one's life ends, all things are nearly lost; one seeks a place to unyoke the carriage but finds no destination. One desires to become a common man, yet this cannot be achieved.

A wealthy elder holds his tally-sticks and calculates, exhausting the strength of mind and heart of a lifetime to bequeath to his descendants, yet the rise and fall of a hundred years is difficult to foresee.
All that remains after death ultimately returns to others; it is like a silkworm spinning its cocoon—this very cocoon is [the source of its own confinement].
When things that entangle the body entwine themselves upon one, whom can one blame? Furthermore, these are merely the possessions of others;
as long as a person possesses this cocoon, who would want you, the worm that spins it? Speaking from this perspective, what joy is there in wealth and status?
It is nothing but suffering. Moreover, when those in wealth and status reach a critical juncture, they are no different from the poor and lowly.
Generally speaking, matters where the wealthy and noble surpass the poor and lowly are all devoid of essential importance. Food is for quelling hunger, and clothing is for warding off the cold;
if one’s clothes are fine and one’s food is exquisite, what essential benefit does this bring to the body and mind? Other matters may be understood by inferring from this.
As for the points of greatest benefit and harm—old age, sickness, and death—one must face these alone with this single body.
When the time comes for the final desperate gamble, as the bells toll and the water-clock runs out, from emperors and ministers down to the common people, there is no one who can take one’s place;
it all concludes in a single stroke, without increasing by even a hair’s breadth. When one reflects on this, how could anyone not feel their heart turn to ash at that very moment?
When Dongpo was in Huizhou, Foyin sent him a letter saying: "A human life in this world is like a white colt passing through a crevice;
in twenty or thirty years, fame, achievement, wealth, and honor vanish into emptiness at a glance.

Why not simply draw a single stroke to sever them all and seek your own original face, which abides eternally through ten thousand kalpas and never falls? Why do you instead remain stuck to the old strings?"
Waiting by the stump for someone to come, you act like one who hates the path; Zizhan, though ten thousand scrolls of books fill your breast, not a single speck of dust remains upon your brush.
Reaching such a state, you do not know where life and nature reside—what is the use of a lifetime of cleverness?
The Buddhas of the three ages are simply men of blood and spirit; if Zizhan can take this up with your own feet, then...
For twenty or thirty years, wealth, honor, and fame are as base as dirt (from the *Hezuan*).
One realizes that this floating life is falsely existent;
though people say having many sons is a matter of security, one who keeps many concubines to broaden the lineage does not consider that the self is but one, and not two.
The body is in peril within this world; many people recognize the perils of their children yet forget the perils of their own bodies.

For the sake of a few pages of examination essays, they pursue ranks in the bureaucracy, amass chests of gold and silk, acquire houses and several acres of farmland, and keep several beautiful wives and concubines.
Amidst these trivialities—neither righteous nor essential—they are submerged by them for their entire lives.
Each and every one of us cannot escape such conventional traps; we have busied ourselves in vain for a lifetime, only to find that our time has already passed—how truly lamentable!
Shao Yaofu said: "If I were granted ten more years, I might still accomplish some small measure of my work; alas, how can it be otherwise?
Within heaven and earth, there is no principle by which the sun rises twice. An ancient proverb says: "Frenzied schemes and far-fetched calculations will never succeed; only..."
There is one with hoary hair who comes as scheduled; he also says, "If you would rest now, then rest; if you seek the moment of realization, there is no such moment.
These are all words that reach the ultimate truth. Why not awaken to this with sudden vigor?
I have often observed those people in the world who are renowned in their time;
though they may be heroes among the hundreds or thousands, they all regard this world as a place where they dwell permanently and will never depart.
To one with clear eyes, every phenomenon is but a passing shadow; in the blink of an eye, so much has already vanished, just like puppets upon a stage.
For a moment, amidst laughter, the creator took that thread and hung it from the top of a pillar. Alas!
Within this enclosure of wood, a space of only one foot and five inches—could this truly be the place where you dwell?
One person came out to mock him, and another followed behind; look before you, how cold and heat urge us on!
Like surging waves or flashing lightning, when one turns back to look at those from forty or fifty years ago, people have suddenly vanished like froth.

Who among us was not deluded by the sorrows and joys of that time? Yet the autumn grasses and winter cicadas—form and resonance alike transformed—have given way to an entirely different scene, beyond our current knowledge.
Those who view the past as the present grieve for the former; the deluded are reckless, while the awakened are detached.
Amidst this endless turmoil and frantic haste, there is but one thing that is real: the urgent pursuit of the path of life and death alone can lead one to the Land of Ultimate Bliss;
otherwise, it will all be in vain—like a flickering flame in the wind. An ancient teaching says: "This day has passed, and with it, one's lifespan is diminished.
A former master addressed the assembly, saying: "You who have left the household life have not yet established yourselves in stability; in an instant, three [kalpas] have already passed."
"It has been forty years," said Zen Master I'an Gwon, weeping as evening fell. "Today, once again, it passes away in this very manner;
I know not what tomorrow will bring. Hearing these piercing words, how could those of us present not tremble in our hearts and have our hair stand on end?
We reflect upon the past and anticipate the future, realizing that we have wasted our limited lifespan on the pursuit of vain and profitless affairs through our attachments.
How lamentable and pitiable! (From the *Hezuan*).
Regarding the delusion of birth and death, Qian Xiaozhi said:
"Since time immemorial, the cycle of birth and death within the three realms has been compared to a prison; yet it is merely this..."

All those born within birth and death are prisoners in the jail of the triple world (*tridhātu*). There are three kinds of such prisoners: the first are those who believe they have no possibility of escape and merely seek a precarious comfort within this confinement; yet one day, when the executioner arrives, they tremble with fear as they face their death. The second are those who pride themselves on being the sons of men of great wealth and do not spare money to arrange their livelihoods, yet their hearts are not resolved [to transcend]. The third... [text fragmentary]... are those who, having already escaped from the prison, still harbor lingering regrets. Among these, the former two are like prisoners who, though they may be released for a time, will surely return to the jail once more. Only the latter kind, having truly escaped, will never again enter the prison. Therefore, one must strive to attain liberation from the triple world. If one does not attain liberation from the triple world, even if one attains the rank of a *cakravartin* king, it is no different from being a prisoner in the triple-world jail. Even if one attains the status of a *śrāvaka* or *pratyekabuddha*, it is likewise no different from being a prisoner in the triple-world jail. It is only by attaining the state of a Buddha that one is truly liberated from the triple-world jail. Thus, one should know that the Buddha is the most supreme among all beings. One should aspire to become a Buddha and diligently cultivate the path. If one does not cultivate the path, one will remain a prisoner in the triple-world jail forever. If one cultivates the path, one will eventually attain Buddhahood. Therefore, one should cultivate the path with utmost diligence. As for those who have already attained Buddhahood, they are like people who have already escaped from the prison and no longer harbor any regrets. Those who have not yet attained Buddhahood are like people who, though they have escaped from the prison, still harbor lingering regrets.
