I shall settle for one thing: to steal the pleasure of wandering through the cauldron; even if the path to rebirth is severed, I shall simply accept my fate with a willing heart.

Yet there is another, a man of stubborn and defiant nature, who cannot endure being bound. When his guards are momentarily distracted, he struggles to break his shackles and rushes forward without looking back.
Seeing such resolute determination, how could he be willing to seek out a mere remnant of pleasure before death?
Whether one is born or escapes, or whether one does not escape, the mind wavers between these two possibilities. Alas! This too is but one model among us within the prison of birth and death.

The first kind of person is found everywhere; they speak loftily of fame, office, wealth, and honor, laboring to acquire them and indulging themselves with the finest palaces, concubines, and attendants. When spoken to about birth and death, they remain utterly unconcerned.
When I spoke of the path beyond birth and death, they remained silent and could only offer a smile, for they lacked the faculty of faith entirely. As for the second type of person,
though born with the roots of past cultivation— worshiping the Buddha, discussing Chan, upholding the teachings, building temples,
and providing offerings to the Sangha without stinting on gold and silver— they have nonetheless become entangled within the net of the world, bound by the snares of fame and profit.
It is like being caught in a thicket of brambles, entangled so that one cannot move freely. For a person, this matter of birth and death is a single great cause and condition;
if one does not apply oneself with single-minded devotion to it, yet hopes to attend to it with only leftover effort, how could there be such a thing as a "crane of Yangzhou"?
Though one may have performed meritorious deeds throughout one's life, at the critical moment of birth and death, one will ultimately fail to leap clear of the cycle.
This is also because their fear of birth and death has not been truly sincere from the beginning.
As with the third type of person, who does not seek wealth or status but applies diligent effort, they are truly able to seek liberation from birth and death.
Now, seeing those in fetters crying out to heaven for their lives, everyone pities their folly and mocks them for not having sought life earlier.
I say that for a condemned prisoner to seek life is too late; compared to those of us like you, it is still a prudent plan.
For the condemned prisoner, the day of execution in autumn comes but once a year, and there is ample time before and after that single day to find respite.
Yet for us, within the prison of the three realms, we may die every year, every month, every day, and at every moment; our death is base, while theirs is noble.
The young die as do the old; the wicked die as do the virtuous. Neither rank nor virtue, nor even age, can prevent it.
With a single breath not returning, one is instantly divided from the past and present.

If you do not prepare yourself early, but instead wait for even a moment—what will you do when, at that very instant, the execution warrant arrives and the executioner stands before you in a state of frantic confusion? How will you resist?
Furthermore, Yuan Zhonglang said: "Sentient beings dwelling in the world of the five turbidities are like prisoners in a jail;
this is because those who enter prison are all criminals, while those who dwell among humans and devas possess bodies that are merely segments of karmic retribution.
Yet, when a criminal enters prison, he seeks release at every moment, for he knows that beyond the thorny walls there exists another world of great peace and bliss."
For this reason, sentient beings today take afflictions as their home and birth-and-death as their garden;
they do not realize that the Great Iron Ring Mountains are the thorny walls of their own domain, nor that beyond the arena of the three realms, each has their own native land and place of bliss.
Out of compassion for them, the Buddhas distinguish between the pure and the defiled, pointing out the path for returning to liberation, yet over the long course of ages, this has been cast aside.
Those who have committed karmic offenses have no place of refuge; therefore, the Buddhas have further constructed great dwellings to settle them.
One serves as a gateway to the hells to manage the pathways, while the other constantly waits outside the prisons to maintain the guesthouses.
For such kindness, with what body could one possibly repay it? As the Sūtra says: "The Tathāgata appears in the world for one great matter. This "great matter" refers to...

This is precisely that matter. Since the Buddhas do not begrudge extending their hands to sentient beings, why is it that they instead cling to this mere hair-tip of a thing, exchanging the small for the great and dying without awakening? (The Parable of the Prison).
People of the world have a saying: "Accumulate moments of joy to prepare for death. Their meaning is this: human life is too bitter and the pure span of existence is too brief;

compared to meeting one's end in a state of panic and distress, what is better than indulging in pleasure to bring about rest? Should one happen to pass away together with the transformations of nature, when reflecting upon one’s entire life, there will surely be many joyful events.
Compared to those who spend their whole lives in poverty and exhaustion, is it not far superior to them? Indeed, it is.

This is of the same category as what people of old said: "Ten times listening to spring crying changes the tongue into that of a nightingale," and "Three times loathing one's own old ugliness leads one to exchange it for the [beauty of] Mount Emei.
I said: "If this were truly so, then it would be like adding weight to a shoulder-load or pouring more wood onto a boiling cauldron;

this is called hastening death, not preventing death. As the Buddha said: 'That which is received is itself empty. When food is set out with various flavors, if one releases the constraints [of attachment], then..."
When one departs empty-handed with a large retinue, it is empty upon arrival; though one may wander and observe all day, it is empty upon returning.
When good deeds are completed through diligent toil, they are empty; yet the white karma remains fully present. When evil deeds are completed with a sense of satisfaction, they are empty;
yet the black karma remains fully present. In this world, those who perform white deeds are few, while those who perform black deeds are many; thus, for a time—
To pursue such fleeting pleasures while creating a vast ocean of karmic karma—is this truly a strategy for preventing death?
Preventing death is the foremost task of a great man; the primary move in preventing death is none other than resolving the matter of birth and death.

To resolve the matter of birth and death, there is no method like reciting the Buddha's name to seek rebirth in the Western Paradise. Furthermore, there is a certain class of people who are shrouded by worldly flavors.

It is not permissible to take lofty ideals as one’s ambition or a life of leisure as one’s disposition; nor to seek to refine the spirit through poetry and wine, or to exchange the mundane world for the chessboard;
nor to fix the mind upon the Five Peaks or to chant amidst the mists and clouds—these are all those who merely waste their time in vain.

As for those above them—the ten classes of flying immortals and the feathered guests of the Three Mountains—it is not that they do not enjoy a carefree existence, soaring aloft on phoenixes and cranes to ascend into the void.

The nobleman was helpless, for his true nature remained unclarified and his cycle of birth and death unresolved. As乐天 (Le Tian) said: "Even if one were to attain longevity, it would only serve to surpass premature death.
To speak of 'long' is inherently to contrast it with 'short'; thus, one has not yet departed from the tracks of birth and death.
It is better, therefore, to study non-arising; where there is no arising, there is no ceasing. Truly profound these words! (To prevent death).

Sūn Dōpō said: "The other day, when Wáng Shí—the son-in-law of Hán Chíguó—came to visit me, he told me that Chíguó considered himself already old and intended to amuse his remaining years with music, song, wine, and women.
Sūn Dōpō replied: 'Precisely because it is one's final years, one should not act in such a manner.
Recently, there was an elderly man who hosted a banquet for his relatives and friends. When the drinking ended, he spoke to the assembly, and as he grew faint and prepared to depart—"
The sons cried out, wishing for him to leave behind a single word as instruction. The old man said, "You should simply rise at the first watch of the fifth watch.

The sons did not understand. The old man said, "Only during the fifth watch can one attend to one's own affairs. What are 'one's own affairs'? They are those things which can be taken with you at the time of death.
Now, as I am about to pass away after a lifetime spent managing my livelihood, what is there that I can take with me?"
My sons have somewhat awakened; I request that you speak to Zhiguo regarding the management of our own household affairs.

Rather than exhausting one's mind on fame and wine, it would be better to prepare for the time when death may come. (The phrase "manage our own household affairs" is to be compiled with what precedes it.)
"To live drunk and die dreaming" is a common saying, yet it is a profoundly true one. Generally, people of the world fall into two categories: the wealthy and noble, and the poor and lowly.
Those who are poor and lowly are certainly busy from morning until night to provide for their food and clothing;

those who are wealthy and noble are likewise busy from morning until night to enjoy sensual pleasures. While their experiences differ, their busyness is one and the same. This busyness continues until death, at which point it finally ceases.
The mind has not yet ceased; carrying this mind along, one is born again and again, busies oneself again and again, and dies again and again.
Birth and death, birth and death—dark and murky, as if intoxicated or dreaming—pass through hundreds of thousands of kalpas without ever reaching an end.
To be clearly and alone awake: such is the way of a great man. (Drunk in life, dreaming in death.)

The layman *Niu* (Put-and-Cow) attained awakening upon meeting the Elder Wumen, saying: "A person of great intelligence, as soon as they hear this matter, attempts to comprehend it with their mind, intellect, and consciousness;
thus, they mistake a reflection for reality. When the thirty days of the twelfth lunar month arrive and the light of their eyes is about to fall, they say to Old Man Yan:
'Wait until I have settled my mind and gathered my thoughts, and then I will go settle accounts with you! This is simply impossible."
It is indeed necessary to investigate with urgency and realize with urgency. Furthermore, Huangbo’s instruction says:

"If you do not strike through [the barrier] beforehand, when the thirtieth day of the twelfth month arrives, you will surely be in a state of frantic turmoil. However, these two characters, "strike through" (dache), must not be read too lightly;
it is not merely a matter of having mastered several volumes of sutras and treatises that constitutes "striking through," nor is it simply a matter of sitting for several incense sticks.
To attain thorough penetration by remaining unmoved and unshaken by incense is not it;
to compose several lines of verse on the recorded sayings and questions-and-answers of ancient worthies, or to perform "picking up the ancients" (niangu), is not it;

to attain thorough penetration by responding with a few lines of the slippery, smooth "verbal samādhi" (koutou sanmei) is not it. One who has attained true and thorough awakening is, in daily life, firmly and securely grounded.

Without moving a blade of grass, one can face the enemy from all eight directions; when impermanence arrives, one remains composed and at ease—neither frantic nor hurried, neither terrified nor confused.
Why wait until you must strain your mind to collect your thoughts and laboriously struggle to sustain yourself?
The ancients said that this matter is as clear as when the bottom of a bucket suddenly falls out, or as refreshing as waking from a great dream, leaving not even a trace of doubt.
Only when one is in a state of doubt can what is called "urgent inquiry and urgent awakening" occur; we should strive diligently for this (to achieve thorough awakening).
Huang鲁直 (Huang Tingjian) said: "If one seeks deeply the joy of Chan and pierces through the root of birth and death, then anxiety, fear, lust, and anger will have no place to take root;
by withering that root, the branches and leaves will naturally wither of themselves. This is an ultimate argument, yet it does not explicitly state who [should do this].
That which serves as the root of birth and death is, furthermore, the failure to penetrate the meaning of the words "illumination" within the essential point of the "joy of dhyāna.

If one attains the joy of dhyāna and deems it sufficient, then internally guarding this secluded tranquility is precisely the root of birth and death. One must exhaustively investigate through diligent inquiry until one clearly perceives one's own original nature;
only then will there be no place for birth and death to set foot. If even birth and death have no place to set foot, then where can sorrow?
Fearing lust and anger, by what means do they arise? (The root of birth and death; above, the transformation of the lotus).
To understand that objects are but delusive conditions, one sees how a thousand kinds of adornment serve only the half-inch eye, and a hundred varieties of music serve only the bean-sized ear.
Agarwood, sandalwood, brain-scented musk, and musk-deer are merely for the sake of two nostrils; food filling a square foot before one is merely for the sake of a three-inch tongue;
exquisite beauty and seductive charms are merely for the sake of a foul and decaying body; and compliance and flattery are merely for the sake of a wild and dissolute mind.
If one can discern this principle, one is a person who possesses no afflictions and dwells in happiness. The Buddha said that sentient beings have none [of these].
From the beginning, one has mistaken the thief for a son and plundered the family treasure; this refers to being deluded by the thieves of the six sense organs and thereby losing one's true nature.
Mencius said that only a sage can truly "fulfill the form," for such a person is not deluded by these things.
There was a courtesan who attained the Way; when Mañjuśrī asked her, "How is it that you do not feel anger? she replied, "I see all sentient beings."
Wu-sheng asked again, "How does one perceive the eighteen realms? He replied, "It is like seeing the kalpa-fire burning the world.
How marvelous these words! They mean that all sentient beings are originally non-existent; they exist only because of the arising of deluded thoughts. Since this is so, what anger could there be?
The eighteen realms refer to the six sense organs, the six sense objects, and the six consciousnesses; it is because of these various factors [that the realms arise].
Thus, one gives rise to immeasurable matters and commits immeasurable evils; therefore, it is as if the kalpa-fire were burning all worlds.
If one awakens to this principle, although one has not yet been born in the Pure Land, one is already as if born in the Pure Land. (The Six Sense Organs)
The *Prajñāpāramitā-hṛdaya Sūtra* states: "Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva, by perceiving that the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) are all empty, transcends all suffering and calamity.

The five aggregates refer to form (*rūpa*), sensation (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), mental formations (*saṃskāra*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*). Because these five accumulate and do not disperse, thereby obstructing and concealing true nature, they are called "aggregates" (*skandha*).
They are also called the "five obscurations" (*pañca-āvaraṇa*), meaning they darken true nature. The physical body ultimately returns to... [end of fragment]
When enjoyments are destroyed, they pass away instantly; are not forms and sensations empty?

Furthermore, when one contemplates an object, once it is obtained, there is no further thought of it; is not thought empty? When one turns back to examine the deeds one has performed, they are still like a dream or an illusion;
are not actions empty? When the ten types of objects of consciousness are exhausted, they are reborn such that consciousness can no longer recognize them; is not consciousness empty?
Is it not empty? All suffering and calamity arise from these five [aggregates].
If one can clearly perceive that the physical body is empty, then one will not be mired in the physical body and will not fear death; this is how one overcomes such suffering and calamity.
If one clearly perceives that sensory experience is empty, then one will not be mired in sensory experience and will not crave sustenance; this, too, is how one overcomes such [suffering].
To perceive that thought is empty is to transcend this kind of suffering and affliction; by not becoming mired in thought, the mind then has nothing to which it clings.
Furthermore, to perceive that action is empty is to transcend this kind of suffering and affliction;
by not becoming mired in action, one can still the traces of activity. To perceive that discernment is... [empty].
If one is empty [of self], one will not be mired in the discrimination of consciousness and can instead achieve "sitting-forgetfulness" (zuowang);
this is yet another way of transcending such suffering and calamity. Therefore, when one perceives that the five aggregates are all empty, one transcends all suffering and calamity.
These five [aggregates] are none of them real; they are merely illusory conditions manifested within the true nature. (The five aggregates are all empty.)
The general purport of the twenty-seven sections of the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states that true nature is entirely non-existent, like empty space.
This empty space is called "insentient emptiness" (*wankong*). Insentient emptiness is simply nothingness. Although true nature is like empty space, it contains [all phenomena] within it;
therefore, it is called "true emptiness" (*zhenkong*) rather than non-empty. Insentient emptiness can be created and can be destroyed.
If this earth were truly hollow, then digging away one foot of soil would result in one foot of void, and removing ten feet of soil would result in ten feet of void;
such would be a "stubborn void" (*wankong*) that can be fashioned.

If this vessel or this room were originally empty, yet becomes solid when objects are placed within it, this too would be a "stubborn void" that can be destroyed. However, the emptiness of true nature (*zhenxing*) cannot be fashioned.
The indestructible original nature inherently contains the world of empty space; how could it be something that can be created?

From beginningless time until this very day, it has never undergone change; how could it be destroyed? Within true nature, nothing exists at all, and thus there is nothing with which it can be compared.
For want of any other alternative, it is compared to "stubborn emptiness" (*wankong*). Thus, the *Prajñāpāramitā-hṛdaya Sūtra* says: "All these phenomena are empty."
They said to one another: "The characteristic that all phenomena are empty is precisely the true nature (*dharmatā*).
Since nothing at all exists, yet there are all sentient beings, these are merely illusory conditions manifested within the true nature.
The true nature is like a mirror, and all who have birth are like reflections; they are reflections manifested within the true nature. While the reflections come and go, the mirror..."
The true nature is ever-constant, even as sentient beings undergo birth and death; once birth and death are eliminated, the true nature manifests.
For birth and death are delusion, while the true nature is reality. Thus, the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* states: "When all delusions have vanished, what need is there for anything other than reality?
This nature has been present from the Buddhas above down to the most minute insects and living beings, without beginning.
That there is something distinct from this distinction is entirely illusory (the true nature).
Liezi said to Confucius: "Abandon the mind and employ the form. This means that the mind is no longer nourished by external things and is thus set aside;
one employs only the physical form to respond to things. I deeply cherish these words; therefore, even though I am exhausted and withered, I do not [desist].
He considered it a failure to lose honor, wealth, and the means of sustenance, rather than a success; this was because his mind did not cling to external things.
He further reflected that while Bodhisattvas have realized the nature of birth and death, they take birth among all sentient beings to establish their teachings;
this is because their minds do not cling to things, and they merely employ their physical forms to respond to circumstances. (Abandoning the mind to employ the form—above is from the *Lóngshū Wén*).
To realize that the thoughts of the mind are illusory:
Once, a brahmin held flowers in both hands and prostrated toward the Buddha. The Buddha said to him, "Let them go.
The brahmin let go of the flowers one by one from his two hands. The Buddha said, "Let them go. The brahmin replied, "I have let them all go. The Buddha said, "Let [your mind] go."
Regarding the meaning of the intermediate state below, later when Guanding heard the Buddha recite this verse, he said:

"If a person sits in stillness for even a single moment, it is superior to constructing stūpas of the seven treasures as numerous as the sands of the Ganges. Those stūpas will eventually turn to dust, but a single moment of stilling the mind achieves perfect enlightenment.
From this we know that the work toward perfect enlightenment begins entirely with stillness; "stillness" means the non-arising of a single thought.
This is what is called the Buddha-mind: supremely still, remaining thus for ten thousand kalpas. If sentient beings can achieve stillness for even a single kṣaṇa, they are Buddhas in that kṣaṇa;
if they can achieve stillness for even a single muhūrta, they are Buddhas in that moment.

Yet the thoughts of sentient beings are restless and agitated, like climbing vines spreading over brambles or silkworms drawing out their cocoons; they never come to rest until they grow weary and fall asleep. Thus it is said.

To have thoughts in a thousand directions is called distraction; to fall into a deep, sweet sleep is called torpor. These two states alternate throughout one's entire life, and it is from this that the cycle of birth and death begins.
Why is this so? The two characters for "birth and death" (生死) carry the meaning of arising and ceasing (*utpāda-nirodha*).
A single thought arising is birth; a single thought ceasing is death. Human existence is entirely comprised of the accumulation of such births and cessations.
To cross over these hundred years, how could one not be subject to the perpetual flux of birth and death throughout eternal kalpas?

This is entirely because there is a single point within the mind that cannot be let go of. If one considers what should be relied upon for contemplation, there is only the Dharma-gate of Buddha-remembrance (*buddhānusmṛti*).
For while remembrance is inherently delusory, by binding it to the Buddha, one uses delusion to dispel delusion.
To investigate through the mindfulness of the Buddha is to investigate the mind with the mind; to awaken through the mindfulness of the Buddha is to attain the mind with the mind.

Although it is said that thoughts arise, in reality there is no arising of thought. Through long-term practice based on this mindfulness, one attains the mind; when the mind is attained, thoughts are forgotten.
When thought reaches the state of non-thought, it is identical to non-mindfulness. Pure, tranquil, and unified, there is only the One True Reality.
Thus, the Bodhisattva Mahāsthāmaprāpta entered the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) by means of the Dharma-gate of mindfulness of the Buddha.
Now, having attained the patience of non-arising, there is no thought. To be without thought is the ultimate state of stillness. The *Zongjing lu* states:

"At the point where the prior and subsequent limits are severed, when not a single thought arises, for a brief moment one is tranquil; with no discursive mind, one correctly abides in this mind. Abiding in this mind is [the goal].

At that very moment is the fundamental substance; if it is the Buddha-mind, it is serene and eternally abiding. To take this mind that abides for a time and train it to gradually ascend is the practice.
Master Lianchi said: "Formerly, when Yangshan was presiding over a Chan monastery, the local deity wished to pay his respects to him but could not do so for a long time.
One day, as the Master entered the kitchen to offer incense, he saw that some food had been damaged."
The Master did not consciously give rise to the thought that "this offering from a faithful donor is to be regretted," and thus his spirit was able to perform the ritual prostrations.
Therefore, it is said that while not a single thought arises, ghosts and spirits cannot know;

yet we, from morning until evening, harbor floating thoughts and chaotic imaginings numbering in the tens of millions and billions. [How can we hope] to transcend birth and death and realize [enlightenment]?
"How could Nirvana be attainable? Master Qian Xiaozhi said: "I think that at the moment of departure, what is there that one cannot let go of?
If you say it is the worldly that one cannot let go of, I fear one will not be able to leap out of them;
one would inevitably return again, so why harbor such attachment? If you say it is this body that one cannot let go of, I fear one will not be able to shake it off."
If you have not yet escaped [suffering], you will inevitably undergo it again; how much more painful that will be!
If you say this mind cannot be let go of, I fear you have not severed it completely—you still harbor it as a seed, so how much more do you cherish it!
If you say the Buddha-dharma cannot be let go of, I fear you have not sprinkled it open; you cling to it and form a fetter of dharmas, so how much more do you love it! If you worry about wisdom...
If the faculties should ever become lost, that which you identify as the faculty of wisdom is precisely the life-faculty and precisely the eight consciousnesses.

That fear of losing even a single thought is precisely the seventh consciousness of ego-clinging; the sixth consciousness of discrimination must be cast off and purified until it is utterly exhausted.
Yet, if you still harbor a protective attachment toward it, then even the state of being fundamentally pure and originally luminous—this wondrous awakening—will not be permitted.
Through discernment, one reaches a state where nothing can be maintained; only when everything is no longer seen and not a single dharma remains can there be total manifestation.
When you were formerly deluded, you brought away all manner of things with you; today, upon awakening, what single thing do you intend to take away?
These words are exceedingly transcendent and may truly be called "unclad as a single thread."
(Setting aside the *Ōzanshō* and the *Renryū Tanka*).

Master Jitsujō of Ryōkai wished to cause all sentient beings throughout the great earth to perceive the Original Buddha Amitābha as their own true nature and to realize the Pure Land of the Mind-Only.
To universally awaken to the wondrous Way of Bodhi, he established the four-character title "Pujue Miaodao" (Universal Awakening Wondrous Way) as its definitive name.

Puji once discussed this, stating: "The realm of all sentient beings is called 'Universal' (Pu); to realize this principle is called 'Awakening' (Jue); for its virtuous function to be boundless is called 'Wondrous' (Miao);
and that which the thousand sages have trodden is called the 'Way' (Dao). Furthermore, "Universal" refers to one's own mind pervading the ten directions.

The essence is the self-mind; awakening is the function of that self-mind’s illuminating wisdom, free from delusion; the wondrous is the practice of that self-mind benefiting others and responding to their capacities;
and the Way is the principle of central harmony and rectitude thoroughly penetrated by that self-mind. This alone is what all Buddhas have realized as eternally wondrous;
this alone is what the patriarchs of successive generations have cultivated; and this alone is that through which one attains birth in the Pure Land.
The earth is for those who will study the Way in the future; this Great Dharma of the Tathāgata’s appearance in the world is entirely for the benefit of sentient beings.

Bodhisattvas practice without the slightest trace of self-interest. Those of later generations should take the Buddha’s mind as their own mind, diligently investigate the source of pure karma, and transmit the authentic seal of the lineage.
One must understand each principle clearly and gain self-confidence in this Dharma.
The Gate itself teaches others to believe in this Dharma-gate; it practices this path itself and teaches others to practice this path;

it vows for its own rebirth [in the Pure Land] and teaches others to vow for rebirth; it realizes its own original nature as Amitābha and teaches others to realize their own original nature as Amitābha.
Each receives the correct cause and together returns to the right path, transforming and delivering one another until the end of the future.
This truly continues the Buddha’s wisdom-life infinitely; how could it differ from that of the World-Honored One? Yet, where there is the correct, there is the deviant.
The correct can awaken the world, while the deviant can further delude it. The True Dharma is difficult to practice, whereas the winds of deviance are easily tainted.

The ten kinds of demonic subjects in the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* all arise from erroneous interpretations, and the ten categories of demonic karma in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* all stem from failing to recognize the true path.

For instance, the teachings of recent times—such as the White Lotus, Wuwei, Yuantun, Nirvana, Changsheng, and Shouchi schools—are all nothing but thefts of the remnants of the Buddhas' and Patriarchs' sutras and treatises;
they have invented "fox-dharma" Chan and spread the evil of the *qiongqi* demon to deceive the ignorant, greedily coveting wealth and inciting disorder.
At first, they attached themselves to Buddhism to propagate their waves; subsequently, they contended with Buddhism to raise their own banners.
Alas! In this final age, the Dharma is weak and Māra is strong; the teachings of Śākyamuni have reached a state of extreme ruin and disorder.

To speak briefly: there are those who erroneously interpret *namo*; there are those who erroneously interpret *prajñā*. Why is this so? There are those who erroneously interpret "Who is Nianfo" (Who is the Buddha-mindfulness);
there are those who falsely divide [the title] into "Male Pǔ" and "Female Miào"; and there are those who falsely divide it into three characters or four characters.

Regarding those who claim that the six characters of the Buddha’s name are divided into false categories—asserting that for laypeople it is the teaching of Amitābha and for monastics it is the teaching of Śākyamuni;
those who falsely claim that Śākyamuni has passed away and Maitreya governs the world; those who falsely claim to see ghosts and spirits by means of candlelight;
those who falsely claim to discern good and evil fortune through the breaking of incense smoke; and those who falsely claim to extract sins, draft men for labor, and collect the Dharma.

Among those who transformed their karmic bodies into male form, there were some who claimed to have received a proclamation from Heaven and been removed from the registers of the Underworld, thereby attaining longevity and transcending the kalpas;

some who, by looking into a mirror, saw themselves wearing the crowns and robes of kings and nobles; some who, through incantations, washed their eyes so that images of Buddhas, dragons, phoenixes, banners, and streamers appeared manifest in the air;
and some who mistakenly perceived husbands and wives as a single, unified entity, or men and women as inseparable.

Among those who practice the dual cultivation, there are those who mistakenly believe that failing to produce offspring constitutes non-arising, and those who erroneously hold that not extinguishing the desire for carnal pleasure constitutes non-extinction.
There are also those who misidentify the "Three Chariots," claiming that the nature is the ox-cart, the mind is the sheep-cart, and the intellect is the deer-cart.

Furthermore, there are various kinds of deceitful people who recklessly defile and falsely claim the Lotus School by employing the methods of Daoist self-cultivation, as if they were mere fabrications.
To grasp the channels of the four great elements as being like an interlaced net of jewels, to point to the colors and mind within the inch-square space as being analogous to Amitābha dwelling there,
to claim that the lungs belong to the West and are thus called the "Golden Land," and that the tongue producing saliva is named the "Flower Pond"—

these are like the arbitrary establishment of thirty-six gates and seventy-two stages of faith to force together strange occurrences; to speak of "seeing one's nature through the six gates" is likewise [a fabrication].
The fabrication of the "Sutra of Sixteen Characters" which instructs one to gather the breath at the navel and exert all effort to send it directly to the *dantian*,
as well as the forged "Treatise on Bodhidharma’s Embryonic Respiration," Zhaozhou’s "Songs for the Twelve Hours," and the "Verses on the Turning of the River Cart" by Layman Pang—
which were secretly transmitted and mutually upheld— are like falsely pointing to the mouth as the gate of all evils and the nose as the path to *nirvāṇa*. These are [false] teachings.

When a person approaches the end of life, they must close their mouth tightly and exert force to restrain the breath so that it exits through the nose, twisting the character [囗@力] (li) as the pivot to pass through this barrier;
this is called taking "one step out the gate. Furthermore, regarding these four characters surrounding it—some say they represent wine, women, wealth, and anger (*jiu-se-cai-qi*);

some say they represent earth, fire, water, and wind (*di-huo-shui-feng*); and some say they represent birth, old age, sickness, and death (*sheng-lao-bing-si*)—I do not know what these characters are called.
The character "A" (pronounced with a departing tone) is taken by the Chan school to describe a sudden awakening, where one abruptly utters this single sound;
how could there be such elaborate explanations? Furthermore, if the ten titles are all manifested, they are unified within the ten titles.

There is the magpie's nest on the journey home, the consecration of the reed sprout piercing the knee, the jade pillar, the coarse trousers, the snake entering the crotch of the trousers, and the Persian offering of jewels.
"The celestial drum does not sound and the lotus ponds dry up; the Second Patriarch cut off his arm and stood in the snow until it reached his waist, yet Shen Guang did not appear.
Those who equate this with the Buddha’s light illuminating both the hidden and the manifest, and thus name it "Surpassing the Light of the Sun and Moon," are deluded people.
They point to the rising sun and moon, instructing others to inhale and swallow their light so that it naturally becomes a treasure within the belly—this is like the *Lotus Sūtra*.

The Praising [of the Tathāgata] states that it is only at the very end that this sutra is preached; it uses the analogy of a wheel-turning monarch who bestows rewards upon his warriors and only at the very end produces the jewel from within his topknot.

This is merely the fabrication of deluded people who point to the circulation of vital energy (*qi*) entering the crown of the head, teaching others that there is a "fleshly protuberance-jewel" (*uṣṇīṣa-maṇi*) atop the Buddha’s head.
As the *Lotus Sutra* says: "All outflows are exhausted," meaning one does not act for the sake of sounds, forms, fragrances, tastes, or tangibles.
To be deluded by the Dharma is the mark of a deluded person who points to the human body as containing the seven treasures that can be transformed into *śarīra*.

They claim that one who has attained the fruit of the outflow-free (*anāsrava*) path should consume everything—eye discharge, nasal mucus, saliva, urine, and excrement alike. This is like the Chan Master Yue of Tuṣita who showed his assembly the "Three Barriers":
first, seeing one's nature; second, understanding birth and death; and third, knowing one's destination. These are merely the claims of deluded people pointing to the human body.

The *dantian* constitutes the three inner passes. Regarding the three outer passes from the feet to the waist, Master Yongjia, when traveling to Caoxi to pay homage to the Sixth Patriarch, recounted his "Song of the Right Path," stating:
"Since I recognized the road of Caoxi, I have known that birth and death are no longer concerned with me.
This refers to the false notion of some who point to the two passes along the spine at the base of the vertebrae as the "single stream of Caoxi."
Furthermore, he falsely claimed that the Sixth Patriarch had said, "It is better to save ten million laypeople than to save even half a monk from the empty gate.
Today, Wúwéi Chángshēng agitates the laity by claiming that the future Maitreya Buddha is currently manifest in the world,

specializing in saving only laypeople (*jūshì*) and not those of the "empty gate," and asserting that only when the ranks of spiritual friends (*shànzhīshí*) are reborn with hair will [the teaching] truly flourish.

When he attained Buddhahood and became a Patriarch, others who heard his teaching responded to him with a "yes. Thereupon, [the Master] said, "In that case, the Maitreya Buddha of King Śibi’s era should also have hair growing from the crown of his head!
The entire assembly laughed heartily. This is not to mention Yongjia’s saying: "The first was Kāśyapa, who transmitted the lamp;
twenty-eight generations in the Western Heaven are recorded in the chronicles. It is further said that in this Eastern Land, Bodhidharma is the first.

The six generations of Patriarchs transmitted the robe, renowned throughout the world; how could there be a principle whereby one in white robes might be ordained while those of the Empty Gate (the monastic community) are not?
For instance, when Master Zhaozhou saw a monk, he invariably asked whether the monk had "arrived" or "not yet arrived," to which he would simply reply, "Go drink tea.

When the temple steward asked why he did this, the Master called out to him; when the steward responded, the Master likewise said, "Go drink tea. It was for this reason that he became known as "Zhaozhou."

According to Cha'an, these are the fabrications of deluded people who claim that rinsing the mouth with saliva thirty-six times constitutes "drinking Zhaozhou’s tea," or who instruct others to take cinnabar tea at the moment of death to realize Zhaozhou’s "mechanism.
There are even those who consider drinking urine to be "drinking Zhaozhou’s tea. All such things are like ghosts and demons, the ravings of drunken dreams and madness.
It is not that these views exclude one another; rather, it is like "one blind man leading a crowd of blind men by the hand into a pit.

When such false views are deep-rooted, the retribution for evil is inexhaustible. An ancient master said: "Those who cultivate the Pure Land must first establish the orthodox teaching and then refute heterodox doctrines.
In this life, you vow to always encounter enlightened teachers and never encounter false views, so that your mind remains free from delusion and does not give rise to indolence."

How grave it is that the paths of the heterodox and the orthodox diverge; this is no minor matter. May the disciples of the Buddhas of the ten directions take care not to be ensnared by the demonic hordes, lest they rush into thorny thickets and fall into the hells; be cautious and exhort yourselves!

Attached is a refutation of the practice of "depositing in the treasury" (jìkù), which is of no benefit. Having examined the entire Tripitaka, I find no mention of such a doctrine as "depositing in the underworld treasury.

I urge all people of the world to use the funds intended for depositing in the treasury to instead invite renowned monks to recite sutras and chant the Buddha’s name, resolving to be reborn in the Western Paradise; if one does not do this, [the merit will be lost].

To devote oneself to the practice of depositing wealth in a treasury, regardless of whether it is for grand aspirations or mere profit, is of no benefit; if your intent is fixed upon the underworld, you will surely enter the underworld after death.
If one claims that what is accumulated in this life is to be enjoyed in the next, then there would be no basis for the retribution of good and evil experienced before birth;
only the ill-gotten gains accumulated through such injustice can serve as the master key to govern both the world of light and the realm of darkness, and to transform the course of one's destiny.
I fear that there is no such obscure principle of Heaven as you suggest.

It is like a person who does not strive to eliminate evil and practice goodness, but instead deposits money with the jailer or the head of the prison, intending to use it to avoid punishment once he has been cast into jail—is this not utterly deluded?

Appendix: Reciting Sutras and the Three Precepts. When reciting sutras, one must strictly avoid giving rise to distracting thoughts or reciting in a distracted manner by blending one’s mind with that of the assembly. To commit such errors will inevitably result in the illness of indistinctness and interruption in the text; not only is it of no benefit, but it is sinful. How can one not be cautious? It is as follows: 1. One must maintain a focused mind and not allow the breath to be disturbed.

2. One must not allow the tongue to tire or the voice to falter. 3. One must not allow the eyes to wander or the body to be restless. If these three precepts are observed, the merit of the recitation will be complete. If they are violated, the fault lies with oneself. Therefore, one should be most diligent. Do not be negligent. Respectfully submitted.
When reciting alone, one must concentrate the mind without distraction in order for each word to be clearly articulated;

when reciting with a group, it is essential that each person holds their own scroll so as to avoid lapses caused by changing breaths. Ancient masters constantly used these words to admonish the world, yet the habit remains unbroken.
Regarding the purification of bodily impurities, one must scrub with soap; furthermore, the monastic regulations state: "Wash..."
Even if one were to scoop up all the waters of the four great oceans to wash [the hands], they could not be purified unless the purification mantra is recited.
The purification mantra says: *Oṃ haṇa miṣṭe svāhā*. The hand-washing mantra says: *Oṃ sugatavākya svāhā*. One should recite these three times;
those who chant the sutras must be especially careful.
The Morning Bell of the Pure Land, Scroll Nine;
The Morning Bell of the Pure Land, Scroll Ten; Accounts of Experiences in Upholding the Pure Land.
That which possesses the principle but lacks the fact cannot serve as a teaching. That which possesses the fact but lacks the verification cannot serve as a teaching.
That which possesses the verification yet is sometimes true and sometimes false cannot serve as a teaching.

Now, this Dharma-gate possesses the principle of purifying the mind and purifying the land, and because it possesses the cause for proceeding to the Land of Peaceful Nurturing (An-yang), [it may be accepted].
Regarding the matter of rebirth, there are instances such as the miraculous manifestation of golden pedestals and jeweled ponds;
furthermore, there are countless various accounts of the rebirth of sages and worthies throughout antiquity and the present. Thus, the Tathāgata’s instruction is not a deception.

As for recording these verified signs, even in remote villages and secluded monasteries within the land of Zhendan (China), there are often those who walk alone like solitary blossoms and, when facing [death]—
How much more so for those who, though once illustrious, are not recorded in the annals and whose names have consequently vanished and been lost to tradition?
Even if one were to take the entire earth as ink and all the bamboo and reeds as pens to write from China throughout the Sahā world and across the ten directions, one could still not exhaust them;
therefore, I have selected the most prominent accounts from past records and compiled them here according to their categories. As for these...
The great masters of the intervening ages were certainly capable of sounding the bells and drums for their own era, and their illuminating influence remains inexhaustible;
yet even down to a common husband and wife, if they sever doubt with a single thought, they possess the strategic resolve of a great man—such individuals serve as models for the vulgar world.
The *Preface to the Collection on Rebirth* states: "When those among the monastic and lay communities read this book, they will point to it one by one, saying, 'This is so-and-so.'"
One is born as such through such liberation; one is born as such through such purity and singleness of mind;
one is born as such through such ultimate sincerity that moves the divine response; one is born as such through such great compassion and great vows;
and one is born as such through such unrelenting repentance that transforms karma at the very moment of falling.
Such-and-such [a person] was reborn in the upper realms, such-and-such in the middle, and such-and-such in the lower;

may this serve as a left-hand voucher for those practicing the pure karma by using the past to verify the present. As for why ancient examples are many while contemporary examples are few—where does the blame lie?
It is, as it were, because their mouths are in the Pure Land while their minds remain in Saṃsāra, and their steadfastness, vigor, and clarity of realization fall short of those of former generations.
In your case, Qingtai, the lotus flowers have both flourished and withered; since you yourself brought this about, what blame can there be for the Pure Land?

In this world, there are those who long for their hometowns and hasten back; having already traveled the path there, this is a precedent for them. This concludes the tenth account of verified experiences.
The Bhikṣu who was reborn [in the Pure Land], the Venerable Master Huiyuan of the Eastern Jin, was surnamed Jia and was a native of Yanmen. His learning encompassed Confucianism;

at over twenty years of age, upon hearing Dharma Master Dao’an lecture on the *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, he attained sudden and clear enlightenment, exclaiming: "The nine schools of Confucianism and Daoism are all mere chaff."

Huiyi subsequently underwent tonsure and took up the monastic life, constantly regarding the Great Dharma as his own responsibility. An Shigao sighed, saying, "If the Way is to flow into China, will it not be through Huiyuan?
Later, Huiyuan entered Mount Lu and planted his staff where he found a spring; wishing to build a monastery (*ārāma*), he lamented the lack of fine timber.
He was moved by a mountain deity who appeared in a dream, and one night there was a great storm of thunder and rain. When day broke, timber was piled up like a forest.
The Provincial Governor Huan Yi, marvelling at his spiritual wonders, memorialized the throne to establish the Donglin Hall, saying:

"Master Shen-yun once remarked that while there are many names for samādhis among the various teachings, those of high merit are easy to attain through the practice of Buddha-recollection (*nien-fo*), which is therefore foremost.

He subsequently formed a *shè* (society) with Huiyong, Huichi, Liu Yimin, and others to recite the Buddha’s name; they were known in the world as the Eighteen Sages. Furthermore, he led a multitude numbering over one hundred and twenty to join them.

Thirteen people together cultivated the pure practice (*śukla-karma*) and fashioned a *padma-ghaṭikā* (lotus water-clock) so that they could perform their liturgical recitations during the six periods of the day without ceasing;

for thirty years, they never entered the secular world. Whenever they saw off guests, they used the Tiger Brook (*Huxi*) as the boundary. Once, when Tao Yuanming and Lu Xiujing arrived, the Master saw them off;
as their paths were in accord with the Way, they did not realize they had already crossed the brook. This is what is famously known in the world as the "Portrait of the Three Laughs. Emperor An...

In the first year of the Long’an era, Huan Xuan urged the Emperor to purge the monks and nuns; however, he claimed that Mount Lu, being a place where the Way and Virtue reside, was exempt from this regulation.
The Master composed a letter to debate this matter, and both parties were spared.

When the Emperor returned to the capital from Jiangling, He Wuji, the Guardian of the State, advised the Master to go out to welcome him, but the Master feigned illness and did not rise. The Emperor sent an envoy to inquire after him, and the Master submitted a memorial to inform the throne.

The Emperor issued a gracious edict in response to this. The monks of the Western Regions all proclaimed that China possessed a Mahāyāna Bodhisattva, and they would regularly face the east to pay him homage.
Kumārajīva sent letters referring to the Master as a "Dharma-protecting Bodhisattva of the East.
On the evening of the final day of the seventh month in the twelfth year of the Yixi era, after emerging from meditative absorption, the Master beheld the vision of Amitābha.
The Buddha’s body filled the void, and within his radiant halo were immeasurable transformation Buddhas; Avalokiteśvara and Mahāsthāmaprāpta stood in attendance to his left and right.
The Buddha said, "By the power of my original vows, I have come to comfort you; seven days from now, you shall be born in my land.
He also saw Buddhabhadra, Huichi, Huiyong, and Liu Yimin by the Buddha's side; they bowed forward to the Master.

He said, "My teacher’s aspiration was for this; why has he come so late? When the Master knew the time had arrived, he said to his disciples, "I first resided here and beheld the holy countenance three times;
now I behold it once more. It is certain that I shall be born in the Pure Land.
On the appointed day, he sat upright and entered nirvana at the age of eighty-three, on the sixth day of the eighth month. The Governor of Xunyang, by imperial decree, erected a stupa for his burial.

Xie Lingyun composed an inscription for him and Zhang Ye wrote a preface; throughout the successive dynasties, he has been honored with posthumous titles. His extant works comprise ten volumes of the *Lushan ji* (Lu Shan Collection).
Examining the history of the Pure Land tradition, although it was transmitted to China, it became established through Fotudeng. From Fotudeng, the Way was attained by Dao’an;
within Dao’an’s school was Master Huiyuan, who bore the ultimate teachings and expanded the Great Holy Way, his fame being esteemed even by the Emperor.
The royal law spread throughout the world for a hundred generations; looking back upon his merit, was it not truly magnificent that he was promoted as the progenitor of the Pure Land school?
Huiying of Jin was a native of Henei; he left home at the age of twelve and subsequently relied upon Master Dao’an together with Master Huiyuan.
At the beginning of the Taiyuan era, he took up residence at Mount Lu. The Regional Inspector, Tao Fan, donated his own residence to become Xilin Monastery for him to dwell in.

He severed all ties with worldly clamor and fixed his mind on the Land of Ultimate Bliss. Later, in the tenth year of the Yixi era, he manifested illness; suddenly, he adjusted his robes and asked for his sandals, wishing to rise.

The assembly was startled and questioned him, to which he replied, "The Buddha has come to welcome me. Having spoken these words, he passed away. A rare fragrance lingered for seven days before finally fading.
Emperor Xuanzong of the Tang dynasty posthumously conferred upon him the title of Great Master Jueji (Awakened Quiescence).

Tan-shun of Jin was a native of Huanglong; in his youth, he followed Dharma Master Kumārajīva to lecture on and explain various sutras. Kumārajīva marveled at him, saying, "This youth is a vessel of extraordinary talent.
Later, while he was practicing the Pure Land path together with others at Mount Lu, Liu Zunkao, the General-in-Chief for Pacifying the Barbarians, established... [the text here is incomplete].

In the temple at Jiangling, Yan-shun began the earnest practice of the *nien-fo san-mei* (Buddha-recollection samādhi). In the second year of the Yuanjia era of the Song dynasty, he passed away while sitting in seclusion from the assembly;
a rare fragrance filled the room.
Hui-rui of Jin was a native of Jizhou; he traveled to study in various regions, journeying as far as India, and upon returning to Guanzhong, followed Kumārajīva.
After the Dharma Master had received and mastered the meaning of the scriptures, he joined the Lotus Society at Mount Lu.
In the sixteenth year of the Yuanjia era of the Song dynasty, he suddenly announced to the assembly, "I am about to depart. Facing west with palms joined, he passed away.
The assembly saw a golden lotus flower appear before Huì’s couch, which vanished in an instant, while five-colored fragrant smoke issued from his room.
Tanheng of Jin was a native of Hedong. Having joined the monastic order as a youth under Master Huiyuan, he became thoroughly versed in both Buddhist and secular classics.

After entering Mount Lu, he devoted himself exclusively to the practice of *nianfo* (recollection of the Buddha). In the fourteenth year of the Yixi era, he sat upright with palms joined and, chanting the Buddha’s name with a resolute voice, passed away.

Dao Bing of Jin was a native of Yingchuan. In his youth, he studied under Master Huiyuan, mastering both the sutras and the vinaya; his words and deeds were in perfect accord. He devoted himself to the *nianfo samādhi* with uninterrupted focus on the mind.
In the fourteenth year of the Yixi era, Wang Qian, the Governor of Yuzhang, entered the mountains to pay his respects and requested that Dao Bing succeed Master Huiyuan on the monastic seat.
The assembly all looked up to him with reverence. In the twelfth year of the Yuanjia era, he gathered the congregation for the practice of *nianfo*. Upon reaching [the end of the session], he...
He attained transformation while seated.
Daojing of Jin was a native of Langye; his grandfather, Ningzhi, served as the Governor of Jiangzhou, and Daojing subsequently left home to become a monk under Master Huiyuan.

At the age of seventeen, he was extensively versed in the sutras and treatises, memorizing ten thousand words a day. He was devoted to the practice of *nianfo* (recollection of the Buddha), never ceasing day or night. During the Yongchu era of the Song dynasty...
In the first year of his reign, Yuan said to the assembly, "The former master has commanded me; it is time for me to depart. Sitting upright, he chanted the name of the Buddha and passed away.
The assembly saw a radiance fill the room, which did not vanish until a long time had passed.

Hui-gong of Jin was a native of Fengcheng in Yuzhang. He studied together with Hui-lan and Seng-guang; Lan and Guang focused their mindfulness on the Pure Land, and at the time of their deaths, both experienced miraculous responses.
Furthermore, five years later, when Hui-gong fell gravely ill, he wept like rain and prostrated himself, vowing to settle his mind in the practice of *anxiang* (recollection of the Buddha).
Without a moment's interruption in his mindfulness, he beheld Amitābha Buddha coming forward to welcome him upon a golden platform, which he mounted.
Furthermore, he saw Lan and the others on the terrace, within the radiance, saying: "Elder, having been reborn, you now dwell in the highest grade;
we are exceedingly joyful and comforted. They then departed with respectful joy and vigorous energy.

Huiqian of the Jin dynasty left home to become a monk at a young age; his observance of the precepts was precise and rigorous. During the Yixi era, he joined the Jiaxiang Temple in Shanyin, where he disciplined his body and led the assembly.
Later, while suffering from illness, he focused his thoughts on the Land of Ultimate Bliss and offered sincere prayers to the Great Being (Avalokiteśvara).

At that time, there was a nun named Jingyan at Beisi who was renowned for her long-standing virtue and steadfast practice. One night, she dreamed that Avalokiteśvara entered through the western city gate, his pure radiance and wondrous form shining with light.

The sun and moon were reflected [in the sky], which was adorned with banners, streamers, and flower canopies made of the seven treasures. The nuns were struck with wonder and prostrated themselves, asking, "Where is the Mahāsattva going?
He replied, "I am going to Jiāxiáng to welcome Master Qián. Qián’s countenance remained as usual; his attendants all smelled an extraordinary fragrance, and he passed away in perfect stillness.
Throughout his life, Song Tanjian dedicated every slight merit toward the Western Pure Land, vowing to behold the Buddha.
One day, while in meditative absorption, he saw Amitābha Buddha sprinkle water upon his face and say: "I wash away your defilements and bathe your mental thoughts;

may your body and speech all become utterly pure. Furthermore, the Buddha produced a single lotus flower from a vase and bestowed it upon him. When he arose from meditation, [the flower] was still there with him.
As the night grew deep during their parting, the temple monk walked alone along the corridor reciting the Buddha’s name until the fifth watch; his voice became increasingly intense.
Then, when his disciple came as usual to inquire after him, he was found sitting cross-legged, motionless, having passed away.

Hui-guang of the Qi dynasty resided in Luoyang and composed commentaries on the *Avataṃsaka*, the *Nirvāṇa*, and the *Daśabhūmika* Sūtras, exhaustively elucidating the profound intent of the provisional and the ultimate.
One day, while ill, he saw celestial hosts coming to welcome him. Hui-guang said, "My vow is to return to the Land of Peaceful Nurturing (An-yang).
Shortly thereafter, transformation Buddhas of the Pure Land filled the void. Hui-guang said, "I only pray that our Buddha will receive me and fulfill my original aspiration."
As soon as he made this vow, he snapped his fingers and cleared his throat, whereupon his speech and breath ceased entirely.

Daozhen of the Liang dynasty lived at Mount Lu and cultivated the practice of Pure Land; in a dream, he saw someone on a boat in the middle of the sea who asked him where he was going, to which he replied, "I am going to the land of Amitābha Buddha.
Daozhen requested to accompany him, but the man replied, "Since you have not yet recited the *Amitābha Sūtra*, how can you go with me?"
After his awakening, he practiced mindfulness of the Buddha and recited the scriptures for many years without ceasing.
Forty-nine days before his death, during the night, it was suddenly as bright as day, and a silver platform descended from the sky. He silently recorded this event within the scripture case.

On the evening of the day his life ended, everything above the mountain midpoint was illuminated by the mutual radiance of thousands of torches like a great conflagration; villagers seeing this from afar mistook it for [the arrival of] various [deities].

The King paid him a visit and audience; it was only after Fazhen’s death that he opened the scripture box and learned that Fazhen had manifested auspicious signs and was destined for rebirth in a Pure Land.

Later, during the Northern Wei dynasty, Tanluan, a native of Yanmen, traveled to Mount Wutai in his youth, where he was moved by spiritual wonders and entered the monastic order; by nature, he was fond of [the teachings of] Long...
Sheng received the *Ten Fascicles of the Immortal Scriptures* from Master Tao Yijun. Later, upon meeting Bodhiruci, he asked, "Does the Buddha possess an art for longevity and immortality?
Bodhiruci smiled and said, "Longevity and immortality are precisely our Buddhist Way.

He then bestowed upon him the *Sutra of the Sixteen Contemplations*, saying, "If you study this, there shall be no further rebirth within the three realms and no further wandering through the six paths; such is the true span of life."
"Even the stone of kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges cannot compare to this; this is the longevity of our Golden Immortal (the Buddha).

Sengluan was greatly delighted and subsequently burned the *xianjing* (immortality scriptures) to cultivate the pure karma (*śuddhakarma*). Whether in cold or heat, or during illness and pain, he never slackened even slightly.
The Wei ruler titled him "Divine Luán. One night, in his chamber, he saw a Buddhist monk who said to him, “I am Nāgārjuna; I have long dwelt in the Pure Land.”
Because you share my same aspirations, I have come to meet you. Sengluan, knowing that the time had arrived, gathered the assembly and instructed them, saying:
"The toil of this weary life continues without end; one must not fail to fear the various sufferings of hell, nor must one fail to cultivate the pure karma of the nine grades.
He then led his disciples to recite the Buddha's name aloud while prostrating toward the west, and he passed away. The assembly heard him.
Celestial music came from the west and ceased only after a long while.
The Great Master Zhizhe of the Sui dynasty, whose name was Zhiyi and whose secular surname was Chen, was a native of Yingchuan.

On the night his mother dreamed that five-colored incense smoke coiled and entered her breast, a divine light illuminated the house on the evening he was born. At the age of seven, he entered Guoyuan Temple and heard the monks [reciting].
Each time he recited the "Universal Gate" chapter once, he would remember it as clearly as if it were something he had practiced since childhood.
At eighteen, while studying under Great Master Wenshi at Mount Dasu, he went there to pay his respects. Wenshi said, "In the past at Vulture Peak, we heard the Lotus Sutra together;

now, driven by our karmic affinity from former lives, you have come here again. He then showed him the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra’s place of practice and expounded for him the four kinds of peaceful and blissful conduct.

The Master entered into meditative observation for twenty-one days, after which his body and mind were suddenly enlightened and his latent spiritual powers manifested. He reported what he had realized to his teacher, Nanyue, who sighed and said, "If it were not you, none could have realized this;
if it were not I, none could have recognized it. This is the *prathama-āvartā dhāraṇī* of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-samādhi*.
In the first year of the Dajian era, he went to Jinling to propagate the teachings; Emperor Xuan of the Chen dynasty established a meditation hall for him to reside in during the Sui dynasty.

Emperor Yang invited the Master to receive the precepts and bestowed upon him the title "Zhizhe" (Wise One). He once wore a single tattered robe while preaching the Dharma at Tiantai for over twenty years.

He composed commentaries on the *Amitābha Sūtra*, the *Ten Doubts*, the *Profound Meaning of the Lotus Sūtra*, and other works, encouraging people to advance in the practice of Pure Land Buddhism—achievements that surpassed those of previous sages.
In the twelfth year of the Kaihuang era, he established a monastery at Mount Yuquan.
Shaguansheng, father and son, manifested their spiritual efficacy and requested to become protectors of the Dharma.

In the winter of the seventeenth year, as he was about to enter parinirvāṇa, he instructed his attendant to chant the name of Amitābha Buddha and the titles of the *Amitāyurdhyāna Sūtra*. He then looked toward the assembly, joined his palms, and praised them, saying:

"The forty-eight vows adorn the Pure Land; its lotus ponds and jeweled trees are easy to reach, yet no one goes there. When the signs of the burning chariot appear, [only those who have cultivated merit can escape]."
Those who repent can still attain rebirth; how much more so for those who cultivate the power of the path through the熏 (*vāsanā*) of precepts and wisdom! Thus, their practice is truly not in vain.

When the recitation of the sutra is finished, he further explains the ten suchnesses, the four non-arisings, the ten dharma-realms, the four immeasurables, the four noble truths, the twelve links of dependent origination, and the six *pāramitās*.
Having finished explaining each of these dharma-gates, he chants the names of the Triple Gem, as if entering the three [refuges].
Later, there was a monk who sought to know the place where he would be reborn. He dreamed of the golden countenance of Avalokiteśvara, several zhang in height.
From behind, Zhizhe told the monk, "Do you wish to resolve your doubts? Upon further verification, it was found that Zhizhe had been reborn in the Western Pure Land.
During the Sui dynasty, Daoyu resided at Kaijue Monastery, where he recited the name of Amitābha Buddha day and night without ceasing. He fashioned a statue of the Buddha measuring only three cun.

Later, while in meditative concentration, he saw the Buddha, who said to him, "Why have you made my image so small? Daoyu replied, "If the mind is great, the image is great; if the mind is small, the image is small.
As soon as he had spoken, he saw the body of the Buddha pervading all of space. The Buddha then told him, "You should bathe yourself."
When the pure morning star appeared, I came to welcome you; when the time arrived, I indeed saw the Buddha arrive with his radiance filling the room, whereupon you sat and passed away.
During the Zhenguan era, the Tang dynasty, Shan Dao saw Master Chao of Xihe at the Nine Grades Practice Hall and said joyfully, "This is truly it."

Entering the essential gateway of the Buddha’s teaching requires that other practices be set aside, for they are scattered and difficult to perfect; only this path is focused and decisive, allowing for swift transcendence of birth and death.
Thus, he was diligent and austere, bowing and reciting day and night, inspiring the fourfold assembly.

Whenever he entered his room, he knelt on his right knee and recited the Buddha’s name, never ceasing until his strength was exhausted. Upon leaving, he would expound the teachings to others. For over thirty years, he never grew weary of this practice.

He would sleep briefly during the day; his daily food and clothing were coarse and simple. Whenever he received offerings or donations, he would transcribe one hundred thousand scrolls of the *Amitābha Sūtra* and create three hundred wall murals depicting the transformations of the Pure Land. He restored dilapidated sites and maintained lamps to keep the light burning.

He did not have others carry his three robes, alms bowl, or water jar, nor did he associate with the multitude for fear of discussing worldly affairs. Those who followed his transformation were extremely numerous.

There were those who recited the *Amitābha Sūtra* one hundred thousand to five hundred thousand times, and those who took it as their daily practice to chant the Buddha’s name ten thousand to one hundred thousand times;
those who attained the samādhi of Buddha-remembrance and were reborn in the Pure Land could not be fully recorded.

Someone asked, "Is one reborn in the Pure Land through the recitation of the Buddha's name? The Master replied, "If you recite the Buddha's name as you do now, you will fulfill your vow; this is indeed self-recollection."
With each utterance, a single ray of light issued from his mouth, increasing from ten to a hundred rays, all of which were likewise so.
His exhortatory verse said: "Gradually the skin becomes like that of a chicken, the hair turns white like a crane; watch as the gait grows increasingly unsteady and decrepit.
Even if gold and jade fill the halls, how can one avoid decay, aging, and the suffering of illness? No matter how many kinds of pleasures you may have, impermanence will inevitably arrive at last."
There was a practitioner on the path who, while single-mindedly reciting the name of Amitābha Buddha, suddenly said to others:
"This body is loathsome; I shall return to the West. He then climbed a willow tree and, facing west, made this vow:

"May the Buddha receive me and may the Bodhisattvas assist me, so that I do not lose right mindfulness and may be reborn in the Pure Land. Having spoken, he threw himself down and passed away. Emperor Gaozong took notice of this.
The Emperor bestowed upon him the temple plaque titled "Guangming" (Luminous). Tradition holds that he was an emanation of Amitābha.

During the second year of the Dali era of the Tang dynasty, Fazhao resided at Yunfeng Temple in Hengzhou; his compassion, forbearance, and meditative concentration were held in high esteem by his contemporaries.
Once, within his alms bowl, he beheld five-colored clouds forming a Brahma-palace called Dasheng Zhulin Temple (Great Sage Bamboo Grove Temple), after which he traveled there.
On Mount Wutai, he beheld a wondrous light and subsequently entered the lecture hall of Zhulin Monastery.

There, Mañjuśrī was seated to the west and Samantabhadra to the east, surrounded by a multitude of ten thousand beings as they preached the Dharma. Zhaoying paid homage and asked: "I am but an ordinary person of the final age;
I do not know what dharma-gate I should cultivate. Mañjuśrī replied: "Among all gates of cultivation, none is equal to the recollection of the Buddha. I myself practice through this recollection."
The Buddha, having attained all-encompassing wisdom (sarvākārajñatā), was asked again how one should practice mindfulness. He replied: "To the west of this world lies Amitābha Buddha;
the power of that Buddha’s vows is inconceivable. You should diligently maintain mindfulness so as not to let it be interrupted, and you will certainly attain rebirth there.

Later, on the first day of the twelfth lunar month, while at the Pure Practice Dharma-Assembly Hall in Huayan Monastery, he finally recalled the prediction of the two Great Beings (Mañjuśrī and Samantabhadra).
When I was about to pass away, I single-mindedly recited the Buddha’s name. Suddenly, I saw the Indian monk Buddhapāli, who said to me, "Your lotus pedestal is already prepared;
three years from now, the flower shall open. When the appointed time arrived, he said to the assembly, "I am going," and passed away sitting upright.

The Master once held five assemblies for the recitation of the Buddha's name at Huduosi Temple on the eastern shore of Lake Dongting; there, he perceived auspicious clouds and a jeweled pavilion, and beheld Amitābha.

The body of Amitābha Buddha and that of the two Bodhisattvas filled the void. Furthermore, during the Fifth Assembly for the Recitation of the Buddha's Name in Bingzhou, Emperor Daizong heard the sound of the recitation within his palace and dispatched an envoy to investigate; he then beheld the Master’s flourishing efforts in exhorting others to practice.

Consequently, the Emperor issued an edict summoning him to the capital to instruct the palace women in the recitation of the Buddha’s name, also conducting five assemblies; thus, he was titled the Dharma Master of the Five Assemblies.
Tang Shaokang was a native of Jingyun Xindu. At fifteen, he mastered the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* and the *Śūraṅgama-samādhi-sūtra*.

During the Zhenyuan era, while visiting Baima Monastery in Luoyang, he saw light emanating from some characters within the hall. Upon examining them, he found they were the "Text for Guiding Others toward the Western Pure Land" by Master Shandao.
The Master prayed: "If I have a karmic affinity with the Pure Land, may these characters emit light once more. As soon as he had finished speaking, [the light shone forth].
As the brilliant light flashed, the Master said, "Even if the kalpa-stone could be worn away, my vow shall never change.
He then proceeded to Chang’an and paid homage at the portrait hall of Venerable Shandao at Guangben Temple.

Suddenly, he beheld Shandao appearing in the air, who said to him, "If you follow my teachings and extensively transform sentient beings, when your merit is perfected, you will surely be reborn in An-yang (Sukhāvatī). Thereupon, he traveled to Xin-ding to seek alms.
He enticed small children to recite the Buddha’s name by giving them one coin for every ten recitations.
For over a year, everyone they encountered—whether young or old, noble or humble—would all chant "Amitābha Buddha. The sound of their recitation filled the roads.
Furthermore, he established a Pure Land practice hall at Mount Wulong; whenever he ascended the seat to preach, the assembly would see a Buddha emerging from [the image].
From his mouth issued ten sounds, and there were ten Buddhas. The Master said, "Those of you who have seen the Buddhas will certainly attain rebirth.
At that time, among the thousands in the assembly, there were those who did not see them; they grieved and reproached themselves, whereupon they redoubled their diligent practice.

Twenty-one years later, on the third day of the tenth month, he addressed the monastics and the laity, saying: "You should give rise to a heart of joyful aspiration for the Pure Land, while regarding Jambudvīpa [with detachment]."
Arousing a mind of weary detachment, you disciples then beheld my radiance; truly my disciples, you subsequently emitted several rays of extraordinary light and departed.
A stupa was erected at Taizi Rock, and he was titled the Dharma Master of Taiyan. Some may doubt that the Buddha emerged from his mouth, deeming it somewhat strange;
yet, alas, when the World-Honored One encountered the intoxicated elephant, golden light issued from the tips of his five fingers like lions.

He said, "How could I have had any intention of warding off the elephant? It was through the power of compassion and patience cultivated by me over immeasurable kalpas that the lion appeared naturally;
I myself did not know it. Now, the manifestation of the Buddha by Lord Kang is likewise the result of his having paid homage and respect over immeasurable kalpas—what is there to wonder at?"

Tang Huaiyu was a native of Taizhou who lived as a layman, eating but once a day and remaining in a seated posture without lying down. He recited the *Amitābha Sūtra* three hundred thousand times and daily chanted the Buddha’s name fifty thousand times. In the first year of the Tianbao era, he beheld Buddhas and Bodhisattvas filling the void; one person came to welcome him with a silver platform. Huaiyu said, "Throughout my life I have practiced nianfo and vowed to obtain a golden platform; why does the Sage bring a silver one? The person replied, "The silver platform is for those who practice nianfo while harboring doubt. Huaiyu immediately prostrated himself on the ground, and instantly a golden platform appeared. He ascended it and passed away. His body was cremated, and his remains were enshrined at the Jingci Monastery in Hangzhou. It is said that whenever the wind blew, a fragrance would emanate from the stupa. Later, during the reign of Emperor Xuanzong, the stupa was opened, and his tongue remained unscathed. It was subsequently enshrined within the Great Tang Temple in Yangzhou. During the Tianfu era of the Later Zhou, the temple was destroyed by fire, yet the tongue remained intact. In the second year of the Dazhong era of the Song dynasty, the relics were moved to the Lingyin Monastery in Hangzhou, where they remain to this day. Furthermore, in the second year of the Dazhong Xiangfu era, when the monk Zhiyuan of the Shengshou Monastery in Yuezhou performed a great assembly, he saw a radiant light in the sky. Upon investigation, he discovered that the relic of Tang Huaiyu had manifested a transformation body and was preaching the Dharma there. Thus, it is known that the power of nianfo is truly inconceivable. Those who wish to attain rebirth in the Land of Ultimate Bliss should single-mindedly practice nianfo. If one can chant the Buddha’s name ten thousand times a day, one will certainly be welcomed by the Buddha upon death. If one chants the Buddha’s name ten million times throughout one's life, one will surely attain rebirth in the Pure Land. One should not harbor doubts. If one practices nianfo without doubting, one will be born in the Western Land. If one harbors doubts while chanting, one will fall into the evil realms. Therefore, one must resolve to practice with unwavering sincerity. If one can maintain this resolve until the end of life, one will surely attain rebirth in the Land of Peace and Bliss. This is the true path to liberation. One should not seek other methods. If one abandons nianfo to pursue other paths, one will wander through the six realms of existence and suffer immeasurable pain. Therefore, one must take up the practice of nianfo with all one's heart. Do not let the opportunity pass. If you encounter this dharma and do not practice it, you will regret it for a thousand eons. The time is now; do not delay. Practice nianfo with diligence and you shall surely attain rebirth in the Pure Land. This is the essential teaching of the Buddhas and the ultimate path for sentient beings. May all beings hear this and practice accordingly. May all attain rebirth in the Land of Ultimate Bliss. The assembly then concealed the jade [image], and [Huiyi] redoubled his diligent practice. After twenty-one days, a golden platform was again brought forth, and it was said:
"The Master has attained rebirth in the highest grade through his diligence; you should sit cross-legged to await him.

Three days later, a wondrous light filled the room, and he said to his disciples, "I have been born in the Pure Land," whereupon he passed away with a smile. Du Gong, the Prefect of the Commandery, composed a verse in praise: [Verse omitted as per instructions]
My Master ascended to the First Ground in a single thought; the celestial music of the Buddha-land has come twice.
Only the ancient locust tree before my gate lowers its branches, as if merely to hang upon the golden terrace.
Daochuo of the Tang dynasty was a native of Wen-shui in Bingzhou; he left home at the age of fourteen to study the sutras and śāstras, and later served under Chan Master Zàn.
