In his study of Chan, he was also deeply devoted to the practice of the Pure Land of Divine Crane (Shenluan). Once, while in meditative absorption, a monk saw Tan-chao holding a rosary that appeared like a great mountain made of the seven treasures.
In his daily life, he lectured on the *Sūtra of Contemplation on the Buddha of Immeasurable Life* for nearly two hundred times.

Each person would hold a rosary and recite the name of the Buddha; at times, even when the assembly dispersed, the resonance of their voices filled the forests and valleys. He performed the six-period prostrations without fail.

He abolished the practice of counting recitations of the Buddha's name daily, limiting them instead to seventy thousand. On the eighth day of the fourth month in the second year of the Zhenguan era, he entered nirvana.
Those who heard the news and came to attend were so numerous that they filled the mountain temple; they beheld a transformation Buddha dwelling in the sky, with celestial flowers falling from above.
Tang Weian was a native of Bingzhou. He took the Pure Land as his true place of refuge and practiced the Vaipulya repentance with diligent and unflagging devotion.
Once, when he was slightly ill, he saw the two Bodhisattvas Avalokiteśvara and Mahāsthāmaprāpta appearing in the air.

Weian summoned a painter, but none were able to depict them. Suddenly, two men appeared who said they could paint them; once the portraits were finished, the two men vanished. Weian then informed everyone.
The disciple said, "I am now going to be reborn in the Pure Land; who will accompany me as my fellow practitioner? There was a young boy who wished to go to the bank to bid farewell to his parents.

His parents thought it was mere child’s play and did not believe him. Shortly thereafter, the boy bathed, changed his clothes, entered the Dharma hall, and passed away while reciting the Buddha’s name.
Huan’an patted the boy’s back and said, "How can you, my little one, depart before me? He then sought out a brush and composed a eulogy.
The two bodhisattvas have made a vow to use their hands of compassion to lift [beings] up and travel together toward the West. Having finished reciting this verse of praise, he passed away.

The Tang monk Xuan was a native of Bingzhou. Initially, he focused his thoughts on Maitreya, hoping for rebirth in the Inner Court (Tuṣita Heaven). At the age of ninety, he met the Chan Master Daocuo and heard about the Pure Land;
only then did he turn his mind toward the Buddha and practice mindfulness of the Buddha, prostrating a thousand times daily with single-minded diligence and without slackening.
Later, when he was ill, he told his disciples: "Amitābha Buddha has bestowed upon me the fragrance of the precepts and robes;
Avalokiteśvara and Mahāsthāmaprāpta have shown me their precious hands. It is time for me to depart. Having spoken these words, he passed away. For seven days, a wondrous fragrance did not dissipate.
At that time, the two Dharma Masters Qifang and Yuanguo witnessed this event firsthand and, at Wuzhen Temple, together broke off willow branches.
Avalokiteśvara made a vow within his hand, saying: "If there is a karmic affinity for this Pure Land, these flowers shall not wither for seven days;
when that time comes, they shall flourish even more. When the auspicious fruit appeared, he rejoiced; day and night he contemplated [the Buddha] without ceasing.

Suddenly, he felt himself approach the Seven-Jeweled Pond and enter a great precious canopy, where he saw the Buddha and the two Great Beings (Mañjuśrī and Samantabhadra) seated upon a jeweled lotus pedestal, their radiance brilliantly reflecting one another. He prostrated before the Buddha.
It was said that those who recite my name shall all be born in my land. Furthermore, I heard Śākyamuni Buddha and Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva praising the Pure Land with Brahma-sounds;
I also saw three jeweled stairways: the first for laypeople, the second for a mixture of monastics and laity, and the third for monks alone.
It was said that those who recite the Buddha’s name with a sincere heart shall attain birth in this land.
Five days later, he suddenly heard the sound of a bell and said, "The sound of the bell is our business. He and his companions passed away simultaneously.
Tang Huai-gan resided at Qianfu Monastery in Chang’an and entered the Buddha-remembrance practice hall for twenty-one days;

when he failed to behold any spiritual omens, he lamented his own deep karmic obstructions and wished to fast to the end of his life. Master Shandao did not permit this, instead exhorting him to be diligent and devout.
For three years he was moved by what he had been taught; later, upon seeing the Buddha’s golden body and the white tuft of hair between his brows, he attained the *nien-fo samādhi*.
He composed the *Jueyi lun* (Treatise on Resolving Doubts) in seven fascicles. At the time of his death, he joined his palms and said, "The Buddha has come to welcome me," and then passed away.
Tang Biancai was a native of Xiangyang. He practiced the Pure Land method in secret for twenty years without ever claiming any special attainment.
He was on good terms only with Ren Gong of Hugong, to whom he said, "I shall certainly be reborn in the Pure Land; my deadline is ten years.
One day, he instructed his disciples to inform Ren Gong, saying, "The time previously promised has arrived. When Ren Gong arrived, Biancai said, "I am departing," and sat in the full lotus posture.
While he was transforming the masses, they heard the music of immortals coming from the west and an extraordinary fragrance wafted through the air.
During the Tang Dynasty, Da Xing resided at Mount Tai to practice the *Samantabhadra Repentance* for three years; he was moved by the manifestation of the Great Being (Bodhisattva).

In his later years, he entered the Great Canon to present his vows, taking up a scroll at random and obtaining the *Amitābha Sūtra*. He recited it day and night until the twenty-first day of the three-week period.
Every day, the Buddha and two great bodhisattvas appeared on the ground of lapis lazuli.

When Emperor Xizong heard of this matter, he issued an edict for him to enter the palace and bestowed upon him the title "Bodhisattva Constantly Diligent. One year later, the lapis lazuli ground appeared once more, and he passed away that very day.
A strange fragrance persisted for ten days, and his physical body remained incorruptible.

Tang Mingzhan resolved to seek rebirth in the Land of Peaceful Nurturing (*An-yang*) in his later years. Some mocked him for doing so late in life, to which he replied, "If one can behold the Buddha through the accomplishment of ten recitations, why should I have any concerns?
Later, while ill at Xingjiao Monastery, he prepared a vegetarian feast to bid farewell to the monastics and the laity;
both the Chief Minister Fang Xuanling and Du Ruhui were present. As noon passed, he composed his demeanor and recited the Buddha’s name.
Suddenly he said, "The Buddha has come! As the two Great Beings also arrived, he straightened his body, joined his palms, and passed away.
The Chan Master Zhijue of Wuyue, whose name was Yanshou, was born into the Wang family of Danyang and later moved to Yuhang.

From the time he was in his early teens, he could recite the *Lotus Sūtra* at a speed of seven lines at once. At the age of twenty-eight, he served as the military commander of Huating, where he used official funds to provide relief.

Born into a life where he was condemned to death for his crimes, his countenance remained unchanged even as he faced execution. King Wenmu, marveling at this, released him and ordered him to leave the household life under the Chan Master Cuoyan of Siming.
There he shaved his head and received full ordination. By day he provided offerings to the assembly, and by night he practiced meditation.

Upon reading the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, he reflected that the people of the world were so depraved and turbid that none could achieve liberation; he concluded that only the holding of the Name could serve to guide and transform them. Thus...
In the Inmyeong Hall, he diligently practiced the recitation of the Buddha’s name forty thousand times. He visited National Teacher Taishan to clarify the essentials of the mind;
while performing the Lotus Repentance, he beheld the Great Being Avalokiteśvara in samādhi, who poured nectar upon him, whereby his wisdom-nature became daily more luminous.
Reflecting on his past vows, yet unable to decide between them, he went to Master Zhizhe at Yan to cast two lots: one for Chan meditation and one for the Pure Land.

With a heart of utmost sincerity and devotion, he performed seven *niēn* (incense offerings) and attained rebirth in the Pure Land; thereafter, he devoted himself exclusively to the practice of Pure Land cultivation.
Later, while residing at Yongming, he recited one hundred and eight items daily; in the evening, he would go to a separate peak to practice the Way and chant the Buddha’s name.

Passersby occasionally heard the sounds of conch shells and celestial music. King Zhongyi sighed in admiration, saying: "Since ancient times, there has never been anyone as single-minded and earnest in seeking the Western Paradise as this man."

He then established the Xiangyan Hall in the western quarter to fulfill his aspiration. He was granted the title Zhijue (Wisdom Enlightenment), and he ordained approximately one thousand seven hundred disciples and about ten thousand others through the precepts.

He constantly conferred the Bodhisattva precepts upon the assembly, provided food for spirits and deities, and released all living beings, dedicating these acts entirely toward the adornment of the Pure Land.
At that time, he was hailed as the descent of Maitreya into this world. He composed the *Zongjing Lu* (Record of the Mirror of the Source) in ten thousand fascicles.
His collected works, including the *Shantongguiji* (Collection on the Shared Return to Goodness) and the *Weixinanxiang* (Peaceful Mind and Nurturing [Land]), numbered several hundred fascicles.
In the second month of the eighth year of the Kaibao era, at the age of ninety-eight, he rose at dawn, informed the assembly, burned incense, sat in the full lotus posture, and passed away.

Later, a monk came from Linchuan and spent a year circumambulating and prostrating before his stupa. When people asked him the reason, he said: "I was ill and entered the underworld, where I saw the King in the left hall of the palace."

Regarding the veneration of the image of Master Yongming Shou: it is said that while all ordinary people must pass through the Netherworld upon death, this Master alone was reborn directly in the Western Pure Land in the highest grade. Therefore, [the Emperor] reverently honored his virtue.
Shitong of Fengxiang, during the Shijin period, was filled with boundless joy upon seeing the ritual for the Pure Land by Master Zhizhe.
From then on, he never spat toward the west nor sat facing away from the west, but focused his mind exclusively on the recitation of the Buddha’s name.
Later, he saw white cranes and peacocks fly down in formation toward the west, and saw lotus flowers opening and closing before him. Shitong said, "The white cranes and peacocks are the Pure [Land]."
The earthly realm is the Lotus Light Realm, the place of rebirth; thus, the Pure Land manifested. Thereupon, he rose to prostrate before the Buddha and passed away.
At his cremation, five-colored auspicious clouds encircled the flames, and the śarīra relics were arranged in scales upon his body.
One must always avoid spitting toward the west and sit facing the west; with mindfulness fixed in this manner, what matter will not be resolved? Some may say: "Is this not excessive attachment?"
Alas! The *Sūtra on Beholding the Setting Sun* contains clear and explicit teachings. When the Great Master Zhi (Zhiyi) was first born, he sat cross-legged facing west;
how could even the virtuous ones who have purified their karma fail to emulate him by sitting facing west when they pass away?

To be so attached to turbid conditions that one remains at ease throughout one’s entire life, yet to feel anxiety about such attachment as soon as one thinks of the Pure Land—how strange and paradoxical this is! Alas! How extraordinary!
Song Wuen was a native of Changshu in Gusu. At the age of thirteen, upon hearing the *Amitābha Sūtra* being recited, he immediately sought ordination.

He maintained the practice of eating only once a day, never parting from his robes and alms bowl, and he accumulated no wealth or treasures. When lying down, he always lay on his right side; when sitting, he sat in the full lotus posture (*paryaṅka*).
During every *poṣadha* ceremony, his tears would flow incessantly. He extensively instructed others in the pure practices of the Western Land as well as the perfect teachings of the One Vehicle.
When someone questioned him for not adjusting his teaching to their capacities, he replied, "I am merely providing them with the conditions for the 'poison drum'.
On the night of the first day of the eighth month in the second year of the Yongxi era, he beheld a white light emerging from the well and said to his disciples, "I am about to depart.

He ceased eating grain and refrained from speech, single-mindedly reciting the Buddha's name. In a dream, he saw a śramaṇa holding a golden incense burner and burning incense, circumambulating his room three times.
He himself said, "I have come here from the consecration ceremony to welcome you. Upon waking from his dream, he called for his disciples; even then, they still smelled a wondrous fragrance.

On the twenty-fifth day, after completing his lectures on the *Zhiguan zhigui* (The Essential Guide to Stopping and Contemplation) and the *Guansin yi* (The Meaning of Contemplating the Mind), he sat upright and passed away.
People heard the sounds of pipes, strings, bells, and chimes resonating brightly in the air; gradually fading and receding toward the west.
Song Shengchang was a native of Qiantang. He entered the monastic order at the age of seven. During the Chunhua era, while residing at Nan Zhaoqing Temple, he admired the spirit of Mount Lu;
consequently, he drew blood to transcribe the "Chapter on Pure Conduct" from the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* and renamed the Lotus Society as the "Society of Pure Conduct Practitioners.
Among the literati who joined the assembly, they were called "Pure Conduct Disciples," and Prime Minister Wang Wenzheng served as their leader. At that time, the public...
The Minister, the Governor-General, and the hundred and twenty officials, along with one thousand bhikṣus, were present.

Su Yijian of the Hanlin Academy composed the preface to the "Chapter on Pure Conduct," stating: "I would not have declined even if I had been required to spread my hair to receive his feet or gouge out my body to request the Dharma;
how much less could I begrudge my mediocre writing and shallow learning? Song Bai, the Director of the Hanlin Academy, composed the inscription for the stele.

What did Yuansun inscribe upon the back of the stele? The Dharma Master Yuan of Gushan composed a record of the Master’s deeds on the twelfth day of the first month in the fourth year of the Tianxi era.
While sitting upright in mindfulness of the Buddha, after a short while, he called out in a forceful voice, "The Buddha has come!
and then passed away peacefully. Following Master Huiyuan, who founded the Lotus Society, came Shandao; subsequently, there was Huiming of Nanyue and the Five Assemblies.
The fame of Master Mingtai Yan reached its zenith, and he was acclaimed as the Seventh Patriarch; how magnificent was the height of his proselytizing!
Zunshe of Song was a native of Taizhou, surnamed Ye. His mother prayed at an ancient Guanyin shrine before giving birth to him.

At the age of twenty, he received full ordination and studied the Vinaya under Shouchu. Subsequently, he entered Guoqing Monastery, vowing to transmit the Tiantai teachings, and burned off a finger at Puxian Hall.

Before the image, he practiced the *Pratyutpanna Samādhi* with great diligence and resolved to be reborn in the Land of Peaceful Nurturing (*An-yang*). He studied so ardently that he vomited blood until death, vowing to persevere.
Suddenly, as if in a dream, he saw Avalokiteśvara extending a finger toward his mouth and drawing out several worms; from the tip of the finger, the Bodhisattva produced nectar, which he drank.
Upon awakening, his body and mind were refreshed and cool, and his chronic illness was completely cured. At the beginning of the Chūnhua era, the assembly invited him to reside at Bao... (Temple).
He preached the Dharma without interruption, leading more than a hundred disciples to liberation and thousands to take refuge.

He took Pure Land as his sole principle, exhorting others to focus on it through the *Jingtu jueyi xingyuan zan* (Praise for Resolving Doubts and Vowing Practice in the Pure Land), the various versions of the *Amitābha Sūtra Repentance Method*, the "Ten Recitations at Dawn" method, and the methods for the meditative visualization of rebirth.
During the Tian-sheng era, as he was about to pass away, he lit incense and prostrated before the Buddha, vowing that all the holy ones...
It is proven that he was reborn in the Land of Ultimate Bliss; he passed away while sitting in meditation at the age of sixty-nine.

When the assembly saw a great star fall from Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa, they acclaimed him as the Great Master Lián Cíyún Chànzhǔ (the Chan Master of Compassionate Clouds). His name was Kèqín. Regarding his method of repentance, he practiced it himself and established it as a model for ten thousand ages;
truly, he is the only such person in all antiquity and the present. As for the burning of fingers and arms, one must attain the stage of a Mahāsattva of Endurance (*kṣānti*) before one can do so.
What one does is not within the realm of a beginner; at its most extreme, it leads to the living cremation of one's own body, possession by malevolent spirits, and the infliction of no small harm.

Those who seek the Western Paradise should study the teachings of Ciyun, practicing with resolute devotion and diligent austerity; they need not imitate others by burning their fingers merely to dazzle the masses.

Song Zongtan was a native of Luzhou and the son of the Shen family. At the age of sixteen, he took refuge under Master Daogong and shaved his head; fifty years later, his reputation spread throughout the monastic academies.

In his later years, while at Qingtai Town in Tangzhou, he devoted himself exclusively to seeking rebirth in the Pure Land, never for a moment neglecting the three karmas or the four modes of deportment.
On the twenty-seventh day of the fourth month in the fourth year of the Zhenghe era, he dreamed that Amitābha Buddha said to him:
"You shall preach the Dharma for six days and then be reborn in the Pure Land. Upon waking, he informed the assembly. On the fourth day of the fifth month, he gathered the multitude and said:
"The convergence and dispersal of causes and conditions must naturally have their time; however, the supreme conditions for the Pure Land depend solely upon the moment.

I pray that the assembly will recite the Buddha’s name to assist me in my rebirth. Having spoken, he sat upright and passed away. Thunder resounded throughout the sky, and white clouds covered the earth. III.
When the Japanese man’s agate rosary slipped from his fingers, the crowd tried to retrieve it but could not dislodge it.

Song Ziyuan, whose style name was Wanshi (All Affairs Rest), was born to a father surnamed Mao and a mother surnamed Chai. His mother had dreamed that a Buddha entered their gate before his birth; for this reason, he was named Folei (Buddha-Come).
Having lost both parents at an early age, he joined the monastic order under Master Zhitong at Yanxiang Temple at the age of nineteen and began his studies.

While in meditative concentration during a day of *śamatha-vipaśyanā*, he heard the cry of a crow and attained realization, composing this verse of awakening: "For over twenty years I have sought on paper;
Seeking and seeking, I grew ever more despondent. Suddenly, hearing the compassionate crow’s call, I finally believe my former efforts were in vain.

Thereupon, his resolve to benefit others became most earnest; he universally exhorted people to recite the Buddha’s name and, on their behalf, performed prostrations and repentance for all sentient beings throughout the Dharma-realm.

He repented and prayed for rebirth in the Land of Ultimate Bliss, establishing the White Lotus Repentance Hall, composing the *Selection of the Four Lands and Three Contemplations*, and illustrating the Diagram of the Buddha’s Selection.
He revealed the "Eyes of the Lotus School" and established the four-character name "Pujue Miaodao" (Universal Enlightenment Wondrous Way) to define his lineage.

Emperor Gaozong summoned him for an audience and bestowed upon him the title Cizhao. Later, on the twenty-third day of the third month at Duocheng, he addressed the assembly, saying: "My transformation..."

"When the conditions for my departure have been fulfilled, I shall go. Having spoken these words, he joined his palms and entered parinirvāṇa. His remains were cremated, yielding countless śarīras, for which an imperial edict granted him the Most Victorious Stūpa (Zuisheng-ta).

The Song dynasty monk Fachih resided at Huadu Monastery, where he practiced the Amitābha Repentance and Vows, seeking to shorten his life in Jambudvīpa so that he might be born early into the Land of Peace.
While she was recovering from a minor illness, she wept rain-like tears and wailed in grief, praying for the Buddha’s guidance. She recited the Buddha’s name with a resolute voice without ceasing;
suddenly, she saw the Buddha’s body, sixteen feet tall, standing upon a pond. She then said to herself, "I have attained rebirth in the Western Paradise," and passed away facing west.
Dharma Master Songji studied under Baoyun and resided at Taiping Xingguo Temple, where he devoted his mind to the practice of *nianfo*.
One day, manifesting illness, he extensively expounded the profound mysteries of the Dharma for his disciples. Suddenly, the assembly saw light appear in the west and music resound through the air.

The Master said, "Amitābha Buddha has arrived together with the two Great Beings," and he immediately passed away while lying on his right side facing west. His remains were enshrined at the temple gate.
A man dreamed that Amitābha Buddha conferred upon him the prophecy of becoming the Tathāgata Chao-shi; another dreamed of his teacher seated upon a pedestal of blue lotuses.
The Dharma-Wisdom Chan Master sighed, saying: "To discuss the profound mysteries while lying ill, and to behold the Buddha at the moment of death—these are truly worthy of reverence.
Song Ruoyu resided at Seontam in Yunchwan and constructed the Muryangsu (Amitāyus) Hall, exhorting both monastics and laypeople to practice the mindfulness of the Buddha with diligent devotion.
For thirty years, he had been friends with the two masters Daoqian and Zechang; Qian was skilled in poetry and sought fame, whereas I and Chang were solely devoted to practical cultivation.
As we were about to follow the world [into death], a divine being appeared and told us:

"Your fellow student Zechang has attained the Samādhi of the Vows and Practices of Samantabhadra and has already been born in the Pure Land; he is now waiting for you. Thereupon, I bathed, changed my clothes, and commanded the assembly.
While reciting the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra*, he sat upright in silence and suddenly said, "The Pure Land has appeared before me; I shall now depart. He wrote a verse and passed away. The verse reads:
"Originally there is no home to which one can return; Who knows that upon the edge of the clouds there is a path to tread?

The light of the stream flickers as the moon sets behind the western mountains— This is precisely the moment the dream of the immortal pond is severed. Furthermore, he said: 'The thousand-petaled lotus net within emptiness is but a dream.'"
Treading upon the lotus ponds of the seven treasures within, he has secured his path to the Western Land, free from even a trace of doubt.
Zongze of the Song dynasty, styled Cijue, was a native of Xiangyang. He took ordination under Chan Master Xiu of Changlu Temple;

his vows were vast and profound, and he attained deep insight into the principles of Chan. During the Yuanyou era, he invited his elderly mother to reside in the eastern chamber of the abbot’s quarters and exhorted her with...

He exerted himself in the practice of mindfulness of the Buddha (*buddhānusmṛti*) for seven years without interruption. When his mother was approaching her end, she indeed passed away without illness.
Following the instructions of the Sugata, he exhorted others to cultivate [the path] and transform sentient beings; adhering to the regulations of Mount Lu, he established a supreme Lotus Assembly.

The method was to recite the name of Amitābha Buddha one hundred, one thousand, or ten thousand times each day, recording the count with ten-character marks beneath each day’s entry. One night, he dreamed of a youth...
A man wearing a black silk cap and white robes, with a refined and elegant appearance, informed the Master that he wished to join the Maitreya Assembly and requested that his name be inscribed.
When Jie took up the brush and asked for his name, he replied, "Puhui. He added, "My elder brother, Puxian, also requests to be included in the record.
Thereupon, the Master Jue said to the senior monks, "In the 'Chapter on Leaving the World' of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, there are two bodhisattvas named Puxian and Puhui."
Satsu assisted in propagating the Buddha-dharma; now, together with the great assembly, he has established a period for mindfulness of the Buddha (*nienfo*) to aspire for rebirth in the Pure Land.

Moved by the profound assistance of sages and worthies, he recorded these accounts, placing the two Great Beings at their head. Far and near, people have turned toward his transformation. He composed the "Admonition on Seated Meditation" (*Zuochan zhen*) and the *Weijiang ji*.
Furthermore, there are one hundred and twenty "Exhortations to Filial Piety" (*Quanxiao wen*); the general purport of these is to encourage the personal cultivation of the Pure Land.
Master Lingzhi Zhao called Master Jie of Yongan a "world-transcending filial son" and a "great master of the Mahāyāna in recent times"—truly so!
At the time of his passing, he sat in meditation while reciting the Buddha’s name and passed away in a state of spiritual transformation.
Zhi-li of the Song dynasty, titled Fazhi, resided at Nanhu and composed the *Miaozongchao*, greatly elucidating the contemplation of the mind and the contemplation of the Buddha.
Every year on the fifteenth day of the second month, he established a *nianfo* (Buddha-recitation) and precept-bestowing assembly that drew more than ten thousand people.

He also composed the *Rongxin jie* (Explanation of Merging the Mind), which clarifies the meaning of the three contemplations within one mind and the four pure lands. Later, on the first day of the new year, he established the *Guangming chan* (Pratyutpanna Samādhi Repentance).
On the fifth day, he summoned the great assembly to preach the Dharma; suddenly uttering the Buddha’s name several hundred times, he passed away while sitting upright.
Zhao Qingxian Gong (Zhao Buan) inscribed a stele for his stupa.
During the Song dynasty, there was a monk named Yan who resided at Chongshan Temple on Mount Chicheng in Taizhou; he studied the Tiantai teachings under Shenxi.

In his later years, he built a thatched hut beneath a jujube tree and called it Zhua’an. Throughout his life, he was devoted to the practice of Pure Land Buddhism and harbored a deep aspiration for the Land of Ultimate Bliss.

His "Poem on Returning to One’s Native Land" was widely circulated during his time. In the fourth month of summer in the first year of the Jiāngzhōng-Jìngguó era, as he approached the end of his life, he beheld a precious pond with a great lotus flower and celestial music arrayed in four rows.
He then composed a "Poem on Departing for the Pure Land" to instruct the assembly. Seven days later, he passed away while sitting in the full-lotus posture.
A light like the moon appeared above his stupa, remaining until three o'clock in the afternoon before fading. Previously, the mirror-like radiance of Fǎxiáng had also manifested.
That the face of Master Yan now appears upon the stupa at the end of the wall, all with a clarity that is translucent throughout body and mind—
this is a manifest proof. Even such things as light filling the room, or golden radiance extending for several hundred li across the river—
alas, how could these be forged?

Song Zhilian resided at Huadu Monastery in Shangyu. Initially, he traveled extensively to consult the masters of the Chan school, but in his later years, he focused his mind solely on the Western Pure Land.

In the eighth month of the autumn of the first year of the Qingyuan era, he took leave of the assembly, saying: "In a dream, I saw Amitābha Buddha surrounded by a great multitude preaching the Dharma.
The Buddha said, 'All you virtuous people, you must concentrate your minds on pure karma so that you may be reborn in my land.'"
"I have seen the supreme signs; my rebirth there is certain," he said, and then wrote this verse: "A wild goose flies across the vast sky, its reflection sinks into the cold water;
neither ceasing nor arising, within the Land of Lotus Flowers. Having finished writing, he turned his body toward the west, performed a mudrā, and passed away.

Song Huaiyi was a native of Leqing, Wenzhou. His father made his living by fishing; while still a child, Huaiyi sat at the stern of the boat and followed his father in catching fish, yet he would secretly throw them back into the water.
His father grew angry and beat him, but Huaiyi felt no regret. He subsequently took leave of his parents to enter the monastic life at Jingde Temple.

During the Tianxing era, he passed the scriptural examinations and received ordination. He received the Dharma from Chan Master Xian of Cui峰 (Cui-feng). He presided over five monasteries in succession, but...
While encouraging the assembly to practice mindfulness of the Buddha and preaching on the cultivation of the Pure Land, Hwa-jung passed away that evening.
His disciple Ji-chai asked, "Now that the construction of the stupa is complete, what is the ultimate matter? The Master raised his fist to show him, pushed aside his pillow, and passed away.
Song Zongben was a native of Changzhou. He possessed a robust and ancient countenance and a straightforward nature.

At an early age, he attended upon Chan Master Huai and attained realization through the practice of *nianfo* (buddha-recitation), subsequently entering deeply into *samādhi*. He initially resided at Rui Guang Temple in Suzhou.

Chen Gong Xiang, the Governor of Hangzhou, earnestly requested him to serve at Jingci Temple for three years to plant roots of merit for this region. Not long after, Emperor Shenzong opened sixty bays of the Xiangguo Temple.

The Emperor issued an imperial decree for the Fourth Court to summon him from Huilin Monastery to an audience at the Yanhe Hall. Once he had retired, the Emperor gazed after him and said to his attendants, "He is truly a monk of both merit and wisdom.
In his daily life, he secretly cultivated the Pure Land practices; in his later years at Lingyan, he remained shut in his room, redoubling his diligent efforts.
When the Dharma Master Cai of Leifeng traveled spiritually to the Pure Land, he beheld an exceptionally beautiful flower and asked about it; the reply was that it was waiting for [Master] Jing.

Furthermore, while Chan Master Ciben was in meditative absorption, the Vinaya Master Xi of Zifusi saw a golden lotus flower and a person who said, "This is the seat of the monk Zongben of the Great Song nation.
He went specifically to visit the Master, prostrated at his feet, offered gold, and departed.

On the day of Jiazi in the twelfth month of the second year of the Yuanyu era, he bathed, informed the assembly, sat upon his seat as if falling asleep, and passed away when shaken. His disciples erected a stupa for him.
His entire body was enshrined at Lingyan, where he was posthumously titled Chan Master Yuanzhao.
Song Yuanzhao resided at Lingzhi, where he propagated the Vinaya teachings and devoted himself earnestly to the practice of Pure Land Buddhism, never ceasing his recitation of the Buddha’s name.

One day, he instructed his disciples to chant the *Amitābha Sūtra* and the "Universal Worthy’s Vow" chapter, and he passed away while sitting in the lotus posture. Fishermen on West Lake all [heard...]
He heard the sound of celestial music in the air.
Huiheng of the Song dynasty resided at Yanshou Temple in Wulin; initially relying on Lingzhi to study the Vinaya, he specialized in the practice of Pure Land for sixty years.

Whenever he encountered others, he invariably exhorted them to recite the Buddha’s name. He constructed a precious pavilion and established statues of the Three Holy Ones, which were most highly praised.
There was a man of extraordinary character named Jiang Ziren who suddenly dreamed that a jeweled throne descended from the sky, with a voice saying, "Master Heng shall ascend this throne.
Shortly thereafter, his lay friend Mr. Sun gave notice of his departure; while still at home, he made a seal and passed away.
Master [Jiang] went to offer incense, and upon returning, he said to his disciples, "Mr. Sun has already departed; I too shall go. Thereupon, he gathered [his followers].
The assembly, mindful of the Buddha, spoke a verse for him, saying: "Reciting Amitābha’s name day by day, contemplating his white ūrṇā-kośa thought after thought;
maintaining this non-retrogressive mind, one will certainly be born in An-yang (Sukhāvatī). He passed away while sitting upright, known as Vinaya Master Qingzhao."
Song Zhiyuan resided on Guoshan in the West Lake, where he extensively commented upon various sutras and focused his mind on the Pure Land.

He composed the *Amitābha Shu* and the *Xizi Chao*, exhorting others toward rebirth in the Western Paradise. At the end of his life, he sat in meditation until death; his remains were interred within a ceramic vessel.
Fifteen years later, after heavy rains caused the mountain to collapse, the vessel was uncovered, and his physical form remained perfectly intact, with his nails and hair having grown long.
Song Ke lived in Mingzhou for many years, constantly reciting the *Lotus Sūtra* with the aspiration to be reborn in the Pure Land; he was then known as Jiu Fahua.
In the eighth year of the Yuanyou era, at the age of eighty-one, he passed away while seated in meditation. Three days later, he returned and said to people:

"I have seen that the realm of the Pure Land accords perfectly with the descriptions in the sūtra. Upon the lotus pedestals, the names of those destined to be born there are all inscribed. A golden pedestal has been marked for me."
In the Guangjiao Monastery of the capital, Xun Gong had one disciple, Mingzhou, and another, Shierlang; Kojiu was a silver-talent official with a disciple from Mingzhou named the Daoist Nun Xu.
After she finished speaking, she transformed and departed again. In the fifth year, the Daoist Nun Xu passed away, and a wondrous fragrance filled the room.
In the twelfth year, Shierlang passed away, and celestial music welcomed him into the void, exactly as Kojiu had described.
The Venerable Master Zhongfeng of the Song Dynasty, whose name was Mingben, was a native of Qiantang. He received the Dharma from Gaofeng Huibian of Tianmu.

He practiced the Pure Land teachings in secret and composed one hundred poems on his longing for the Western Paradise. His moral character was as eminent as a mountain, and he was visited by both dragons and elephants among the monastic community.
The imperial court repeatedly dispatched envoys to bestow upon him gold and silk, and he was granted the posthumous title of National Teacher Puying. He passed away at the age of sixty-two.
On the day he entered nirvana, a brilliant light shone forth from Mount Taishan.
Song Yingke, who had received his precepts at Yaoshan in Xiachuan, was once feasting on wine and meat without restraint when he suddenly thought to himself, "My pure conduct is deficient;

I fear I shall continue to wander through the cycles of rebirth. He then sought out the *Biographies of Zen Masters Who Attained Rebirth* (*Wangsheng zhuan*) to read it. Upon reading a single biography, he attained full realization.

Thereafter, he arranged a meditation chair facing west within his room, abstained from food, and recited the Buddha’s name. After three days had passed, he dreamed that the Buddha told him, "Your remaining lifespan is still ten years;
you should exert yourself. Baoke replied to the Buddha, "Even if I were granted a hundred years, in this defiled and evil Jambudvīpa it would be easy to lose one's right livelihood.
My wish is only to be born early in the Land of Peaceful Nurturing (Sukhāvatī) to serve the multitude of sages. The Buddha said, "Your resolve is as follows..."

Three days later, he was to welcome you; when the appointed time arrived, he commanded the assembly to recite the *Amitābha Sūtra*, whereupon he said, "The Buddha and the great assembly have all arrived," and he passed away in silence.
Yuanshanzhu, whose style name was Yunwu, was a native of Suzhou.
By nature, his character was lofty and pure; he did not pursue fame or profit, and he remained shut within his room, practicing the six periods of meditation.

He practiced the recitation of the Buddha’s name, upheld the Mahāyāna teachings, and performed prostrations and repentance; though he suffered from chronic illness for a long time, he remained steadfast.

Among those in the Wu region who cultivated the Pure Land, this Master was the most eminent, and both monastics and laypeople took him as their model. At the time of his death, a rare fragrance filled the room. His *An-yang chuan* (Biographies of the Pure Land) and *Gu-xiang ji* (Collection of Echoes) circulate in the world.
Yuantiru Weize was a native of Luling who received the Dharma from Zhongfeng Miaowu.
He established Shizi Lin Puti Zhengzong Temple in the city of Suzhou, which contained two chambers named "Lying in the Snow" and "Standing in the Snow," where he sat daily reciting the Buddha’s name.

Students who came to study followed one after another; beyond his practice of directly pointing out the nature of mind through single-minded instruction, he also composed the *Jingtu hewen* (Questions on the Pure Land).
He exhorted others until his passing, when auspicious omens appeared within a single year. At the age of sixty-nine, he was interred at a pagoda on the plain west of the water.
Yuan Pu-du was a native of Dan-yang; he left home to become a monk in his early twenties and first studied under Chan Master Hui of Bao-shan, who held him in high esteem.

He resided at Dong-lin Temple on Mount Lu, where he devoted himself to the cultivation of the *nien-fo* samādhi and authored the ten-fascicle *Lian-zong bao-jian* (Treasury of the Lotus School) to elucidate its teachings.

He presented his treatise to the State Preceptor for Empowerment at Fawang Temple in the capital. An imperial decree was issued praising him, and the work was printed and circulated throughout the realm.
It contained such phrases as "guiding humans and devas" and "continuing the Buddha’s wisdom-life to once again revitalize the East Lin.
At the end of his life, he bid farewell to the assembly, passed away while reciting the Buddha’s name, and was posthumously titled the Patriarch Udumbara.
Mingchu Qi was a native of Shu who possessed profound faith in the Western Paradise. Upon arriving in Yanjing (Beijing), he heard the sound of the tower drum and attained great enlightenment.

In the third year of the Hongwu era, he was summoned three times by imperial decree to preach the Dharma in the capital, which greatly pleased the Emperor. Later, he built a residence called Xizhai (Western Studio) and devoted himself single-mindedly to the practice of pure karma.
He once had a vision in which a great lotus flower filled the entire world; Amitābha Buddha sat within it, surrounded by a multitude of holy beings.
When he was about to pass away, he wrote a verse to address the assembly, saying: "I am going. Someone asked, "Where will you be reborn? He replied, "The Western Land.
Another asked, "Is there a Buddha in the West, but none in the East? Thereupon, he let out a piercing shout and passed away in stillness.
Mingzuxiang was a native of Xinyu in Jiangxi. He cultivated the Pure Land practices with great diligence at Longtan Temple in Shandong.
A layman named Wang Jie constructed a hermitage to invite him; after a short time, he said to Jie, "I am about to return home. When Jie asked where his home was, he replied, "My home is An-yang.
At the appointed time, he arranged his seat facing west and passed away. His remains were carried to the mountains in a coffin.
He manifested a fire to immolate himself.

This was Master Lianchi, whose style name was Zhuhong and whose secular surname was Shen of Hangzhou. Having set his mind upon the Buddha-vehicle at the age of twenty, he received the tonsure under Wumen Xingtian in the Bingyin year of the Jiajing era.
He subsequently received full ordination and traveled with a single calabash and a pair of sandals, visiting various spiritual teachers.

At that time, Bianrong and Xiaoyan were the most prominent figures of the two Chan lineages; he studied under them extensively and attained profound resonance with their teachings. While traveling north to Mount Wutai, he was moved by the manifestation of Mañjuśrī’s radiance.
In the *Xinwei* year of the Longqing era, seeing that the mountains and waters of Yunqi were secluded and tranquil, he settled there, constructing a thatched hut to spend the rest of his life.

Tigers abounded around the mountain and caused frequent disasters, but as the Master recited sutras and performed the ritual of offering food (*bali*), the tiger menace was pacified. During a drought, he followed the irrigation channels across the fields.
As he traveled on foot chanting the Buddha’s name, timely rains fell wherever he went; from this point on, his path of transformation flourished greatly.
The Master alone pioneered the single gate of Pure Land, synthesizing the Three Baskets of scripture to show that their ultimate aim points toward the Mind-only.

Monastics and laypeople from all quarters prostrated themselves before him, and those who heard the Way followed one after another. Illustrious officials and high-ranking dignitaries, such as Lu Guangzu, Zhang Yuanjian, Feng Mengzhen, Tao Wangling, and Yu... [continued].
Tingxi, Song Yingchang, and others were all so moved that they bowed their hearts in submission and took refuge in him. By nature, he was profoundly filial;

whenever he carried his ancestral tablet while traveling, he would prepare offerings for its sustenance. He cared for the solitary in the monasteries and offered memorial services for the deceased of the Shen clan, extending his compassion to the netherworld.

He personally practiced the *Yankou* (Feeding the Hungry Ghosts) ritual and frequently presided over the distribution of alms. There were many who beheld the image of the Tathāgata appearing upon his seat.

It was through the power of his contemplation that he rescued the lives of sentient beings. He composed the "Essay on Refraining from Killing and Releasing Life" (*Jiesha fangsheng wen*), and established ponds for releasing life both within and outside the city, as well as in the mountains.
During the Wanli era, Empress Dowager Cisheng sent an eunuch to inquire after his health and bestow upon him purple robes and gold;
the envoy returned with the gold to the monastic community, while the robes were offered to the High Hall, never even being worn upon his body. The Master carried them upon his shoulder.

In the *Zhengfa xiu si anle xing yi nianfo sanmei pu she san gen zhu Mituo shu chao* (Commentary on the Four Practices for Cultivating the True Dharma and the Universal Inclusion of the Three Faculties through the Buddha-Recollection Samādhi), it is recorded that more than twenty types of practices from the *Yunqi fahui* (The Collected Works of Yunqi) were circulated in the world.

Fifteen days before his passing, he entered the city to bid farewell to his former acquaintances and disciples, including Song Shouyi and others, saying: "I am about to depart; returning to the mountain to part with the assembly shall be as it was before."

When his disciples wished to bid farewell to visitors, he would invariably reside at Changshou Monastery, leaving no one to fathom the reason for this. Upon reaching this point, he faced west and recited the Buddha’s name with composure until his passing.
The assembly mournfully entreated him to remain and leave instructions; he opened his closed eyes once more and said, "Recite the Buddha’s name with sincerity; do not change the subject.
This was on the fourth day of the seventh month in the forty-third year of the Wanli era; he was eighty-one years of age.

With fifty years of monastic seniority (*saṃgha-lakṣa*), he was the patriarch of the Lotus School on Mount Kuang; by the time of Yongming, the seven [patriarchs] were established throughout the realm, and with the Master added, they were reckoned as the Eight Patriarchs.
In Huangzhou, Hubei, there was an anonymous monk who exclusively recited the name of Amitābha Buddha day and night without ceasing. Following...
Whatever he saw, he would address as "Amitābha Buddha. In the *guīwèi* year of the Chóngzhēn era, the General Huang Dǐng defended the prefectural city.
The Master loudly chanted the name of the Buddha as he encountered the general on the road and was seized by him.

Later, when Zhāng Xiànzhōng attacked Hángzhōu, the Master remained upon the city walls at night, chanting the Buddha’s name and repeatedly calling out to wake the sleeping soldiers. They detested him, bound him, and threw him down from the wall; however, he did not die.

Several times he remained atop the city walls reciting the Buddha’s name; thus it was four times: when he was below the eastern wall, he was atop the western wall, and when below the southern wall, he was atop the northern wall.

The commander of the central army reported this to the Generalissimo, who then began to pay him respectful homage. At that time, Huangzhou was suffering from a great famine and people were eating one another.
When the Master went outside the city, a starving person holding a knife approached him, seeking for the Master to sacrifice his body. The Master took off his robe and showed it to him.
The crowd said, "Wait until we have recited the Buddha’s name a thousand times, and then we shall eat.

When he had reached three hundred recitations, the crowd grew anxious and were about to take up their blades when suddenly troops and horses appeared from the sky; the starving people scattered in terror, and the Master was already inside the city.
A hunter in the mountains caught a large tiger, and the Master entreated him to release it. The hunter demanded thirty pieces of gold, which the Master [gave].
He managed to capture four tigers. A hunter said, "If you can grasp a tiger by its ear and circle it three times without harming it, I shall give you that tiger as your master.
He then conferred this instruction upon him. The monk grasped the tiger by its ear, circled it three times, and released it;
the tiger returned to him and did not leave. The master lived together with the tiger in the Vajra Cave on Mount Hwangma. General Lu Gude of the Inner Ministry led his troops there.
Passing through Huangzhou, he went to the mountain to visit him, wishing to see Master Hu. He told Hu that he wished to see him fully;
Hu then let out a great cry and leaped outside. Lu also took refuge in him as his teacher.

One day, while walking through the streets, the master saw a chicken chanting the Buddha’s name in a loud voice, and the chicken followed along with the sound. In the year of Gengyin, the master intended to go to Wulin.
While staying at a lodging by the Qinhuai River near the White Gate, Daojing saw a large pleasure boat on the river during the Dragon Boat Festival.
He called out, "Mr. Qian! You who once took refuge with the Master—are you also on this boat? Mr. Qian was indeed in the boat. Upon disembarking, he saw the Master;
the Master asked his companions who he was, and they told him it was so-and-so. Mr. Qian then wailed aloud, saying: "Sentient beings take suffering for pleasure, just like..."
Qián Kěn requested instruction on the essentials of practice. The Master said, "Single-mindedly recite the name of Amitābha Buddha.
He further said, "After I have passed away, if you have any doubts, you may ask Juelang; he is a man of clear vision. Someone asked Táng Yízhī, "Who is this Master?
He replied, "The Dharma-realm is the body of Amitābha Buddha; the Master exclusively upholds this."
Jue Shi must have been an emanation of a Buddha or Bodhisattva; his supernatural powers and wondrous functions were merely incidental matters following his realization of the nature.
By singling out Master Jue to inspire people’s yearning, one can also know the extent of his cultivation and realization.

Shi Haibao of Tianting Monastery in Jinling during the Ming dynasty initially encountered rotten vegetables in the meditation hall. Every morning upon rising, he would leave several loads of these rotten vegetables at the monastery gate;
whenever he met passersby, he would solicit money and place it atop the vegetables. Once they were restored, he would have the sellers take them away.

When he first brought them inside to provide for the monks, he encountered those who were unwilling to give alms; he would follow them for as far as a *li*, never treating them with disdain as he exhorted them to practice charity.
I changed my residence during this period; at the age of twenty, I visited the Xunzhai studio of Master Yici.
Finding him eccentric and simple, I spoke to him, but he did not respond with even a single word, merely looking at me with a laugh. His tattered robe was full of lice;

when he had leisure, he would sit on the ground reciting the Buddha’s name, constantly picking lice and moving them from one place to another, never leaving them off his person. After more than a year, he would beg for vegetables and rotten food, besides which—

He further begged for small increments of money until he had accumulated several taels of gold; he then earnestly requested the assembly to recite sutras and perform repentance rites, followed by mindfulness of the Buddha and the dedication of merit.
He continued this practice for many years. During the Chongzhen era, Zheng Zuochang of the literary academy invited the Master to visit the South Sea, but the Master declined.
After setting sail, Zheng saw the Master walking ahead of him on land whenever they met, unable to catch up with him. Eventually, they reached the mountain and entered [the temple].
The Magistrate also saw the Master upon it offering incense; he dispatched an envoy to observe him, who returned to report that the Master had not yet arrived at the prefecture.
Zheng immediately went to the temple to wait for the Master. His disciples said, "The Master has been lying in bed for over a month and has not taken even a sip of tea or water;

only yesterday did he ask for a drink and rise. Zheng then recounted the Master’s spiritual wonders, whereupon the people of the prefecture came to revere and believe in him. One day, Liao... [text ends]
"You may come to bid farewell to your teacher," the Master instructed him. "On such-and-such a day, we shall meet to bring our worldly affairs to an end.
Liao arrived as scheduled. The Master brewed tea and poured it out, saying, "I trouble you, Layman, to paint a small portrait of this old monk.
You must capture it so that not only are the form and spirit perfectly rendered, but even my tattered robes and the lice upon them appear vividly moving, as if they were alive."
It was a work of meticulous brushwork (*gongbi*). Over ten days later, he sat in meditation reciting the Buddha’s name and passed away.

In the autumn of the Wuzi year, having just returned from a long journey, I paid homage at the Master’s portrait and was moved by a profound sense of sorrow. Upon completing the transcription of this account of the Master’s life in the early winter of the Jihai year, I have recorded these broad outlines as they are.
The Official Who Attained Rebirth:

Liu Chengzhi, courtesy name Zhongsi, was a native of Pengcheng and a descendant of Liu Chang, the Prince Yuan of Han. Having lost his father at an early age, he served his mother with such filial piety that it became renowned.

Possessing great talent, he did not conform to the vulgar customs of his time. Upon first leaving the plain white robes of a student, he served as a military aide (*canjun*) for a provincial administration, whereupon he immediately retired to Mount Lu to live in seclusion.
When Liu Yu sought to stabilize the dynasty, he repeatedly recommended him for office, but Huiyuan declined, styling himself a "Remnant Man" (Yimin).
He joined the Lotus Society of Master Yuan Hui and, together with Lei Cizong, Zhou Xuzhi, Zong Bing, Zhang Quan, and others, cultivated the Pure Land, carving inscriptions upon stone as a vow.

He also composed the *Nianfo Sanmei Shi* (Poem on the Samādhi of Buddha-Recollection) to express his earnest resolve; after half a year of seated meditation and focused visualization, he beheld the light of the Buddha within samādhi.
The ground was illuminated everywhere, turning entirely golden. After fifteen years, while he was practicing the mindfulness of the Buddha, he again saw Amitābha Buddha;

the light from his jade-like brow-mark shone forth, comforting him and touching the crown of his head. One day, while practicing the mindfulness of the Buddha, he again saw himself enter a pool of the seven treasures, where the lotuses were blue and white and the water was limpid and clear.
A person with a circular halo around the neck and a *svastika* on the chest pointed to the water of the pool and said:
"Drink from these waters of eight virtues. Cheng drank the water, which was exceptionally sweet and delicious; even upon waking, he still perceived a wondrous fragrance emanating from his pores.
He then addressed the assembly, saying, "The conditions for my rebirth in the Pure Land have arrived. Facing the image [of Amitābha], he burned incense and made this vow:
"By virtue of the bequeathed teachings of Śākyamuni, I know that there is the Compassionate Father, Amitābha. This incense shall first be offered to him."
Having made offerings to the Tathāgata Śākyamuni, he next offered them to Amitābha Buddha, saying, "May all sentient beings be born together in the Pure Land.
Having finished speaking, he faced west, joined his palms, and passed away. This was the sixth year of the Yixi era. A rare fragrance wafted forth and did not cease for seven days.
Master Huiyuan composed an inscription to commemorate his virtues. Master Tanluan remarked that the *Amitāyurdhyāna Sūtra* describes the practices of pure karma.

Since filial piety toward one’s parents is the foremost cause, it is fitting that these lay disciples, having devoted themselves minimally to the duties of filial support, have further entered deeply into the Samādhi of Buddha-Recitation and repeatedly experienced auspicious signs;
their rebirth in the highest grade is indeed appropriate. This serves as a model for lay practitioners of the Pure Land path to emulate for ten thousand generations.
Zhang Ye of the Jin dynasty resided in Xunyang; he was proficient in both Chinese and Sanskrit literature and was particularly skilled in composition.

Having been nominated for the position of Mocaicai (Mao Cai) and repeatedly summoned as a Sanqi Changshi (Attendant-in-Ordinary), he declined both appointments. He entered Mount Lu to join the Lotus Society (*Lianshe*) to cultivate the Pure Land practices.
In the fourteenth year of the Yixi era, he took leave of his family, entered his room, sat upright, and passed away.

Song Wang Zhonghui served as a *Sishu Canjun* (Assistant Magistrate) in Guangzhou and frequently visited Chan Master Tianyi Hui for instruction, gaining realization through the practice of mindfulness of the Buddha.
When Yang Cigong, while serving as Governor of Danyang, repeatedly sought his guidance, he asked:

"The sutras instruct people to seek rebirth in the Pure Land, yet the Patriarchs say that the mind itself is the Pure Land and there is no need to seek it elsewhere. How is this to be understood? Yang Gong replied: "Try it for yourself—"
He reflected: "If one were already within the realm of the Buddha, there would be neither purity nor defilement; what need would there be to seek rebirth?
If one has not yet emerged from the realm of sentient beings, how could one fail to recite the Buddha's name with a sincere heart, abandoning this defiled land to seek rebirth in a Pure Land?

The Officer of Personnel (Sishi) was moved by this realization and departed with joyful leaps. Two years later, while Master Yang was in Danyang, he suddenly dreamed that the Officer of Personnel said to him: "Previously, I received [your favor]..."
The Master indicated that he had already attained birth [in the Pure Land] and came specifically to express his gratitude. A few days later, the news of his passing arrived;

it was said that seven days prior, the Official of Rites (Sishu) had foreseen the arrival of the time of death, bid farewell to his kinsmen, and passed away—precisely at the moment the dream occurred. (This should follow Yang Jie’s entry in the Song dynasty.)

Ma Ziyun of the Tang dynasty was selected as a filial and incorrupt official (*xiaolian*) and appointed as the magistrate of Jing County. While escorting grain taxes to the capital, his boat was wrecked by a storm and he was imprisoned.
Thereupon, he devoted himself single-mindedly to the recitation of the Buddha’s name for five years. Upon encountering a general amnesty, he entered a mountain temple in Nanling to live in seclusion.

One day he said to others, "Throughout my life I have been diligent in the recitation of the Buddha’s name; now that my karma for the Western Pure Land is perfected, I shall soon be reborn in An-yang."
The next day, he bathed, dressed in new clothes, sat upright with palms joined, and as a wondrous fragrance filled the room, he said with joy, "The Buddha has come to welcome me.
Having spoken these words, he passed away.
During the Tang dynasty, Bo Juyi, styled Lètiān, held the office of Junior Tutor to the Crown Prince; in his later years, he dismissed all his concubines and attendants and donated his residence.

He took the name "Incense Mountain Layman" (Xiangshan Jushi) after the Xiangshan Temple, spent thirty thousand coins from his own salary to have a painting of the Western World of Ultimate Bliss created, and made a vow to prostrate before it daily while reciting the Buddha’s name. He praised it with this verse:
"The Land of Ultimate Bliss is a pure realm, Free from all evil paths and manifold sufferings. May those like my own body—aged and infirm— Be reborn together therein."
In the *Amitāyus Sūtra*, there is another verse that says: "I am seventy-one years old; I no longer devote myself to chanting.
My eyes grow dim as I labor at my worldly duties, yet I fear the toil of such exertion. How can I deliver my mind’s eye?
With one call of 'Amitābha,' whether walking I am Amitābha, or sitting I am Amitābha—even if I were as busy as a rushing arrow, I would not cease my Amitābha. There is a man of distinction."
It is said that when the eminent Master Le Tian was about to depart for Penglai, he composed a verse of farewell: "The mountains and seas of the ocean are not my place of departure;

if I must return, I shall return to Tuṣita Heaven. Now, having again relinquished Tuṣita to seek rebirth in the Pure Land, is this not what is meant by "the more one chooses, the more refined one becomes"?
That he passed away peacefully while sitting upright at the end of his life is a manifest proof of his rebirth in the Pure Land.

Zhang Di of Song was a native of Qiantang who served as an Assistant Teacher (*jiàozhù*). He received the Bodhisattva precepts from Vinaya Master Yuanjing and inquired after the Dharma-gates of Pure Practice (*jìngyè*).
He applied himself with earnest devotion to their cultivation, vowing to be reborn in the Land of Peaceful Nurturing (*Ān-yǎng*).

Whenever he practiced mindfulness of the Buddha, he would chant with such vigorous and loud voices that he would lose his voice, yet he would not stop. One day, he said to Yuanjing, "In my meditative concentration (*dìng*), I saw a white *piñgā* bird."
After dancing and whirling before him for another three years, he sat upright facing west, recited the Buddha’s name, and passed away.

Wang Ri-xiu of Song was a native of Long-shu and a Jìn-shì graduate of the National Academy; having extensively mastered the classics and histories, he suddenly renounced them all, saying, "These are all merely habitual practices and not the ultimate Dharma.
I shall instead seek my return to the Western Land. From that time on, he applied himself with diligent progress in mindfulness.
At the age of sixty, the Buddha wore simple robes, subsisted on vegetarian food, and performed a thousand prostrations daily before retiring to sleep at midnight.

He composed a text on the Pure Land, exhorting the world with words that were both fervent and earnest. Three days before his passing, he took leave of all his relatives and acquaintances, saying they would not see him again.
On the appointed day, as he was reciting his usual prayers, he suddenly raised his voice and called out, "Amitābha Buddha! and proclaimed, "The Buddha is coming!"
When he came to welcome me, he stood firm and motionless, like a tree planted in the ground. Examining his daily recitations, they amounted to nine hundred and twelve thousand five hundred;
these were pasted upon the walls. A person of the local community dreamed that two youths in green robes led the Master westward.
From then on, every household painted his portrait and venerated him. Zhou Bida, the Chancellor and Duke of Yiguō, composed a eulogy for him, and Zhang Yuhu also wrote one.
Preface.

Ge Fan of Chengjiang in the Song dynasty attained the imperial examination at a young age and served as high as the Court Scattered Rank (*chao-san*). In his daily life, he constantly practiced acts of benevolence;

whether in public offices or private residences, he invariably established pure chambers, installed Buddha images, and would regularly enter them to perform prostrations, recitations, and chantings, with śarīra relics accompanying him.
He descended from the sky and returned to the world of men, where he universally exhorted both monastics and laypeople through his pure karma; many were moved by his transformation.
Later, while a monk was traveling spiritually through the Pure Land in meditation, he saw Fan there. Subsequently, without illness, Fan sat upright facing west and passed away.
Hu Yin, the Prefectural Governor of Xuan-yi during the Song dynasty, had long believed in the Buddha-vehicle but was not yet familiar with the Pure Land teachings.
At the age of eighty-four, as his illness grew critical, his son invited the Vinaya Master Qingzhao to request his guidance.

Qingzhao asked Yin, "Do you know where one establishes one's life and finds peace? Yin replied, "When the mind is pure, the Buddha-land is pure. Qingzhao said, "You have already attained realization yourself."
In the past, did you have defilements from discursive thoughts? Zhiqin replied, "Since one dwells in the world, how could there not be discursive thoughts?

Tanyao said, "If this is so, how can the mind be pure and the land be pure? Zhiqin replied, "By reciting the Buddha’s name once, how can the heavy sins of birth and death for eighty billion kalpas be extinguished? Tanyao said, "It is because Amitābha Buddha possesses the power of his great vows."
To extinguish immeasurable sins by reciting their names just once is like the brilliant sun dissolving frost and snow; how could there be any doubt? Thereupon, Yin attained realization.
That very day, he invited monks to practice Buddha-recitation. The next morning, Zhao went to visit him and said, "Master, why have you arrived so late?
By then, the two Great Beings had already descended. Zhao then led the assembly to recite the Buddha's name with a resolute voice, whereupon Yin...
He passed away with palms joined at the city gate; having attained rebirth in Qingzhao, he was welcomed by Qingzhao himself. Is this not the height of filial piety?
There are those in the world who, clinging to minor attachments, violate the precepts of fasting for their parents; their error is indeed profound.

Yang Jie of Song was a native of Wuweizhou and styled himself the "Master of Non-Action" (Wuweizi). Having passed the imperial examinations in his youth, he served as the Director of the Court of State Ceremonies and later as the Commissioner for Judicial Review of the Two Zhejiang Circuits.
He held the Buddha-dharma in high esteem and attained clear realization of the Chan school.

He taught that while the capacities of sentient beings vary—some being sharp and others dull—and thus their paths may be either easy to understand or easy to practice, the Western Pure Land is such that anyone who can single-mindedly contemplate it will have all scattered thoughts gathered together.

Relying on the power of the Buddha’s vows, he resolved to be born in the Land of Peaceful Nurturing (*An-yang*). He once composed the *Preface to the Ten Doubts about the Pure Land* (*Tiantai Shiyi lun xu*), the *Preface to Wáng Gǔ’s Direct Pointing to the Pure Land:
Resolving Doubts* (*Zhízhǐ jìngtǔ juéyì xu*), the *Record of the Precious Pavilion of Amitābha* (*Mítuó bǎogé jì*), and the *Thirty Praises of the Land of Peaceful Nurturing* (*Ān-yǎng sānshí zàn*).

He extensively propagated the teachings and contemplations of the Western Paradise to guide future generations. In his later years, he painted an image of the sixteen-foot-tall Amitābha Buddha, which he would carry with him as he practiced mindfulness and visualization.
On the day of his death, he was moved by the Buddha’s arrival to welcome him; sitting upright, he passed away.
During the Xuanhong era, the consort of the Prince of Jing traveled in spirit to the Pure Land and saw the Master sitting upon a lotus flower together with Ma Yu.
When Wen Lu Gong of the Song dynasty, whose name was Yanbo, was serving as Governor of Luoyang, he once went to Longshan Temple for a ritual fast to pay homage to the Buddha.

Upon entering the hall, he suddenly saw that a statue had collapsed and fallen to the ground; he showed it no sign of reverence. A monk questioned him about this, and the official replied, "Since the image is already broken, what benefit is there in gazing upon it?
The monk said, "The image is neither new nor old; the Way is neither born nor extinguished. Upon hearing this, the official [was moved].

After paying his respects and departing, he later attended Master Jingyan, where he vowed to assemble one hundred thousand people for a Pure Land assembly to universally exhort them to recite the Buddha’s name;
he passed away peacefully at the end of his life through the practice of mindfulness of the Buddha.
Song Ma Yu, style name Dongyu, served as a Grand Secretary. During the Yuanfeng era, the monk Guangyi bestowed upon him the *Ten Doubts on the Teachings of Tiantai*.
He was greatly delighted and said, "I have finally found my guiding principle. For twenty-five years, he recited the Buddha’s name with a sincere heart.

During the Chongning era, while suffering from a minor illness, he changed his clothes and passed away while sitting upright. A vapor like a blue canopy emerged from his door, ascending into the sky and vanishing. His family... [observed this].
Everyone dreamed that Ju was reborn in the Upper Grade.
Zhongli Jin (style name Gongyu) of the Song dynasty passed the examinations in the third year of the Xianping era and served as an Attendant Gentleman of the Longtu Pavilion.

He was exceptionally filial; when his mother, Lady Ren, passed away, he lived in a hut by her grave and practiced cultivation. After his period of mourning ended, while traveling for official duties, he made it his daily practice [to recite the scriptures].
After serving for twenty years, he was transferred to the post of Judicial Commissioner of Zhejiang. By imperial decree, he was granted special honors as the Master of the Ciyun Repentance Ritual.

Having heard the essential instructions from Master Jue, he devoted himself earnestly to the practice of the Pure Land. Later, while serving in Kaifeng, he exerted his utmost in state affairs when abroad, yet upon returning home, he would focus his mind on reciting the Buddha’s name.

Suddenly one night, he urged his family members to rise, requested a bath, changed his robes, and passed away while seated. The entire family saw the Master sitting upright at the moment of his death.
Blue-lotus celestial music led the way as he traveled westward.
Yan Bangrong of Puzhou, during the Song dynasty, had recited the *Nianfo Wangsheng Zhou* for twenty years.

As he was about to pass away, his family members dreamed that the Buddha emitted light to welcome Bangrong. At dawn, Bangrong sat cross-legged facing west; suddenly he rose and walked several paces, saying, "I..."
As he was departing, he stood with his hands hanging down, forming a mudrā and smiling; his wife, startled, supported him, and he passed away.
Song Jiu-ding, whose courtesy name was Shengzhai, served as an instructor at the prefectural school and devoted himself exclusively to the Pure Land practice.

He once produced large-scale *bākō* (block-print) illustrations to distribute and encourage people to recite the Buddha’s name, and every month on the second and eighth days, he gathered monks and laypeople to recite the Buddha’s name and chant the *Amitābha Sūtra*.
In the fourth year of the Jiading era, Zhihuilun dreamed of a youth dressed in green who told him, "The Supreme Honored One summons you; three days hence, you shall attain rebirth.
When the appointed day arrived, he bathed, changed his clothes, and while reciting the Buddha's name, he passed away while seated.
Feng Jia of Song, styled Jichuan, was a native of Suining who attained the jinshi degree through the Imperial Academy. Initially, he sought the Way within the Chan forests;
in his later years, he devoted himself exclusively to the Pure Land practice. He composed the *Xifang wen* (Text for the Western Paradise) and the *Mituo chan yi* (Amitābha Repentance Ritual).

Later, serving as a Remonstrance Official (*Ji shigong*), he was dispatched to lead the military administration in Lunnan, where he led both monastics and laypeople in holding "Mindfulness Assemblies" (*Xilian hui*). While serving as the Prefect of Qiongzhou, he would personally go to the rear hall at the end of each day to perform these rites.

When he was appointed to a high seat, he faced the palace and performed a solemn prostration; when donning his monastic robes to ascend the seat, he thanked the officials and, leaning his staff against his knees, passed away.
Master Lian asked: "The *Chuan deng lu* records that the Master first studied under Longmen Yuan and later under Miaoxi, attaining realization at each stage.
At the end of his life, he set a specific date to ascend the seat and departed without speaking of 'reciting the Buddha's name' or 'rebirth in the Pure Land. Why is this so?"
This is truly because biographers each establish their own principles according to what they emphasize.
Those who emphasize the direct pointing to the human mind naturally focus exclusively on clarifying the "mind-ground" while omitting details regarding the Pure Land;

this is exemplified by the fact that although Huaiyu visited the Jintai (Golden Terrace) twice and Yuanzhao was named after the lotus seeds, neither is recorded. Conversely, those who emphasize the ultimate return to the Pure Land provide detailed accounts of their lives.
When the retribution for one's life is exhausted through the practice of Buddha-remembrance, one is reborn and realizes the nature of the mind, attaining mastery therein;
as it is said, "Once you have seen Amitābha, why worry about not attaining enlightenment? Those who practice the pure karma should vow to believe this with firm conviction and without doubt.

Song Wang Gu, courtesy name Huizhong, was a native of Dongdu who served as Minister of the Court of Rites. Compassionate and kind toward all living beings, he was deeply attuned to the Chan school and further realized the excellence of the Pure Land dharma-gate.
He composed the *Direct Pointing to the Pure Land: A Collection for Resolving Doubts*, which was prefaces by Yang Cigong.

Throughout his life, he was diligent in the practice of nianfo, never letting his prayer beads leave his hand; whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, he remained constant in this practice.
Taking the pure contemplation of the Western Paradise as his Buddhist practice, there was a monk who traveled in spirit to the Pure Land and saw Gu and Ge Fan both present there;
it is fitting that his rebirth there would be of the highest grade.
During the Zhizheng era of the Yuan dynasty, Wu Zicai (style name Xinsou), a native of Suzhou, practiced together with his disciple Zhang under Master Yun.

Wu Xinsou, who had received the Dharma-door of mindfulness of the Buddha, practiced with unceasing diligence. After his son Cai retired from office, he prepared a coffin in advance and slept within it at night.
He would have a youth strike the coffin and sing: "Wu Xinsou, go back! Go back! There is no peace in the three realms; they cannot be dwelt in.
The Western Pure Land has lotus wombs; go back, go back, and follow [the Buddha] there. The son would then join in the chant.
Later, he passed away peacefully while sitting without illness; his son, Zhang, likewise met his end serenely, reciting the Buddha’s name as he transformed.
During the Song dynasty, Su Shi—styled Dongpo and serving as Hanlin Academician—was exiled to the south. While traveling, he painted a single scroll of Amitābha and wore it with him at all times.
When people asked about it, he replied, "This is my official warrant for birth in the Western Paradise. His mother, the Lady... [text ends].
Upon the death of Lady Cheng, she bequeathed her personal jewelry and assets to the artisan Hu Xi, instructing him to paint an image of Amitābha to assist her in attaining rebirth in the Pure Land.
Furthermore, Sū Shunqian (Laoquan) once commissioned images of the Six Bodhisattvas at Jile Temple; thus, it was evident that the Su family had long turned their hearts toward the Triple Gem.
There are those in the world who have carved "Testimonials for the Western Paradise," adding colloquial vernacular to them and falsely claiming they originated from Su Dongpo.
This is a slander. Let those with discerning eyes not lose the truth because of this falsehood (this should have been placed before Wang Rixiu).

Ming Zhu Gang was a native of the capital who studied Confucianism and passed the provincial examination. Although he failed three times at the Imperial Academy, he subsequently took office in two government departments and retired from service to devote himself exclusively to the Pure Land path.
He recited the Buddha’s name thirty thousand times daily for fifteen years without the slightest negligence.

At the moment of death, sitting upon his couch, he held a prayer bead in both hands and recited the Buddha’s name without ceasing. A wondrous fragrance filled the room, and he exclaimed, "The Buddha is coming!
He passed away while continuously chanting the name.
During the Wanli era of the Ming Dynasty, Master Gu Baocang (whose secular name was Yuanzhi) cultivated the Pure Land practices together with his Dharma friend, the elder Zhang.
The gentleman was gravely ill; he gathered a group of monastics and laypeople to chant the ten recitations of Amitābha Buddha’s name in continuous unison, including Zhang Yuyan.
The gentleman said to him, "At this moment, I do not perceive any movement. Zhang replied, "You are greatly mistaken; why harbor such doubts?

You must be single-minded and diligent, rousing your spirit to recite the Buddha's name. After a short while, the assembly suddenly smelled a wondrous fragrance filling the room, and the gentleman saw it for himself.
As his body sat within the lotus flower, his disciples were overcome with grief and longing. He consoled them, saying: "Where do you think I am going?
Wherever you are, that is where I am. The Buddhas have come to welcome me; having struck the drums at dawn, I set forth. My own vow is now fulfilled, and thus your vows shall also be comforted.
When the appointed time arrived, he departed with a smile. Master Yin Qiuming, the Vice Minister of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices, composed a biography of him titled *The Great Lotus*.
The Master said: "As for 'the body sits within the lotus'—to be born there means one will certainly be born there;
as for 'where is it?'—it is right here. To go there, in reality, one does not go. This is a contemporary fact that those with clear eyes should examine. Someone asked me:
"I believe your cultivation is indeed like this, yet the single phrase 'not seeing movement or stillness' cannot help but give rise to doubt. I replied: "This is precisely your going."
Right mindfulness has arisen; because its recognition is certain, one’s aspiration is fervent and one’s expectation is earnest, thus the waiting is urgent.
It is like one parched by a great drought looking toward rain, hoping for its swift arrival and fearing only that it might not come—how could there be any doubt about the rain?
When Ming Haiyan’s Zhu Yuanzheng was a student, he expounded the teachings of Confucius and Mencius with integrity and rectitude.
After the age of sixty, he immersed himself deeply in Chan practice; in a dilapidated three-bay building behind his residence, he closed the gate and withdrew from domestic affairs.
He inscribed the six characters "For example, I am already dead" above the door. His daily devotions consisted of reciting the *Lotus Sūtra* before noon.
One scroll. Afternoon: One thousand recitations of the Buddha’s name. On the fourth day of the month of Gengshen, Tang Yizhi, together with his disciple Chen Zeliang, visited Master Zhigong.
Yizhi said to Zeliang, "I previously sent you a letter urging you to cultivate the practice of the Pure Land;
you should listen to it most earnestly. Subsequently, Zeliang said, "The Master is advanced in years; why not relax the prohibition against wine for a little? The Master replied: [He did so].
