He said, "Do you think that in my declining years I should rely on several cups of wine to regulate my qi and nourish my blood?

You do not know that my life has already been severed; why speak of such things? When he said his life was severed, he took a brush and drew a line across the table, thereby manifesting his mastery over birth and death. On the seventh month, without illness, he suddenly said to his son: "I..."
"There is nothing more to be done here," he said. When his son asked where he was going, he replied, "I am going to the West. His son and grandson earnestly entreated him to stay, and he consented.

On the first day of the twelfth lunar month, he manifested illness and ceased eating. His family members were in a state of panic, preparing for his funeral arrangements, when the Master said, "Do not be anxious;
this shall happen at midnight on the eighth day of this month. He further instructed his family that, upon his departure, they must not allow women to be present.
He came back two or three times, yet even then he did not weep. When the time arrived, he sat upright and passed away.
It was then just before dawn; when his kinsmen finally arrived and began their wailing, the Master woke up again, opened his eyes, but did not speak.
He merely shook his head to have the women removed, then closed his eyes and passed away. At that time, his coming and going were as free as this.

Mingding Mingdeng, styled Jianhong, was a native of Jiangpu. In the *jǐyǒu* year of the Wanli era, he took refuge with the Great Master Yunqi and became a devoted believer in the Pure Land Dharma-gate, changing his style name to Lianlü.
In the *jǐsī* year of the Chongzhen era, he received the fourfold precepts from Yinyi; in the *gēngwǔ* year, he received the Bodhisattva precepts from Dahui.
In the *bǐchén* year of the Wanli era, he passed the imperial examinations and served as an official in Wēnlíng, where he traveled frequently.

Through great deeds for transcending the world, he transformed both monastics and laypeople, leading many to profound realization. While serving as Magistrate of Quzhou, he strictly prohibited the slaughter of cattle.
When a reckless man who had violated the law was pursued by authorities, he learned that the man respected the clergy; he immediately shaved his head and presented him to the Master.

He instructed the local headman to monitor him closely and punish him severely should he return to secular life. That man resolved to practice with diligence and eventually became a renowned monk. This was his first official appointment.

The Judicial Commissioner of Quanzhou issued a decree of flogging and public censure. He established a regulation permitting those who wished to contribute rice to do so for the purpose of providing sustenance for impoverished prisoners.
During the summer months, he renovated the prison cells and provided *xiangru* (patchouli) decoy and *huai* fans; in the winter months, he installed warming boxes containing pepper and ginger.

He selected physicians to attend to the sick and purchased over a hundred strings of plain prayer beads to distribute among the prisoners, encouraging them to constantly recite the Buddha’s name. He spoke thus to the people.
He said, "Many people resolve their minds toward the Dharma when they are in distress; I shall take advantage of their remorse to guide them toward the practice of *nien-fo*.
Fortunately, they have been released from prison and have become good citizens. However, I feel compassion for the women within the inner chambers who do not hear the Buddha-dharma.

I request that you, O Zen Master, expound upon the Mahayana so that they may listen from behind the curtains. At that time, four members of the family shaved their heads and became monks, hearing [the teachings] from within the lotus-like enclosure.
The Great Master said: "There was an old woman who claimed that her husband had recited the Buddha’s name with single-minded focus and without distraction until his death.
He requested one final invitation before departing, and from this the woman gained deep faith in the Pure Land. The Master himself also resolved to leave the household life from this point on.

He drew a picture titled "One Final Invitation" and hung it in his meditation hall, inscribing a poem upon it: "I have given you my one final invitation; in a flash, you have departed. Cherish our meeting—how many times shall we encounter again?"

In the winter of the Year of the Rooster (1765), when my illness was severe, on the first day of the eleventh month, I prepared a memorial to inform the Buddha of my firm resolve and earnestly sought rebirth in the Pure Land.
I burned one memorial each day until the tenth day, at which point my consumption of rice gruel and drink remained normal and my facial complexion was radiant and smooth.

He repeatedly and earnestly exhorted his relatives and acquaintances to be reborn together in the Western Paradise; then, reclining upon his bed, he lay still and passed away peacefully. This account has been compiled for the sake of future generations.
The "Village News," "Lotus Waterclock Pure Sounds," "Mustard Seed Fire and Lotus Calyx," and "Faint Conversations on the Ten Kinds" are all essential texts for the Pure Land school;
the remainder are recorded in the "Successor Prince Han-sheng’s Leftovers from the Lotus Fragrance Pond."

Appendix: Three Accounts of Master Bianrong’s Release from Prison through Mindfulness of the Buddha during the Wanli Era. During the Wanli period, Chan Master Bianrong was imprisoned on account of slanderous rumors.

A prison guard, knowing that the Master was highly esteemed for his reputation, demanded a large sum of money as a reward. Master Bianrong replied, "Where would a monk obtain money? The guard then produced a chest containing the loot from a robbery.

Regarding the distinction concerning the bed-casket, Gong faced the void and chanted: "The Avataṃsaka Sūtra of the Buddha, the Flower Ornament; may the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas of the Avataṃsaka assembly fill this casket.
The bed then rattled and clattered, its locks snapped and the frame shattered. When this event was reported to the prison warden, it reached the Imperial Court.
By imperial decree, he was summoned to bring forth the contents.
During the Chongzhen era, there were many high-ranking officials imprisoned; if their cases involved matters of defense or the frontiers, none escaped the death penalty.
At that time, Yu Jisheng (Da Cheng), the Governor of Shandong, was in prison and first proposed chanting the Buddha’s name, which most of the other officials followed.
When the date for their execution arrived, they gathered together and chanted the Buddha’s name day and night without ceasing. Suddenly, images of the Buddha appeared covering the walls.
A brilliant light flashed, startling everyone, who all bowed in reverence; subsequently, they received an imperial edict of grace.
Mo Jisheng and Shen Yanwei, both of whom were sentenced to execution for their roles in border defense, were instead spared and sent to military colonies rather than being released from prison.
In the sixth year of the Shunzhi era, Chan Master Juelang was imprisoned at Taiping Prison for publishing works that offended the authorities.

While there, Master Lang instructed the prisoners to recite the Buddha’s name and used virtuous words to exhort the prison guards to change their hearts; the guards also began to observe the fast and recite the Buddha’s name.
Every time the first watch arrived, Master Lang would take up a small mallet while the guards held long incense sticks; passing by each numbered cell, he would call out, "Da! (Great!).
The assembly was single-minded in their mindfulness of the Buddha; those who violated this precept could not help but weep aloud as they recited the Buddha’s name.

Laypeople provided offerings and alms, which were distributed entirely to relieve the poor and destitute. Within less than five months, the Prefect of Taiping arrived at the prison and personally released Master Lang;
because of this, the prisoners were reviewed for clarity, and those with minor offenses were largely granted clemency and release.
Ming Tang Yizhi, whose courtesy name was Shi, was a native of Huzhou. He attended upon Master Lianchi and diligently cultivated the Pure Land practice.

Initially serving as a Vice Governor (Biejia) of Shouyang by virtue of his mastery of the Confucian classics, he later assisted in the governance of Xiangguo. His entire family and kinsmen all took refuge in the Triple Gem;

each morning they would each recite the scriptures, and each evening they would gather together to chant the Buddha’s name. In the second month of the spring of the Xin-si year of the Chongzhen era, the rebel leader Chang escaped with his troops and captured Xiangyang.
At the end of the public referendum, while inside the well to the left of the Endli Gate, his family members assisted him in climbing out; though his breath had already ceased, he revived.

Having been summoned for interrogation by imperial decree, he was granted leniency under the broad amnesty. He subsequently requested leave to return to his home village, yet on the fifth day of the last month of winter, Xiangyang fell once again.
Thus, he did not die at the hands of the rebels, nor did he die in the well, and in the end, he did not die by the law—is this not [a testament to his fortune]?
The merit of his compassionate, silent protection is inconceivable. Ye Gong himself described how, over several years, there was a profound resonance between the Way and his practice.

On the eighth day of the twelfth month in the Dinghai year, while reciting the Buddha’s name and paying homage at the stupa in Changgan Temple, he beheld the Buddha’s form within the light of the stupa.
The Buddha’s golden light was like snow, like ice, and like a clear mirror. On the fifth day of the seventh month in the Wuzi year, he [continued] his recitation.

While the Buddha was in his meditation hall, he opened a window and suddenly beheld Mount Zhong floating upon a vast ocean. A golden Buddha stood majestically, its auspicious radiance brilliant and dazzling;
the tiles, rubble, walls, and enclosures, as well as the tall trees and thickets, were all empty and vanished from sight.
Now, ordinary people, when told that the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss lies beyond ten trillion Buddha-lands, immediately consider it remote; yet, judging by what was seen here, [it is not so].
Ten billion buddha-lands are right before one’s eyes; to exhaust one’s life in the space of a finger-snap and be reborn therein—is this not indeed to be born within the square-inch of one’s own mind?
As the *Lotus Sūtra* states: "With the eyes born of one's parents, one can see all that is above and below heaven;
walls, enclosures, mountains, and valleys present no obstruction. Thus, seeing the worlds of the ten directions is like looking into empty space.

This is merely a matter of the internal events. During the assembly at the Lotus Sutra, the light from the Tathāgata’s white tuft of hair illuminated the ground everywhere, making it all pure lapis lazuli;
there were no villages, cities, rivers, seas, mountains, or valleys, nor did hells or hungry ghosts exist, as the entire land became a Buddha-field.
Is this not truly so? Recalling the year of Guisi (1593), I was still able to receive your instructions in Baixia, and subsequently heard [of these matters].

The auspicious responses of his westward journey were manifest and clear; yet, I am ashamed that my own defilements and afflictions remain so persistent that I have not had the leisure to examine the historical records.
Nevertheless, based on the fact that he repeatedly beheld the Buddha during his lifetime, it is fitting that after his rebirth he should serve by the Buddha’s side.

In the *Jinyu Cheng* (Collection of the Head Coachman), there are transcriptions of the *Sutra of the Lotus World*, the *Dharma-sound*, and the *Peacock Sound*, as well as further accounts of the Tathāgata.

This single volume of correspondence with the World-Honored One’s teachings of his lifetime—spanning several millennia from the Zhou and Qin dynasties through the Song and Ming—is a testament to the spirit of virtuous friends (kalyāṇamitra).
Within its pages, the profound flavor of the Dharma as expounded by emperors, kings, ministers, and officials is brilliantly displayed;
among lay practitioners who have realized the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, you alone are such a person in recent times.
While the common people were seeking rebirth at the Jin palace gates, Gongze entered Mount Lu’s Lotus Society and attained the samādhi of buddha-remembrance.
After his death, a friend performed a memorial sacrifice for him at night within the White Horse Temple in Luoyang; suddenly, all the trees and the temple buildings turned entirely golden.
In the midst of the empty sky, a voice spoke, saying: "I am Gue Gongze. I sought the Land of Ultimate Bliss and have now attained rebirth there.
Having finished speaking, he vanished from sight.

Zhou Xuzhi of the Song dynasty was a man from Yanmen; he mastered the Five Classics and the Five Weis at the age of twelve, earning him the title "The Child of the Ten Classics. He lived as a recluse...
Zhi lived in seclusion; though summoned by high officials from all quarters, he declined them all. He resided at Mount Lu with Dharma Master Huiyuan, who was a member of the Lotus Society.

When Emperor Wen ascended the throne, he summoned Zhi for an audience, and after their discussion, the Emperor was greatly pleased. Someone asked him, "Is it appropriate for one who calls himself a recluse to frequent the royal court?
He replied, "Those whose hearts run toward the imperial palace regard the rivers and lakes as shackles; those whose feelings have transcended both [the secular and the monastic]..."
The marketplace and the court were, for him, no different from a mountain cave; he was thus titled "Master Tongyin" (the Master Who Penetrates Both Secular and Recluse Life).

Later, he resided on Mount Zhong, where he devoted himself single-mindedly to the recitation of the Buddha’s name with increasing sincerity as he grew older. One day, facing the sky, he said, "The Buddha has come to welcome me," and with palms joined, he passed away.
Sun Liang of Song was a native of Qiantang who lived in seclusion and studied the Tripitaka, gaining a profound mastery of the essential principles of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*.
Having received the Bodhisattva precepts from Vinaya Master Dazhi, he recited the Buddha’s name ten thousand times daily for twenty years without ceasing.

One day, he instructed his family to invite monks to recite the Buddha’s name to assist him in his rebirth. When the monks had gathered and had been chanting for only half a meal’s duration, Sun Liang joined his palms toward the void.
It is said that the Buddha and the Bodhisattvas had already graced him with their presence, whereupon they withdrew and entered parinirvāṇa (this should be placed later in the Song dynasty record).
Yu Xian of Xinye, during the Liang dynasty, was summoned by Emperor Wu to serve as a Gentleman of the Yellow Gate but did not go. Six times each day he recited the name of the Buddha.
One night, he saw a practitioner who called himself Master Yuan; he addressed Yu Xian as "Master Shangxing" and, after handing him incense, departed.

After four years, he wished for the Master to return, but the Master then passed away into transformation. A voice spoke from the air, saying: "Master Shangxing has already been reborn in the Land of Peaceful Nurturing (An-yang).
Sui Songman was a native of Changzhou. He counted his beans while reciting the Buddha’s name until they accumulated to thirty *shi*.

On the ninth month of the eighth year of the Kaihuang era, Amitābha and Avalokiteśvara appeared, holding him as they went to beg for alms. Songman said, "I, your disciple, vow to be reborn in the Western Paradise to provide offerings to my Master."
Deeply comforted in his long-held aspiration, after the meal was concluded, the three monks departed toward the sky. Man then sat in meditation and passed away;
people saw celestial flowers and extraordinary fragrances proceeding westward from the edge of the clouds, never dispersing.

Song Wang Tian was a native of Siming, surnamed Wugong Seng (the Elder Without Merit). He had a profound mastery of all the fundamental tenets of the Chan school as well as the teachings of the Tiantai school.
He authored the *Jingtu Zixin Lu* (Record of Self-Confidence in the Pure Land). In his later years, he devoted himself exclusively to the recitation of the Buddha’s name;
he sat facing west and passed away amidst a fragrant aura of rare incense. When his coffin was cremated, one hundred and eight śarīras were recovered.

Fan Yan of the Song dynasty was a native of Renhe who had completely severed his ties to worldly affairs. When his son could not manage the household, Yan paid it no mind, saying only, "I am merely a guest here.
He recited the *Lotus Sūtra* daily and chanted the name of Amitābha Buddha with undivided and tireless devotion.
Suddenly, he beheld Samantabhadra Bodhisattva riding a six-tusked white elephant and emitting golden light, who informed Yan that [the time for his departure] was near.

At the hour of the Rabbit (卯) on that day, he was about to pass away when, in the middle of the night, Buddhas and Bodhisattvas came to welcome him; he took his seat, joined his palms, and passed away.
Sun Zhong of Siming in the Song dynasty was a man who had long admired the Western Paradise. He built a hermitage east of the prefectural city to practice *nianfo*.

Later, falling ill, he invited one hundred monks to recite the Buddha’s name for him. Suddenly, looking up at the sky with palms joined and his hands forming the double-seal mudrā (*yinyin*), he passed away peacefully.
The entire city heard celestial music and a wondrous fragrance gradually vanished toward the west. The two sons followed one another in reciting the Buddha’s name and passed away while seated.
In the family of Shen Quan of Qiantang during the Song dynasty, he and his wife Shi focused their minds exclusively on the Pure Land; all their various good deeds were dedicated toward that goal.
Later, when both husband and wife reached the end of their lives, they were moved by the response of the Transformation Buddha, who appeared holding a monk’s staff to welcome them away.
Ji Gong of Song was an ironworker from Taoyuan in Siming. At the age of seventy, his two eyes had lost their sight.

Zhan Xuelun of the village provided him with "broke-cone" (large-character) diagrams of Buddha images to distribute as offerings, encouraging people to recite the Buddha's name. When Ji Gong first received one diagram, he recited the name thirty-six hundred thousand times;
by the time he reached the fourth diagram, both his eyes were restored to clear vision. He continued in this manner for three years until he had completed ten million recitations.

On the seventh day of the first month, while reciting the Buddha’s name, he suddenly lost consciousness. After half a day, he revived and said, "The Buddha has commanded that six charts be given to Xuèyù Ķǎn, for he was the leader in encouraging others;
one chart is to be given to Lì Èr Gōng, for he was the person who displayed the charts.
He instructed his son to go and offer thanks, and having finished speaking, he bathed, faced west, and passed away.

Song Jin was a native of Kuaiji who made his living by fishing. Suddenly, he attained a profound realization and began to observe the precepts with diligent vigor, reciting the Buddha’s name ten thousand times daily without fail for a long time.
Later, without any illness, he said to his family members, "Amitābha Buddha, accompanied by two Bodhisattvas, has come to welcome me;
I am returning to the Pure Land. He then burned incense, sat upright, and passed away amidst the admiration of the local people.
A rare fragrance was perceived and celestial music resounded throughout the day without ceasing.
Liu Tongzhi, a native of the capital, was a man of sincere devotion who recited the Buddha’s name with diligence. At the age of fifty-two, he fell ill; his recitation became even more earnest.
His neighbor Li Baizhai had previously passed away, yet when [Tongzhi] lost consciousness from morning until noon, he revived. He said to his family members:
I recently saw a boat departing for the Pure Land, and thirty-six people were on board, including Baizhai.
I was also among their number; however, my robes were not fresh or clean, and I had forgotten to bring my prayer beads.
The boat stopped to wait for me, and my family members hurriedly changed my clothes and hung the beads around my neck. A short while later, I passed away.
Ming Tang Yan-ren was a native of Lanxi, styled the Layman Tiri (Tirushi). Filial and fraternal, his integrity was innate.
Having studied in the schools during his youth, he gained a reputation; subsequently, realizing the impermanence of the world, he turned his heart toward the Ultimate Way.

He studied under Yunqi and received the *nien-fo* samādhi, which he then practiced with vigor for thirteen years as if they were but a single day. His resolve toward the Western Paradise was steadfast and singular.
In the middle winter of the *guimao* year, on the occasion of his sixtieth birthday, he suddenly said to his sons, "On the eleventh day of the New Year, I shall return.

Several days prior, his ritual recitations were as usual; when the appointed time arrived, he washed and rinsed his mouth, adjusted his robes, sat upright, formed mudrās with his hands, and while chanting the names of the Buddhas, passed away with a smile, as if entering meditative absorption.

Ming Yang Jiawei, style name Banghua, was a scion of a prominent family from Taichou. At the age of thirteen, he observed the precept against taking life, ensuring that not even a louse or a flea suffered harm.
He devoted himself to the Pure Land school of Dharma, reciting the *Amitābha Sūtra* twenty-three times daily.
After studying at the Southern Capital Academy (Nanyong), he suddenly fell ill and passed away on the nineteenth day of the second month of winter in the year Wanshi Yisi. Upon his death...
Previously, while dreaming, he traveled to the hells and saw the Great Being Kṣitigarbha in the Hall of the Living and the Dead.
Upon waking, he released all living beings, invited monks to recite sutras, and chanted the Buddha’s name, saying to others, "I am about to pass away. A blue lotus has appeared before me;

could this not be a vision of the Pure Land? Thereupon, he chanted the Buddha’s name day and night without ceasing. He ordered the candles extinguished, saying, "You people rely on candles for light."

To clarify that he did not require a candle because he was always within the light, [the Master] asked, "What do you see? He replied, "Lotuses blooming in four colors. [The Master] asked, "Do you see Amitābha?
He replied, "I see Amitābha manifesting a body one thousand *zhang* tall. [The Master] asked about Guanyin: "Is his body equal to that of Amitābha?

He replied, "It is. [The Master] asked about Shizhi: "Do you see him? He replied, "I do not. Having finished speaking, he suddenly leaped up, took up incense, and spoke in a continuous stream of words.
He said, "The merit of the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra* is unspeakably unspeakable; I have already attained the highest grade [of rebirth] and shall pass away in serene stillness.
His elder brother, Jiazuo, recorded this account and vowed: "If I have ever uttered a deceptive word, may I fall into the Hell of the Plucked Tongue.
Is this not a vision of truth, and are these words not uttered with such urgency? Those who do not believe in the Pure Land should reflect upon this."

Ming Hao Xicai was a native of Qiantang; his Dharma name was Guangding. Throughout his life, he was loyal, trustworthy, and free from deceit, earning a reputation for his virtuous conduct within the schools.
In his later years, he turned to Buddhism, reciting the scriptures with increasing devotion day and night. In the second month of the spring of the Xinhai year of the Wanli era, he fell ill.
Every time he awoke from sleep, he would say: "In my dream, I sought an audience with the Buddha in the mountains; I did not see the Buddha, but I saw hundreds of birds."
Having gathered in this manner for many days until the twenty-seventh, at the hour of midnight, he suddenly said: "Two youths have come to welcome me;
I see myself seated upon a lotus pedestal before me. I am going; I shall pass away in auspiciousness. Thus he departed.

Mingge, whose dharma name was Guangtai, was a native of Qiantang. He was exceptionally filial and had long accumulated virtuous deeds, yet he remained deeply reclusive, seeking no recognition from others.
In his later years, he devoted himself with sincerity to the Buddha and formed two seasonal societies with the Lingzhi monk Xuansu to practice nianfo and recite the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* five times.
Suddenly, he said to those around him, "My great life-limit is about to reach its end."
As he was preparing the provisions for his journey to the West, he recited his prayers in his chamber morning and night without ceasing.

Having fixed the date of his departure for the twenty-first day of the twelfth lunar month, two nights prior to that, he and his mother looked at one another and choked with grief. The layman smiled and said, "Birth must inevitably end in extinction;
why grieve? I am now concentrating my spirit on the Pure Land to behold Amitābha face-to-face. You all should be careful not [to disturb me]."

Because worldly attachments disturbed his right mindfulness, he earnestly exhorted [his family] to assist him with recitation without any distracting speech; when the appointed time arrived, he passed away in silence.
Ming’s grandson, Shu Zi, whose Dharma name was Dayu, was naturally gifted and fond of learning from childhood; at the age of twelve, he followed his father, Jing.
My Master Gong brought an image of Amitābha Buddha made in accordance with the Forty-eight Vows to Yunqi. Thereupon, he received the five precepts and renounced meat and strong flavors.
He resolved his will upon the recitation of the Buddha’s name, vowing to attain rebirth on the Golden Terrace. Through his diligent and arduous efforts, he did not spare even his own life;

suddenly, he saw two bhikṣus holding lotuses to certify his single-minded devotion to the Pure Land. Furthermore, he saw a manifested person reciting the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* for an entire day.
At night, he suddenly rose from his seat in a state of alertness and said, "Amitābha and Avalokiteśvara have both come to welcome me.

He formed the *vajra-muṣṭi-mudrā* and called out "Amitābha Buddha" several times, after which he passed away peacefully. This occurred on the eleventh day of the second month of winter in the *xinhai* year of the Wanli era.
A "Song of the Twelve Hours of the Pure Land" was subsequently transmitted to the world; its details are fully contained in the biography of the Imperial Historian Wu Xisheng.

The nun Da-ming, a *bhikṣuṇī* of the Sui dynasty, was devoted to pure cultivation and vowed to be reborn in the Pure Land. Whenever she entered her room to perform prostrations and recitations, she would first don clean robes and hold aloeswood incense in her mouth.
Emperor Wen’s consort held her in high esteem; on the day of her passing, the assembly suddenly smelled the fragrance of aloeswood.
Suddenly, the entire room was filled with a radiance like clouds that gradually faded away toward the west.
The Tang nun Jingzhen resided at Jixian Temple in Chang’an; she wore patched robes, begged for her food, and recited the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* one hundred thousand times.
Devoted to the practice of mindfulness of the Buddha, she said to her disciples: "Within this fifth month, I have seen the Buddha ten times and beheld the jewels twice."

"I have already attained birth in the highest grade in the Lotus-Flower World," said the Youth Playing upon the Lotus. Having finished speaking, he sat in the full-lotus posture and passed away, while auspicious light filled the hermitage.
The Tang nun Wuxing lived on Mount Lu; there she met Master Zhao, who instructed her to make vows and practice mindfulness of the Buddha, practicing with diligence during the six periods of the day.
Jin-yi-chie-bu-luan (Zongmi). In the sixth year of the Dali era, he suddenly fell ill.
Hearing music coming from the west through the air, he said to those around him, "My spirit has traveled to Sukhāvatī, and I have already attained rebirth in the highest of the middle grades.

I see that all my fellow practitioners who sincerely recite the Buddha's name have lotus flowers awaiting them; you all should each exert yourselves. Having spoken these words, his face manifested [a radiant expression] as he passed away.
At the age of twenty-four, she was golden-hued.
A nun from Qiantang named Nengfeng, who specialized in the practice of Pure Land, once dreamed that Buddha-light illuminated her body and heard kind words from the air consoling her.
She told her disciples: "When I am about to be reborn in the Pure Land, you will hear the sound of 'Nianfo' (Buddha-recitation). Nengfeng passed away shortly thereafter.

Her voice was very forceful as she rushed to see him; he was found sitting facing west with palms joined, having passed away. A rare fragrance filled the room, and the sound of music drifted toward the west.
The nun Fazang of the Song dynasty resided in Jinling; her precepts and virtue were extremely strict, and she diligently practiced the mindfulness of the Buddha every four months of the year.
Shuo gathered his fellow practitioners to recite the sutras and maintain mantras; the great assembly of faithful believers unanimously followed his transformative influence.
On the night he passed away, they saw the golden images of Buddhas and Bodhisattvas appear within his chamber, their radiance illuminating the temple. He sat upright and departed from this life.
Regarding women who attain rebirth:
Empress Gao Yang of the Sui dynasty, though dwelling in the royal palace, deeply loathed her female nature and constantly recited the name of Amitābha Buddha.
When she passed away on the day of Jiazi in the eighth month, various kinds of music spontaneously resounded from the north of the Yong'an Palace.
A wondrous fragrance filled the chamber, arriving from the void. The Emperor asked Jñānagupta, "What auspicious omen is this?
He replied, "In the Pure Land there is a Buddha named Amitābha; because the Empress’s karma is exceptionally sublime, she shall ascend to that realm, and thus this auspicious sign has appeared."

Ge Jizhi of Juqiong in the Song dynasty was a descendant of Ge Zhichuan. Throughout his life, he pursued the study of the immortals. His wife, Lady Ji, alone possessed singular sincerity in the recitation of the Buddha’s name.
In the thirteenth year of the Yuanjia era, while she was at her loom, she suddenly felt the air become transparent and luminous.
She cast aside her shuttle and looked upward, clearly beholding the Buddha manifesting in the west amidst precious canopies, banners, and pennants against the Milky Way. She said with joy:
The scripture speaks of the Buddha of Immeasurable Life; was this perhaps him? Ji bowed to the Buddha in person, struck with wonder at being thus saved.
He approached the site, and Ji pointed out where the Buddha had appeared; the one who had been saved also saw the Buddha’s half-body.
Suddenly, he vanished, leaving behind auspicious clouds of five colors that were witnessed by all the neighbors. From then on, many turned to the Buddha-dharma.

The nun Yao Po of the Tang dynasty was exhorted by the nun Fan Xing to practice the recitation of the Buddha’s name. Later, as she approached her death, she saw the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas coming to welcome her.

She said to the Buddha, "I have not yet taken my leave of the nun Fan Xing; I pray that you, World-Honored One, will remain suspended in mid-air for a moment. When Fan arrived, Yao Po passed away instantly.
Wen Jingwen’s wife, a native of Bingzhou, had been bedridden for a long time due to illness. Wen Jingwen encouraged her to recite the Buddha’s name.

After one year, she suddenly beheld the Pure Land and told her husband, "I have already seen the Buddha; I shall depart in the month to come. She then instructed her parents, saying, "I have now attained rebirth following the Buddha.
I pray that you will recite the Buddha’s name with single-minded devotion, so that we may meet again in the Western Paradise in days to come. Having spoken these words, she passed away.
She passed away.
Zheng of the Song dynasty was a native of Qiantang who daily recited the Avalokiteśvara Sūtra and practiced mindfulness of the Buddha without ceasing. Later, while ill, she requested a bath;
having finished, she sat facing west and asked her family, "Do you hear the sound of the chime? The sages of the Pure Land have already arrived, as has Avalokiteśvara."
Holding a golden platform in her hands, the Tathāgata received her and led her to ascend the seat; she then suddenly passed away.
Lady Wang, the consort of the Prince of Jing during the Song dynasty, was devoted to the practice of Pure Land Buddhism, being diligent and earnest from dawn until dusk.

Among those who served her, there was none who did not follow her example, with the sole exception of one maidservant who was indolent and disrespectful. The lady rebuked her, whereupon the maidservant repented and applied herself with vigor. Suddenly, she became free of ailment.

Before long, she passed away and appeared in a dream to another concubine, saying, "I have received the instruction of my lady and have been reborn in the Land of Peaceful Nurturing (*An-yang*). The lady did not yet believe her.

Suddenly, she too dreamed that she was traveling with the concubine to the Jewel Pond (*Ratnahrada*). There they saw a lotus flower upon which celestial robes fluttered; inscribed on them was the name "Yang Jie.
Upon another flower sat one dressed in court attire; inscribed on it was the name "Ma Yu. They further beheld a golden terrace of shimmering brilliance, where the concubine [was seated].
He pointed and said, "This is where that woman lived. Once she had awakened, she redoubled her efforts in practice.

At the age of eighty-one, on the morning of her birthday, she held a candle and burned incense, standing before the Guanyin Pavilion. While those around her were preparing the ritual offerings for her long life, she passed away while still standing.
King Jing was a paternal uncle of Emperor Zhezong.

Lady Feng of Guangping Commandery in the Song Dynasty, whose name was Faxin, was the daughter of Xu Xun, who had been posthumously honored as a Junior Preceptor. She married Chen Encong, a Director of the Imperial Secretariat for Propaganda.

From her youth, she suffered from chronic illness that physicians could not cure. Upon receiving instruction from Chan Master Cishou Shen regarding the observance of precepts and the recitation of the Buddha’s name, she came to believe it with sincerity and practiced it diligently.
After ten years of unwavering effort, her illness was cured. Suddenly, she grew weary of the world, which was a source of wonder to those around her.
He said, "I have lost mindfulness within the Pure Land and have arrived here in China; my karmic conditions are exhausted and I shall now return to the West—what is there to wonder at?
At the moment of death, after his breath had ceased, he revived and said to his family, "I have returned to the Pure Land and seen the realm of the Buddha;
it is no different from what is described in the *Sixteen Contemplations Sutra* of the *Avataṃsaka*. " Thereafter, he passed away. Three days later, when they lifted his corpse...
A rare fragrance was produced, as sweet and pervasive as incense.
Lady Lu of Song, a native of Qiantang and the wife of Wang Yu (a court official), had long recited the *Lotus Sūtra* with a sincere devotion to the Pure Land.
She would perform one session of liturgical repentance while chanting the Buddha’s name ten thousand times, doing so for thirty years. Due to a slight illness, she suddenly heard a celestial voice.
The drum sounded spontaneously, and the people were struck with wonder. He then sat facing west, formed mudrās with both hands, and passed away.

Lou Huijing of the Song dynasty was then serving as the Director of the Temple Library; Zhou Yuanxiang once examined and studied the *Chuan Deng Lu* (Record of the Transmission of the Lamp) with him, whereupon he clarified his realization of the Dharma-ground.
He took the practice of purity as his true cultivation and never ceased reciting the Buddha’s name. In his later years, while suffering from illness, he suddenly saw a purple lotus pedestal.
Countless transformation Buddhas appeared, and various extraordinary fragrances filled the room as they told her family members to urgently recite the Buddha's name; she passed away in an instant.
In Song, at the home of Qin Shi Jingjian in Songjiang, there was a woman who loathed her female body and lived separately from her husband, diligently observing the precepts and fasts.
She read the Avataṃsaka, Lotus, Prabhāsa, and Prajñāpāramitā Sūtras every day without fail, and performed the Amitābha Repentance ritual morning and evening.
After the Buddha had performed a thousand prostrations for a long time, a radiance entered the room; he sat facing west and passed away.

A daughter of the Wang family from Jixian during the Song dynasty recited the *Amitābha Sūtra* and the "Universal Gate Chapter" of the *Avalokiteśvara Sūtra* daily, chanting the Buddha’s name and seeking deliverance.
When her mother died and was already encoffined, blood flowed and dripped profusely. The daughter vowed, saying: "If my filial heart has moved the Buddha, may my mother's impurities [be cleansed]."
After she finished speaking, her vital energy ceased and the bleeding stopped. Later, her father took a secondary wife and they practiced together for the Pure Land.

When the daughter approached the end of her life, she requested a monk to explain the visualization methods of the Pure Land. She changed her clothes and lay down auspiciously; while holding the banner of Great Compassion, she passed away in perfect stillness.
Originally from Qiantang, Lady Zheng Jing’an spent every day of her life reciting the Buddha’s name. When she fell ill, she heard a voice in the air saying, "Your time to depart has come;
do not allow yourself to be indolent. She then saw the golden body of the Buddha and immediately rose, sitting upright facing west.
She summoned her ordained son, Yixiu, and had him chant the *Amitābha Sūtra*. Suddenly, she passed away. Her daughter subsequently dreamed of her.
The mother replied, "I have already attained birth in the Pure Land. She said this upon hearing the words of various masters who had practiced cultivation.
Originally surnamed Tao and named Lianniang, she was a native of Xuchun Village in Changshu. At the age of twenty-six, she became a widow and remained childless;

she vowed to be reborn in the Pure Land and constantly recited the *Amitābha Sūtra* and the *Avalokiteśvara Sūtra*. Suddenly, she dreamed of a person dressed in white robes leading her by the hand toward a lotus flower.
After eating one flower, her state of mind became quite different from before. She subsequently built a small pavilion facing west to recite sutras and chant the Buddha’s name.
Within three years, she saw the Buddha manifest in radiance; upon the scripture case, there was a sphere of fire the size of a marble.
Fearing it would burn the scriptures, she hurriedly struck it with her hand and obtained a single *śarīra*. At the time of her death, a transformation Buddha came to welcome her.
She departed from the assembly.
Mingyu was the mother of Yu Gui, a villager in Shao Village, Changping County. She had long accumulated the merit of reciting the Buddha’s name.

One day, while washing clothes until they were exceptionally clean, she said to her son, "I shall be reborn in the Pure Land. Her son did not yet believe her. When the appointed time arrived, she took a small table and placed it [before her].
As she sat upon a small table in the courtyard, a rare fragrance emanated from her body, and the divine music was heard by all the neighbors.
Mingfang Shi’s student, Wu Yingdao, had been widowed at thirty and remained faithful to her vow, turning to Buddhism and exclusively practicing the Pure Land path.
An elderly woman also observed the precepts alongside her for twenty years. In the year Wanyli Badyou (1585), she was fifty...

At the age of ten, she fell slightly ill; she called for her elderly nursemaid, and the two faced one another, reciting the Buddha’s name without ceasing, never uttering a single word regarding other matters.
On the day before her death, she bathed, changed her clothes, burned incense, and paid homage to the Buddha. She then sat upon a single mat and passed away.
Her son, Yongxian—a former palace scholar—was upright and sincere, never speaking falsely. He recorded these events and requested a commemorative inscription.

Ming Dynasty, Lady Xue of the Wutang noble clan. When she was born, her mother dreamed that the long-geng (Venus) entered her breast. Later, she married into the Zhou family and bore five sons before becoming a widow.
She maintained her integrity and took a vow of chastity, offering incense to Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva, from which lotus flowers emerged—people marveled at this.
She devoted herself single-mindedly to pure practice, never tiring of giving alms. For fifteen years, her recitation of the Buddha’s name was as constant as a single day. (Wanli era).
On the day of Dinghai in the fifth month, he fell ill. When a physician offered him disordered gruel, he resolutely refused it; he subsequently ceased all food and set aside all medicinal treatments.
On the sixth day of the ninth month, he invited monks to perform repentance rites and said, "In four days my affairs shall be concluded.
He then faced west toward an image of Amitābha, maintaining mindfulness day and night, and instructed his sons to assist him while forbidding any women from entering.
In accordance with his final instructions, the shrine was prepared and the outer and inner coffins were removed; no money or silk was burned, nor were the deities of the soil sacrificed.
It being the Double-Ninth Festival, this was precisely the fourth day. Early the next morning, he requested water to wash his hands and recited the Amṛta-mantra.

Donning his pure robes and the hat of Master Zhigong, he knelt long before the Buddha, chanting verses of praise while burning incense and reciting the Buddha’s name one hundred and eight times with his prayer beads.
At noon, he sat cross-legged, formed a mudrā, and passed away with his spirit and breath serene. At that time, the assembly all smelled the fragrance of lotuses filling the chamber;
the sons of the deceased, by imperial command, entered the shrine, and several thousand spectators joyfully prostrated themselves in worship.
Mingji Dao-long’s mother, Lady Li, was forty years old when she began a lifelong fast (*zhāizāi*) to recite the Buddha’s name.
She did not understand how to read the sutras, so she renovated a single quiet room to enshrine images of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, burning incense and prostrating morning and evening.

Whenever it was her birthday, she instructed her sons and daughters-in-law not to arrange celebratory feasts; instead, they were to perform one day or three days of repentance rituals. She continued in this manner for twenty years.
In the year preceding the conclusion of his fifth year [of practice], he employed the proceeds from his spinning to invite monks for a seven-day and seven-night rite of repentance.

During the night, he dreamed that the Great Being (Mahāsattva) appeared holding a string of white beads and showed them to him, saying: "I bestow these upon you; the number of beads is the period of your rebirth.
He counted them in his dream and found there were fifty-three beads, yet he did not understand their significance until the thirteenth day of the fifth month in the year Gengzi.
One day, he suddenly told his family, "I am departing today; you should all recite the Buddha's name with a loud voice to assist me in my journey to the West.
His sons and daughters-in-law all sat before his couch, reciting the Buddha’s name, and as they sat upright facing west, he passed away.

In the Ming dynasty, Lady Tao, mother of Zhang, was the secondary wife of Changshui Shouyue. On the day the Layman (Shouyue) passed away while engaged in the Buddhist transformation, he had been reciting his daily liturgy without interruption.
When the Layman went out to pay his respects at Putuo [Mountain], the Lady said to her two sons:

"I have daily contemplated these two phrases: 'This mind makes the Buddha' and 'This mind is the Buddha. Only now do I realize their meaning; on the fourth day of the first month, I shall depart. When that time arrived, she passed away.
He passed away sitting upright; on the following day, when the layman returned and completed the enshrouding, five blue lotus flowers suddenly emerged from atop the coffin.

The layman was greatly struck with wonder and remorsefully realized that his own understanding of the Master’s spiritual practice had been so superficial. All who saw or heard of this, near and far, could not help but sigh in admiration.
The mother of Sun Ming, a eunuch of the inner court, had observed the precepts and recited the Buddha’s name throughout her life.

When she was elderly and slightly ill, she knew that her time had come and told her son that she wished to pass away while seated in meditation. Her son wept and tried to dissuade her, but she would not be stopped. He then prepared a coffin for her;
when the appointed time arrived, she entered the coffin, sat upright, and passed away.
Ming Dynasty: Lady Xu, mother of Lu, was a native of Jiading. After her husband’s death, she lived as a widow, dedicating herself to the Pure Land practice.

Her late husband had once lent her a thousand pieces of gold; she burned the promissory notes and did not seek repayment. She gave away all her marriage dowry to others and constantly performed prostrations and recitations before the Buddha without ceasing.
After ten years of such practice, one night she suddenly called to her attendant, saying, "Look, has the light appeared in the east? It is time for my rebirth."
"It is enough! You all should assist me by reciting the Buddha’s name aloud with palms joined, and then pass away.
Ming, a native of Yuzhang named Yang Zhuan Yi, lived at Dinghuai Gate in Jinling. His wife called herself Xuan Yi Niang;

she gave birth to a son at age thirty and thereafter lived separately from her husband, allowing him to take concubines. She maintained a lifelong vegetarian diet and recited the Buddha’s name until the year Jichou.

Fifteen years had passed when, in the eighth month, she suddenly suffered from a piercing pain in her back that reached to the very bone. She saw a malevolent ghost who used a knife to slice the flesh from her back;
a powerful deity then drove the ghost away. Her suffering vanished as if she had been liberated. She immediately said to her husband, "I am about to depart.
There are four youths who come to welcome me; you may offer them pure tea. Her husband suspected this was merely a delusion born of her illness.
In his delirium, he asked where he was going; when told, "To the West," he joined his palms, recited the Buddha’s name, and then passed away.

In the tenth month of the following year, the mother of Tang Gongfu, a Daoist practitioner from the Ximen district of Jiangning, who was eighty-one years old, had long maintained a vegetarian diet and recited the Buddha’s name, making ten thousand recitations as her daily practice at dawn and dusk.
On the first day of the new year in the year of Gengyin, Gongfu invited Rongwu to observe [the funeral rites].
As two preceptors were devoutly practicing the Great Amitābha Repentance, at the fifth watch on the fourth day they entered the altar.
A Daoist from the Tang dynasty was striking the signal bell outside the altar when, at dawn, he suddenly saw dozens of white cranes circling above the roof.
Within the altar, both the monastics and the laity all saw lotus flowers sprout beneath the Buddha’s seat, while a golden light from within and without covered the sky.

Mountains, rivers, and the great earth were entirely without obstruction; such was the state of realization that a single branch of incense remained until the conclusion of the ritual, at which point it was extinguished upon descending from the altar.
These were all manifest proofs of Tang Mu’s devoted cultivation of the Pure Land, and her rebirth in the highest grade is certain.
Tang Yizhi witnessed this himself and requested me to record it.
On the Rebirth of the Wicked:
Zhang Shanhe of the Tang Dynasty, whose occupation was slaughtering oxen, saw a herd of oxen speaking human speech at the moment of his death, demanding his life.

Stricken with great terror, he called to his wife, saying, "Quickly invite monks to perform a repentance rite for me. When the monks arrived, they instructed him, citing the *Amitābha Sūtra* (*Guānjīng*).

In the *Zhong* (the *Zhongsheng jing*), it is said that those who encounter evil omens at the time of death will attain rebirth in the Pure Land simply by reciting the Buddha’s name with a sincere heart.
A commentary states: "The hells are so urgent that there is no leisure to fetch an incense burner.

Thus, he supported a flame with his right hand and held incense with his left, facing west and intoning the Buddha’s name with single-minded intensity without ceasing. After more than a day, he passed away peacefully.

Tang Xiongjun resided in Chengdu; his courage and bravery surpassed those of others, and he did not observe the monastic precepts. He once left the monastic life to join the military, but soon returned to being a monk.

Upon hearing the words of the sutras—that reciting the Buddha’s name even once extinguishes the heavy sins of eighty billion kalpas of birth and death—he was greatly delighted and said, "I am fortunate indeed to have this.
From that time on, he ceased his transgressions and never stopped reciting the Buddha’s name.
In the second month of the *dingwei* year, he died suddenly; after one night had passed, he revived unexpectedly and said that he had been brought before the presiding judge of the underworld.
The judge sentenced him to enter hell, whereupon Jun spoke out in a fierce voice, saying: "I have no defense for entering hell, yet even the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas cannot avoid speaking falsehoods.

The *Amitābha Sūtra* states that those of the lowest of the low grade, though they have committed the five heinous crimes, may still go [to the Pure Land] through ten recitations at the moment of death."

"Although Seongjun has committed sins, he has not yet committed the five heinous crimes; moreover, he has repented and recited the Buddha’s name countless times. Having said this, he attained rebirth.

Later, he entered the mountains to observe the fasts and recite the Buddha’s name. Four years later, in the third month of the *xinhai* year, monks and laypeople gathered together, and he declared, "My time has come.
You should return to the city and see my relatives and acquaintances; ask them to tell Seongjun that I am reciting the Buddha’s name."
One must not regard those who attain birth in the Pure Land as people who have escaped the net of hell.

While in the midst of conversation and laughter, Song Zhongming, who resided at Ba’en Temple in Shanyin, sat upright and passed away. His habitual conduct had exceeded the bounds of propriety, yet due to his illness, he spoke to his fellow students, saying: "The Way..."
Ning said, "My mind and consciousness are now so distracted; what medicine can cure this? Ning then instructed him to practice mindfulness of the Buddha by following his breath.
Following these instructions exactly, after seven days, his strength was already exhausted and weary. Ning then had him visualize a Buddha image before his eyes.
After a long while, he suddenly saw two Bodhisattvas, and subsequently saw the Buddha. With his eyes closed, he passed away.
Wu Qiong of Lin’an, Song Dynasty, was originally a monk who later left the monastic path to return to secular life. He married twice and fathered two sons;

there was no occupation he would not engage in, including butchery and selling liquor. Whenever he slaughtered chickens, ducks, and other poultry in his kitchen, he would hold them up and chant, "Amitābha Buddha!
Son, may you be well released from this body! He would thus repeatedly recite the Buddha’s name before applying the blade to cut the meat.
He practiced the recitation of the Buddha’s name without ceasing. Later, a tumor the size of a chicken egg grew on his forehead, which caused him great anxiety and fear.
He constructed a grass hut, separated from his wife and children, and spent day and night as if he could not wait to practice the recitation of the Buddha’s name and perform repentance rituals.

In the twenty-third year of the Shaoxing era, he told others, "Qiong will depart at the hour of Xu (7–9 p.m. tomorrow. Everyone laughed at him; however, that following evening, he exchanged his cloth shirt for wine.
Having finished drinking, he wrote a verse which said: "Like wine, all is empty; what need is there to ask about the Chan school?
Today, with deep respect for the bright moon and clear breeze, I sit upright with palms joined, reciting the Buddha's name, and pass away."

Chen Qi of Longshu in the Song dynasty had once committed murder. Later, he encountered a ghost who appeared before him; Qi was struck with great terror and urgently called upon the name of Amitābha Buddha.
Because he did not cease his recitation of the Buddha’s name, the ghost could not approach him and eventually vanished. When his time came, he passed away while sitting upright in meditation.
In the winter of the fifteenth year of the Yuan Zhi Zheng era, Zhang Shicheng attacked Huzhou.
The Chancellor of Jiangzhe engaged him in battle and captured forty men, whom he placed in cangues and sent to the authorities. They were lodged for the night at Niaoke Temple on West Lake.

It happened that Chan Master Mudao Mou was walking leisurely along the corridor; when the prisoners saw the Master’s dignified and elegant bearing as he recited his prayers without ceasing, they said to him: "Long..."
The old man who had saved them said, "I cannot save you; however, if you recite 'Namo Jiu ku jiu nan Amituofo' with utmost sincerity, you shall indeed be saved.
There were three among them who believed and accepted these words, and they recited them without ceasing. At dawn, their fetters were removed and they were released from prison;
by chance, when they arrived at the place of execution, there were insufficient instruments for the three of them, so they were bound only with ropes.
Subsequently, upon thorough investigation, it was found that the individuals in question were actually honest citizens who had been abducted, and they were thus released.
Reflecting on the Dharma-gate of the Buddha’s Recollection (Nienfo), people know it as the destination for those who have passed away, yet they do not realize its benefits for those still living.

Therefore, upon hearing that reciting mantras yields spiritual efficacy, they immediately change to reciting mantras; upon hearing that giving lectures yields eloquence, they immediately change to giving lectures; and upon hearing of [the benefits of] engaging in construction...

To create merit and receive its retribution, to hear of vegetarian assemblies and gain the favor of others, or even to hear of methods for nourishing the body and attain longevity—these are all various forms of conditioned change that can never be grasped or maintained.
How can one hope for the fulfillment of pure karma while the mind remains distracted?

To speak according to reality, the fundamental purpose of seeking birth in the Pure Land is to achieve Buddhahood in order to save sentient beings; it is certainly not intended merely for the sake of one's posthumous state.
Regarding such joy, what need is there to calculate whether one’s benefit prior to this life was great or small?

Take for example the case of a parrot kept by the Pei family of Hedong during the Zhenyuan era of the Tang dynasty; it constantly recited the Buddha’s name and would not eat after noon. At the time of its death—
After ten recitations of the Buddha’s name, his breath ceased and he was cremated, yielding more than ten grains of *śarīra* that shone brilliantly.
The monk Huiguan constructed a stupa using earthen bricks to commemorate this marvel. Wei Gao, the Governor of Chengdu, composed an inscription for it, containing the lines:
"In the midst of non-thought, he interfuses with the void; though his true bones remain after his death..."
In Song dynasty Huangyan, at Zhengdeng Temple, Master Guan kept a myna bird that could speak; it constantly recited the Buddha’s name without ceasing. One day, it passed away while standing upright.
He buried it in a hole in the earth, and shortly thereafter, a single purple lotus flower emerged from the tip of its tongue.

Vinaya Master Lingzhi once composed a praise for this event, containing the lines: "To die standing upright and be confined within a cage is but a trivial matter; to transform into a purple lotus flower is truly marvelous."
Formerly, there was a monk in Tanzhou who raised a myna bird, which the locals called "Baba-er. The bird constantly recited the name of the Buddha.
When it died, he buried it in a coffin, whereupon a single lotus flower suddenly sprouted from its mouth. One who composed a verse about this said:
"There was a spiritual bird, Baba-er, Who understood to follow the monk’s lips in reciting Amitābha. Buried in the level earth upon death, A lotus flower blossomed from the person."
If one does not turn the mind [toward awakening], what can be done? I have carefully examined the World-Honored One’s vow, which states:
"Any sentient being who calls my name shall surely be born in my land. Generally speaking, "sentient beings" include those above from devas and humans down to insects and even the smallest creatures.
Judging by this, this myna bird must surely be born in the Western World, where it will join with the kalaviṅka in chanting the sounds of the Dharma.
"Can a human being truly be inferior to a bird? This account is recorded in the *Tanzhou Zhi* (Gazetteer of Tanzhou), and to this day, the city gates are named after the "Eight Eights.
During the Chongzhen era of the Ming dynasty, Master Wu Xueya served as the Judicial Administrator of Fuzhou; throughout his life, he was a devout follower of the Tathāgata. Every...

When he went to Kaiyuan Temple to pay respects to the Buddha and recite the sutras, he had long heard that the monks there consumed many vegetables and meat, and that this temple in particular kept livestock for slaughter and consumption.

The official petitioned the provincial governor and military commander to issue a strict edict and erect a stone inscription to prohibit such practices; yet, the stubborn customs could not be entirely eradicated.
One day, while the official was reciting the Buddha’s name in the meditation hall, a chicken heard him and also began to recite the Buddha’s name. The official [was moved by this].
He rebuked the monks, saying, "You claim that no livestock has been kept in this temple for a long time; how then can there be a chicken?

When he found it, the monk recited the Buddha’s name, and the chicken likewise recited the Buddha’s name. The Master then severely reprimanded the monks, saying, "Observing this animal now, it still possesses the Buddha-nature (*buddhadhātu*).

You who have shaved your heads and donned the robes, yet violate the precepts, are far worse than this animal. There is no doubt you will fall into the realms of suffering. The monks wept and repented.

He repented, saying, "From this day forth, I and my fellow monks shall make great vows and maintain our precepts with sincerity. Upon hearing the news, those throughout the province were alerted and took warning;
the community of śramaṇas underwent a complete transformation. Later, while serving as an official, Gong raised this rooster in his residence and constantly recited the Buddha’s name without ceasing.
Subsequently, when he was transferred to the post of Danyang, he took the rooster with him and sent it into Haihui Monastery, as it served as a means for receiving guests.
This caused those far and near to give rise to faith. On the day the rooster arrived at the hermitage, he immediately recited the Buddha’s name and passed away while standing upright;
Gong erected a stupa to commemorate this event. This account is from Tang Yizhi’s *Jinyu Cheng*.
Ming-dynasty Zou Zuyin of Jiangxi served as the Military Commissioner (Bingxian) of Guangdong; there was a paramilitary general who knew his own past lives across three generations.
In his first life he was a snake; in his second, a scholar; and in his third, his present office.
Once, while leading troops to campaign against the Man tribes of the caves, he passed a mountain and addressed his soldiers, saying: "In a former life, I once dwelt upon this mountain as a snake.

Now, as we advance into the mountains to visit my former abode, you must not be alarmed. Upon entering, they saw countless snakes within the cave; the General of the Left (Cān Jiàng) had become a snake.
The snake spoke, saying: "I and you were born here together in the past; it was only because I was able to recite the Buddha’s name even once that I attained birth among humans.
Now I am a great general, so why do you not recite the Buddha’s name to seek deliverance from this suffering?
The snake bowed its head in the manner of one receiving instruction. On the day the Colonel returned in triumph, he entered the cave again to observe them, and there were ten thousand snakes.

"All these people should have been transformed and delivered through the practice of Buddha-recollection (nien-fo) before they died. When Master Zou heard this, he found it extraordinary and recorded the account for posterity.

During the Chongzhen era of the Ming dynasty, the monk Jueyuan of Zhongzhou was exceptionally strict in his observance of the precepts. He made a vow to provide meals for the monastics at Donglin Temple on Mount Lu and established a donation station to solicit offerings.
At that time, a monk guarding the station returned from begging alms at the Hua family’s residence, where there was a rooster.
When they reached the halfway point, the monks realized it was a chicken and sent it back to Pāṭaliputra, where it was taken in. Consequently, its door was closed;

the chicken flew out from atop the roof and followed them to the city gate, circling there and refusing to leave. It remained with Master Daojue at the gate for three years. Afterward, when Daojue took it to Donglin Monastery, he conferred the precepts upon it.
When the assembly entered the hall to recite the Buddha’s name, the chicken suddenly followed along, chanting the Buddha’s name as well. It continued this way until—
When the occasion for providing alms to the monks during the year-long retreat concluded, the rooster sat in *jhāna* (meditative transformation) and was buried beside the temple.

Furthermore, records relate that there was a cat that sat in transformation at Luzhou, a monkey that sat in transformation in Xiaoxia, a sparrow that stood in transformation at Zhagao Town in Chao County, and a pig that sat in transformation after being released by Grand Councilor Huang Daci.
Such various spiritual wonders truly suffice to manifest the transformative power of the Dharma infinitely.
Thus ends the tenth fascicle of the *Jingtu chenzhong* (The Morning Bell of the Pure Land).
